items.question: What If Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century?
human_answers: Where would the Dutch stand on this? I'm guessing they don't want to see France gain anything in the Low Countries. But, would it be better to swallow a bitter pill in order to make gains themselves and not be left out in the cold getting nothing? The Dutch are past their prime as a power, but I guess they're still something, if not much. Financially, France is on so-so footing, having recovered from the double beat down of the WoSS, then the Mississippi Bubble burst. Britain is usually seen as being on firm financial footing. Spain is typically meh, while Austria typically needs propping up. I'm guessing Britain/France holds the upper hand in the finance department. Britain, although not yet the naval powerhouse of a century later, is undoubtedly the supreme naval power of these four countries. On land, Spain is rather meh. France has its ebbs and flows, and I'm not sure which way the tide is going in the late 1720s. Austria has Eugene, but I'm thinking he's aging. Overall, with Britain and France in bed together, I think they hold the upper hand. The Dutch siding with B/F would seal the financial and naval superiority. The Ottomans have to figure in there, too. I don't really follow their history, but I know they went at it against Austria a bunch. The German realm will get involved. I'm not sure if Austria can invoke HRE involvement, but I'm thinking the usual some Germans in one camp, some in the other, will be the case. It is my impression that Spain thought Austria was going to be more of an active ally, while Austria didn't agree. The buffoon Spain sent to negotiate the alliance sold Philip/Elizabeth on it being much more than it really was. Thus Austria basically laughed at Spain's request for assistance when the bullets started flying. This situation would need to be remedied. Perhaps Britain/France having the audacity to divvy up Austrian soil might do the trick.

If forced the Dutch would probably accept, since at that time the barrier treaty of 1715 was still in place. I would go a bit furhter, if the Dutch were forced to (and backed by the British) deafcto, annex parts of the Austrian Netherlands they probably try to get a better deal, rather than a difficult to defend coastal strip of the county fo Flanders. I would say they will try to get as much as the earlier Townsend treaty of 1709, in order to get as much as possible closed line of forts and fortyfied cities. The British would see the benefits of this from a military perspective. In this scenario this would then be, the entire county fo Flanders, Ducy of Brabant and a large or complete, part of Hainaut, the Austrian bts of Guelre and Over Maas, which leaves, Namen and Lucembourg to the French. Since the ducy of Luxembourh and her city and Namur were quite strategical and important stronghold, the British and Dutch might ask Dunkirk in return for it, even Lille, since this was an imprtant strongh old as well. The earlier Townsend agrement of 1709 was torpedood by the British since it would gieve the Dutch republic too much marked and trade. In this proposal the British would have a strong influence and part of trade in this Austrain Netherlands

well if it happens, France has just gained without a fight a direct border with Holland and the rest of the HRE ( making its ability to influence and successfully intervene militarily even greater than Otl ) to remove the Habsburgs from its border ( which in the long run will be more good for Austria than for others, since he will be able to concentrate exclusively on the fight against France on the Italian front, he will consider the Rhine as a minor front for his troops ( since there will be contingents from the entire empire for that ) to weaken Holland ( Catholics will not want to stay in a country that discriminates against them) all thanks to English stupidity which in doing so has lost the only ally on the continent may contain French hegemonic aspirations ( because I doubt France and England will be friendly to each other in the long run )

This partition plan (Stanhope and Townshend) would require worse Anglo-Austrian relations. Britain would have to be convinced that Austria is the biggest threat to the European balance of power and stability. So had Emperor Charles VI gone ahead to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos, then we would see a more solidified Anglo-French alliance as a counterweight. A Bourbon-Hapsburg alliance would reshuffle the post-Utrecht European order and a war could be a real possibility (Europe plunged into a wider war during the OTL Anglo-Spanish War of 1727). After the war, this partition plan could be the basis of peace negotiations (if the Anglo-French alliance gained the upper hand), and Austria could be compensated with Tuscany like in OTL. Personally, I am more interested in James Stanhope's first idea of giving Austrian Netherlands to Leopold or Francis of Lorraine. Suppose that Don Carlos married Maria Theresa and France captured Lorraine in a war, then France could annex it while giving the Austrian Netherlands to Leopold/Francis.
items.original_question: What if Partition of the Austrian Netherlands in the 18th Century? Hi, everyone. This is my second post sharing some lesser-known yet fascinating PoDs in European history. I stumbled upon a historical academic journal written by Frederik Dhondt, a history professor from the Ghent University in Belgium titled " So Great a Revolution’: Charles Townshend and the Partition of the Austrian Netherlands, September 1725 " (2012, Journal of Low Countries Studies). According to the article, Charles Townshend, the British Northern Secretary (equivalent to the Foreign Minister) and his predecessor James Stanhope (†. 1721) had proposed a partition of the Austrian Netherlands. The plan would see Austria surrendering its holdings in the Low Countries. The article summarised three possibilities. Some background before moving on. In the Nine Years' Year and the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria had allied with the Dutch Republic and Great Britain (or England-Scotland before 1707) to counter French ambitions in the Low Countries and the Rhineland. Towards the end of the Spanish Succession War, Britain became weary of increasing Austrian power. In 1716, it allied with France. The Austro-Spanish alliance confirmed by the Treaty of Vienna rang alarm bells in London. Not only did it reconcile the enmity between Emperor Charles XI and King Philip V, the combined power of Spain and Austria threatened the established balance of power. There were even talks to marry Maria Theresa to Don Carlos (future Charles III). Prime Minister Walpole and Townshend, therefore, desired to weaken the power of Austria. These plans were never made public, Townshend only discussed them with the ambassador in Paris, Horace Walpole. On page 56, Townshend suggested the partition plan could be implemented if the marriage between Maria Theresa and Don Carlos took place. James Stanhope first suggested that the Duke of Lorraine could receive Austria Netherlands. Alternatively, Stanhope suggested awarding it either to the Elector of Cologne or the Elector of Trier. The Electorate would be secularised. Townshend outright dismissed these ridiculous ideas, and offered his own solution. The Dutch will annex some territories including Antwerp. Ypres, Bruges, and Ostend would fall under joint Dutch-British control while the inland and southern portions of the Austrian Netherlands will go to France. What will be the geopolitical and diplomatic consequences of one of these plans was realised? Although I personally doubt the likelihood of this happening, nevertheless the ramifications will be interesting. You can access the article here through your university: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1179/0309656411Z.0000000002 .

items.model_answer:
If the Austrian Netherlands (roughly modern-day Belgium and Luxembourg) had been partitioned in the 18th century—most likely divided between the Kingdom of France and the Dutch Republic—the geopolitical map and balance of power in Western Europe would have been fundamentally permanently altered. Historically, the Habsburg Monarchy viewed this disconnected territory as a strategic liability that was difficult to defend, frequently exploring ways to trade it, such as the proposed Bavarian Exchange. A successful partition would have allowed Austria to shed this burden and consolidate its power entirely within Central Europe. With its resources no longer stretched to the English Channel, Austria could have focused its military and diplomatic might on countering the rise of Prussia, expanding against the Ottoman Empire, and likely absorbing Bavaria to create a massive, contiguous German-Austrian bloc.

For France, acquiring the southern, Francophone regions of the territory (modern Wallonia and parts of Hainaut) would have fulfilled a centuries-old strategic ambition of securing its vulnerable northern frontier. This expansion would have provided France with a massive demographic and economic boost. Crucially, securing the rich coal and iron deposits of Wallonia would have accelerated French industrialization in the 19th century, potentially allowing it to better rival Britain's industrial supremacy. However, this French expansion would have been a strategic nightmare for Great Britain. British foreign policy relied heavily on keeping the Low Countries out of the hands of a hostile hegemonic power to protect the English Channel. A partition heavily favoring France would have forced Britain into an even more aggressive, uncompromising anti-French posture, likely accelerating global colonial wars and prompting Britain to heavily militarize its southern coast.

The Dutch Republic, absorbing the northern, Flemish-speaking provinces (such as Flanders and Brabant), would have gained a vital territorial buffer against France but at the cost of severe internal instability. Integrating a large, staunchly Catholic population into a politically dominant Calvinist structure would have triggered intense religious and social friction. Economically, the Dutch would likely have continued to keep the Scheldt River closed to protect the mercantile dominance of Amsterdam, deliberately stifling the economic potential of Antwerp and breeding deep resentment among their new Flemish subjects. 

Ultimately, the most profound consequence of this 18th-century partition would be the erasure of the modern state of Belgium, which historically gained independence in 1830. Without a unified administrative history under Austrian and later French and Dutch rule, the distinct Belgian national identity would never have coalesced. Instead, Wallonia would have been thoroughly assimilated into the French nation-state, while Flanders would have become a permanent, culturally distinct, and likely restless southern province of a Greater Netherlands, shifting the linguistic and political fault lines of Western Europe forever.

edus.text: If the Austrian Netherlands (roughly modern-day Belgium and Luxembourg) had been partitioned in the 18th century—most likely divided between the Kingdom of France and the Dutch Republic—
the geopolitical map and balance of power in Western Europe would have been fundamentally permanently altered.
Historically, the Habsburg Monarchy viewed this disconnected territory as a strategic liability that was difficult to defend,
frequently exploring ways to trade it,
such as the proposed Bavarian Exchange.
A successful partition would have allowed Austria to shed this burden
and consolidate its power entirely within Central Europe.
With its resources no longer stretched to the English Channel,
Austria could have focused its military and diplomatic might on countering the rise of Prussia,
expanding against the Ottoman Empire,
and likely absorbing Bavaria to create a massive, contiguous German-Austrian bloc.
For France, acquiring the southern, Francophone regions of the territory (modern Wallonia and parts of Hainaut)
would have fulfilled a centuries-old strategic ambition of securing its vulnerable northern frontier.
This expansion would have provided France with a massive demographic and economic boost.
Crucially, securing the rich coal and iron deposits of Wallonia would have accelerated French industrialization in the 19th century,
potentially allowing it to better rival Britain's industrial supremacy.
However, this French expansion would have been a strategic nightmare for Great Britain.
British foreign policy relied heavily on keeping the Low Countries out of the hands of a hostile hegemonic power
to protect the English Channel.
A partition heavily favoring France would have forced Britain into an even more aggressive, uncompromising anti-French posture,
likely accelerating global colonial wars
and prompting Britain to heavily militarize its southern coast.
The Dutch Republic, absorbing the northern, Flemish-speaking provinces (such as Flanders and Brabant),
would have gained a vital territorial buffer against France
but at the cost of severe internal instability.
Integrating a large, staunchly Catholic population into a politically dominant Calvinist structure
would have triggered intense religious and social friction.
Economically, the Dutch would likely have continued to keep the Scheldt River closed
to protect the mercantile dominance of Amsterdam,
deliberately stifling the economic potential of Antwerp
and breeding deep resentment among their new Flemish subjects.
Ultimately, the most profound consequence of this 18th-century partition would be the erasure of the modern state of Belgium,
which historically gained independence in 1830.
Without a unified administrative history under Austrian and later French and Dutch rule,
the distinct Belgian national identity would never have coalesced.
Instead, Wallonia would have been thoroughly assimilated into the French nation-state,
while Flanders would have become a permanent, culturally distinct, and likely restless southern province of a Greater Netherlands,
shifting the linguistic and political fault lines of Western Europe forever.

None of them had colonies in the Western hemisphere (or anywhere else) and, IIRC, at that time the former colonies were not ideologically, not to mention economically or militarily, of a any serious importance for the continental Europe. Which, putting aside Spain, leaves “certain trade arrangements” and the obvious question is what these arrangements would be? Would they hurt or benefit France? In OTL to a great degree the French bellicosity was supported by the strategic factor called “Bonaparte” who, besides military glory, provided looting (both on state and individual levels) on the “industrial” scale. It seems that ITTL French government behaves “Napoleonic” without Napoleon, which brings some obvious questions without clear answers to which episode with tearing the document looks as an act of imbecility. AFAIK, none of the OTL generals of that period were that good in both areas and without Bonaparte the war of 2nd coalition most probably would end due to the exhaustion of both sides without too much to show for it (in OTL in 1799 the French were kicked out of Italy and exercises on the Danube led to nowhere for either side so the only area of clear success was Switzerland). Which means that enthusiasm in France is unlikely and, in OTL the Directory was in almost permanent fiscal crisis. So, it would be quite interesting to find out in more details how the things were proceeding (including financial aspect) without Nappy? Were ITTL any indications of the Russian desire to conquer Hungary? Anyway, this was clearly not an consideration during the 2nd Coalition when Austria asked for the Russian help (at least in OTL). BTW, without Nappy, is Paul still on the throne? If yes, and if the 2nd Coalition ended along the OTL lines, the issue would be not Francis’ reluctance but Paul’s refusal to deal with a former ally who screwed him up. Alexander hated Napoleon on a personal level, which mostly defined his actions in the 3rd and 4th coalitions, but, while being pro-British, was not actively anti-French in general. Anyway, it does not look like he would be doing Francis’ bidding. Why not Greenland? The XVII - XVIII centuries coalition wars against the Ottomans demonstrated to the Russians that the Austrians are, at best, useless as the allies and impotent as the enemies. If Austria is at war with France, whoever is the Russian emperor, can start war with the OE without paying any attention to Vienna’s position. Besides, how would Russia simultaneously fight the French and the OE? Obviously, expecting that after the French war the Hapsburg emperor is going to honor his generous promise to grant Russia the Ottoman territories (how about the Ottoman consent?) assumes a rather unrealistic level of a naivety on the Russian side. Which is of no importance to Vienna and Berlin by the obvious reason: none of them has colonies in the Americas. Then, the US in the early 1800s as a serious military threat? In 1812 it had less than 10,000 troops when war started and its navy had 12 frigates. Yes, and the question is how an obvious idiot managed to become the head of the French government and how his actions got approval of the parliament?
items.original_question: My Alternative History Scenario: What if Napoleon couldn't make it to France at 1799? EPISODE THREE​ German Pact ​ ​ A sudden storm breaking out across Europe had created a massive shockwave. Austria, still struggling to recover from the economic and military wounds of the War of the Second Coalition, was deeply displeased by France’s abrupt rekindling of hostilities. Emperor Francis II had been expecting a long period of peace, one he intended to devote to revitalizing Germany. Unfortunately, history had once again disappointed him. His federalist ambitions had not yet completely faded, but this meant confronting French republicanism earlier than anticipated. Moreover, following the referendum held on 18 February 1803 and the subsequent election, the country transitioned into what was called a presidential system. As a result, Fourier—who came to power and was a prominent representative of socialist thought—began spreading his ideas more widely across Europe. This signified a gradual shift of the German peoples toward republicanism. Although the Kingdom of Prussia and the Habsburg Monarchy did not hold each other in high regard, they shared a common enemy: France and republicanism. Approximately one week had passed since the outbreak of the Franco-Spanish War. French armies advanced rapidly, exploiting the dire condition of the Spanish forces to seize Catalonia and push toward Eastern Aragon. The Basque region had also fallen. Emperor Francis convened his cabinet, and they debated at length what course of action should be taken. Johann Amadeus Franz, the Minister of Finance of the era, was firmly opposed to breaking the peace with France, as any potential war would further devastate Austria’s already fragile economy. József Alvinczi, the Chief of the General Staff, argued that this war represented an opportunity to eliminate both France and the spread of republican ideas on the European continent. He maintained that, as demonstrated in the previous conflict, the Austrian army was not in as poor a condition as believed and demanded that an open ultimatum be issued to France. However, the Emperor had a different plan in mind. Although there was no certainty it would succeed, he deemed it worth attempting. For this reason, he decided to send a delegate to the Kingdom of Prussia, carrying a note requesting a private meeting with the King. The delegation set out on 15 March 1803. Meanwhile, across Europe, no clear decision had yet emerged from the British Isles. Prime Minister Henry Addington had no desire to see Spain under French control, but he also believed that the British Army was not yet prepared. After lengthy discussions with other statesmen, he sent an envoy to the Kingdom of Portugal to further expand the Anglo-Portuguese Alliance and present several proposals. In the meantime, the delegation sent by Austria to Prussia returned two weeks later. The Emperor’s proposal to the King of Prussia was to intervene in the Franco-Spanish War by forming a German coalition. The Prussian King, eager to enhance his prestige among the German states, responded favorably and announced his acceptance. Thus, the German Pact was formed. Both sides began final preparations for their already mobilized armies, and within approximately two weeks, everything was ready. A note bearing the personal signatures of both the Emperor and the King was delivered to the French delegates by a joint Austro-Prussian mission. The note demanded that France sever its alliance with the United States, withdraw from Spain, and agree to certain trade arrangements. French President Charles Fourier tore the original document to pieces in parliament. This act provided the Habsburg Monarchy and the Kingdom of Prussia with sufficient legitimacy to launch a military intervention against France. Emperor Francis II was deeply uneasy about Russia’s ambiguous stance. He neither wanted Russia to emerge excessively strong nor excessively weak. Poland could be the first step, and the Russian flag might one day fly over Hungary or the borders of the Holy Roman Empire. Taking such a risk seemed irrational. Therefore, depending on the course of the war, he considered enticing Russia into joining their side by offering the Balkan territories of the already weakened Ottoman Empire—despite his preference for preserving the balance of power in the Balkans and Eastern Europe. The French threat, however, took precedence. Although the United States did not yet pose a direct threat to Europe, it continued to threaten the colonial powers in the Americas. While it had not yet entered the conflict, such an involvement was not impossible. On the other hand, the Emperor foresaw that the French government’s aggressive and overly idealistic actions would ultimately lead to its downfall. By initiating this war, France had effectively shot itself in the foot, and these events would pave the way for a rise in anti-French sentiment throughout Europe.

criteria.name: Point-of-divergence fidelity and immediate 1799 feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer treats the counterfactual premise precisely: Napoleon is unable to return from Egypt to France in 1799, and the immediate consequences follow from realistic naval, military, political, and communications conditions of that year.
criteria.1-2: Ignores or changes the premise, e.g. lets Napoleon return anyway or makes unrelated changes without justification.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges Napoleon’s absence but gives vague or implausible immediate effects with little attention to Egypt, Britain, or France in 1799.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible short-term setup, including Napoleon’s isolation/capture/death and some effects on Egypt and France, but misses key constraints.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains how Napoleon fails to reach France and traces credible immediate effects on Egypt, the British, the Directory, and French morale.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the divergence in 1799 conditions and integrates naval interception, Egyptian campaign collapse, information delays, French politics, and coalition timing.

criteria.name: French domestic political trajectory without Brumaire
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how well the answer reasons through the fate of the Directory, possible alternative coups, republican institutions, generals, finances, public opinion, and the absence of Napoleon’s personal authority.
criteria.1-2: Assumes France simply follows the same Napoleonic path without Napoleon or gives no domestic political explanation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions instability in France but does not identify actors, institutions, fiscal crisis, or plausible alternatives to Napoleon.
criteria.5-6: Discusses the Directory, coup risk, and military politics, but relies on broad claims or underdeveloped mechanisms.
criteria.7-8: Explains credible alternatives such as Sieyès using another general, a continued Directory, Jacobin/royalist pressure, or military stalemate.
criteria.9-10: Deeply analyzes factional politics, army patronage, fiscal exhaustion, legitimacy, and why any successor regime would or would not reproduce Bonapartist outcomes.

criteria.name: Second Coalition and military-diplomatic causality
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly models the 1799-1802 war without Napoleon’s return, especially Italy, Switzerland, the Danube, Austria, Britain, Russia, and the likelihood of peace or continued war.
criteria.1-2: Presents arbitrary victories or defeats with no relation to actual 1799 military and diplomatic conditions.
criteria.3-4: Names some coalition powers but gives simplistic outcomes, such as automatic French collapse or automatic French dominance.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that France was under pressure in Italy and Europe, but gives only partial causal links to coalition behavior.
criteria.7-8: Connects Napoleon’s absence to campaigns, coalition coordination problems, Austrian and Russian aims, British strategy, and peace prospects.
criteria.9-10: Balances French resilience with coalition limitations and gives a nuanced account of likely military stalemate, altered treaties, and divergent Austrian/Russian/British incentives.

criteria.name: Long-range European and global downstream effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage and coherence of major downstream consequences after the immediate crisis, including whether the Napoleonic Wars, Holy Roman Empire, German and Italian reorganization, Spanish crisis, Louisiana, Britain, Russia, Austria, and Ottoman affairs change plausibly.
criteria.1-2: Provides little beyond 1799 or jumps to distant outcomes without causal bridges.
criteria.3-4: Lists some later differences but treats them as disconnected speculation.
criteria.5-6: Covers several major effects, such as no Empire or altered coalitions, but omits important knock-on consequences.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent medium- and long-term chain affecting France, Germany, Italy, Britain, Russia, Austria, Spain, and colonial affairs.
criteria.9-10: Shows sophisticated long-range reasoning across European institutions, nationalism, war finance, imperial reform, colonial policy, and Ottoman/Russian dynamics while preserving causal continuity.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, plausibility, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and speculative outcomes; avoids contradictions with the premise and known constraints; and does not overstate obscure or unsupported claims.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, anachronisms, or confident claims that violate the premise or basic historical facts.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible ideas but also unsupported leaps, internal inconsistencies, or overconfident deterministic conclusions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with some uncertainty noted, but includes gaps or weakly justified assumptions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly signals uncertainty, explains assumptions, avoids deterministic overreach, and maintains internal consistency across the timeline.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates high-probability consequences from speculative branches, flags evidentiary limits, and rigorously checks all claims against the 1799 counterfactual logic.

items.model_answer:
If Napoleon Bonaparte had failed to return to France from Egypt in 1799—whether due to interception by the British Royal Navy, disease, or death in combat—the immediate consequence would have been a drastically different outcome for the French government, though a coup would still have occurred. By late 1799, the French Directory was bankrupt, deeply unpopular, and facing severe threats from royalist uprisings and the armies of the Second Coalition. The political mastermind Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès was already plotting to overthrow the government and needed a popular military hero—a "sword"—to enforce it. Historically, Napoleon filled this role and quickly hijacked the Coup of 18 Brumaire for himself. Without him, Sieyès would likely have turned to General Jean Victor Marie Moreau or General Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte. Because neither possessed Napoleon’s ruthless political ambition or overarching charisma, Sieyès likely would have succeeded in implementing his original constitutional vision: a complex, oligarchic republic with a divided and relatively weak executive branch, avoiding the autocratic dictatorship Napoleon established.

Militarily, France would not have immediately collapsed. Competent generals like Moreau, who historically won the decisive Battle of Hohenlinden in 1800, could have successfully defended France's borders against the Second Coalition and forced a favorable peace treaty. However, without Napoleon's unparalleled military genius and insatiable ambition, the ensuing decade and a half of relentless expansion known as the Napoleonic Wars would never have occurred. France would likely have fought defensive or limited regional conflicts rather than attempting to subjugate the entire European continent. Consequently, the Holy Roman Empire might have survived its historical 1806 dissolution, the disastrous Peninsular War and the 1812 invasion of Russia would have been averted, and millions of European lives would have been spared.

Domestically, the absence of Napoleon would mean the loss of his massive centralizing reforms. The Napoleonic Code, which fundamentally shaped modern civil law across Europe and Latin America, would not have been written in its historical form, and the Concordat of 1801 might not have reconciled the French state with the Catholic Church so swiftly. Without Napoleon's iron grip stabilizing the nation, France would have remained politically volatile. This ongoing factional instability would likely have paved the way for an earlier restoration of the Bourbon monarchy, as the exhausted French public eventually sought a return to traditional order without a military dictator to rally behind. 

Ultimately, the geopolitical trajectory of the 19th century would have been entirely rewritten. Napoleon's conquests inadvertently exported the ideals of the French Revolution—such as meritocracy, secularism, and the destruction of feudalism—while simultaneously sparking fierce nationalistic backlash in places like Germany and Italy. Without his continent-spanning empire to act as both a modernizing force and a common enemy, the unification of Germany and Italy would have been significantly delayed or taken entirely different paths, and the map of Europe would have remained heavily fractured, altering the balance of power leading into the 20th century.

edus.text: If Napoleon Bonaparte had failed to return to France from Egypt in 1799—whether due to interception by the British Royal Navy, disease, or death in combat—
the immediate consequence would have been a drastically different outcome for the French government,
though a coup would still have occurred.
By late 1799, the French Directory was bankrupt, deeply unpopular, and facing severe threats from royalist uprisings and the armies of the Second Coalition.
The political mastermind Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès was already plotting to overthrow the government
and needed a popular military hero—a "sword"—to enforce it.
Historically, Napoleon filled this role
and quickly hijacked the Coup of 18 Brumaire for himself.
Without him, Sieyès would likely have turned to General Jean Victor Marie Moreau or General Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte.
Because neither possessed Napoleon’s ruthless political ambition or overarching charisma,
Sieyès likely would have succeeded in implementing his original constitutional vision:
a complex, oligarchic republic with a divided and relatively weak executive branch,
avoiding the autocratic dictatorship Napoleon established.
Militarily, France would not have immediately collapsed.
Competent generals like Moreau,
who historically won the decisive Battle of Hohenlinden in 1800,
could have successfully defended France's borders against the Second Coalition
and forced a favorable peace treaty.
However, without Napoleon's unparalleled military genius and insatiable ambition,
the ensuing decade and a half of relentless expansion known as the Napoleonic Wars would never have occurred.
France would likely have fought defensive or limited regional conflicts
rather than attempting to subjugate the entire European continent.
Consequently, the Holy Roman Empire might have survived its historical 1806 dissolution,
the disastrous Peninsular War and the 1812 invasion of Russia would have been averted,
and millions of European lives would have been spared.
Domestically, the absence of Napoleon would mean the loss of his massive centralizing reforms.
The Napoleonic Code,
which fundamentally shaped modern civil law across Europe and Latin America,
would not have been written in its historical form,
and the Concordat of 1801 might not have reconciled the French state with the Catholic Church so swiftly.
Without Napoleon's iron grip stabilizing the nation,
France would have remained politically volatile.
This ongoing factional instability would likely have paved the way for an earlier restoration of the Bourbon monarchy,
as the exhausted French public eventually sought a return to traditional order
without a military dictator to rally behind.
Ultimately, the geopolitical trajectory of the 19th century would have been entirely rewritten.
Napoleon's conquests inadvertently exported the ideals of the French Revolution—such as meritocracy, secularism, and the destruction of feudalism—
while simultaneously sparking fierce nationalistic backlash in places like Germany and Italy.
Without his continent-spanning empire to act as both a modernizing force and a common enemy,
the unification of Germany and Italy would have been significantly delayed or taken entirely different paths,
and the map of Europe would have remained heavily fractured,
altering the balance of power leading into the 20th century.

items.question: What If the Greek 'Great Plan' had succeeded and the Greek War of Independence had triggered an early collapse of the Ottoman Empire?
human_answers: A more decisive Ottoman defeat against Greece can give birth to the "Megali Idea" before 1844. In such a scenario, a larger independent Greek state can invited Louis-Philippe d’Orléans to become its king, before 1830 of course. This arrangement can be supported by both France and its Bourbon king, who might want to sideline a troublesome cousin, and by the United Kingdom. For the British, the presence of a Great European power south of the Straits, one aligned with neither Austria nor Russia can further divide the continental great powers and serve British strategic interests. With France satisfied in Greece and Austria compensated with territories along the Adriatic coast, Britain can focus on securing Egypt for itself. Even if the Suez Canal is not even a dream, control of Egypt is already strategically valuable for strengthening connections with India. By 1829, railway projects are already under consideration, making overland transit increasingly plausible and reinforcing Egypt’s geopolitical importance. And if its happen after 1830, Louis-Philippe has enough sons (6 minus one who died in 1828) to send one to Greece.

Considering their interest is not even religious (GB: Protestant, France: Catholic, Russia: Orthodox) and that really none of these Great Powers saw the Greek War of Independence with positive eyes (to them it was no different than the revolutions in Spain, Portugal and Naples; which, btw, they sent huge armies to crush). There was later a British change, but even the Metternich, Alexander and so on weren't super happy about it. Remember: at this point, the memory of Napoleon is far fresher than that of the Ottoman invasions into the Balkans, so the concern, far above Islam, is revolutionary sentiment. What I do see happening is them deliberating and taking too long to make a decision that the situation ends up devolving on its own (it took them like 3 years to agree to send an invasion to Spain). Then again, the French were sympathetic to Muhammad Ali while the British aided Ali Pasha plenty of times (through Maitland, specifically). They will always prefer a rotting corpse of the Ottoman empire maintaining power over the ambitious and reformist Albanian Pashas in power, this is why they went out of their way to put them out IRL, but when shit hits the fan, they have to re-examine their approach of course.

Agreed that the Great Powers, including even Russia under Alexander, don't want a full Ottoman collapse. That's not the same as saying they would intervene to stop it. It's hard to conceive of a situation in which Great Britain, France, or Russia would go to war to suppress Christian rebels fighting against the Sultan, particularly after the various atrocities committed at Chios and other places. There were also similar atrocities committed by the Greeks against Muslims, but this did not register in the European consciousness of the time and would not be a factor. It's also not a given that any intervention would be successful at stopping chaos and preserving the Empire, even if it did somehow occur. This would be a formidable job if the situation became so extreme that the Ottomans asked for such support. More likely the intervention would be directed towards managing the collapse and achieving a partition either formally or in terms of spheres of influence.
items.original_question: What if 'Great Plan' more or fully successful - Greek War of Independence causes early Ottoman collapse? There have been many threads about the Greek War of Independence here, but one what if I haven't seen anyone talk about might be one of the most crazy ones. Mark Mazower states the following in his book on the Greek War of Indepdendence: Of course, aside from the revolt in the Peloponnese, none of these plans ever came close to succeeding. These plans were modified or abandoned entirely when the focus of the revolt shifted from the Peloponnese to the Danubian Principalities. There was a letter sent to cause terror in Constantinople, but the letter never made it and plans were changing so often that no action was taken. Now this seems like an insane scheme which would be insanely hard to pull off, even if all the circumstances were right, but let's hypothetically ask, what if some, or all of them did? Would this cause the Ottoman Empire to collapse entirely, or enter a prolonged period of unrest? A torching of the fleet, coordinated with the assassination of Mahmud II, coupled with all the other issues the empire was facing in the early 1820's seem like they would be a complete headache, who would even be Sultan had this happened, considering Abdulmecid wasn't even born yet and Mahmud II had no sons? Edit: Turns out Mahmud II had a single surviving son by this point, Abdulhamid. But he died in 1825 IOTL, which, if it still happens, might actually make things even worse if the revolt didn't fizzle out by then.

items.model_answer:
If the Greek "Great Plan" (the vision of the Filiki Eteria to spark a pan-Balkan uprising) had succeeded in the 1820s, resulting in the capture of Constantinople and the premature collapse of the Ottoman Empire, a sprawling, neo-Byzantine Greek state would have emerged to dominate the Aegean and the Bosporus. This early death of the Ottoman Empire would have instantly detonated the "Eastern Question," fundamentally altering 19th-century global geopolitics by removing the vital buffer state that kept European imperial rivalries in check.

The most immediate consequence would be a massive Great Power scramble and likely a major European war. Russia would view the new Orthodox Greek state either as a natural vassal to secure its long-desired warm-water access to the Mediterranean or as a dangerous rival for control of the Straits. Great Britain and Austria, terrified of Russian expansion and the disruption of the balance of power, would aggressively intervene. This power vacuum would almost certainly trigger an early, highly destructive equivalent of the Crimean War, as Britain and France rushed to secure naval dominance and trade routes to India, while Austria fought to contain Russian and Greek influence on its southern borders.

Internally, this enlarged Hellenic empire would be highly unstable. The Greek vision of a Hellenized, resurrected Byzantium would clash violently with the emerging nationalisms of Serbs, Bulgarians, and Romanians. Instead of slowly uniting against a decaying Ottoman state over the 19th century, these populations would immediately turn against Greek hegemony. This would spark a series of early, brutal Balkan Wars, forcing the new Greek state to expend immense military and economic resources attempting to pacify its northern frontiers and govern a vast, multi-ethnic population. 

In the Middle East and North Africa, the sudden Ottoman collapse would create a vast geopolitical void. Muhammad Ali of Egypt, who already possessed a highly modernized military in the 1820s, would likely seize the Levant, Syria, and the Hejaz, establishing a powerful, independent Egyptian-Arab empire decades ahead of schedule. Simultaneously, European powers would accelerate their colonization of the region. Britain and France would begin carving up Mesopotamia, the Levant, and North Africa to secure their imperial lifelines, effectively moving the post-World War I Sykes-Picot dynamic nearly a century into the past. 

Finally, the Turkish and Muslim populations of the former empire would face catastrophic displacement. A rump Turkish state would likely form in the rugged interior of central and eastern Anatolia, serving as a staging ground for continuous revanchist wars against the expanded Greek state on the coast. The resulting demographic shifts and ethnic conflicts would define the region's borders through perpetual warfare, leaving the Eastern Mediterranean in a state of volatile militarization and preventing the new Greek Empire from ever achieving true stability.

criterion_evaluations.name: Counterfactual Premise Integration and Point of Divergence
criterion_evaluations.reason: The answer clearly centers the specified premise: a successful Greek 'Great Plan' in the 1820s leads to capture of Constantinople and an early Ottoman collapse, and it explicitly traces consequences across the Balkans, the Straits, Egypt/Levant, and Great Power politics. It gives real mechanisms of destabilization—power vacuum, Orthodox/imperial rivalry, anti-Greek reactions among other Balkan peoples, and Muhammad Ali exploiting the collapse—so this is well above generic Ottoman-decline discussion. However, it does not rigorously develop why Greek success itself produces systemic Ottoman breakdown in military, fiscal, ideological, and legitimacy terms; it mostly asserts collapse once Constantinople falls. items.question: What If the French become one of the largest communities in the US
human_answers: Hordes of Catholics, even if not all that devout, descending on the US will cause some tension. On the flip side, though, France is one of the civilized nations, and they're seen as more desirable shade of white. Timing matters, too. Napoleonic era, when immigration is still low, is a whole lot different than the final decades of the 19th century, when millions is a drop in the bucket. Location matters, too. Are the French hordes joining into the crowded East, where they likely assimilate? Or are they carving out a big chunk of the midwest/west as largely French? Reason for the diaspora might matter. If we mess with the Napoleonic era, especially if we butterfly it (not killing off a generation or two of males would be a good start in having excess population to export), the state of the world could affect the state of the USA (maybe even the size if no Mex-Am War/Texas). With such a generic What if, we can only talk in generics. If we stipulate a recognizable world, more or less the same, except a massive French diaspora for some reason that hasn't caused OTL to derail.... I would guess the French would be like any other large group. There'll be tension, but everyone will adapt. It's an age of racism, and French are in the top class, so I suspect they'll have an easier time of it. (caveat edit: In no way am I saying French are better than any other nation, but reality is that skin color mattered. My understanding is that not all whites were considered equal)

I would assume rather than staying in the east, the French would largely settle in former Louisiana- centring probably on New Orleans. Texas and Florida as well are likely spots for French settlement. Of the 13 colonies, I would guess it’s the southern ones which would be most amenable to French settlement- though how that affects racial dynamics in the south, and how that affects potential north south tensions is difficult to say. It’s difficult as well to say what the economic impact of French settlement would be- I’d say as a community they’d probably be more educated and thus better off than the Irish or Italians, perhaps more comparable to German or Swedish immigrants. Perhaps the planter class ends up going fully bilingual. Depending on how the 19th century goes you could end up with an Alt-confederacy that stays independent because it has so many French speakers and Catholics that the north simply isn’t interested in reintegrating them.
items.original_question: What if the French become one of the largest communities in the US Let’s suppose that millions of French flocked to the US in the 19th century for one reason or another—for example, because harsher Napoleonic Wars and a more severe Congress of Vienna plunged France into a deep economic crisis, while the Irish and Italians would be less numerous in the US, for example because the Irish Great Famine never happened and the Italian peninsula unified and modernized earlier. No PoD before 1780. How would the French be treated in the US? Would they face xenophobia and form a distinct community like the Irish and Italians, or would they be assimilated among the WASPs within one or two generations like the Germans did IOTL? French culture was admired, but I’m not sure that the arrival of millions of French people (with a Latin culture and Catholic religion) would be particularly well received.

items.model_answer:
If the French had become one of the largest demographic communities in the United States, the nation's cultural, linguistic, and political landscape would be fundamentally transformed. Linguistically, French would likely rival Spanish as the nation's second most spoken language, leading to widespread bilingualism in public education, government, and media. Cities with historical French colonial roots—such as New Orleans, St. Louis, Detroit, and Chicago—would likely have developed into massive Francophone cultural hubs, retaining distinct French architectural and social identities rather than fully assimilating into the Anglo-American mainstream.

Culturally, everyday American life would be deeply infused with French traditions. American cuisine would feature a heavier, more mainstream reliance on French culinary techniques, baking, and viticulture, potentially making the US an even larger global center for wine and gastronomy. Furthermore, the historical dominance of Anglo-Protestantism in the US would have been challenged much earlier. A massive French population would have significantly bolstered the American Catholic Church, likely reducing the severe anti-Catholic prejudice that later Irish, Italian, and Hispanic immigrants faced, thereby shifting the moral and social frameworks of early American society.

On a political and legal level, the influence of French Civil Law—which is currently isolated to Louisiana's state legal system—might have spread to other states or influenced federal law, creating a more prominent hybrid of English Common Law and the Napoleonic Code across the country. In foreign policy, a powerful French-American voting bloc would have demanded closer diplomatic and economic ties with France. This could have altered the United States' isolationist stance during early European conflicts, potentially accelerating US entry into World War I and World War II, and reshaping the geopolitical alliances of the 19th and 20th centuries. Ultimately, the United States would operate as a deeply bicultural Anglo-French nation, acting as the primary bridge between the Anglosphere and the Francophonie.

items.question: Independent Naples: What If Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505?
human_answers: I wouldn't say that Philip is foolish, simply naive, since it is impossible for him to imagine that Ferdinand II and Catherine are plotting against him, to shape Joanna and especially the little Charles into a figure totally different from his own ( so that he may become the perfect archetype of a Christian Monarch ), but in any case I am certain that Queen Isabella would never do anything wrong in compromising her nephew's chances of inheriting his father's possessions ( Burgundy and Austria ) or preventing him from aspiring to the imperial throne, after all doing this risks it compromise to the international prestige of his family ( the Trastamaras ) let's say that the Catholic Monarchs only want to make sure that the future King of Castile and Aragon is not too accommodating to French wishes, it is realistic to think that Charles was initially educated at his mother's court, and then, when he was sure he could face a sea voyage, he was transferred to his grandfather Maximilian

Oh, please… the POD is interesting but the development is full of things that are blatantly false. OTL Isabella and Ferdinand were the ones that wanted Catalina’s remarriage to the future Henry VIII, and insisted that her marriage with Arthur was not consummated. Henry VII OTL was bullied in accepting the engagement of his second son to Catalina as he believed she was too old for his son. He would have zero troubles in giving back the half of her dowry he had already received (for all that getting back her dowry meant that Catherine had no right to any English money or lands) and send Catherine back at home as he had no use for her. Catalina’s aunt, the Dowager Queen of Naples would first try to marry her own daughter to the new Ferdinand III of Naples, as Giovanna was still in her mid-20s (or she would expect to see another match arranged for her daughter before agreeing to support Catalina as future Queen of Naples. Sea journeys at the time were extremely dangerous (I don’t remember if Catalina got lucky, but both Joanna and Margaret got close to die in their respective wedding journeys) reason for which Philip used his friendship with the French King for securing a land passage into France for going to receive the investitures. Eleanor and Charles at the time were too little for making safely the long journey, for not talking about baby Isabella, and Philip would never agree to bring them in Castile in any case. And if she had been so inclined Catalina, being the youngest of her sisters, could very well be allowed to take the veil. In 1502 Juana had three children and Maria one and both were likely to have soon more…

The year 1502 starts very rough for Catalina of Aragon. She and her husband, Arthur , Prince of Wales had both fallen ill at the end of March and when she recovered, she discovered that her husband had died. She could not believe it. She was a widow after only five months of marriage. She knew that she was not pregnant, as her marriage was unconsummated. One month after she was made a widow, Catalina was moved to Durham House in London and was visited by King Henry VII and his wife, Queen Elizabeth of York. Catalina told them that she had bled already and there was no hope for an heir from their late son, so his younger brother, Prince Henry, Duke of York, was officially declared as the heir. When the news to Catalina's parents, King Fernando II of Aragon and Queen Isabella I of Castile, they were disappointed that the alliance seemed to have fallen through and that their daughter was widowed at only sixteen years old. This began a struggle over Catalina. Queen Isabella was adamant that her youngest child be returned to her, since there was not a hope of an English grandchild to seal the alliance with Spain and England. King Henry VII, however, did not want to lose her or her dowry. He offered to marry her to his younger son and she could still be Queen of England one day. Queen Isabella made up her mind and told her husband that she wanted their daughter to be returned home. King Ferdinand sent an ambassador to tell King Henry that the Princess would be returned to Spain, either with her entourage or by force. When King Henry VII heard this, he was furious, but also terrified. He needed this alliance with Spain and he did not want to let his daughter-in-law go. Finally, an agreement was finally reached. The Infanta would return to her parents and half her dowry would be returned with her and she would retain her status of Dowager Princess of Wales and would still receive her marriage jointure for the remainder of her life. Her English attendants, like Margaret Pole, would remain in England. When she was told Princess Catalina had a mix of grief and relief. She was happy to return home to her parents, especially since her older sister, Juana, who was now Princess of Asturias, was back home as well. On August 1, 1502, Princess Catalina and her entourage arrived at Dover, preparing to board the ship that will cross the sea once again. Prince Henry, the young Prince of Wales accompanied her, just like he escorted her down the aisle to marry his late older brother. The eleven year old, who was talkative and social, was unusually quiet through the journey. Princess Catalina gave him a little kiss on his forehead and told him that she will never forget him or her time in England and she knew that one day, he will be the greatest King that England ever had, before she boarded the ship. Thankfully, this journey was much easier than her original one taking her to England. She and her entourage arrived in Laredo on the 15th of August. Princess Catalina found herself smiling, as she saw the familiar Castilian villages and knew she was home. However, she then was wondering what would happen to her and her future. Due to the deaths of her older brother, sister and nephew, she knew that taking holy vows was not an option, as he parents only had three surviving daughters. Would she just remain a spinster? Would she be married off again to a foreign Kingdom, even France? Her father was definitely ambitious and was a shrewd ruler, so she knew that she would not remain unmarried for long, but she was still looking forward to just feeling her mother's embrace once more.
items.original_question: Independent Naples: What if Catherine of Aragon marries Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505? Hey all! This question has been on my mind a little too. What if instead of the long seven years in England in virtual poverty, Catherine of Aragon returns to her parents in the summer of 1502 and they arrange a marriage for the young King of Naples, which is still an independent Kingdom in this timeline? In this timeline, Henry VIII will instead marry Eleanor of Austria instead.

items.model_answer:
If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505, the geopolitical landscape of early modern Europe would have been radically transformed, most notably by averting the English Reformation and establishing an independent, sovereign Kingdom of Naples. 

In 1505, Catherine was living in a state of political limbo in England following the death of her first husband, Arthur Tudor. Her betrothal to the future Henry VIII was stalled by diplomatic and financial disputes between Henry VII and her father, Ferdinand II of Aragon. Historically, Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, was the heir to the deposed Neapolitan branch of the House of Trastámara and was living as a captive of Ferdinand of Aragon. If the Aragonese king had chosen to marry his daughter to the Duke, it would have been a strategic masterstroke to pacify the rebellious Neapolitan nobility. By restoring the native Neapolitan heir to the throne alongside his own fiercely loyal daughter, Ferdinand of Aragon would have transitioned Naples from a contested territory into a secure, semi-independent client kingdom, rather than absorbing it as a direct Spanish viceroyalty.

The most profound global consequence of this union would be the alteration of English history. Without Catherine of Aragon in England, Henry VIII would have married a different European royal—likely a French princess or a Habsburg. Consequently, the specific dynastic crisis that defined Henry’s reign—his desperate pursuit of an annulment from Catherine to secure a male heir—would never have occurred. Without the "King's Great Matter," Henry’s schism with Rome would be entirely averted. England would likely have remained a staunchly Catholic nation, profoundly altering the religious demographics of Europe, preventing the eventual rise of Puritanism, and completely erasing the historical Tudor succession of Mary I and Elizabeth I.

In Italy, the establishment of an independent Naples under Catherine and the Duke of Calabria would have shifted the balance of power during the Italian Wars. Rather than being heavily taxed and administered by Spanish viceroys, a sovereign Naples would have retained its wealth, fostering a distinct Southern Italian Renaissance. Catherine, known historically for her formidable political acumen and education, would have been a highly effective queen consort or regent, helping to centralize Neapolitan power and defend the kingdom against French incursions. The Neapolitan court would have become a major diplomatic hub in the Mediterranean, serving as a buffer state between the Papal States, the expanding Ottoman Empire, and rival European powers. 

Furthermore, this marriage would have lightened the administrative burden on the future Emperor Charles V (Catherine’s nephew). Historically, Charles inherited Naples along with Spain, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Americas, leading to massive imperial overextension. With Naples ruled by a cadet branch of his family, Charles would still enjoy a reliable military ally in the Mediterranean without the financial drain of directly garrisoning the territory. Ultimately, this single marital pivot in 1505 would have preserved the religious unity of Western Europe while permanently altering the map of Italy, allowing a sovereign Southern Italian kingdom to flourish centuries before the historical unification of the peninsula.

edus.text: If Catherine of Aragon had married Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria in 1505,
the geopolitical landscape of early modern Europe would have been radically transformed,
most notably by averting the English Reformation
and establishing an independent, sovereign Kingdom of Naples.
In 1505, Catherine was living in a state of political limbo in England following the death of her first husband, Arthur Tudor.
Her betrothal to the future Henry VIII was stalled by diplomatic and financial disputes between Henry VII and her father, Ferdinand II of Aragon.
Historically, Ferdinand, Duke of Calabria, was the heir to the deposed Neapolitan branch of the House of Trastámara
and was living as a captive of Ferdinand of Aragon.
If the Aragonese king had chosen to marry his daughter to the Duke,
it would have been a strategic masterstroke to pacify the rebellious Neapolitan nobility.
By restoring the native Neapolitan heir to the throne alongside his own fiercely loyal daughter,
Ferdinand of Aragon would have transitioned Naples from a contested territory into a secure, semi-independent client kingdom,
rather than absorbing it as a direct Spanish viceroyalty.
The most profound global consequence of this union would be the alteration of English history.
Without Catherine of Aragon in England,
Henry VIII would have married a different European royal—likely a French princess or a Habsburg.
Consequently, the specific dynastic crisis that defined Henry’s reign—his desperate pursuit of an annulment from Catherine to secure a male heir—would never have occurred.
Without the "King's Great Matter,"
Henry’s schism with Rome would be entirely averted.
England would likely have remained a staunchly Catholic nation,
profoundly altering the religious demographics of Europe,
preventing the eventual rise of Puritanism,
and completely erasing the historical Tudor succession of Mary I and Elizabeth I.
In Italy, the establishment of an independent Naples under Catherine and the Duke of Calabria would have shifted the balance of power during the Italian Wars.
Rather than being heavily taxed and administered by Spanish viceroys,
a sovereign Naples would have retained its wealth,
fostering a distinct Southern Italian Renaissance.
Catherine, known historically for her formidable political acumen and education,
would have been a highly effective queen consort or regent,
helping to centralize Neapolitan power
and defend the kingdom against French incursions.
The Neapolitan court would have become a major diplomatic hub in the Mediterranean,
serving as a buffer state between the Papal States, the expanding Ottoman Empire, and rival European powers.
Furthermore, this marriage would have lightened the administrative burden on the future Emperor Charles V (Catherine’s nephew).
Historically, Charles inherited Naples along with Spain, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Americas,
leading to massive imperial overextension.
With Naples ruled by a cadet branch of his family,
Charles would still enjoy a reliable military ally in the Mediterranean
without the financial drain of directly garrisoning the territory.
Ultimately, this single marital pivot in 1505 would have preserved the religious unity of Western Europe
while permanently altering the map of Italy,
allowing a sovereign Southern Italian kingdom to flourish centuries before the historical unification of the peninsula.

human_answers: India has only recently emerged as one of the world’s chief polluters; some two decades ago, Russia and Japan had a bigger mark, and in 1980 Canada was the bigger polluter. Depending on how decarbonized the economies of the First World are by 2000, India’s subsequent economic growth could be magnitudes cleaner than it was OTL. China you have a better point about, though first, their massive economic rise in the three decades after Mao’s death or so is pretty contingent, and second, they still only caught up to the already carbon stagnant EU in 2002. Imagine if the US was still comparable, as they were OTL until the mid 1980’s; now imagine, as China is getting ready to join the WTO in the late 90’s and early 2000’s, the west is also pushing a world climate treaty that (among other things) pushed these three major blocs (the US, Europe, and China) to curb their emissions going into the future. Even if India still sees their emissions rise, wouldn’t the fact that by far the largest producers are simultaneously cutting emissions lead to net reduction?

Well, is the point of your question, can we limit temperature rise by today , or in perpetuity? If the former, then greater adoption of nuclear energy in the West is probably a good enough answer; by the time Chinese and Indian energy use spikes, the resultant temperature spike won't come until after today. Maybe. But that seems like the wrong question, I interpret it as how to prevent such a spike from EVER occurring, rather than just occurring 10 years late. And for that, there's a big challenge. How do developing countries get off the ground? Hydrocarbons are great for that. If the big emitters of the 60s all switched to nuclear, that's fantastic--but China and India can't afford to START with nuclear, nobody can, which means a huge amount of hydrocarbons being burned when they start heavily industrializing. As a solution, perhaps their rise as industrial powers can be delayed a few decades? If they started industrializing in 2025 instead, they might use shale gas or solar, which are now the cheapest sources of power. But the production of those isn't domestic to China, which is a huge part of their use of coal--they don't have to import it. Tentatively, maybe the Soviet Union needs to have greater economic development and a softer landing when it falls? If they can be an industrial exporter while powered off domestic nuclear and natural gas, and remain so in the 1990s, then Chinese growth will be very different, and overall emissions will be lower. Cars and planes are obvious problems. I would also posit beef as a problem--methane is significantly more powerful than carbon in greenhouse effect, and is estimated as responsible for 20 to 30 percent of human-origin warming. Sixty percent of methane emissions are estimated as human-caused, with a big one being agriculture, and beef is responsible for a LOT of agriculture. So a poorer world, that eats less meat, would have lower methane emissions. So too would a world with fewer wetlands, so perhaps a little more paving of swamps would be good from the perspective of this question. Just thoughts. I'll be back for more, probably.

No, because they're already too anti-nuclear. The R&D and thus cost curves on silicon-based solar cell production, and on improved battery capacity, are both pushed pretty hard historically by electronics industry spinoffs. It's hard to see any sort of policy pushes for renewables accelerating those more than marginally, and dramatic acceleration is what you need to make them cost-viable decades ahead of schedule. On the other hand, nuclear was deliberately hobbled by US policy in the 1970s. People like to blame 1979's Three Mile Island, but (for a couple examples) the AEC to NRC switchover was passed by Congress and signed by Ford in 1974, while Carter's anti-reprocessing moratorium was in 1977. If you instead have the US adopt its own version of France's Messmer Plan in 1974 (which is tricky, because Messmer was able to simply ignore anti-nuclear sentiments due to government and economy structure in ways the US government couldn't), you get nuclear power economies of scale driven by the joint US-French demand that make it a more-attractive alternative throughout the rest of the industrialized world. Imagine Thatcher's government nuclearizing Britain in part to undercut the coal unions, for example. Then, if US electricity is something like 75% nuclear in 1990 (like France in 1990, instead of the historical 20%), with the UK fast-following? Now you have the necessary condition (it not hobbling the US) for international trade treaties and the like based on carbon emissions, after a decade of greenhouse effect publicity (since the 1979 NAS report), with the first IPCC report coming out. (Yes, sure, butterflies will scramble the details, but "coal is bad" science, if anything, will be better-funded if the US is transitioning from coal.) If Japan has (as is likely) lagged the US/France/UK in adoption of nuclear, this will be a particularly easy sell, since everybody in the West in 1990 is looking for an excuse to be protectionist against "Japan, Inc." And with that set up, you have the trick for going forward. If China (etc.) has to avoid coal power to export to Western markets, China either will figure out how to avoid coal, or it won't develop because it won't have markets to sell into.

I can give you two, PODs, One being no 3 Mile Island and the other being no John Sununu. So the real easy way to cut down on CO2 emissions is to cut down on coal use, and both PODs give easy ways to do just that. After the banning of CFCs in the late 80s, momentum existed for much harder caps on carbon than were discussed later. In particular, serious curtailment of coal as an energy source in the developed world was mooted. However, this momentum was handicapped with a lack of US Presidential support, with Bush Sr being advised against supporting these efforts by his Chief of Staff, John Sununu. Remove Sununu, and US support for carbon caps become more likely earlier. In addition with no 3MI incident, nuclear technology in the west could become less taboo, giving a viable alternative to coal fired power earlier. I could see a scenario where industry, much like CFCs, sees the financial opportunities in replacing coal with a nuclear/gas mix, and does not get in the way of any cuts to carbon emissions. A good book on the subject in your timeframe is Loosing Earth, by Nathanial Rich, which goes into detail about the drive to curtail emissions in the late 80s. would highly recommend giving it a read.
items.original_question:
AHC: Curb Global Warming after 1980

So you know how Global Surface Temperatures have increased 1.3°C over pre-industrial levels at present, and how a big part of the current Climate Movement is trying to limit further change as much as possible, 1.5°C being the best known* goal? Well, as recently as circa 1980, GST above PIL was only about 0.3°C, and had been hovering just below those levels for decades since the aftermath of WWII; in other words, a full degrees celsius of global warming only happened in the past 45 years alone. This is actually pretty astonishing when you realize how much of a turning point circa 1980 was to global carbon emissions -- both the biggest producers world-wide at the time, the US and Europe, initially saw their emissions peak, with Europe remaining controlled even as the US reversed course after a few years; Japan and Canada have a similar "false peaks" around the same time as the US; the USSR, of course, collapse circa 1990 and saw their emissions collapse thereafter, never to recover; and China was about to undergo a massive economic expansion that would see them become the world's largest emitters. So what I want to determine here is -- what is the latest PoD for avoiding this massive escalation of climate change, or of making it as small as possible? Could a PoD in the late 1970's (eg a continuation of Carter's energy policies in the US) have done the trick? If avoiding a full degrees celsius of warming wasn't seriously avertable by, say, 1975, how early do we need to go? 1960? The aftermath of WWII? In the event we can come to a consensus on the latest possible PoD and what would do the trick, we might also discuss how those changes to said countries' energy polices and to the global economy as a whole would have changed things overall. Thanks. *I'm really trying to avoid getting sidetracked in this discussion for the thread, so for anyone wanting to weigh in on whether its still feasible or how big of a deal missing that goal is, please take that to one of the Chat discussions -- much thanks!

rubrics.question_focus: What If Curb Global Warming after 1980

criteria.name: 1980 Baseline and Emissions Chronology Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately anchors the counterfactual in the post-1980 emissions landscape, including which countries/blocs mattered when, and avoids anachronistic assumptions about China, India, the USSR/Russia, Japan, Canada, the EU, and the US.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the 1980 baseline or treats present-day emitters as if they had the same role in 1980; little connection to historical emissions timing.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes some major emitters but gives a shallow or partially anachronistic chronology of who drove emissions after 1980.
criteria.5-6: Mostly accurate on broad emissions timing, distinguishing early Western dominance from later Chinese and Indian growth, with minor omissions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly tracks major emitter shifts across the 1980s, 1990s, 2000s, and later, using this chronology to shape the counterfactual.
criteria.9-10: Precisely integrates historical emissions sequencing, industrialization timing, and bloc-level comparisons to evaluate whether post-1980 warming could plausibly be curbed.

criteria.name: Decarbonization Mechanism Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the specificity and plausibility of proposed mechanisms for curbing warming after 1980, especially nuclear expansion, coal displacement, renewables cost curves, efficiency, carbon treaties, and fossil-fuel lock-in.
criteria.1-2: Offers vague claims such as 'use clean energy' without explaining feasible mechanisms or constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions plausible technologies or policies but ignores cost, deployment speed, political resistance, or energy-system inertia.
criteria.5-6: Provides one or two workable mechanisms, such as Western nuclear buildout or coal limits, with some attention to feasibility.
criteria.7-8: Explains multiple mechanisms and constraints, including nuclear politics, renewable timing, grid deployment, coal dependence, and international policy leverage.
criteria.9-10: Builds a highly plausible decarbonization pathway with detailed technological, economic, political, and institutional mechanisms appropriate to the 1980 onward timeline.

criteria.name: Developing-World Industrialization and Trade Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the central downstream issue: how China, India, and other developing economies industrialize if the West curbs emissions, and whether trade, technology transfer, delayed growth, or carbon standards change their trajectories.
criteria.1-2: Ignores China, India, and developing-country growth or assumes they simply copy Western decarbonization without constraints.
criteria.3-4: Mentions China or India but gives little explanation of energy affordability, domestic coal, export markets, or development incentives.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that developing-country industrialization is a major challenge and links it to coal, trade, or technology access.
criteria.7-8: Analyzes how Western decarbonization, carbon tariffs, WTO-era trade, Soviet/Russian alternatives, or technology transfer could alter Chinese and Indian emissions.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced account of developing-world growth paths, including affordability, domestic resources, export dependence, geopolitical contingencies, and whether global emissions fall despite later industrialization.

criteria.name: Climate Outcome Reasoning and Greenhouse-Gas Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Measures how well the answer connects emissions changes to climate outcomes, including cumulative CO2, timing of warming, methane, land use, transport, agriculture, and the distinction between delaying warming and preventing it in the long run.
criteria.1-2: Conflates annual emissions with temperature outcomes or ignores cumulative emissions and climate lag.
criteria.3-4: Makes broad claims about reduced warming but gives little explanation of cumulative carbon, timing, or non-CO2 gases.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that lower emissions reduce warming and includes some discussion of climate lag or non-CO2 sources.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes short-term delay from long-term prevention and covers major sectors such as electricity, transport, industry, agriculture, and methane.
criteria.9-10: Rigorously links sectoral emissions pathways to cumulative forcing and temperature outcomes, explicitly assessing whether warming is merely postponed or durably limited.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses the overall counterfactual chain from post-1980 interventions to late-20th and 21st-century outcomes, including internal consistency, handling of contingencies, and calibrated confidence.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims, deterministic assertions, or contradictions that break the counterfactual chain.
criteria.3-4: Has a recognizable scenario but weak causal links, unsupported leaps, or unacknowledged conflicts between assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Maintains a mostly coherent chain with some uncertainty acknowledged, though parts remain underdeveloped or loosely connected.
criteria.7-8: Develops a consistent multi-decade causal pathway, flags key contingencies, and avoids major contradictions.
criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly reasoned long-range scenario with explicit causal dependencies, alternative branches, uncertainty calibration, and careful distinction between necessary and sufficient conditions.

items.model_answer:
If the world had successfully acted to curb global warming after 1980—capitalizing on the scientific consensus established by the 1979 Charney Report and the political momentum of the 1970s energy crises—the trajectory of global technology, geopolitics, and environmental health would be radically different today. 

To achieve this, governments would have had to aggressively pivot away from fossil fuels, likely sparking a massive, sustained renaissance in nuclear power while accelerating the commercial maturity of solar and wind technologies by decades. The automotive industry would have faced strict emissions regulations much earlier, pushing the widespread adoption of electric vehicles into the late 1990s or early 2000s rather than the 2020s. 

Economically and geopolitically, the early decline of the fossil fuel industry would have severely curtailed the wealth and global influence of petrostates. Nations heavily reliant on oil exports, such as the Soviet Union, Saudi Arabia, and Iran, would have faced premature economic crises, potentially altering the outcome of the Cold War and reducing the frequency of oil-driven conflicts in the Middle East. Meanwhile, early implementation of global carbon pricing—enacted before climate change became a hyper-polarized political wedge issue—would have reshaped global supply chains, favoring energy efficiency, localized manufacturing, and nations leading in green technology.

Environmentally, the Earth would have avoided the drastic temperature spikes of the 21st century. The Arctic ice cap would remain largely intact, global sea-level rise would have been minimized, and marine ecosystems would have been spared from catastrophic mass bleaching and rapid ocean acidification. Furthermore, the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, such as mega-wildfires, super-hurricanes, and deadly heatwaves, would be significantly lower, saving millions of lives and trillions of dollars in disaster recovery. 

Ultimately, climate change would be viewed today as a successfully managed 20th-century environmental triumph—much like the mitigation of acid rain or the closing of the ozone hole—rather than an existential and deeply polarizing global crisis.
