items.question: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won?
human_answers: From another convo regarding this: "In Axis Victory scenarios, [Germany]is presumed to implement late war policies fully. This is unlikely because those were developed via a process of increasing radicalization caused by losing the war. The harder they win early on, the less radical they are .If they win, they (for example) keep the network of client parties who lead aligned states & it's just Bormannite Gau-Federalism all the way down. Until he dies & the EU (racist) forms, especially if they impose a continental system as some economists desired. Funny ideas would likely be restricted to the SS as a counterelite and the source of a youth counterculture. This is perhaps the only thing TNO understood well about Germany (and then forgot)." Some Notes: Any Brown Scare would basically devolve into Southern Democrats gleefully lecturing Republicans about the virtues of Anti-Fascism whilst holding up anti-lynchings and halting civil rights bills. Midwestern Republicans and America Firsters( who include liberals like Sargent Shriver) go tell the Dixiecrats to pound sand and the issue becomes a partisan football much like the McCarthyite hearings. If America is never at war with Germany, then a major obstacle between America and Germany wrt trade is gone. The same business types that pre-war were pro-Britain out of a fear that a German-dominated Europe would close itself off to American exports would be at the close of ww2, be pushing hard for a renormalization of ties in trade or otherwise because again, Europe is THE most developed part of the world in 1940. There are no other countries or regions that even comes close save maybe The Dominions/Argentina/Brazil and even then they're a far cry from what Europe is. Even if Hitler postwar is ideologically against it because he feels Germany no longer needs to cooperate "Anglo-American-Judeo-Capitalism", Goering is definitely going to be in favor of improved trade ties as well as the bulk of the German industrial community as well(especially if there is any chance these American multinational corps have of keeping tighter control of their German subsidiary). Given the KMT's territorial irredentism especially towards Hong Kong,Macau, East Manchuria, and Chiang Kai Shek's ego. I could definitely see the KMT pivoting to being Pro-German and seeking investment from them to build up the economy and engage in import substitution industrialization and modernization of their own military. Some form of zionist state would be established post-war with allied support and would probably survive any initial confrontation with Arab armies. This means that middle eastern politics is quite *fun* for the next 50 years as Italy and Germany have an easy vector to appeal to arab support, especially once Baathism starts being intellectually developed, with much of its socialist skin being shorn off and replaced with corporatism. Addendum

The Germans would control everything up to the Urals or at least the AA line since anything less and the Soviets keep fighting. So that situation honestly is unlikely. I think this is based more on wish fulfillment more than anything. The reality is that the wishes of the South American and US ambitions would increasingly separate specially since there is not Sovier or socialist groups or ideology to unite both groups towards a common vision. If anything I would imagine South America to be closer to neutral to actively playing both sides to get as much for themselves as possible. Your also ignoring that the European markets would be gone to both the US and South America causing it own issues. Unlikely if only due to the nature of the Reich. This isn't the Soviets who at least had in theory an encourager of minorities and such. This is the reich where any minority would have been killed, Germanized, or enslaved. More importantly unlike the Soviets the Reich doesn't have the prospect of losing millions of their own people to either invasion or self inflicted socialist violence and ideological economic policies. Would things go well for the reich? Probably not but if the Soviets lasted decades and the PRC is still standing the Reich can do the same.

Germany will want everything, I agree, but they still have to focus on digesting the rest of Europe beforehand, which leaves the periphery less stable. That's not to say that Germany can't ultimately beat the partisans completely, but I'd imagine there'd still be room on the German-USSR border for a few years. As for Portugal and Norway, the allies don't have presence there. Portugal never joined the war, but they also have no real ideological reason to challenge Germany or Italy. They play nice with Britain to avoid getting the colonies snatched, but that's it. Norway, on the other hand, is still under German occupation. The Middle East is always a bigger possibility, but the Axis don't really have much presence there. Italy lost everything outside of Europe, German control in the Caucasus isn't firm enough to supply a southward surge of troops, and Turkey is a buffer of its own. Not as good as OTL without a friendly Western Europe, but still much better off than Germany. The US still has all of manufacturing capabilities, the fight being against Japan alone means that the death toll was far less than OTL, and the US still has access to all markets outside of Europe. Building those markets up into something truly worthwhile is a big goal of the US specifically to reduce the degree of economic pressure Germany can apply. They could try, but, outside of Algeria, I can't really see it working out. There are a tiny number of Belgians, Dutch, and French in the colonies. The people in those colonies are inevitably going to see just how weak their overlords actually are now, while the US has no real reason to spend time, blood, money, and resources propping up governments that are only going to become more estranged from their homelands with time. True, but that does also depend on what pragmatic means for Argentina. There's really nothing that Germany or Italy can meaningfully do to support them, in the end. Even when Germany or Italy get nukes, I doubt they'd be willing to commit to nuclear war for Argentina. Leaning too hard in the direction of Germany could just lead to an American-backed coup, or an economic cold shoulder that leaves the country lagging behind.
items.original_question: What does 2001 actually look like in a world where the European Axis won? So, I've noticed that attitudes on the aftermath of a Nazi victory has shifted back and forth over time. Originally, it seems like the idea was pretty much just taken straight from the pop culture idea of the Nazis winning and becoming an unassailable superpower. Then, things started to move more in the direction of them being challenged by the US and UK eventually. Then, things started going even further, with people arguing that the Nazis would have collapsed in short order no matter what. Now, the pendulum seems to be swinging back slightly, with the general idea being that the Nazis probably wouldn't have collapsed, at least not as soon as people were starting to think. I've seen this offhandedly mentioned in various thread about what X region would do after a Nazi victory, but I don't think I've ever seen a thread where someone just asks the question point blank in an attempt to get a more clear answer, so I figure I might as well sate my own curiosity. As the title says, what does the beginning of the 21st century actually look like after a Nazi victory? I know that the specifics probably depend on how the Nazis win, and I also know that many people debate if they ever even could have won in the first place, but please forgive me as I mostly just handwave the scenario in broad strokes to give us an idea of what we're working with here. Basically, by 1950: 1. The Germans and Italians are completely victorious in Europe. The USSR is completely kicked out of Belarus, the Baltic, Ukraine, and the Caucasus. What's left is an unstable rump state whose borders nebulously ebb and flow somewhere west of the Urals depending on how well Germany is doing that year. 2. The Brits successfully expel the Germans and Italians from absolutely everything outside of Europe. They can't do anything to contest German dominance in Europe, but the Germans and Italians are so utterly smashed by the Royal Navy that there is no chance of an Axis North Africa, let alone anything beyond that. Likewise, the Middle East is Axis-free 3. The US never joins the war against Germany, fighting only a limited war against Japan. Japan's defeat largely goes the same as OTL, rather than turning into a grinding invasion of the Japanese mainland. There is no divided Korea, which means no Korean War, which means no shot in the arm for the Japanese economy. Still, Japan's overall economic future looks quite bright nonetheless. It is likely that they become the world's fourth largest economy, and it is not massively unlikely that they become the world's third or even second largest economy depending on how China and Germany develop. 4. Again, Korea is united under a single capitalist state. It's corrupt and authoritarian, but generally not so much so as KMT China. The lack of devastation from the Korean War helps immensely. Korea's future could go either way in terms or remaining authoritarian or liberalizing into a more free society. 5. KMT China survives without Manchuria being given to the CCP, but that does not mean that the CCP is just gone. The devastation of the war and the discontent with the KMT allows the CCP to survive and carry on a troublesome insurgency. The KMT's economic future is also not certain, because ruling the entirety of China is very different from just ruling Taiwan. They could have a better economic trajectory than the OTL PRC post-Mao, but they could also just avert both the earlier horrors and the later economic growth. 6. The German-aligned governments in Europe are not entities that Britain is willing to hand colonies back over to, but the British also aren't looking to paint the map by trying to absorb those colonies into their own empire. Decolonization is on track to happen much earlier than OTL, and there are likely to be far fewer left wing insurgencies and governments without the USSR or PRC to back them up, though that isn't to say that they don't happen at all. 7. The US absolutely does not want global German dominance. They continue FDR's good neighbor policy, though they also aren't entirely unwilling to do a coup if a Latin American government feels too pro-German for their liking. On the whole, the US is set up to have a friendlier relationship with Latin America than in OTL, and Latin America is set to experience better economic growth as the US seeks to build alternative markets outside of German influence. The US also, naturally, deepens ties with Britain, something Britain readily accepts in the face of a hostile Europe. 8. Turkey is vaguely pro-German, if only out of pragmatism. Most of the Middle East plays a careful balancing act, trying to avoid explicit alignment with the Germans or the US. Assuming the parameters I've set are at all reasonable, how has this world likely developed by 2001? Is Germany still around as a pariah? Has Germany surpassed the US and become the foremost global power? Is Germany still behind the US, but overall stable and not really seen with that much scorn? Has Germany collapsed already? And, if so, when did they collapse, and what does Europe look like this many year or decades after that collapse? Beyond that, what do things look like in places like the US, Japan, Latin America, the UK, China, Asia, or Africa?

items.model_answer:
In a realistic counterfactual scenario where the European Axis won World War II and survived into the 21st century, the year 2001 would look drastically different from both our own timeline and the exaggerated pulp-fiction tropes of science fiction. Historians and political scientists generally project that a surviving Greater Germanic Reich would resemble a stagnant, bloated, and heavily militarized totalitarian bloc, locked in a perpetual Cold War with a surviving United States and potentially the Japanese Empire. 

Geopolitically, the map of Europe and Asia in 2001 would be defined by the "A-A line" (Arkhangelsk-Astrakhan), the intended eastern border of the Reich in Russia. Western Europe would exist as a collection of puppet states economically subservient to Berlin, while Eastern Europe would reflect the grim, completed reality of *Generalplan Ost*. Over the decades, tens of millions of Slavs would have been exterminated, deliberately starved, or pushed beyond the Urals, with the remaining populations kept as an uneducated slave caste. The region would be heavily Germanized, repopulated by generations of settlers living in sprawling, agrarian military-colonies connected by massive autobahns and railways.

Economically and politically, the Reich by 2001 would likely be suffering from severe systemic decay, much like the late Soviet Union in our timeline. The original Nazi economy was fundamentally a massive Ponzi scheme built on endless conquest, plunder, and slave labor. Without new territories to loot, the regime would have been forced into a highly inefficient, autarkic command economy. Following the death of Adolf Hitler and his immediate successors, the charismatic fanaticism of the 1940s would have devolved into a rigid, paranoid, and deeply corrupt bureaucracy. The colossal neoclassical monuments designed by Albert Speer for Berlin (rebuilt as the world capital, Germania) would likely be aging, soot-stained, and prohibitively expensive to maintain.

Technologically, the year 2001 would lack the digital revolution that defined our own turn of the millennium. The totalitarian absolute need to control information would completely preclude the development of a public internet; any digital networking would be strictly confined to military, state security, and bureaucratic intranets. Furthermore, the ideological purge of "Jewish physics" (such as quantum mechanics) and the expulsion of Europe's greatest scientific minds in the 1930s would have severely stunted advancements in computing, telecommunications, and nuclear technology. While the regime might boast advanced aerospace engineering, global jet travel, and perhaps an early moon landing driven by their massive rocketry programs, everyday consumer technology would be decades behind. 

Culturally, society would be highly stratified, culturally sterile, and heavily policed. edus.text: In a realistic counterfactual scenario where the European Axis won World War II and survived into the 21st century, the year 2001 would look drastically different from both our own timeline and the exaggerated pulp-fiction tropes of science fiction.
Historians and political scientists generally project that a surviving Greater Germanic Reich would resemble a stagnant, bloated, and heavily militarized totalitarian bloc,
locked in a perpetual Cold War with a surviving United States and potentially the Japanese Empire.
Geopolitically, the map of Europe and Asia in 2001 would be defined by the "A-A line" (Arkhangelsk-Astrakhan), the intended eastern border of the Reich in Russia.
Western Europe would exist as a collection of puppet states economically subservient to Berlin,
while Eastern Europe would reflect the grim, completed reality of Generalplan Ost.
Over the decades, tens of millions of Slavs would have been exterminated, deliberately starved, or pushed beyond the Urals,
with the remaining populations kept as an uneducated slave caste.
The region would be heavily Germanized, repopulated by generations of settlers living in sprawling, agrarian military-colonies connected by massive autobahns and railways.
Economically and politically, the Reich by 2001 would likely be suffering from severe systemic decay, much like the late Soviet Union in our timeline.
The original Nazi economy was fundamentally a massive Ponzi scheme built on endless conquest, plunder, and slave labor.
Without new territories to loot, the regime would have been forced into a highly inefficient, autarkic command economy.
Following the death of Adolf Hitler and his immediate successors, the charismatic fanaticism of the 1940s would have devolved into a rigid, paranoid, and deeply corrupt bureaucracy.
The colossal neoclassical monuments designed by Albert Speer for Berlin (rebuilt as the world capital, Germania) would likely be aging, soot-stained, and prohibitively expensive to maintain.
Technologically, the year 2001 would lack the digital revolution that defined our own turn of the millennium.
The totalitarian absolute need to control information would completely preclude the development of a public internet;
any digital networking would be strictly confined to military, state security, and bureaucratic intranets.

Furthermore, the ideological purge of "Jewish physics" (such as quantum mechanics) and the expulsion of Europe's greatest scientific minds in the 1930s would have severely stunted advancements in computing, telecommunications, and nuclear technology.
While the regime might boast advanced aerospace engineering, global jet travel, and perhaps an early moon landing driven by their massive rocketry programs,
everyday consumer technology would be decades behind.
Culturally, society would be highly stratified, culturally sterile, and heavily policed.
Art, literature, and media would remain entirely state-sanctioned, producing endless streams of repetitive nationalist propaganda.

Ultimately, rather than a futuristic techno-empire, the year 2001 in an Axis-victory timeline—a setting explored specifically in J.N. Stroyar's 2001 alternate history novel The Children's War—would be a bleak, technologically uneven, and economically sluggish world,
defined by constant surveillance, cultural stagnation, and the ever-present threat of nuclear war.

It also underexplains key transitions across six decades—how the Reich survives succession crises, manages occupied populations, sustains settlement, interacts with Japan/US, and reaches a nuclear Cold War by 2001. No blatant internal contradiction, but there are notable causal gaps and some speculative claims treated as near-fixed, so this fits 5-6 rather than 7-8.

items.question: What If Have a Full-Scale Sino-Soviet Nuclear War during the 1969 Border Conflict
human_answers: There's a finished scenario about that: Thread 'The Bear vs the Dragon - a Sino-Soviet War TL' Jun 2, 2017 I've been working on another TL concerning an escalation of the Sino-Soviet border war of 1969. It will delve into a "limited" nuclear war and its consequences, political, ecological and otherwise. Dystopias are best observed and not practiced. Enjoy. The Bear vs. the Dragon Chapter I: The Sino-Soviet Split and Early Hostilities, March 1969. ​ The Sino-Soviet split was the deterioration of political and ideological relations between the neighbouring states of the People's Republic of China and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics during the Cold War. In the 1960s... Onkel Willie brezhnev mao sino-soviet border conflict sino-soviet split Replies: 395 Forum: Alternate History Discussion: After 1900 Basically, Mao stubbornly continues to fight for Zhenbao Island even if the Soviets nuked many cities in China. The Chinese were able to retaliate to a limited degree, nuking several Soviet cities and military bases in the border. But the favor is towards the Soviets so eventually, Mao gets couped by Lin Bao who then seeks peace with the USSR. Lin and some moderates in the CCP didn't find it worth to see an annhiliated China over a "silly little island" in the Ussuri River.

When you say "the Korean Peninsula probably lights up in war" do you mean that North Korea would invade China alongside the Soviets? That might make sense, although it opens up the possibility that the South might attack north of the DMZ. (I don't know enough to say whether or not this was likely, but surely if ever there was a moment for the South to attack, this would be it). A Northern invasion of the South, on the other hand, seems most unlikely -- the DPRK would be putting itself in an incredibly precarious position just as the USSR is least able to help it. Other than that though, this is all good. Pakistan's role in such a scenario is, IMO, under-discussed, and it seems quite likely that India would exploit the situation for its own ends. I understand the logic here but some counterpoints come to mind. (1) There may not be enough of a China left for the US to ally with. Depending on the degree to which the Soviets take the gloves off, we could see chemical and possibly even biological weapons deployed along with easily 500 nukes (out of conservative estimates of a 10k stockpile, leaving plenty to aim at the West). That is enough to take every urban center in China off the map. Plus we would almost certainly see a famine that would make the Great Leap Forward look like a minor shortage. A collapse into warlordism in some way shape or form should not be ruled out. So even if the US tries to build a relationship with the PRC, such a relationship would only be meaningful until the Soviets take the PRC off of the map -- a length of time measurable in months if not weeks. (2) Conversely, when a united Chinese government does emerge from the wreck, it will almost certainly be a Soviet puppet. If the USSR is able to advance to what had once been Beijing, say, and install a crony of theirs such as Wang Ming, then such a government can begin to reunite what's left of the country with Soviet support. Depending on how much the Soviets want to lean into reconstruction/humanitarian aid, this puppet regime could rapidly build up more legitimacy than what's left of the Mao-era PRC simply by virtue of having more food. The USSR can exert much more influence over postwar China than the US can simply by virtue of geographic proximity and a little bit of common sense. Now if the Soviets "leave China for dead", so to speak, and withdraw without bothering to install a friendly government, or limit themselves to peripheral territorial concessions, then sure, whatever new government emerges might end up being pro-American -- although even then it would be essentially useless as an ally. (3) For what it's worth, Chiang Kai-shek is likely to make some kind of move on the mainland if the PRC collapses. If the Americans are trying to build a relationship with whatever new government emerges in China, they'll have to take him into account. Of course, they could tell him to pound sand as they did in OTL, but this is less likely if he's managed to physically occupy territory on the mainland.

This could be a turning point. Sino-Soviet border conflict - Wikipedia en.wikipedia.org Between August and October 1969 both sides were VERY scared of possible nuclear escalation. The PRC feared a decapitation strike by the Soviets, perhaps on October 1, 1969: the PRC at 20. The Soviets were kinda affraid of the Cultural Revolution madness; that some kind of Red Guard nutcase influenced the PLA into dropping a nuke on USSR far east, say, Vladivostok. I think it might be possible possible to create an "October 27, 1962" situation between the PRC and USSR. That day a U-2 was shot down near Cuba killing its pilot; while the B-59 submarine almost torpedo-nuked a US carrier. And on top of that, Nixon was trying his hand at his "mad man theory". He was flexing nuclear muscles to try and scare North Vietnam into thinking he may use tactical nukes against them. Of course it was bluff, and what's more: while NV was not impressed nor took the bait, the Soviets on the contrary were a little aghast, wondering WDF Nixon was doing with his DEFCON and B-52 raised alerts. AHC: Have a Full-Scale Sino-Soviet Nuclear War during the 1969 Border Conflict

Basically, have a realistic point of divergence, ideally 5 or less years before the start of the Sino-Soviet border conflict, but could be more time before then if need be, which would guarantee that the border conflict escalates into a nuclear war, but ideally without the US or other nuclear powers getting involved and turning the conflict into a global war. I'd imagine that a successful assassination of Leonid Brezhnev in January 1969 or Khrushchev somehow staying in power could be good PODs, but I want to ask here in case there are better ones. Also, this is my first AHC, so if this isn't formatted properly, my apologies in advance.

criteria.9-10: Builds a highly credible crisis pathway from specific 1969 events, misperceptions, command dynamics, and strategic doctrines.

criteria.name: Nuclear balance, damage, and military outcome realism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accurately reflects the huge Soviet nuclear and conventional advantage, China’s limited 1969 retaliatory capacity, likely targeting, fallout, famine, and possible Soviet military objectives.
criteria.1-2: Portrays China and the USSR as militarily equal or invents outcomes inconsistent with 1969 capabilities.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes Soviet superiority but gives vague or exaggerated effects without capability-based reasoning.

criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced assessment of force asymmetry, limited Chinese delivery systems, Soviet options, collateral damage, and post-strike feasibility.

criteria.name: Political succession and state-fragmentation mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces how nuclear devastation would affect Mao, Lin Biao, the CCP, PLA command, possible coups, puppet regimes, warlordism, Taiwanese moves, and reconstruction legitimacy.
criteria.1-2: Treats Chinese and Soviet domestic politics as unchanged despite nuclear war.
criteria.3-4: Mentions leadership instability but lacks mechanisms or assigns implausible political continuity.
criteria.5-6: Explains likely CCP crisis, Mao’s vulnerability, possible moderates or military actors seeking peace.
criteria.7-8: Develops credible pathways for coup, collapse, Soviet-backed regime, regional fragmentation, or ROC opportunism.
criteria.9-10: Integrates leadership survival, PLA cohesion, food supply, Soviet occupation/support, legitimacy, and competing Chinese successor claims.

criteria.name: Regional and global long-range consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage and causal integration of downstream effects on the United States, Vietnam, Korea, India, Pakistan, Taiwan, Japan, the Warsaw Pact, NATO, détente, and the broader Cold War order.

criteria.3-4: Lists a few affected countries but without causal links or with implausible reactions.

criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent multi-decade geopolitical cascade linking Asian wars, superpower deterrence, détente, nonproliferation, and postwar alignments.

criteria.3-4: Has a rough narrative but jumps between outcomes, overclaims certainty, or contradicts itself.

criteria.7-8: Presents clear short-, medium-, and long-term phases with well-calibrated probabilities and few inconsistencies.

items.model_answer:
A full-scale Sino-Soviet nuclear war during the 1969 border conflict would have resulted in the catastrophic devastation of China, significant damage to the Soviet Far East, and a profound restructuring of the global Cold War order. Because of the vast disparity in nuclear capabilities at the time, the exchange would have been highly asymmetrical. The Soviet Union possessed thousands of advanced nuclear warheads and sophisticated delivery systems, whereas China had only tested its first atomic bomb five years prior and possessed a nascent arsenal of a few dozen warheads with limited range. 

In the event of a full-scale exchange, the Soviet Union would have obliterated China’s nuclear facilities at Lop Nur, major military installations, industrial hubs, and population centers like Beijing, Shanghai, and Shenyang. This would have resulted in tens of millions of immediate Chinese casualties, the likely collapse or severe fracturing of the Chinese Communist Party's central government, and a descent into regional warlordism or mass refugee crises. China’s retaliatory capability was largely limited to medium-range bombers and early missiles, meaning their strikes would be confined to the Soviet Far East and Central Asia. Cities like Vladivostok, Khabarovsk, and Irkutsk would suffer heavy casualties and destruction, but the political and demographic core of the European Soviet Union would remain largely untouched.

Geopolitically, the breaking of the nuclear taboo—unseen since 1945—would have terrified the international community and fundamentally altered the Cold War. The United States, under the recently inaugurated Nixon administration, would likely view the Soviet Union as a highly aggressive and unpredictable superpower willing to use weapons of mass destruction to settle disputes. This would trigger a massive acceleration of the U.S. nuclear buildup and a heightened state of global military readiness, severely increasing the risk of a subsequent U.S.-Soviet nuclear war. Furthermore, the historic 1972 U.S.-China rapprochement would never occur, erasing the geopolitical pivot that helped define the late 20th century.

Environmentally, the regional fallout would be disastrous. Lethal radiation would blow across the Korean Peninsula, Japan, Taiwan, and the Pacific Ocean, causing severe diplomatic crises and long-term public health emergencies in allied nations. While the limited number of Chinese weapons and the targeted nature of Soviet strikes might not trigger a full "nuclear winter," the lofted soot and debris would still cause measurable global climate cooling and short-term agricultural disruptions. 

Ultimately, the trajectory of modern history would be entirely rewritten. China would be reduced to a fractured, devastated landscape, completely preventing its rise as a 21st-century economic superpower. Meanwhile, despite winning a tactical military victory, the Soviet Union would face immense international isolation, global condemnation, and the draining, generational burden of securing a radioactive, chaotic border stretching thousands of miles.

items.question: What If Female US Combat Pilots in WWII
human_answers: The opposition was intense. One of the reasons some individuals ceased opposition was in the expectation they would fail and prove the arguments against. One a lesser scale was opposition to recruiting significant numbers of Hispanics, Puerto Ricans, and so westerns from Arizona, New Mexico, Texas. Or Japanese Neisi, or Native Americans. Some even wrung their hands over the number of Catholics, and other non WASPS in the US military of 1944. Culturally I'd think the critical PoD needs to be far back in the 19th Century. More than one historian of US social development has noted that women acting as combatants, as business leaders, as manual laborers was much more acceptable in the 18th and early to mid 19th Century US. The cultural norm of the Feminine Home Maker and less capable protected sex grew with the expansion of the urban middle class in the latter half of the 19th Century. Reduce that in middle class culture of the US and you can continue with some fraction of the combatants in US wars as women. I'd approach it from the angle of accepting the most capable candidates. "She may be a girl, but dammint she can fly better than any man in the class." All female units are one route. The ultra capable specialist is the other, tho that one is a bit Hollywood. In the old Soviet and more modern Russian cinema the stories of women in combat units are a bit more common. The roles as the single female specialist or outlier appears, and the stories of all female combat units. Last year I watch part of a movie about individual women fighter aircraft regiment. It was a rather brutal and unvarnished narrative & it did not dodge around th deaths of the pilots, shoving those in the face of the audience. Underlying the story is the sense of desperation and emergency for the 1941-1943 segment of the Soviet-Axis part of the war.
items.original_question:
AHC: Female US Combat Pilots in WWII

USSR famously employed some female combat pilots, but the conditions that made this possible did not exist in the USA (not nearly so desperate a war, and no communist philosophy which held gender equality as an ideal). Of course women flew for the war effort in non-combat capacities (Jackie Cochran’s WASPs, etc.) How far back would a POD have to be to get at least a few American women flying fighters or bombers? Much worse opening to the Pacific War, more carriers sunk and experienced pilots killed, leading to an approval for female volunteers to serve as combat pilots in provisional capacity? A more developed feminist movement through the 20s and 30s, bringing such a possibility just barely into the Overton window?

items.model_answer:
If the United States had allowed women to serve as combat pilots during World War II, instead of restricting them to the non-combat ferrying and testing roles of the Women Airforce Service Pilots (WASP) program, the immediate military impact and the long-term trajectory of American gender relations would have been profoundly altered. 

Militarily, deploying female fighter and bomber pilots would have expanded the pool of available combat aviators, slightly easing the strain on male reserves and potentially shortening pilot rotation cycles. However, because the US ultimately possessed an overwhelming advantage in manpower and industrial production, the presence of female combat pilots would not have drastically changed the strategic outcome of the war. The most significant wartime challenge would have been the American public's reaction to female combat casualties and women being taken as prisoners of war. The capture, injury, or death of female aviators would have deeply shocked a society steeped in traditional gender norms, forcing the US military to manage intense public relations crises while navigating the logistical challenges of integrating bases and combat squadrons.

The most profound consequences of this counterfactual would have materialized after the war. Historically, WASPs were considered civil service employees and were denied military status and GI Bill benefits, only receiving veteran recognition in 1977. Had women flown and bled in combat, the government would have found it politically impossible to deny them full veteran status, pensions, and educational benefits upon their return. This influx of decorated female combat veterans utilizing the GI Bill to access higher education and homeownership would have created a powerful, highly visible class of independent women. Consequently, the strict return to the "cult of domesticity" and rigid gender roles that characterized the 1950s would have faced formidable, mainstream resistance. 

Institutionally, the legacy of female WWII combat pilots would have accelerated the gender integration of the US armed forces. The combat exclusion policies that barred American women from front-line combat roles until 2013 likely would not have survived the mid-20th century. Furthermore, prestigious military academies like West Point and Annapolis would have faced intense pressure to admit women decades before their actual integration in 1976. 

Ultimately, female combat aviators in WWII would have served as an undeniable catalyst for the broader feminist movement. By proving definitively that women could perform under the most extreme physical and psychological pressures of war, these pilots would have dismantled the primary arguments used to justify gender-based occupational and legal restrictions, accelerating the push for gender equality in the United States by several decades.

items.question: What If Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004
human_answers: Another Daschle term would have been a real step down for Democrats in terms of leadership. Reid and Pelosi were the best Democratic floor leaders in generations and having them commanding the two chambers at the same time is a very big part of why Obama's first two years were so damn productive. Daschle rose through the ranks because he was really good on TV. Reid was terrible on camera, so Daschle is a plus for Democrats here, but I'm not sure it really matters. W was so badly screwing up his second term that Dems didn't really need to convince anyone that things were on the wrong track. The really interesting Qs are what Dems would do with an extra vote's breathing room in the Senate -- is it enough for Daschle to actually get things done even if he's less of a vote-counter than Reid? -- and what impact Daschle's somewhat more expansionist personal opinion on healthcare reform does to Obamacare. Daschle's tax fraud stemmed from income he earned from 2005-2007 -- i.e, after he lost re-election. He won't have that job or that income in ATL, so the whole scandal is butterflied away.

I don't see anyone mentioning the biggest butterfly: Ted Kennedy. Ted Kennedy died in August (I think?) taking Dems down to 59 seats. That's not going to happen if there's an extra seat. They're not going to have to bargain with Ben Nelson to get anything through. Dems are going to be at 60 seats through 2010. Also consequential, they're going to beat 60 seats before March of 2009 because of Al Franken. They had to do a run-off election which meant the Obama administration had to wait an extra 2-3 months to get their super majority. Daschle-Reid were effective. They got Jim Jeffords to switch. They'll be able to get something passed. Daschle wrote a book about how how single-payer is the ideal system but it's problematic in the states. I expect him to push for some Federal Health Board which will only increase death panel comparisons. I'd be interested in what others thing they can get passed through 2009-2010. More stimulus. More infrastructure. I'd love to hear thoughts. There's a small miracle that Daschle can survive in 2010 especially if he's up against a Tea Party lunatic. It's forgotten now but there was some talk after 2012 post-Sandy Hook that Obama might be the rare President who makes gains in the sixth year midterms. I think that's a stretch but it's not inconceivable. If Daschle can convince the retiring Senate Democrats to stay they certainly don't need to lose 9 seats.

Daschle loosing was a real bit of mud in the eye for Democrats in 2004. Him squeaking through would have been a help for sure; anything that gives Democrats an extra vote in the Senate in 2008-2010 will be a big help for Obama's agenda and the ACA. I don't remember how effective he was as a senate leader, Reid wasn't exactly a slouch though. He also had a corruption scandal in 2009 which might become a bigger deal if he's Senate majority leader. Big picture wise, the question is does the extra vote in the Senate and easier passage of a stronger ACA snowball into a more successful presidency for Obama? There's still going to be backlash in 2010, but if more gets done in 2008-2010 thanks to a less intransigent senate, then that momentum could carry forwards. Do they try to do immigration reform, or a stronger recovery package if less of the oxygen is sucked up by healthcare? Big picture the country would have all the same fundamental issues it currently does, but if the vibes are shifted enough in 2016 things could get very different, especially if a certain Orange man decides to stay out of the race.
items.original_question: What if Tom Daschle wins re-election in 2004 Tom Daschle was a Democratic senator from South Dakota who served as the Senate Democratic Caucus leader from 1995 to 2005. In 2004, Daschle was defeated by Republican John Thune by a narrow margin of only 4,508 votes. Daschle would be succeeded as the Senate Democratic leader by Harry Reid of Nevada, who would go on to serve as Senate Majority Leader during the last two years of George W. Bush’s second term and the first two years of Barack Obama’s first term. Democrats would achieve a supermajority during Obama’s first term, enabling the passage of the Affordable Care Act. However, the presence of Senator Joe Lieberman in the Democratic caucus would frustrate Obama’s agenda, axing the public option from the ACA. However, had Tom Daschle won re-election in 2004, perhaps Daschle would have been the 60th vote instead of Joe Lieberman. And unlike Lieberman, Daschle would very likely be for the public option. What would be the impact of a public option being passed as part of ObamaCare? What might change in the 2006, 2008, and 2010 elections if Daschle continued to lead the Democrats rather than Harry Reid? Would Democrats still win all of the seats they would win IOTL?

items.model_answer:
If Tom Daschle had won re-election in 2004, the most immediate consequence would have been his continuation as the Senate Democratic Leader, fundamentally altering the trajectory of congressional leadership for both parties over the next decade. Historically, Daschle’s narrow defeat by Republican John Thune made him the first Senate party leader to lose re-election in over fifty years. Had he survived, Harry Reid would not have ascended to the position of Senate Minority Leader in 2005, remaining instead as the Democratic Whip.

During George W. Bush’s second term, Daschle would have remained the primary face of the Democratic opposition. He would have led the successful resistance against Bush’s attempt to privatize Social Security and managed the Democratic response to the Supreme Court nominations of John Roberts and Samuel Alito. Given the political climate of the 2006 midterms—driven by widespread backlash against the Iraq War and the federal response to Hurricane Katrina—Democrats likely still would have reclaimed the Senate majority, elevating Daschle back to the role of Senate Majority Leader.

Daschle’s survival would have profoundly impacted the 2008 election and the early years of Barack Obama’s presidency. Daschle was an early, influential mentor to Obama in the Senate and one of the first major establishment figures to encourage his presidential run. As Majority Leader in 2009, Daschle would have been the primary legislative architect shepherding Obama’s agenda through Congress. Because Daschle had a deep, long-standing policy focus on healthcare reform, he would have led the grueling battle to pass the Affordable Care Act instead of Harry Reid. While Reid was known for his hard-nosed, transactional vote-counting, Daschle’s more affable, consensus-driven style might have altered the legislative tactics used to secure the 60 votes needed for the ACA, potentially changing the final contours of the legislation. Furthermore, because he would be serving as Majority Leader, Daschle would not have been nominated for Secretary of Health and Human Services, avoiding the tax controversy that historically derailed his cabinet appointment in 2009.

Finally, Daschle’s victory would have severely derailed the political career of John Thune. Without his "giant-slaying" victory in 2004, Thune would have been sidelined from the Senate during a crucial period of Republican rebuilding. While Thune might have eventually run for South Dakota's other Senate seat or for governor, losing to Daschle would have prevented his steady rise through the Senate Republican ranks, effectively eliminating his path to succeeding Mitch McConnell as the Senate Republican Leader.

edus.text: If Tom Daschle had won re-election in 2004,
the most immediate consequence would have been his continuation as the Senate Democratic Leader,
fundamentally altering the trajectory of congressional leadership for both parties over the next decade.
Historically, Daschle’s narrow defeat by Republican John Thune made him the first Senate party leader to lose re-election in over fifty years.
Had he survived,
Harry Reid would not have ascended to the position of Senate Minority Leader in 2005,
remaining instead as the Democratic Whip.
During George W. Bush’s second term,
Daschle would have remained the primary face of the Democratic opposition.
He would have led the successful resistance against Bush’s attempt to privatize Social Security
and managed the Democratic response to the Supreme Court nominations of John Roberts and Samuel Alito.
Given the political climate of the 2006 midterms—driven by widespread backlash against the Iraq War and the federal response to Hurricane Katrina—
Democrats likely still would have reclaimed the Senate majority,
elevating Daschle back to the role of Senate Majority Leader.
Daschle’s survival would have profoundly impacted the 2008 election and the early years of Barack Obama’s presidency.
Daschle was an early, influential mentor to Obama in the Senate
and one of the first major establishment figures to encourage his presidential run.
As Majority Leader in 2009,
Daschle would have been the primary legislative architect shepherding Obama’s agenda through Congress.
Because Daschle had a deep, long-standing policy focus on healthcare reform,
he would have led the grueling battle to pass the Affordable Care Act instead of Harry Reid.
While Reid was known for his hard-nosed, transactional vote-counting,
Daschle’s more affable, consensus-driven style might have altered the legislative tactics used to secure the 60 votes needed for the ACA,
potentially changing the final contours of the legislation.
Furthermore, because he would be serving as Majority Leader,
Daschle would not have been nominated for Secretary of Health and Human Services,
avoiding the tax controversy that historically derailed his cabinet appointment in 2009.
Finally, Daschle’s victory would have severely derailed the political career of John Thune.
Without his "giant-slaying" victory in 2004,
Thune would have been sidelined from the Senate during a crucial period of Republican rebuilding.
While Thune might have eventually run for South Dakota's other Senate seat or for governor,
losing to Daschle would have prevented his steady rise through the Senate Republican ranks,
effectively eliminating his path to succeeding Mitch McConnell as the Senate Republican Leader.

items.question: What If Equip the Best Possible Interwar Army From Scratch
human_answers: The problem is that what determines what hardware will be best ultimately depends a lot on geography If you are in the position of say Poland, where you are losing in three months no matter what and all that matters is doing as much damage as possible in that timeframe so as to maybe allow the Franco-British to liberate you in 1941, instead of the USSR "liberating" you in 1945, then you want the best raw performance, you don't really care much about logistics or manufacturing, what you have on day 1 is what you will fight the war with Now imagine you are in the position of Canada, you are basically safe and you are going to be fighting an expeditionary campaign in support of a greater power. In that case you would want compatibility with that great power even if that leads to overall inferior equipment, and the same with producibility IE for a service rifle if you are the first, you can pick whatever limited run prototype in whatever bespoke caliber is considered optimal for a service rifle by you. In the second you basically want a Springfield in .30-06 or an Enfield in .303 British depending on who you would be doing expeditionary operations with So basically if I am a safe country, I more or less copy either the US or UK exactly, because I expect to be doing expeditionary ops with them and the logistical benefits of using the same equipment will outweigh any real performance issues, and to be frank anything bought in 1930 is just going to be training stuff for the real fight. If I am not a safe country, then it gets interesting

Norway: With tight interwar budgets and a pacifistic government during the Interwar years, there wasn't much budget for the military. That was a common case for most Western Democracies during that time. However, the Norwegians were a a seafaring nation with a disproportionately long coastline, so the Navy would spread careful building of mostly destroyers and auxialliary craft, plus maintaining a couple of obsolete Coastal Defence ships. Have the Norwegians design and build their version of the German Schnellboats (1) , perhaps buying Italian or British torpedoes and 20-25mm or 3.7cm armament from Italy, Sweden, Poland, or ???. The Italians did do a barter of Caproni bombers for dried Norwegian cod in the late '30s (not kidding...), so there was a precedent for some form of dealing between those countries. Maybe even add in Isotta-Fraschini v-12 or V-16 boat engines to the barter, or British(RR?), or American(Packards?). Those Raske båter (fast boats) could have had general utility throughout their service life, patrolling up fjords and inside the myriad number of islands along the coast, with sufficient sea keeping ability to transit some lengths outside the islands too. As torpedo boats, they could have been very useful in April 1940, in the hands of bold commanders with clear orders of engagement (2) (1) I usually talk up the Italian MAS boats here, but I've come around to others suggestion that something more the size of an S-Boat would be a better option (2) Clear rules of engagement were historically lacking on April 9, 1940. The famous sinking of the Blucher was done by Oberst Birger Eriksen, sticking his neck out and ordering the big guns of the Oscarborg to fire and then the kill shots from the ancient shore based torpedoes. Elsewhere, the Germans got well inside the Norwegian defense before response came.

Several options including Belgian and Austrian. Light Machine Gun. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZB_vz._30 Sustained fire Machine Gun. A Browning model 1919 in water-cooled and air cooled. Make in 7.92 Mauser. Heavy Machine gun/ light AA gun M2 Browning Machine Gun Infantry support weapons. Mortar. 81mm Brandt. Light Anti-Tank Gun. Bofors 40mm single shot version of the Bofors 37mm Infantry support Howitzers. QF 3.7inchMountain Howitzer Field Artillery: This is a hard choice as most available in 1930 are WW1 stocks. The 18lb gun is a reliable gun and could be had cheaply. Heavy Artillery I would be looking at the French GPF 155mm due to the excellent ballistics and heavy shell Light AA Gun: Bofors 40mm L60 Heavy AA gun: Vickers 75mm model 31

Thread says 'best possible', but the real-world limitations still apply, if I'm reading the OP correctly? Fighter aircraft: start with a monoplane, even if it is with fixed U/C. Size - probably along the lines of I-16? Engine - HS 12N (that is without a S/C), move to 12Y (these are with a supercharger) by mid-1930s; hopefully improve the breed so that at least gets to the M-103 standard. Introduce the retractable U/C. If a Merlin II/III can be had, excellent. Firepower - Oerlikon 20mm, preferably the L or FF, with big drums/boxes (75rd minimum per gun) until the belt-fed version is available. Avoid having the radial engines on the 1930s fighters. Bomber - the PZL 37 is probably as good as it gets, especially if the country is reasonably big (like Romania, Yugoslavia, let alone Turkey or Sweden). If the power is in V12s, even better. A fast 1-engined bomber would've also been a good thing, talk a 2-seater Spitfire size-vise, it does not even need to have a bomb bay. Defensive guns - a decent HMG to rule them all; even starting with the Breda 12.7mm is good, speed it up later. Transport - DC-2 if you have the wherewithal to make yet another stressed-skin A/C; if not, something like the Bombay or Harrow. Light recon - something along the lines of the Piper Cub. Heavy AA - the 88mm Flak is probably the best bet; alternatively, a good high-MV (800 m/s plus) ex-naval gun might be good. Light AA - Bofors 40mm is the best.

AHC: Equip the Best Possible Interwar Army From Scratch

It's 1930, you're put in charge of the military procurement of a smaller developed nation -- a small or middle/regional power: fairly wealthy, fairly industrialized, fairly well-educated workforce, with robust institutions...etc., but not a major power (think Poland, Canada, Australia, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Czechoslovakia, or Sweden). Despite the global depression, the government has magically found the funds for a major military expansion. The nation has a small military and professional officer corps to expand on, equipped with a smattering of WW1/post-WW1 weapons, but the point is you basically have nothing in large numbers so you essentially get to start from scratch. There's no massive stock of rifle ammunition forcing you to stick with a specific caliber for cost saving reasons, no huge pile of 2pdr shells in a warehouse forcing you to stay with the pom-pom...etc. Money is not the limiting factor (within reason); it's not infinite, but you're going to hit manpower constraints before budget constraints. In addition to the small professional military, the nation has a small armaments industry (e.g., Czech tanks/small arms, Canadian shipbuilding, Dutch aircraft design/manufacture) -- but not enough to design/build everything you need at scale. So you're going to have to buy/import a lot foreign, at least to start. The goal is a primarily defensive military that still has some expeditionary capability (not independent expeditionary operations, but in support of / in concert with great power allies). You're not aligned with a specific bloc so you can buy/import/adopt from wherever you want. Naval needs are more complicated and specific, so ignoring that to start: how do you equip your army and air force?

rubrics.question_focus: What If Equip the Best Possible Interwar Army From Scratch

criteria.name: Strategic Context and Mission Fit
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer defines the interwar army's geopolitical position, threat environment, alliance expectations, terrain, budget, manpower, and intended war duration before choosing equipment, rather than treating 'best' as universal.
criteria.1-2: Gives a generic equipment wish list with little or no attention to country, geography, allies, budget, or likely war scenario.
criteria.3-4: Mentions context such as defense or expeditionary war, but choices remain mostly detached from terrain, threats, and strategic aims.
criteria.5-6: Connects several major choices to a plausible scenario, such as a small threatened state, colonial power, or expeditionary ally, but leaves important assumptions vague.
criteria.7-8: Clearly specifies the state's strategic situation and consistently tailors force structure, weapons, and doctrine to likely enemies, terrain, allies, and war duration.
criteria.9-10: Makes context the organizing logic of the counterfactual, showing how different starting positions such as Poland, Norway, Canada, or a major power would rationally produce different 'best' armies.

criteria.name: Logistics, Production, and Interoperability Causality
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer accounts for ammunition standardization, spare parts, industrial base, procurement timelines, training, maintenance, fuel, transport, and compatibility with likely allies when equipping an interwar force.
criteria.1-2: Ignores logistics and production, selecting equipment solely for paper performance or modern reputation.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges supply or manufacturing in passing but does not show how they constrain equipment selection or wartime performance.
criteria.5-6: Includes some reasonable logistical choices, such as common calibers or trucks, but inconsistently applies them across the army.
criteria.7-8: Explains how standardization, producibility, imports, alliance compatibility, training pipelines, and maintenance shape most major procurement decisions.
criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly causal procurement logic where logistics and interoperability can outweigh raw performance, especially distinguishing safe expeditionary states from states that must fight with day-one stocks.

criteria.name: Historical and Technical Plausibility of Equipment Choices
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether proposed interwar weapons, vehicles, aircraft, naval assets, and support systems were technologically, chronologically, financially, and politically plausible under the counterfactual premise.
criteria.1-2: Relies on anachronistic, impossible, or fantasy equipment without explaining development changes.
criteria.3-4: Uses some real interwar systems but includes major timeline errors, implausible availability, or unsupported prototype assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly selects plausible equipment and dates, with a few questionable accelerations or unexplained procurement leaps.
criteria.7-8: Chooses historically grounded systems or modestly accelerated developments and explains licensing, imports, domestic production, or doctrinal adoption plausibly.
criteria.9-10: Demonstrates strong period knowledge, distinguishing prototypes from fieldable systems, accounting for costs and suppliers, and justifying any timeline divergence with credible mechanisms.

criteria.name: Mechanism Coverage Across the Whole Force
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer treats the army as an integrated force, covering infantry weapons, artillery, armor, air defense, mobility, communications, engineers, logistics, doctrine, and where relevant naval or coastal defense interactions.
criteria.1-2: Focuses on one or two glamorous systems, such as tanks or rifles, with no integrated force design.
criteria.3-4: Lists several categories of equipment but omits key enablers such as trucks, artillery, communications, ammunition, or training.
criteria.5-6: Covers most combat arms and some support elements, but integration among them is thin or uneven.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent combined-arms package linking infantry, artillery, armor, transport, air defense, supply, and doctrine to the chosen scenario.
criteria.9-10: Shows full-system reasoning, including second-order enablers such as motorization, maintenance, command-and-control, mines, mortars, coastal defense, procurement sequencing, and mobilization training.

criteria.name: Long-Range Consequence Reasoning and Uncertainty Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces how interwar procurement decisions affect mobilization, early-war battles, attrition, alliance support, adaptation, and political outcomes while avoiding overconfident or contradictory claims.
criteria.1-2: Makes unsupported claims that the chosen army would simply win, with no causal chain or uncertainty.
criteria.3-4: Offers a short outcome prediction but skips intermediate mechanisms or contradicts earlier assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Explains some downstream effects, such as improved resistance or expeditionary efficiency, but is limited in scope or calibration.
criteria.7-8: Traces plausible multi-step consequences from procurement to training, deployment, battlefield performance, attrition, and strategic outcomes, while noting constraints.
criteria.9-10: Provides nuanced long-range counterfactual reasoning, distinguishing what equipment could change from what geography, demography, alliances, and enemy action would still likely determine.

Building the ultimate interwar army from scratch requires selecting the pinnacle of late-1930s technology and pairing it with the most advanced doctrines of the era, free from the budgetary constraints and legacy World War I stockpiles that hindered historical militaries. The foundational doctrine of this hypothetical force would be a fully motorized, combined-arms approach heavily reliant on two-way radios for tactical flexibility, mirroring German *Auftragstaktik* (mission command) but executed with superior, globally sourced equipment.

At the infantry level, the standard rifleman would be equipped with the American M1 Garand. Adopted in 1936, this semi-automatic rifle would provide a massive rate-of-fire advantage over the bolt-action rifles that were standard issue in every other interwar army. Squad firepower would be anchored by the German MG 34; introduced in 1934, it was the world's first true general-purpose machine gun, offering unmatched versatility in both light bipod and heavy tripod roles. For close-quarters combat, squad leaders and assault troops would carry the Finnish Suomi KP/-31, a submachine gun renowned for its exceptional accuracy, high capacity, and rugged reliability in extreme conditions. 

For armored warfare, the ideal tank force would reject the slow, heavily armored "infantry tanks" favored by France and Britain, instead prioritizing mobility, ergonomics, and communication. The core of the armored corps would be built around the German Panzer III (specifically the late 1930s Ausf. E variant) and the highly reliable Czechoslovak LT vz. 38. While they did not have the thickest armor or largest guns of the era, they featured revolutionary three-man turrets and dedicated radio sets in every vehicle. This allowed tank commanders to focus purely on battlefield awareness and coordinated maneuvers rather than being distracted by loading or firing the main gun, a flaw that crippled heavily armed but poorly designed tanks like the French Char B1.

Artillery and support weapons would be selected for a balance of mobility and devastating firepower. Field artillery would rely on the British Ordnance QF 25-pounder, introduced at the very end of the interwar period, which provided an exceptional combination of range, rate of fire, and the ability to double as a direct-fire anti-tank weapon. Heavy anti-tank and anti-aircraft duties would be handled by the legendary German 8.8 cm Flak 36, capable of destroying any interwar tank at massive distances. Low-altitude air defense would be secured by the Swedish Bofors 40mm autocannon, widely considered the best light anti-aircraft gun of the era.

Crucially, this army would be entirely motorized. Using reliable, mass-produced utility vehicles like the German Opel Blitz or American multi-ton trucks, the military would ensure that infantry, artillery, and logistical supplies could actually keep pace with the armored spearheads. 

Finally, close air support would be integrated directly into ground operations. The German Junkers Ju 87 Stuka would be utilized for precision dive-bombing to break hardened strongpoints, protected by top-tier late-interwar fighters like the British Supermarine Spitfire Mk I or the German Messerschmitt Bf 109E to guarantee air superiority. 

By combining American semi-automatic rifles, German machine guns and armored ergonomics, British artillery, and total motorization, this hypothetical force would possess a devastating combination of situational awareness, operational speed, and sheer volume of fire that no actual interwar military could have withstood.

items.question: What If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade in World War II?
human_answers: The RN and other allies can only block the marine trade, so the first thing is to look at who Germany has land borders with. Then, which of those countries might have food or other essentials that Germany needs. If these are willing and able to trade [1], then Germany can maybe get by but if not then they either make do or try to take things by force. Nazi Germany chose force instead of negotiation and trade to try to beak the blockade. Why? because their leaders were mad bastards who were completely untrustworthy to trade with, thought they were better than everyone else, thought that violent conflict was good and who wanted to take over Russian lands for themselves: it ended badly. [1] Italy, for example, might have been willing to trade with Germany, but getting goods into Italy by sea is difficult with the British blocking imports intended for or suspected to be intended for Germany.

Yes its difficult to imagine it now but in 1939 the British had a near monopoly on merchant shipping and many nations merchant ships and their cargos would be 'under written' that is insured by British firms. And much of a nations cargos would likely travel on British ships or ships owned by British firms. In WW1 the blockade of Germany had been part physical i.e. warships stopping ships and inspecting cargos and manifests etc and part commercial pressure. Indeed it was discovered that many of the cargos that had been going to Germany pre war were instead going to Neutral nations like the Netherlands and Denmark and simply continuing on to Germany overland. By 1915 this 'loop hole' was effectively stopped using the commercial apparatus to quite simply restrict goods to no more than had been going to those neutral nations before the war meaning that very little would be left to sell on to Germany.
items.original_question: What if what if successful WW2 German breaking of the blockade I'm new here (and I'm a student, so please don't be too harsh, this is my first post), and I had a question, What if the Germans somehow broke the British blockade, or at least got any form of a sustainable food and oil (and rubber, and many other things, though the main question is about food) source that wasn't pillaging and murdering all of Eastern Europe and inspiring massive insurgencies? Now, the methods can be as creative as you'd want, was extra development of agriculture/synthetics possible (I know I said breaking of the blockade, but anything that gives the Germans a good food source counts)? I do know there were programs for rationing, but it still involved lots of pillaging in everywhere. My personal take on this is using U-Boats for trade, though I have zero idea who they would trade with. Was that even possible? How big was a U-Boat anyways?

items.model_answer:
If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade, World War II in Europe would have been significantly prolonged and vastly more destructive, though the ultimate outcome of an Allied victory would likely remain unchanged. 

With an abundance of oil and rubber, the Wehrmacht and Luftwaffe would have maintained their high mobility, logistical efficiency, and operational tempo throughout the conflict. Strategic military decisions driven by resource desperation—most notably the 1942 offensive into the Caucasus (Case Blue) to seize Soviet oil fields—could have been avoided. Instead, German forces could have concentrated their efforts on more strategically sound objectives, such as neutralizing the Red Army or capturing key political and industrial centers. Furthermore, a sustainable food supply would have prevented the collapse of civilian morale, maintained the productivity of the German home front, and mitigated the severe rationing that plagued the country in the later years of the war.

Militarily, the Allied strategic bombing campaign, which eventually focused heavily on crippling synthetic oil and rubber plants to paralyze the German war machine, would have been far less effective. This would have forced the Allies to shift their bombing focus entirely to civilian or broader industrial targets. On the ground, German mechanized units and aircraft would not have been grounded by fuel and tire shortages during crucial late-war operations, making their defense against the Soviet advance in the East and the Allied invasions in the West far more formidable. Battles like the Ardennes Offensive (Battle of the Bulge) would not have failed due to a lack of fuel, exacting a much heavier toll on Allied forces.

However, despite these massive logistical advantages, Germany would still have faced the overwhelming combined manpower, overall industrial capacity, and multi-front pressure of the United States, the Soviet Union, and the British Empire. The war in Europe would have dragged on well past May 1945, resulting in millions of additional military and civilian casualties. Ultimately, this prolonged timeline would have intersected with the successful completion of the Manhattan Project in the summer of 1945, making it highly probable that the United States would have dropped the first atomic bombs on German cities to break the stalemate and force a final surrender.

edus.text: If Germany had secured a sustainable wartime supply of food, oil, and rubber despite the Allied blockade,
World War II in Europe would have been significantly prolonged and vastly more destructive,
though the ultimate outcome of an Allied victory would likely remain unchanged.
With an abundance of oil and rubber,
the Wehrmacht and Luftwaffe would have maintained their high mobility, logistical efficiency, and operational tempo throughout the conflict.
Strategic military decisions driven by resource desperation
most notably the 1942 offensive into the Caucasus (Case Blue) to seize Soviet oil fields
could have been avoided.
Instead, German forces could have concentrated their efforts on more strategically sound objectives,
such as neutralizing the Red Army or capturing key political and industrial centers.
Furthermore, a sustainable food supply would have prevented the collapse of civilian morale,
maintained the productivity of the German home front,
and mitigated the severe rationing that plagued the country in the later years of the war.
Militarily, the Allied strategic bombing campaign,
which eventually focused heavily on crippling synthetic oil and rubber plants to paralyze the German war machine,
would have been far less effective.
This would have forced the Allies to shift their bombing focus entirely to civilian or broader industrial targets.
On the ground, German mechanized units and aircraft would not have been grounded by fuel and tire shortages during crucial late-war operations,
making their defense against the Soviet advance in the East and the Allied invasions in the West far more formidable.
Battles like the Ardennes Offensive (Battle of the Bulge) would not have failed due to a lack of fuel,
exacting a much heavier toll on Allied forces.
However, despite these massive logistical advantages,
Germany would still have faced the overwhelming combined manpower, overall industrial capacity, and multi-front pressure of the United States, the Soviet Union, and the British Empire.
The war in Europe would have dragged on well past May 1945,
resulting in millions of additional military and civilian casualties.
Ultimately, this prolonged timeline would have intersected with the successful completion of the Manhattan Project in the summer of 1945,
making it highly probable that the United States would have dropped the first atomic bombs on German cities
to break the stalemate and force a final surrender.

items.question: What If nuclear fission had been discovered early enough for a practical reactor to be built around the 1900s?
human_answers: Well, according to Google "Canada's first CANDU prototype, the Nuclear Power Demonstration (NPD) reactor, required a significant amount of heavy water (D2O) for its moderator and coolant, generally around 1 tonne of heavy water per megawatt (MW) of capacity, translating to roughly 20-25 tonnes for its small 20 MWe output..." and "In the 1930's Norwegian company Norsk Hydro began industrial-scale extraction of heavy water (deuterium oxide) at its Vemork plant in Rjukan, using electrolysis as a byproduct of fertilizer production, " Finally from Wikipedia (yes, I know this may well be nonsense) "It was the world's first site to mass-produce heavy water (as a byproduct of nitrogen fixing), with a capacity of 1.2 tonnes per year. " So, by the late 1930's / early 1940's it might well be possible to build a 1 or 2MW CANDU stream generator using just one or two years production from the single Norsk Hydro plant. I assume Canadian hydro plants were built with higher capacity since they (the Canadians) managed to build commercial output (GW) plants requiring 200-300 tones of heavy water in a 'reasonable' timescale (ie. less than 200 years )

Believe it or not, my first engineering degree was in Nuclear Engineering (it was a dead field when I graduated 30 plus years ago, and still is, so I got another degree in Manufacturing Engineering). Yes, you can run reactors with natural enrichment, and the right neutron moderator - heavy water (as in the water molecules have Deuterium instead of your usual one proton no neutrons hydrogen) or graphite come to mind. Both would avoid the need to enrich the fuel (which is a major hassle to do). BUT, that's only part of the story - you need the instrumentation for monitoring the nuclear reactions (to make sure they're occurring, and not getting out of control) which is basically electronic in nature (sorry mechanical won't cut it). In the early 1900s, the field of electronics was embryonic at best. Then there's the material science aspect - you need materials seriously capable of dealing with the high reactor temperatures, and radiation effects (oh yeah, and the material can't interfere excessively with the neutron flux, which would disrupt the reaction) - sorry not happening, material science was in its infancy IMO. There is also the safety aspect - you need shielding for any radiation emitted from the reactor. The health aspects of radiation exposure were basically unknown, resulting in many people getting exposed to and dying of cancer (Marie Curie, early X-Ray technicians, the so called "Radium Girls" who painted the glowing dots on watch faces). In certain cases of extreme exposure (due to reactor surges, etc.), you can die from the radiation days after the exposure. In short, IMO, having a viable nuclear reactor in the early 1900s is a non-starter.

To your first part: Fair enough. It seems like this might require ASB, like just magically gifting people the entire lexicon of nuclear understanding and teaching them how to make purer graphite. I'm not sure I entirely agree with the second part. Were the engineers that built the Chicago Pile doing sophisticated core analysis? Did they know the neutron flux? I feel like you could "fly blind" and just go by heat/steam output, especially since "won't immediately melt down and ruin my investment" is probably considered sufficient by 1900s standards of safety (especially if the health effects of radiation are not yet understood). Granted, it seems very, very likely that the long term effects of this mentality would make for a much more radioactively contaminated world... Ah, but I didn't say for generating electricity, per se. A nuclear boiler just for steam would be useful. And I doubt they'd come up with a design that requires steam generators or controlling boron concentration in the coolant: I wouldn't expect anything like a PWR with its separation between a primary and secondary loop. More like a BWR or RBMK, where the radioactive steam is directly used. If the objective is electricity, it may require a bit longer than early 1900s. But by the time you have coal plants coming online, you have everything you need for the conventional thermal plant.

To elaborate on some things: as far as I can tell, there are possibly 3 historical reactor designs that used unenriched/natural uranium: heavy-water moderated CANDU reactors, graphite-moderated gas-cooled reactors (Magnox and UNGG), and possibly the graphite-moderated Soviet RBMK reactors (although RBMK reactors typically used low-enriched uranium). Heavy water's out of the question; it was only discovered in the 1930s, and even WW2-era methods for extracting heavy water were massively energy-intensive. NPD, the first CANDU reactor producing some 20 MW of electricity, required 28,660kg of heavy water. Using pure electrolysis to extract the heavy water - the initial method used to extract heavy water at Vemork - required about 58,000 kilowatt hours per pound of heavy water, or 3.6 billion kilowatt-hours to produce all the necessary heavy water. As a quick comparison, the US' entire monthly electricity generation in April 1922 was about 3.6 billion kilowatt hours. That means the NPD reactor, if it obtained heavy water using pre-WW2 methods, could run for 20 years straight and not break even on the power needed to create the heavy water necessary to run the plant (not to mention some heavy water will be lost in operation) before the development of postwar heavy water production methods. UNGG and RBMK definitely used zirconium cladding for their fuel elements (necessary because zirconium has a smaller neutron absorption cross-section and is resistant to corrosion); the issue is that metal zirconium wasn't commercially synthesized until 1925, and it wasn't commercially synthesized cheaply until after WW2. The specific zirconium alloys used in the fuel claddings weren't developed until the postwar either. RBMK reactors operate with water at pressures of about 1,000 psi; that wasn't achieved by land-based power generation systems until 1925. Uranium metal used in the gas-cooled reactors is difficult to work with considering it corrodes a lot of metals when molten, thus requiring graphite molds of decently high purity (maybe not as pure as nuclear graphite, but boron has to be minimized). Also the furnaces used to cast the uranium were vacuum induction furnaces, a technology not invented until the 1920s. Turning the uranium metal into fuel rods that can be inserted also required a ton of research and development to the point where it was once considered the most critical job at Hanford for the Manhattan Project.
items.original_question: What if A nuclear reactor, four decades early? I posit that with the technology of the early 1900s, a nuclear reactor could've been theoretically possible had the theory been understood. Uranium enrichment is entirely out of the question, but not all reactor designs require it. The industrialists of the 1900s had access to graphite, yellowcake, and boron, which would allow the creation and control of a graphite-moderated natural uranium reactor, so long as the graphite was pure enough (I am admittedly unsure if that level of purity would be possible, but I am presuming so given what little I know of the process). Is there any plausible scenario where the discovery of nuclear fission is pushed back far enough for our enterprising titans of industry to begin harnessing nuclear steam, short of dropping off a modern nuclear physics textbook in their engineers' laps? If so, what effects would this have on the world?
