items.question: What If the Allies lose on the Salonica front?
human_answers: Alan Wakefield (IWM expert on Salonika, among other subjects) commented that most of the Bulgarian forces in September 1918 facing the British were well motivated, apart from the 1st Macedonian Bde that consisted of many men of Serbian origin. It was the collapse further west when the French & Serbian forces broke through three lines of defence, followed by the Greek breakthrough at Petit Couronne and Doiran Hill to the Bulgarian second line that unhinged the Bulgarian defences. Bulgarian C-in-C Todorov met with the German commanders von Steuben (German 11th Army) and von Reuter (Division Reuter) on 18 September, and agreed that Bulgarian 1st Army would be pulled back from positions east of the Vadar River, while the German 11th Army and Bulgarian 3rd Division would maintain contact. However the orders to 1st Army came as a severe blow to morale as the men were celebrating their stalling the British attacks, They started marching to Kosturino Pass but there was a serious shortage of draught animals, and of the survivors: " The majority of horses & oxen were absolutely unfit for work and they had need of at least six months rest in the interior, where they could be well nourished, Others had need of at least 45 days rest" - Major Nedeff, 9th Division, quoted in Under the Devil's Eye (Alan Wakefield & Simon Moody) from which much of the first three paragraphs are sourced. This was when the RAF caught the Bulgarian withdrawal through the passes, causing serious casualties & further delays. With foreign troops now on Bulgarian soil, political opposition to the war in the Sobranie was widespread. The PM, Malinov, was pro-western and had been appointed that June by Tsar Ferdinand with the purpose of proposing an armistice to the Allies, and on 26 September emissaries were sent through the lines to start discussions, although Franchet d'Esperey would only accept an unilateral unconditional armistice, which the Bugarian government then agreed to give, So it looks like the Bulgarian army was in generally good morale status until the final victories sparked by the French, Serbian & Greek forces, when the order of and losses taken on the retreat caused a final decline. But it looks like the home front collapsed first, if the Tsar was considering an armistice in June, so not sure what caused the domestic problems that drove the government to seek peace (I understand that a military rebelliion / mutiny at Radomir formulated by Bulgarian Agrarian National Union attempted to overthrow the government and establish a republic). Wiki suggests the following reasons: - Extreme war weariness, given Bulgaria had been at war since 1912 (short break 1914-15). Exhausted manpower (see #1 above) - I would add this resulted in dissatisfied minority groups supplying more troops, such as Macedonian Serbs & Greeks, diluting the Bulgar core. Both military & civilians suffering extreme food shortages (result of your point regarding harvests?). Troops poorly supplied - not only food but ammunition, clothing, boots, etc. Troops believing profiteers making hay at home at their expense. Feeling of betrayal by their allies, principally Germany, especialy regarding promised levels of supplies not being met, and lack of support for Bulgarian territorial ambitions at expense of Romania. Not sure how far the German troop levels had been reduced as you comment. The impact of the Russian Revolution. The impact of Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points (maybe a surrender would't be as bad as keep fighting) Recommended is 'The Enemy is Behind Us': The Morale Crisis in the Bulgarian Army during the Summer of 1918 - Richard C Hall, War in History Vol. 11 No. 4 which again refers to the collapse in morale starting by June 1918. Bulgarian C-in-C Nikola Zhekov reported to Tsar Ferdinand on 121 June that: "Today it is impossible ton have any illusions that the spirit of the soldiers is the same as at the beginning of the war, or even last year." I can't access as I don't have a school account! It does look like some units, such as the 9th (Pleven) Division, kept their high morale almost to the end. My main comment on demoralised forces would apply further north and primarily to the Austro-Hungarian troops who fell apart in October 1918, when I daresay no one suggests they were of high morale status. Earlier in the war that would not be the case, and I reckon me & a mountain goat could hold the Neretva Valley!

When you mentioned the Allies, I almost thought it was World War II. In reality, due to the division of Greece, neither the Entente nor the Central Powers could make any progress on the Thessaloniki front. Launching a large-scale offensive meant turning Greece into a battlefield, alienating more Greeks, and pushing more Greeks to the other side. The Entente was able to launch its offensive on the Macedonian front in 1917-1918 because the Entente countries had a large surplus of French reserves, willing to do everything except attack the Germans, such as conducting political work with the Greeks (Germany's reserves were smaller but more elite, and needed to do more important things; Bulgaria and the Ottomans were absolutely unacceptable to the Greeks). Ultimately, the deployment of hundreds of thousands of soldiers from the core countries of the Triple Entente only resulted in the defeat of one vassal state. The Central Powers could not accept this waste of reserves (unless Italy joined the Central Powers, providing some low ability soldiers). Even so, the problem of resource shortages must be taken into account.

It's my impression that it's something of a convention on this post 1900 forum to use "Entente" instead of "Allies", presumably to avoid confusion with the Allies of WW2. IMVHO I do prefer "Allies" for the WW1 military coalition because "Entente" is a derivation of the "Triple Entente" which applies to France/Russia/Britain, but by the end of WW1 the key great powers were Britain/France/Italy/America (and Russia was out) and there were multiple smaller allied powers. Why couldn't the Central Powers advance? Like, I thought Gallipoli ultimately failed because it was a trench-warfare stalemate; the Allies couldn't overcome a German client state. IIRC the proximal reason for the Gallipoli evacuation was that Bulgaria had joined the Central Powers, providing a route for German war material (not merely advisor personnel) like heavy siege artillery to be delivered to Turkey, which the Allies thought would be decisive. Was that assessment correct? Are you saying the Ottomans (with German support) could do something (push an Allied army into the sea) the Bulgarians (with their German support) could not? Or do you think that if the Allies had dug in on the Gallipoli peninsula in 1916, they might have obtained a stalemate which lasted until 1917/1918 when further offensives could be launched? I read that because of the potential futility of the front, Britain (and France) contemplated withdrawing their troops from mainland Greece before lines were solidified. Surely the Central Powers could have conquered Greece under those circumstances, no? I suppose in a grand strategy sense I recognize Germany was trying to fight a multi-front conflict against [the entire rest of the world] and was ultimately all but certain to lose the war. But in the narrower sense of "could the Balkan theater have played out differently", isn't it possible that the Central Powers could have achieved more success? Like, what if some resources from a different offensive (which surely would see less success than in OTL) devoted towards breaking through on the Macedonian front?

The allies couldn't overcome a German ally with more than 50 divisions and more than a million men on the field you mean, which in 1915 were about as well armed as their own troops. This is not 1942 in the Eastern front. But to get to the actual question in the fall of 1915 Greece was fully mobilized with 16 divisions and 325,000 troops in Macedonia and the Germans were doing their level best to keep Constantine in control and Greece out of the war. If they invade Greek territory you can kiss that neutrality goodbye and these 16 divisions just come into play added to the British and French divisions already landed in Salonica. And you'd better time it after the Serbs have been pushed into retreating into Albania, if your invasion comes before you just saved the lives of a couple hundred thousand Serbs. No. You essentially suggest Berlin says "to hell with the shenanigans to keep the Greeks neutral, let's invade them too. " So you just about gave numerical parity to the defenders... who don't have to move everything but food and fodder for the Macedonian and Turkish fronts though a single track railway going all the way back to Vienna. Before Dobro Polie and Desperate Frankie advancing all the way to Hungary and Austria putting the final nail in the Austro-Hungarian empire's coffin the actual front looked a pretty good deal to Berlin. Over 400,000 allied troops before the Greeks joined, that could be fighting elsewhere contained through mostly Bulgarian manpower... which could not be used elsewhere. Biggest POW camp in the world jokes and all that.

Well, Alternate History Challenge: An equivalent of Dobro Polie and subsequent desperate Frankie advances happen six months to a year earlier than OTL, *before* the Germans start getting pushed back on the western front, not after, and perhaps as a consequence, we get to see see the desperate Frankie international force *keep advancing* through the territory of capitulated Austria-Hungary, and over onto German territory from its southern and eastern borders (to Munich, Passau, Dresden, Gorlitz, Liegnitz or further to Cottbus or Berlin) before the Germans actually capitulate. Could this have ever happened in the right combination of circumstances? Could an earlier resolution of the Greek political divide in favor of the Venizelist side, committing the full Greek Army to the Entente side earlier, have helped with this? What might it take, faster French seduction? Or, going the opposite direction, more in line with what the OP wants, is there any way the Venizelist side could have been so marginalized that the Royalist side in Greece became willing to openly side with the Central Powers and openly welcomed/sought CP support in expelling Allied forces from Salonica and any other parts of Greece at any point during the war?
items.original_question: What if the Allies lose on the Salonica front? As I loosely understand it, the Salonica front was established after the Serbian army was routed. What if the Central Powers were able to continue advancing into Greece and expelled the Allies from the mainland Balkans? The Salonica front in some ways seems to resemble Gallipoli (an Allied lodgment supplied by sea) and the Central powers were able to prevail at Gallipoli, so it seems possible. The Allies also had to deal with the fact that the Greek government was divided - if the Central powers were more successful it seems possible Greece would have “switched sides”, or at least had a compliant government installed.

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise definition and historical anchoring
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines what it means for the Allies/Entente to lose on the Salonica/Macedonian front and anchors the divergence in the real military, political, and logistical conditions of 1917-1918.
criteria.1-2: Treats the premise vaguely or anachronistically; confuses WWI with WWII or ignores the Salonica/Macedonian context.
criteria.3-4: Identifies the front but gives an unclear or implausible Allied defeat with little reference to real 1918 conditions.
criteria.5-6: Defines a plausible defeat, such as failed Entente offensive or withdrawal, with some correct historical anchors.
criteria.7-8: Specifies a credible point of divergence tied to Doiran, Vardar, Bulgarian morale, Greek participation, or Entente logistics.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the counterfactual, distinguishes limited tactical defeat from strategic collapse, and grounds it in documented constraints of the Macedonian front.

criteria.name: Causal fidelity to Balkan military mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the military mechanisms by which an Allied loss could occur and what immediate effects it would have on Bulgaria, Greece, Serbia, and Central Powers operations.
criteria.1-2: Relies on unsupported claims of easy conquest or collapse; ignores terrain, supply, morale, and force composition.
criteria.3-4: Mentions military outcomes but with weak or inaccurate causal links, such as assuming Salonica alone decides the war instantly.
criteria.5-6: Addresses some relevant mechanisms, including defensive terrain, Bulgarian forces, Entente reserves, or Greek involvement.
criteria.7-8: Connects battlefield outcomes to Bulgarian morale, Serbian recovery, Greek politics, supply bottlenecks, and Central Powers priorities.
criteria.9-10: Provides a robust operational chain showing how Allied defeat affects withdrawals, lines of communication, Balkan armies, and feasibility of further Central Powers advances.

criteria.name: Integration of Bulgarian domestic collapse and alliance constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for Bulgaria’s internal war weariness, food shortages, manpower exhaustion, mutiny risk, relations with Germany, and the limits these imposed even after an Allied defeat.
criteria.1-2: Portrays Bulgaria as either effortlessly triumphant or inevitably collapsing without explaining domestic conditions.
criteria.3-4: Mentions Bulgarian morale or politics only superficially and misses why Bulgaria sought an armistice historically.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes some domestic pressures such as shortages, war weariness, or agrarian unrest but underdevelops their implications.
criteria.7-8: Explains how an Allied defeat could delay or alter, but not automatically remove, Bulgaria’s morale and political crisis.
criteria.9-10: Carefully weighs military success against structural exhaustion, minority troop issues, Radomir-style unrest, Malinov’s policy, and German failure to meet Bulgarian expectations.

criteria.name: Long-range strategic consequences for World War I
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the coherence and plausibility of the answer’s downstream chain from an Allied loss at Salonica to wider outcomes for the Central Powers, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire, Italy, Germany, and the 1918 armistices.
criteria.1-2: Jumps directly to sweeping conclusions such as Central Powers victory or unchanged history with no causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Gives a broad outcome but neglects key theaters or timing, especially the Western Front and Austria-Hungary’s collapse.
criteria.5-6: Discusses several downstream effects, such as delayed Bulgarian surrender or altered pressure on Austria-Hungary, with partial coherence.
criteria.7-8: Builds a plausible sequence linking the Balkan result to Serbia, Greece, Ottoman communications, Danube/Balkan security, and Germany’s worsening overall position.
criteria.9-10: Balances local Central Powers gains against decisive global constraints, showing how Salonica might delay or reshape armistices without overclaiming reversal of Germany’s strategic defeat.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer distinguishes likely, possible, and unlikely outcomes, avoids internal contradictions, and handles ambiguous terms such as 'Allies lose' with appropriate caveats.
criteria.1-2: States speculative outcomes as certain, contradicts itself, or ignores the ambiguity of the premise.
criteria.3-4: Uses some caveats but still makes deterministic or mutually inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Shows moderate uncertainty awareness and mostly avoids contradictions, though some assumptions remain unstated.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates immediate, medium-term, and long-term probabilities and flags dependencies such as scale of defeat or German reinforcement levels.
criteria.9-10: Maintains consistent assumptions throughout, compares multiple plausible branches, and calibrates confidence in each major causal claim.

items.model_answer:
If the Allies had lost on the Salonica (Macedonian) Front during World War I, the most immediate consequence would have been the prolonged duration of the war, as the historical breakthrough there in September 1918 was the catalyst that triggered the rapid collapse of the Central Powers. An Allied defeat—whether through a forced evacuation akin to Gallipoli or a decisive military rout—would have secured absolute Central Powers hegemony over the Balkans. Serbia would have remained entirely occupied with its exiled army destroyed or captured, and Greece, already deeply divided by the National Schism, would likely have been forced into full submission or an alliance with the Central Powers. Consequently, Bulgaria would have emerged as the undisputed dominant power in the region, securing its territorial ambitions in Macedonia, Thrace, and Dobruja.

Strategically, an Allied defeat would have permanently secured the vital overland supply route between Germany and the Ottoman Empire. Unharassed by the Allied presence in northern Greece, the railway corridor from Europe to the Middle East would have allowed a continuous flow of German munitions, coal, and military advisors to the Ottomans. Bolstered by these uninterrupted supply lines, the Ottoman Empire could have mounted a much stiffer resistance against British offensives in Palestine and Mesopotamia, potentially stalling the Arab Revolt and delaying the collapse of the Ottoman fronts. 

Furthermore, the elimination of the Salonica Front would have freed up hundreds of thousands of Bulgarian, German, and Austro-Hungarian troops. These forces could have been redeployed to reinforce the vulnerable Austro-Hungarian lines along the Italian Front or sent to the Western Front to bolster German defenses against the advancing British, French, and American armies. For the Allies, a defeat at Salonica would have been a humiliating political disaster, severely damaging morale in Paris and London and sparking political crises.

Ultimately, without the domino effect initiated by Bulgaria’s historical surrender in September 1918—which exposed Austria-Hungary’s southern flank and convinced the German High Command that the war was unwinnable—World War I would have almost certainly dragged on well into 1919. The Allies would have been forced to achieve victory exclusively through grinding, bloody attrition on the Western Front, resulting in hundreds of thousands of additional casualties and potentially altering the post-war borders and diplomatic treaties of 20th-century Europe.

the most immediate consequence would have been the prolonged duration of the war,
as the historical breakthrough there in September 1918 was the catalyst that triggered the rapid collapse of the Central Powers.
An Allied defeat—whether through a forced evacuation akin to Gallipoli or a decisive military rout—would have secured absolute Central Powers hegemony over the Balkans.
Serbia would have remained entirely occupied with its exiled army destroyed or captured,
and Greece, already deeply divided by the National Schism, would likely have been forced into full submission or an alliance with the Central Powers.
Consequently, Bulgaria would have emerged as the undisputed dominant power in the region,
securing its territorial ambitions in Macedonia, Thrace, and Dobruja.
Strategically, an Allied defeat would have permanently secured the vital overland supply route between Germany and the Ottoman Empire.
Unharassed by the Allied presence in northern Greece,
the railway corridor from Europe to the Middle East would have allowed a continuous flow of German munitions, coal, and military advisors to the Ottomans.
Bolstered by these uninterrupted supply lines,
the Ottoman Empire could have mounted a much stiffer resistance against British offensives in Palestine and Mesopotamia,
potentially stalling the Arab Revolt and delaying the collapse of the Ottoman fronts.
Furthermore, the elimination of the Salonica Front would have freed up hundreds of thousands of Bulgarian, German, and Austro-Hungarian troops.
These forces could have been redeployed to reinforce the vulnerable Austro-Hungarian lines along the Italian Front
or sent to the Western Front to bolster German defenses against the advancing British, French, and American armies.
For the Allies, a defeat at Salonica would have been a humiliating political disaster,
severely damaging morale in Paris and London
and sparking political crises.
Ultimately, without the domino effect initiated by Bulgaria’s historical surrender in September 1918—
which exposed Austria-Hungary’s southern flank
and convinced the German High Command that the war was unwinnable—
World War I would have almost certainly dragged on well into 1919.

resulting in hundreds of thousands of additional casualties
and potentially altering the post-war borders and diplomatic treaties of 20th-century Europe.

items.question: What If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine?
human_answers: 1 - as noted by the fellow member, the P-40F and L used the Merlin 2 - it was a pretty simple upgrade 3 - engine itself does not require a laminar flow wing; a laminar flow wing will cut some drag, however, and thus allow for some speed increase 4 - historically, it offered some 30 mph over the P-40E at 18000 ft and above, IOW it was an improvement the P-40 badly needed 5 - P-51s used the better Merlins, these with 2-stage supercharger; a P-40 with such an engine would've probably be as fast as the Spitfire IX, but not as fast as the Merlin Mustang, nor as rangy - and thus the answer is 'no' 6 - as-is, the performance was better on the P-40F than on the ubiquitous P-40E; with 2-stage Merlin, it would've probably been good for 400+ mph, and much better rate of climb (the XP-40Q did 420+ mph with a 2-stage supercharged V-1710)

I'll have to take your word for it as I'm forbidden from your links but that sounds about right. A more advanced Merlin won't really help the P-40 though. There are availability issues with the Merlin, as ever, which historically forced Curtiss to revert to the V-1710-81 for the P-40M, despite more than half the production run going to the RAF. Not even every P-40F/L received a Merlin as some were completed as V-1710-81 engined P-40Rs. More though, there is the tale of the XP-60, which was a P-40D fuselage with a new laminar-flow wing. It was an improvement, with 387mph at 22,000ft. Modified as the XP-60D with an enlarged tail, it may or may not have received the V-1650-3 slated for it by the time of it's destruction in a crash on 6th May 1943. It certainly didn't perform any substantive testing with it. By that time the Merlin Mustang was established as superior in performance and was already entering production. The XP-60A with 1425hp V-1710-75, good for 420mph at 29,000ft, was part-cancelled in January 1942 (with the remainder following in June 1943) in favour of P-40Ks, Ls and P-47Gs. I think that is going to be the fate of any advanced or improved P-40 variant. Cancelled in favour of sustained production of known quantities.

items.model_answer:
If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed from the outset around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, rather than the Allison V-1710, its combat role, aerodynamic profile, and the early trajectory of Allied air power in World War II would have been significantly altered. 

Historically, the P-40 was severely handicapped at high altitudes because early Allison engines lacked a multi-stage supercharger, forcing the aircraft into low-to-medium altitude tactical roles. If designed around the Merlin—which possessed an excellent supercharger—the early P-40 would have been a highly capable high-altitude interceptor from the very beginning of the war. Allied pilots in the Pacific, North Africa, and Europe would have had a fighter capable of matching the Messerschmitt Bf 109 and the Mitsubishi A6M Zero in high-altitude vertical combat, drastically reducing the tactical disadvantages suffered by early USAAF and RAF squadrons.

Aerodynamically, a ground-up Merlin P-40 would have looked different from the iconic early models. The Allison engine required a distinctive top-mounted carburetor intake scoop, which would have been absent. While Curtiss did eventually retrofit Packard-built Merlins into later variants (the P-40F and P-40L), an airframe designed natively around the Merlin’s specific dimensions, weight distribution, and cooling requirements would have been better optimized, likely resulting in a lighter, sleeker, and more aerodynamic fighter than the historical retrofits.

However, this design choice would have created a massive logistical bottleneck. In 1939 and 1940, Rolls-Royce was struggling to build enough Merlins to supply Britain's own Spitfires and Hurricanes, meaning they could not have exported engines to Curtiss. To make the aircraft a reality, the United States would have had to negotiate and establish the Packard license-production agreement of the Merlin (the V-1650) a year or two earlier than it actually did. If this early production hurdle could not be cleared, the P-40 might have suffered severe manufacturing delays, depriving the Allies of the one fighter they had in mass quantities when the war broke out. 

Ultimately, if the engine supply issue had been solved, an early Merlin-powered P-40 would have given the Allies a world-class fighter in 1941. This success might have even altered the development timeline of the P-51 Mustang. While the Mustang would still have eventually surpassed the P-40 due to its revolutionary laminar-flow wing and lower drag, the desperate urgency that led to the Mustang's rapid development and its own eventual mating with the Merlin engine might have been lessened if the USAAF already possessed a high-altitude capable P-40.

edus.text: If the Curtiss P-40 had been designed from the outset around the Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, rather than the Allison V-1710,
its combat role, aerodynamic profile, and the early trajectory of Allied air power in World War II would have been significantly altered.
Historically, the P-40 was severely handicapped at high altitudes
because early Allison engines lacked a multi-stage supercharger,
forcing the aircraft into low-to-medium altitude tactical roles.
If designed around the Merlin—which possessed an excellent supercharger—
the early P-40 would have been a highly capable high-altitude interceptor from the very beginning of the war.
Allied pilots in the Pacific, North Africa, and Europe would have had a fighter capable of matching the Messerschmitt Bf 109 and the Mitsubishi A6M Zero in high-altitude vertical combat,
drastically reducing the tactical disadvantages suffered by early USAAF and RAF squadrons.
Aerodynamically, a ground-up Merlin P-40 would have looked different from the iconic early models.
The Allison engine required a distinctive top-mounted carburetor intake scoop,
which would have been absent.
While Curtiss did eventually retrofit Packard-built Merlins into later variants (the P-40F and P-40L),
an airframe designed natively around the Merlin’s specific dimensions, weight distribution, and cooling requirements would have been better optimized,
likely resulting in a lighter, sleeker, and more aerodynamic fighter than the historical retrofits.
However, this design choice would have created a massive logistical bottleneck.
In 1939 and 1940, Rolls-Royce was struggling to build enough Merlins to supply Britain's own Spitfires and Hurricanes,
meaning they could not have exported engines to Curtiss.
To make the aircraft a reality,
the United States would have had to negotiate and establish the Packard license-production agreement of the Merlin (the V-1650) a year or two earlier than it actually did.
If this early production hurdle could not be cleared,
the P-40 might have suffered severe manufacturing delays,
depriving the Allies of the one fighter they had in mass quantities when the war broke out.
Ultimately, if the engine supply issue had been solved,
an early Merlin-powered P-40 would have given the Allies a world-class fighter in 1941.
This success might have even altered the development timeline of the P-51 Mustang.
While the Mustang would still have eventually surpassed the P-40 due to its revolutionary laminar-flow wing and lower drag,
the desperate urgency that led to the Mustang's rapid development and its own eventual mating with the Merlin engine might have been lessened
if the USAAF already possessed a high-altitude capable P-40.

items.question: PT-109: What If JFK Died on 7/2/43?
human_answers: It seems plausible to me that if Jack were to die in the Pacific, Sr would use connections to ensure that Jr would come home in one piece so that grooming for public office could begin. That said, I've read several accounts that suggest/indicate Jr was not as approachable/astute/able to think on his feet as well as Jack. That might make a political career more challenging: still feasible, but more challenging and quite possibly more costly (Sr might have had to write more and/or larger checks to make things happen?). I could see Jr with a House, and later a Senate seat. Then the question becomes: could he work his way into such a position that Adlai Stevenson might consider him as a running mate in 1956? Arguably, that propelled Jack into the limelight enough to become a presidential contender in 1960. My sense is that Jr would not get the same consideration ITTL that Jack did IOTL. Rather, he would plausibly have tried a presidential run having something like 8-10 years of Senate experience under his belt in 1960. We're talking a crowded field for the Dems in 1960: Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Jr, and the usual cast of favorite sons. Johnson might be the favorite, but not a prohibitive favorite: coming from Texas would assure that. Too manybut Lodge won northerners would be skeptical. On the other hand, Humphrey would definitely not play well in the south. Could Jr emerge as a compromise candidate? Maybe, but he'd be a tough sell in the south given his Catholic faith. My sense is that a protracted, multiple ballot convention would ultimately result in a Johnson nomination, with a middle of the road midwesterner (I'll yield to someone else here) as a VP candidate. Nixon will still be the GOP nominee, but Lodge won't be his running mate: don't need to counter a Kennedy. I suggest it would be MD governor Theodore McKeldin, a man who knew how to work with both sides (he was the last GOP mayor of Baltimore). McKeldin would bring a great deal more to the ticket than Lodge, but that's a pretty low bar. While we're at it, look for the 1960 campaign to be nasty. Lyndon Johnson had few scruples if any as far as that went, so I wouldn't be surprised if he started it. Then all Nixon has to do is take the high road and point out how well things have gone during Ike's tenure, and pump up his role (maybe this time Ike wouldn't make his famous "...if you give me a week..." remark?). And I don't see Richard Daley doing much to help Lyndon Johnson in Chicago, so IL might well flip to the GOP. Long story short: Nixon wins in '60. That leaves 1968 as Jr's next shot at the White House: he wouldn't try to unseat Nixon unless something totally unforeseen happened.

I once posted on another thread about a different pathway that Joe Jr's career would look like. IOTL JFK had the choice of running for Congress or for Lt. Governor of Massachusetts, and he chose to run for Congress in 1946. My alternate path for Joe Jr. had him running for Lt. Governor in 1946 and getting Statewide exposure, IOTL the Democratic ticket lost, but with Joe Sr's money the Democrats win. Joe Jr. runs for US Senate against Republican incumbent Leverett Saltonstall in 1948 and wins in a Democratic year. The main character flaw of Joe Jr. was his fierce loyalty to his father. There is a story about how Joe Sr. was on the Harvard baseball team and by playing on the Harvard-Yale game he would get a letter, but due to anti-Catholic bigotry, he was left on the bench and didn't get a letter. When Joe Jr. as a senior on the team, he was the first baseman and made the final put out of the Harvard-Yale game, and by tradition the ball is given to the team captain and Joe Jr. kept it himself and gave the ball to his father. How this would play out is uncertain, how far would he go in defending Joe Sr.'s isolation? JFK was able use his service to separate himself against any criticism against his father, but could Joe Jr. do that?

Both are possible, but I do think that Jor Sr trying to pull some strings would be more plausible (at least to me). But if Joe Jr still does his mission (maybe the dates between Jack's death and Joe's mission are too close), it could be that Robert gets chosen as the next. That being said... This was something I didn't think about, but from what I read it would make sense. Robert was always known as the black sheep of the family. If Ted was chosen by Joe Sr, he may very well have been thrown into Korea. The only question would be where Ted's future would go: He would have been far too young to run for President in 1960, but he could have won a seat as Senator in Massachusetts (although it would have been difficult). Maybe eight years later (say 1968), Ted might try to make his move, although 1972 might be more plausible.
items.original_question: PT-109: What if JFK Died on 7/2/43? In 1943, John F Kennedy's patrol boat PT-109 was rammed by the battleship Amagiri. After PT-109 exploded, JFK was able to survive, swimming from the wreck to a nearby island to stay alive while also saving his fellow soldiers. The moment cemented Jack as a war hero, and after his brother Joe died in a special mission, Jack was seen as next in line to join the Senate, before finally becoming President (which we all know how it ended). But what if things went slightly differently? Maybe Jack is closer to the blast and dies in the initial explosion. What next? What would happen to Joe Jr, and by extension, the Kennedy family? In our timeline, Joe Jr was killed in a special mission, but could the death of JFK stopped Joe Jr from going on the mission, and continue to stay alive to be the frontrunner of the family? Joe Jr had approved of Hitler, but his ideals could have easily morphed over time. Could Joe have done what Jack did and become President, and how would his presidency have looked? And if Joe Jr did in fact die anyway, who would replace him? Robert would have been far too young, along with Ted. Would the Kennedy family fade out of the limelight? What would become of the 1960 elections? The more obvious question, with Jack dead, who would be the man to lead the Democrats against Nixon? The most likely options are Hubert Humphrey, Lyndon Baines Johnson, and (although less likely), Adali Stevenson. Who would have been able to win the primaries, and could they have dealt with Nixon? With whoever becomes President, how would their Presidency look, and what could happen to them if they were also assassinated? For me personally, the most likely ticket would have been Johnson, causing him to be President.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise Fidelity and Immediate Wartime Response
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly anchors the divergence in JFK dying in the PT-109 incident on July 2, 1943, and plausibly traces the Kennedy family's immediate response during WWII, especially Joe Sr.'s effort to preserve or redirect the family's political ambitions.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or treats JFK as still politically active; little or no attention to 1943 wartime context.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges JFK dies but gives only vague or implausible immediate consequences for the Kennedys.
criteria.5-6: Correctly uses JFK's death and identifies Joe Sr.'s likely search for another political heir, but with limited wartime detail.
criteria.7-8: Plausibly explains how JFK's death affects Joe Jr., RFK, or Ted in the war and family strategy, with mostly sound timing.
criteria.9-10: Strongly grounds the divergence in 1943, integrates military timing, Joe Sr.'s influence, family succession pressures, and avoids anachronistic assumptions.

criteria.name: Kennedy Family Succession and Candidate Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates the depth and plausibility of reasoning about which Kennedy becomes the political heir after JFK's death, including Joe Jr., RFK, and Ted, and how their personalities, ages, records, and limitations would affect viability.
criteria.1-2: Ignores the question of Kennedy succession or assumes another Kennedy simply replaces JFK without justification.
criteria.3-4: Names a successor but gives shallow reasoning about why that person would or would not succeed.
criteria.5-6: Discusses at least one plausible heir, such as Joe Jr. or RFK, with some attention to experience, age, or family backing.
criteria.7-8: Compares multiple Kennedy heirs and links their traits, wartime service, and Joe Sr.'s patronage to political prospects.
criteria.9-10: Nuanced comparison of Joe Jr., RFK, and/or Ted, including personality, public appeal, Catholic identity, age constraints, family dynamics, and realistic career paths.

criteria.name: Long-Range Political Chain Coherence, 1946-1968
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer constructs a coherent downstream timeline from the 1940s through at least the 1960 election, and preferably toward 1968 or later, covering congressional, Senate, convention, and presidential implications.
criteria.1-2: Provides disconnected speculation with no sustained timeline beyond JFK's death.
criteria.3-4: Mentions later politics but skips major transitional steps or gives a chronologically confused chain.
criteria.5-6: Offers a basic timeline for a Kennedy heir and some national political effects, though with gaps.
criteria.7-8: Builds a mostly coherent chain through House/Senate prospects, Democratic nomination politics, and the 1960 election.
criteria.9-10: Presents a well-sequenced long-range chain from WWII through 1946, 1948, 1956, 1960, and possible 1968/1972 effects, with each step causally motivated.

criteria.name: Coverage of Major Downstream Actors and Electoral Mechanisms
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer accounts for key non-Kennedy actors and mechanisms affected by JFK's absence, such as Joe Sr., Adlai Stevenson, Lyndon Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, Richard Nixon, VP selection, anti-Catholic voting, regional blocs, party conventions, and machine politics.
criteria.1-2: Focuses almost entirely on the Kennedys and ignores broader electoral structures.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few national figures but does not explain how JFK's absence changes their incentives or outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant actors or mechanisms, such as LBJ, Nixon, Catholicism, or Democratic convention dynamics.
criteria.7-8: Explains how JFK's absence reshapes Democratic nomination contests, Republican strategy, regional voting, and VP choices.
criteria.9-10: Richly integrates multiple actors and mechanisms, including party factions, electoral geography, campaign style, running-mate logic, and machine support, without overclaiming.

criteria.name: Plausibility Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer presents uncertainty appropriately, distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes, and avoids internal contradictions or conflicts with known historical constraints.
criteria.1-2: Highly deterministic, internally contradictory, or dependent on clearly impossible historical claims.
criteria.3-4: Some plausible ideas but frequent overconfidence, unsupported leaps, or timeline inconsistencies.
criteria.5-6: Generally plausible and mostly consistent, but with some weakly supported assumptions or underexplained contingencies.
criteria.7-8: Uses calibrated language, notes alternative paths, and maintains consistency with ages, offices, elections, and known personalities.
criteria.9-10: Carefully balances uncertainty and causal confidence, explicitly flags contingencies, avoids contradictions, and preserves historical constraints throughout the counterfactual chain.

items.model_answer:
If John F. Kennedy had died during the PT-109 incident in the summer of 1943, the trajectory of the Kennedy political dynasty, the Cold War, and American domestic policy in the 1960s would have been fundamentally altered. 

Immediately, his death would have shifted the intense presidential ambitions of his father, Joseph P. Kennedy Sr. Historically, Joe Sr. focused his hopes on his eldest son, Joe Jr., and only shifted to John after Joe Jr. was killed in action in 1944. If both of the eldest sons had died in World War II, the immense pressure and financial backing of the Kennedy political machine would have fallen directly onto the third son, Robert F. Kennedy. Robert would likely have been groomed for a Massachusetts congressional seat in the late 1940s instead of serving as John’s campaign manager and eventual Attorney General, fundamentally changing Robert's political development from a behind-the-scenes enforcer to a frontline candidate much earlier in life.

Without JFK in the political arena, the 1960 presidential election would have looked entirely different. Kennedy’s youth, charisma, and mastery of the emerging medium of television were the deciding factors in his razor-thin victory over Richard Nixon. Without him, the 1960 Democratic nomination would likely have gone to Lyndon B. Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, or Stuart Symington. Because the historical margins were so close, it is highly probable that Richard Nixon would have won the 1960 election, ascending to the presidency eight years earlier than he actually did.

A Nixon presidency in 1961 would have drastically reshaped the Cold War. Nixon was a staunch, hawkish anti-communist who likely would have authorized direct U.S. military air support during the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, potentially overthrowing Fidel Castro but risking an immediate military confrontation with the Soviet Union. If the Cuban Missile Crisis still occurred under his watch, Nixon’s reliance on military advisors might have led him to favor preemptive airstrikes rather than the naval blockade JFK utilized, significantly increasing the risk of a global nuclear war. Furthermore, the early stages of American involvement in Vietnam would have been directed by Nixon, potentially accelerating the deployment of U.S. ground troops.

Domestically, the absence of JFK would mean the cultural mythology of "Camelot" would never exist, depriving the early 1960s of its signature youthful idealism. More importantly, Kennedy would not have been assassinated in 1963. The national grief following his martyrdom was the primary emotional catalyst that Lyndon B. Johnson used to strong-arm the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the sweeping "Great Society" welfare programs through a reluctant Congress. Under a Nixon administration, civil rights progress likely would have proceeded at a much slower, more moderate pace, and the modern American welfare state would look vastly different today.

nodes.text: If John F. Kennedy had died during the PT-109 incident in the summer of 1943,
the trajectory of the Kennedy political dynasty, the Cold War, and American domestic policy in the 1960s would have been fundamentally altered.
Immediately, his death would have shifted the intense presidential ambitions of his father, Joseph P. Kennedy Sr.
Historically, Joe Sr. focused his hopes on his eldest son, Joe Jr.,
and only shifted to John after Joe Jr. was killed in action in 1944.
If both of the eldest sons had died in World War II,
the immense pressure and financial backing of the Kennedy political machine would have fallen directly onto the third son, Robert F. Kennedy.
Robert would likely have been groomed for a Massachusetts congressional seat in the late 1940s instead of serving as John’s campaign manager and eventual Attorney General,
fundamentally changing Robert's political development from a behind-the-scenes enforcer to a frontline candidate much earlier in life.
Without JFK in the political arena,
the 1960 presidential election would have looked entirely different.
Kennedy’s youth, charisma, and mastery of the emerging medium of television were the deciding factors in his razor-thin victory over Richard Nixon.
Without him,
the 1960 Democratic nomination would likely have gone to Lyndon B. Johnson, Hubert Humphrey, or Stuart Symington.
Because the historical margins were so close,
it is highly probable that Richard Nixon would have won the 1960 election,
ascending to the presidency eight years earlier than he actually did.
A Nixon presidency in 1961 would have drastically reshaped the Cold War.
Nixon was a staunch, hawkish anti-communist
who likely would have authorized direct U.S. military air support during the 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion,
potentially overthrowing Fidel Castro
but risking an immediate military confrontation with the Soviet Union.
If the Cuban Missile Crisis still occurred under his watch,
Nixon’s reliance on military advisors might have led him to favor preemptive airstrikes rather than the naval blockade JFK utilized,
significantly increasing the risk of a global nuclear war.
Furthermore, the early stages of American involvement in Vietnam would have been directed by Nixon,
potentially accelerating the deployment of U.S. ground troops.
Domestically, the absence of JFK would mean the cultural mythology of "Camelot" would never exist,
depriving the early 1960s of its signature youthful idealism.
More importantly, Kennedy would not have been assassinated in 1963.
The national grief following his martyrdom was the primary emotional catalyst
that Lyndon B. Johnson used to strong-arm the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the sweeping "Great Society" welfare programs through a reluctant Congress.
Under a Nixon administration,
civil rights progress likely would have proceeded at a much slower, more moderate pace,
and the modern American welfare state would look vastly different today.

items.question: What If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981?
human_answers: The core problem with these discussions is that you wind up with a lot of people who had personal experience with home computers imagining their home computer was a long-term viable platform particularly killed by the IBM PC. The inherent market dynamic was, instead, that all the home computers were doomed to extinction at the hands of the standard business personal computer platform. It is businesses that care about backward compatibility with their internal installed base, while the home computer user market has an observable willingness to abandon old platforms and adopt new ones. This means home-targeted versions of the business platform can easily be adopted by the home market, while business-targeted versions of home platforms can only get adopted by businesses if they have a specific compelling business advantage. And then, as soon as the business platform clones the advantage, the home platform is again on the defensive. Home platforms are thus in an inherently weak position, and will be smashed flat by the standard business platform. And, well, there was already a standard business personal computer platform in 1980-1981 -- the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. You could buy that platform as an Osborne 1, or as a Xerox 820, or from any of dozens of other of other makers. You even had the Microsoft Softcard (originally, "Z-80 Softcard", but Zilog complained) which used an Apple II as a host for a 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The major problem that the CP/M-80 platform had going forward was that it had run up against the 64k RAM addressing limit of the 8080/8085/Z80, at a time when RAM prices had dropped enough that it was entirely practical to buy more. And since none of the chipmakers had had the sense to make a 8080-compatible processor with wider addressing, the only real way forward was the 8086/8088, since 8080 assembly code could be easily machine-translated into 8086 code. Everybody was just waiting on Digital Research to get CP/M-86 out. The IBM PC then arrived, with an OS that was arguably even more compatible in its system calls with CP/M-80, and the ability to use all the RAM anybody could practically afford. (Even if Gates never said 640K was enough for anybody, in 1981 that was true. Indeed, the first version of the PC's BIOS had a 544K limit.) It was the perfectly natural successor to the 8080-compatible running CP/M-80. The IBM endorsement made the transition smoother, and did have some secondary consequences (killing the S-100 bus, for example), but the true key to the IBM PC's success is that it was the natural successor-host for a software ecosystem that had grown up on top of the Altair 8800. What happens in the absence of the IBM PC is simple enough. Digital Research will release CP/M-86. At which point the CP/M-86 systems take over the business market, and eventually all the home computer platforms are killed by the multi-manufacturer business standard, just as in the original timeline.

As I understand it, the IBM machine was intended as an 'intelligent terminal' for their mainframes .. Businesses already had mainframes & dumb terminals but because the terminals were dumb the mainframe had to do everything - which led to limits on the numbers - and whilst IBM would be happy to sell (rent) you another mainframe they then run into the problem of getting the mainframes to talk 'seamlessly' to each other ... so IBM work on evermore powerful / more expensive mainframes as the number of users go up .. If, however, you can off-load some of the 'housekeeping' (things like deciding how to repaint the screen as the user edits a file, without the entire screen contents having to be resent from the mainframe, for example) onto the terminal, you can roll out cheap low end mainframes (at the same cost as the high end ones, naturally) able to cope with 100's more users .. Other companies wanted to 'get in on' IBM's business but had difficulties building mainframes as powerful as the IBM ones = thus, sooner or later, some-one else is going to come up with the concept of 'intelligent terminals' .. after which the PC becomes more or less inevitable ..
items.original_question: What if no IBM PC (2026 ed.) In short - the IBM PC (model 5150) was not an inevitable thing, the IBM leadership was highly skeptical of the project and it would not have seen the light of the day had things gone just slightly differently. So, what if that computer had never been created? My take - the personal computer market would look a lot like mobile or console market - a walled garden of 2-3 incompatible standards, probably Apple and Commodore (which, would do better financially without the competition from PC clones). It's interesting what would happen in Japan and (later) China.

items.model_answer:
If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981, the personal computer market of the early 1980s would have remained highly fragmented for a much longer period. At the time, the industry was divided among incompatible proprietary systems from companies like Apple, Commodore, and Tandy, alongside a loose ecosystem of CP/M-based machines. Without IBM’s entry, CP/M would have likely remained the standard operating system for early business microcomputers, and software developers would have continued to face the burden of rewriting their programs for dozens of different, incompatible hardware platforms. 

The most profound immediate impact would have been the delayed adoption of personal computers in the corporate world. In 1981, microcomputers were still largely viewed by enterprise IT departments as hobbyist toys. The IBM brand provided the crucial legitimacy that convinced large corporations to trust desktop computing, famously summarized by the adage, "Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM." Without this stamp of approval, businesses would have likely prolonged their reliance on mainframes and minicomputers accessed via dumb terminals, slowing the transition to decentralized workplace computing by several years.

Furthermore, the absence of the IBM PC would have prevented the rise of the "PC clone" industry and the subsequent "Wintel" (Windows and Intel) duopoly. Because IBM built its PC using off-the-shelf parts and an open architecture, competitors like Compaq were able to reverse-engineer the system, creating a massive, standardized hardware ecosystem. Without this open standard, the Intel x86 processor architecture and Microsoft’s MS-DOS would not have become universal defaults. Microsoft might have remained a moderately successful vendor of programming languages rather than an operating system monopoly, and Intel would have faced much stiffer, prolonged competition from alternative chips like the Motorola 68000.

Ultimately, the computing industry would have still standardized out of economic necessity, but the winner would have been entirely different. Apple might have successfully captured the corporate market with the Macintosh, establishing a computing monopoly based on closed hardware and software. Alternatively, a consortium of manufacturers might have eventually negotiated a unified hardware standard. Regardless of the victor, the technological landscape today would look drastically different, likely characterized by a slower initial evolution of hardware, isolated software ecosystems, and a completely different dominant operating system in place of Microsoft Windows.

edus.text: If the IBM PC had never been released in 1981,
the personal computer market of the early 1980s would have remained highly fragmented for a much longer period.
At the time, the industry was divided among incompatible proprietary systems from companies like Apple, Commodore, and Tandy,
alongside a loose ecosystem of CP/M-based machines.
Without IBM’s entry, CP/M would have likely remained the standard operating system for early business microcomputers,
and software developers would have continued to face the burden of rewriting their programs for dozens of different, incompatible hardware platforms.
The most profound immediate impact would have been the delayed adoption of personal computers in the corporate world.
In 1981, microcomputers were still largely viewed by enterprise IT departments as hobbyist toys.
The IBM brand provided the crucial legitimacy that convinced large corporations to trust desktop computing,
famously summarized by the adage, "Nobody ever got fired for buying IBM."
Without this stamp of approval, businesses would have likely prolonged their reliance on mainframes and minicomputers accessed via dumb terminals,
slowing the transition to decentralized workplace computing by several years.
Furthermore, the absence of the IBM PC would have prevented the rise of the "PC clone" industry and the subsequent "Wintel" (Windows and Intel) duopoly.
Because IBM built its PC using off-the-shelf parts and an open architecture,
competitors like Compaq were able to reverse-engineer the system,
creating a massive, standardized hardware ecosystem.
Without this open standard, the Intel x86 processor architecture and Microsoft’s MS-DOS would not have become universal defaults.
Microsoft might have remained a moderately successful vendor of programming languages rather than an operating system monopoly,
and Intel would have faced much stiffer, prolonged competition from alternative chips like the Motorola 68000.
Ultimately, the computing industry would have still standardized out of economic necessity,
but the winner would have been entirely different.
Apple might have successfully captured the corporate market with the Macintosh,
establishing a computing monopoly based on closed hardware and software.
Alternatively, a consortium of manufacturers might have eventually negotiated a unified hardware standard.
Regardless of the victor, the technological landscape today would look drastically different,
likely characterized by a slower initial evolution of hardware, isolated software ecosystems, and a completely different dominant operating system in place of Microsoft Windows.

items.question: What If No P51 Bomber Escort?
human_answers: The P-51B/C/D was clearly a better dogfighter at medium and low altitude, but at 25-30,000ft the R-2800 engine in the P-47 maintained power even better than the Packard Merlin and the DB-605 engine in the Bf-109G. The P-47 was made to rule at 30,000ft. The P-47 shootdown almost the same number of fighters as the P-51, and the highest scoring USAAF groups in the ETO were P-47 units. Yes, the P-51 was shooting down more German fighters from mid-1944 on but that was because the P-51 was given the high-altitude job where they would encounter more enemy fighters while the P-47 was given most of the low altitude work like CAS, and interdiction missions. This is not to take away any credit from the P-51 but in most histories the Mustang gets the glory, and the Thunderbolt is relegated to being a ground support aircraft. The Mustang was clearly given the right name. She was fast and graceful and could dance with the best of them. The Thunderbolt had the right name as well. She was a warhorse that could absorb more punishment and bring her pilot home while raining thunder on the enemy. The P-38 Lightning is another also run for more complicated reasons, but she has her admirers for many reasons. And in 4th place the P-40 Warhawk held the line from 1940-43. Strangely it's the Mustang and the Flying Tigers Warhawk that are remembered best.

Hence my post about Big Week, P-47 provided 80% of the escort fighters during that effort. I doubt very many people realize that. P-38 is an interesting plane, read an interview with a high scoring German ace who said that provided it was being flown by a pilot who knew how to handle it he thought the P-38 was the toughest Allied fighter he faced. It also presented the Japanese with a difficult tactical problem in that it flew higher and faster than both the Zero and the Oscar. General Kenney liked it best because of the two engines. His pilots flew a lot of missions over water and he appreciated what two engines provided in that sense. General Chennault did not like for the same reason. He was at the ass end of a long logistics chain in a lower priority theater. To him two engines just meant twice the engine maintenance. The P-40 deserves much more credit that it gets. Only the P-51 and P-47 were produced in greater numbers (for US fighters), it was used extensively in the MTO, PTO, and CBI theaters well into 1944 and it was used by more Allied air forces than any other fighter. It was not a thoroughbred by it was definitely a work horse and sometimes that is what you need.

Cost to buy and operate the P-47 was not a factor - USA have had the money, material and fuel. They were after all buying and using the P-38, that offered no savings in any category. P-47 was made in more than 15000 copies. The P-47 was turned into a ground attack aircraft after the fact, and fact being that Merlin Mustang was rangier, a bit faster and a better climber. A combination of the P-51 getting the drop tanks earlier, and the better mileage on internal fuel made it the premier LR fighter of the war. Two very common 75 gal drop tanks make the P-51 going much further than if two 75 gal drop tanks are carried by the P-47 or the P-38. Some mix-up happened there. As-is, it could not do the job. With a bit of foresight, it might've come close. People at USAAF will need to request that P-47 is outfitted with wing racks from day one (ie. already in 1942, so it is debugged and ready for 1943), and there should be the drive to increase the internal fuel tankage. In OTL, the 1st increase was achieved by removing the stuff between the main tank and the top of fuselage so the main tank can get bigger, now with 270 instead of 205 US gals. That change upped the internal fuel tankage to 370 gals, that, together with 2x 150 gal drop tanks, enabled the theoretical 600 mile combat radius under the demanding ETO rules (that included cruising at more than 300 mph TAS at 25000 ft). There is also the need for the actual drop tanks to be available in the UK, with clear contracts with the suppliers. The know 'bubbletop' P-47Ds were the 1st with the main tank being at 270 gals. If there was the earlier go with adding some fuel tanks in the wings - even if it is not a 'surgery' as what was done with the P-47N, but perhaps 2x 50 gals? - together with a drop tank under the fuselage, the radius would've been increased even more, equaling the best P-51D values.

The P 47 was an incredible fighter and despite it's sheer size was fairly good in a dogfight. The P-51 Mustang was until the Rolls Royce Merlin was used a low level fighter at best. The V-1710 engine was fine but needed the two stage supercharger and the like which did happen it just took time. Drop Tanks and education on how to achieve maximum range needed to happen in order to make the Mustand what it became. The P-51 B was the start of the Merlin engines and gave it excellent high altitude performance. The P-47 on the other hand did not need an engine swap to be effective. Instead doctrine and production numbers made the difference. The most important use of the daylight bomber offensive, was the decimation of the Luftwaffe and this occurred in measurable ways. The P-38 was suffering from poor pilot training and tactics. THe presence of 3 high performance fighters whose abilities compliment each other is very desirable.
items.original_question: What if No P51 Bomber Escort? From Jan 1944 the Merlin engined P51 could escort the Bombers all the way to Berlin and beyond and destroyed the Luftwaffe in doing so. However, I would argue the P47 could have done the same job but The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft. twice the cost in construction and fuel consumption. Really the game changer was the drop tank although the P51 was the best host for them by far I think of the P51 as the sleek technical European sports car sipping fuel, with the P47 as a brute, "cubes is everything", American muscle car guzzling gas like there was no tomorrow. The POD would be North American builds P40s instead of creating the new P51 design for the British. The distance the P-47 could cover evolved rapidly as new tanks were engineered: Early 1943 (No tanks): ~175 miles. (Could barely reach the Dutch border). Mid 1943 (75-gal belly tank): ~230 miles. (Reached Antwerp/Ruhr Valley). Late 1943 (108-gal belly tank): ~375 miles. (Reached Frankfurt). Early 1944 (Maximal 3-tank setup): 475–500+ miles. The P47 did not get the escort gig because it was twice the cost and it was a superb ground attack aircraft with its radial engine. OTL the Mustang was a dangerous aircraft to strafe German airfields while a much better dogfighter than the P47 [fixed after tomo mentioned]. I believe more P51s lost to ground fire than air combat. But I would argue that the Mustang was the best solution to the need for an escort, but the P47 could have done the job. Standardising on the P47 would simplify the training and operations of the fighter arm but at double the cost would it have been as effective and escort in numbers? I look forward to your thoughts.

items.model_answer:
If the P-51 Mustang had never been introduced as a long-range bomber escort during World War II, the Allied strategic bombing campaign and the overall trajectory of the war in Europe would have been drastically altered. Historically, the P-51 provided the critical range and combat performance needed to escort heavy bombers deep into German territory, effectively destroying the Luftwaffe in the air and on the ground. Without it, the United States Army Air Forces (USAAF) would have continued to suffer the unsustainable bomber losses experienced during unescorted deep-penetration raids in 1943, such as the disastrous strikes on Schweinfurt and Regensburg.

Faced with catastrophic casualties, the USAAF would likely have been forced to abandon daylight precision bombing entirely and join the British Royal Air Force in conducting less accurate nighttime area bombing. Alternatively, the military would have had to pour immense resources into extending the range of existing fighters like the P-47 Thunderbolt and P-38 Lightning through massive drop tanks and aerodynamic modifications. While the P-38 had the range, it suffered from severe engine and heating issues at high European altitudes, and while the P-47 was highly capable, it burned fuel too quickly to be an efficient deep-penetration escort. 

The most significant strategic consequence would have been the survival of the Luftwaffe as a potent defensive force well into 1944. Total Allied air superiority was a strict prerequisite for Operation Overlord. Without the P-51 aggressively sweeping the skies ahead of the bomber streams and decimating German fighter squadrons, the D-Day landings in Normandy would have been fiercely contested from the air. This threat likely would have forced Allied commanders to delay the invasion until 1945 or risk catastrophic failure on the beaches. 

A delayed Western Allied advance would have prolonged the war in Europe by many months. Geopolitically, this delay would have allowed the Soviet Union's Red Army to push much further west before meeting American and British forces, potentially bringing all of Germany and even parts of the Low Countries under Soviet control, drastically redrawing the post-war Iron Curtain. Furthermore, if the European war had dragged into late summer 1945, the first atomic bombs developed by the Manhattan Project might have been dropped on German cities rather than Japan.

items.question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982?
human_answers: If GB got beat up per the OPs post and had to give up and go home I am not sure why Argentina would care about upsetting BG with the treatment of British Citizens on an “Argentine island”. They didn’t care about upsetting GB when the invaded and that was before the Royal Navy got beet like a stray dog and sent home with its tail between is legs. So why on earth would Argentina worry about what GB would think? I suspect a lot of folks will leave the Island and i expect Argentina would do everything it could to encourage that. Including being a bit heavy handed and sending over a good number of “settlers” and giving control of everything to its citizens and such. And I would not be surprised that Argentina was a bit brutal. Not the point of blatant executions as that would put them over the line internationally and they don’t really want that kind of reputation for no good reason, frankly I doubt the then current government really cares what happens to the locals or on the island its goal was to take it and use that propaganda to shore up the government. So yes it won’t be fun on the island and many will leave but I doubt it gets to bad, I suspect the local economy goes to hell but I don’t trully know enough about that to say.

What seems to have happened is that the Argentinian occupation forces initially expelled a small number of Kelpers, which attracted international criticism, then a further 14 potential 'troublemakers' were sent to Fox Bay East and placed under house arrest. Otherwise, the occupying forces seem to have been generally respectful - the principal exceptions being at Goose Green, where the civilian population was locked up in the social hall, and Patricio Dowling overstepping his authority as chief of police. The latter was apparently sufficiently objectionable that he was removed by the Argentinian forces. If the islands remained under Argentinian control, I would expect that those 14 might get deported, and favourable conditions offered for anyone wishing to leave voluntarily. Argentinian settlers seem like a given, at a bare minimum to replace departed Kelpers and possibly more - probably subsidised to do so, which won't help the condition of the Argentinian public purse. What, exactly, they would do there I don't know. I'd expect a boom in the popularity of mutton in Argentina as a 'patriotic' product of the 'liberated' islands. Over time the administration would surely revert to the mean of whatever was happening in mainland Argentina. It would be interesting to see what happens if/when Argentina undergoes its economic troubles. If the replacement of Kelpers with Argentinians hasn't progressed very far, I could easily see loud voices for ' erm... can we have the British back now?' on the islands.

I've studied this topic quite a bit and can say with confidence that Arg military did not go in with any concrete, long term plans on what to do with the locals. Their initial move was to try and keep a low profile (correctly) fearing that any incidents would only strengthen the UK's position, but this was more of on the spot decision by General Menendez than anything. My best guess is, if the UK fleet is defeated, eventually most of the locals will end up leaving on their own. Argentinean society is very Kafkean, and complex paperwork is needed for the most simple things. Unless islanders try to work with new local authorities, they will soon find themselves without the ability to drive cars (no driving licenses), lack of permits and licenses to practice trades, unable to open bank accounts, and unpaid property taxes piling up. Solving these things would entail applying for Argentinean ID cards, which could be interpreted as accepting Argentinean rule. I figure most people would refuse and just leave (unless the new authorities go out of their way to accommodate them.)

Probably nothing, except perhaps deporting a few troublemakers and using bureaucracy to force them to take Argentine ids. Even if Argentina wins the war, the Latin America debt crisis will be hitting by August '82, so I don't see that dictatorship lasting and, by that time, it wasn't as murderous as it was prior to 1980. The government, either the dictatorship or a new democratic government replacing it later, may enact tax breaks in the islands, like it had been done with Tierra del Fuego, to attempt to populate them. It doesn't need to be very successful, as they only had about 2000 inhabitants and Argentina had a population of about 30 million. As long as 3000 people move in, the locals become a minority. That may lead to ethnic tensions down the line, but they are just too few people in a too isolated place and facing a country that earned a reputation by going against one of the world's leading military powers and winning IITL.

Argentina would have gone as far as She could (and probably beyond) to accommodate them. It is of course possible that someone in the Islands would misbehave. That person would be crushed. The whole Argentina (Anaya) assumption was the Goa* Hypothesis. They are not going to come, there is not going to be a war, AND our US friends** shall help us. They were very, as in very, very, conscious of their international public reputation. Had they won the situation of the Kelpers and what the world was shown would be one of their primary preoccupations. As in fact it was during the war * https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Goa ** Argentina, and it's armed forces, was used by the Reagan Administration in the dirty wars in Centro America. Galtieri*** was absolutely convinced that he was an personal friend to most in the Pentagon. And most probably he was right. *** (He was not the one that was all out for Operation Rosario **** that was Anaya that made it an condition on the Navy supporting Galtieri when he, mini, couped Viola and take charge of the Junta) **** https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_invasion_of_the_Falkland_Islands
items.original_question: How would the population of the Falklands have been treated if Argentina had won in 1982? Let’s suppose that HMS Hermes and HMS Invincible had been sunk, forcing the British to make peace and accept the loss of the Falklands. Let’s also suppose that this victory gave the Argentine junta a reprieve of 2-3 additional years, but that it still eventually collapsed so that Argentina followed a political path similar as IOTL. What would the Falklands population have faced? It's almost certain that Buenos Aires would have sent thousands of Argentine settlers to Puerto Argentino/Port Stanley in order to, at least, make the Anglo population a numerical minority and to extinguish any secessionist aspirations. But would this Anglo population have been allowed to remain and then obtain full Argentine citizenship, perhaps even some degree of cultural autonomy, or would it have faced a complete ethnic cleansing in order to permanently erase the Anglo identity of the Falklands? There are fewer than 2,000 people, so if Argentina decided to do it, it wouldn’t have any problem doing so.

items.model_answer:
If Argentina had won the 1982 Falklands War, the treatment of the islanders would have been dictated by the integrationist goals of the Argentine state and the authoritarian nature of the military junta ruling the country at the time. Based on Argentina's actions during its brief occupation of the islands and the junta's domestic track record, the population would have faced forced cultural assimilation, demographic shifts, and a loss of democratic rights.

During the actual 74-day occupation, Argentine authorities began implementing immediate integration measures. They made Spanish the official language, renamed Port Stanley to Puerto Argentino, mandated driving on the right side of the road, and began altering school curricula. Had Argentina secured a permanent victory, these policies would have been expanded to fully absorb the islands into Argentina's legal and economic systems. The Argentine government had publicly promised to respect the islanders' customs and offered them dual citizenship, largely to legitimize their territorial claim and avoid international condemnation. To solidify control, the state almost certainly would have incentivized mainland Argentines to settle on the islands to dilute the British-descended majority and shift the demographic balance.

Politically, the islanders would have lost their local democratic institutions. Because Argentina was under a right-wing military dictatorship, the civil liberties of the islanders would have been suspended, mirroring the lack of political freedom on the mainland. 

While the junta might have initially exercised restraint to maintain international approval, the fierce pro-British sentiment of the islanders would have inevitably led to friction. Given the junta's brutal history of suppressing dissent during the "Dirty War"—which involved the forced disappearance, torture, and murder of tens of thousands of political opponents—any organized resistance or vocal opposition by the islanders would likely have been met with harsh repression. Dissidents would have faced arbitrary detention, imprisonment, or deportation. Consequently, historians generally agree that an Argentine victory would have resulted in a mass exodus of the original Falklands population to the United Kingdom or other Commonwealth nations.
