rubrics.question_focus: What If Everyone on Earth Pointed a Laser Pointer at the Moon?

criteria.name: Ordinary Laser Pointer Outcome and Scaling
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons from the actual premise of billions of ordinary laser pointers aimed at the Moon, including visibility limits, beam spread, and comparison with solar illumination.
criteria.1-2: Claims ordinary laser pointers would visibly brighten, damage, move, or significantly heat the Moon with little or no quantitative support.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes the effect is small but gives vague or flawed reasoning, omitting key scale comparisons such as sunlight versus milliwatts per person.
criteria.5-6: Correctly concludes ordinary pointers are not visible from Earth and explains this mainly through total power or beam dilution, with limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Uses sound order-of-magnitude reasoning: only part of humanity can see the Moon, beams spread over a large area, and sunlight overwhelms milliwatt lasers.
criteria.9-10: Clearly shows why the effect is negligible using relevant scales such as billions of 5 mW lasers, lunar surface area, atmospheric loss, beam divergence, and solar illumination around kilowatts per square meter.

criteria.name: Geometric and Observational Setup
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of Moon visibility, lunar phase, aiming, atmospheric transmission, and whether the illuminated region could be observed from Earth.
criteria.1-2: Ignores geometry entirely or assumes everyone on Earth can point at the Moon simultaneously without qualification.
criteria.3-4: Mentions visibility or phase but handles it inconsistently, such as placing the Moon overhead for everyone or confusing new, full, and quarter Moon effects.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges that only a fraction of people can see the Moon and that lunar phase matters, but gives only a rough setup.
criteria.7-8: Accounts for hemisphere/time-zone constraints, atmospheric distortion or absorption, target phase, and why aiming at the dark portion would matter for detectability.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent observational scenario: maximizes participating population, chooses a phase that aids contrast, distinguishes day/night viewing issues, and keeps beam focus and surface coverage physically plausible.

criteria.name: Power Escalation and Brightness Thresholds
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores how increasingly powerful light sources would change the result, rather than treating all lasers as equivalent.
criteria.1-2: Uses a single unsupported claim for all laser powers or confuses brightness, energy, and visibility.
criteria.3-4: Mentions stronger lasers but gives implausible thresholds or no causal explanation for when the Moon becomes visibly brighter.
criteria.5-6: Explains that higher-power devices would be needed and gives approximate qualitative stages, but lacks clear comparisons to lux, sunlight, or lunar illumination.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes ordinary pointers, watt-class lasers, searchlights/projectors, and megawatt-class lasers, with reasonable visibility and power-demand consequences.
criteria.9-10: Accurately tracks escalating regimes: consumer pointers fail, very bright lamps barely help, massive focused searchlights become visible, and megawatt-per-person lasers approach solar-level lunar illumination while requiring planetary-scale power.

criteria.name: Extreme-Energy Lunar and Terrestrial Consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates reasoning about far-counterfactual cases involving enormous lasers, including atmospheric plasma, reflected light, heating, vaporization, ablation, and lunar orbital effects.
criteria.1-2: Jumps to spectacular outcomes such as instant Moon explosion or harmless visibility without mechanisms or scale.
criteria.3-4: Mentions heating or destruction but misses major processes such as atmosphere interaction, reflected radiation, or ablation.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that extreme lasers could heat or vaporize lunar material and endanger Earth, but gives a short or partially incomplete chain.
criteria.7-8: Explains that sufficiently extreme beams would ionize air, ignite or sterilize Earth, heat lunar regolith, vaporize rock, and produce thrust through ejecta.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent high-energy sequence: atmosphere would become plasma unless assumed transparent, reflected Moonlight could exceed sunlight, lunar surface vaporizes into plasma, laser ablation acts like a rocket, and the Moon could be pushed from Earth orbit over time.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence, Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the counterfactual chain remains internally consistent, appropriately caveated, and calibrated across ordinary, powerful, and impossible laser scenarios.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible transitions, or uncaveated certainties that violate earlier assumptions.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct pieces but mixes incompatible assumptions, exaggerates precision, or changes the premise without noting it.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with some caveats, but leaves gaps between stages or overstates uncertain long-term outcomes.
criteria.7-8: Maintains consistent assumptions about power, focusing, atmosphere, and duration; marks speculative parts such as ablation efficiency and later orbital evolution.
criteria.9-10: Separates realistic from deliberately impossible cases, states assumptions before using them, avoids false precision, preserves conservation-of-energy intuition, and treats long-term Moon trajectories as uncertain but causally motivated.

items.model_answer:
If everyone on Earth—about 8 billion people—simultaneously pointed a standard 5-milliwatt laser pointer at the Moon, absolutely nothing noticeable would happen. The combined effort would not change the Moon's appearance, nor would the light be visible to anyone looking up from Earth.

First, the total power output of 8 billion standard laser pointers is roughly 40 megawatts. While this sounds like a massive amount of energy on a human scale, it is practically nothing on a cosmic scale. By comparison, the sunlight hitting the Moon delivers tens of petawatts (tens of millions of gigawatts) of power, completely washing out any artificial light we could shine on its illuminated side. 

Even if humanity coordinated to aim their lasers at the dark side of a new moon to maximize visibility, the experiment would still fail due to beam divergence and atmospheric interference. A standard laser pointer does not shoot a perfectly straight, tightly focused beam forever; the light spreads out as it travels. By the time the beams cross the 384,400 kilometers of space to reach the Moon, a single laser dot would spread out to be hundreds of kilometers wide. 

Furthermore, the Earth's atmosphere would absorb, scatter, and distort a large percentage of the light before it ever reached space. The fraction of the 40 megawatts that actually survived the journey and reached the lunar surface would be spread so incredibly thin that it would provide only a tiny fraction of a milliwatt of illumination per square meter. This artificial light is vastly dimmer than "Earthshine," which is the natural sunlight reflecting off the Earth and faintly illuminating the dark side of the Moon. Consequently, the combined laser light would be completely overwhelmed by natural light and perfectly undetectable to the human eye.

items.question: What If a Giant Water Hose Focused on the Sun?
human_answers: In today’s article, I give short answers to several reader questions. Your brother might be surprised to learn that the water would actually make the Sun hotter! [Image: image] Water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, which is fuel for the Sun’s fusion. But more importantly, the extra mass also makes the Sun heavier. This crushes it together more tightly and makes fusion happen faster. This means it will burn more brightly and run through its fuel more quickly. As you keep adding water, the Sun will go through a lot of wacky fusion phases. (During one phase, called a helium flash, the reaction rate is proportional to the 40th power of the temperature—which is probably the largest exponent I’ve ever seen in a physics equation!) But one way or another, eventually the whole thing will collapse in on itself, blow off its outer layers, and become a black hole. This black hole will keep soaking up water, spraying off X-rays in the process, until finally the municipal water department notices what you’ve been doing and shuts off your service. Believe it or not, you’ve been lied to all your life—there’s no such thing as one-way mirror glass. Glass either lets light through or reflects it, but there’s no glass that lets light through one way and reflects it the other way. The glass in police shows is partially reflective (on both sides). The key is that the room on the prisoner’s side is brightly lit, so the reflection washes out the small amount of light from the observers’ side. [Image: image] He’d most likely black out and die somewhere between 100 and 400 meters. [Image: image] The human body handles pressure remarkably well. With the right preparation, we can survive pressures over a dozen atmospheres. Different body systems break down at different depths, but one of the trickiest limits is created by High Pressure Nervous Syndrome (http://archive.rubicon-foundation.org/xmlui/handle/123456789/2661). Below about 100 meters, divers become jittery and excitable (especially if the pressure increase is rapid), and at the same time begin slipping in and out of sleep. The reason may be direct pressure on the brain (http://jn.physiology.org/content/92/6/3309.full.pdf). But let’s suppose Michael Phelps were immune to all those things. In that case, it simply becomes a question of speed. There aren’t very many records for underwater swimming, but based on how quickly this guy (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vox9KOxC1ZA) completed the 50m backstroke, it would probably take Michael about ... \[ 2\times\text{Depth of Marianas Trench}\times\frac{23.1\textrm{ seconds}}{50\textrm{ meters}}\approx3\textrm{ hours} \] … to make the trip. Someone recently blew my mind by telling me I’d been misinterpreting that scene all my life. I like their take on it way better: Superman wasn't exerting a force on the Earth. He was just flying fast enough to go back in time. (Faster than light, I guess? Comic book physics.) The Earth changed direction because we were watching time run backward as he traveled. It didn't actually have anything to do with the direction he was flying. Now that I see it, it makes a lot more sense. I mean, as much sense as a red-cape-and-outside-underwear time traveler can make. A discussion of the reversal of the Earth’s spin—and what that even means—will have to wait for another article. \[ \frac{\text{Red light wavelength}}{\text{Green light wavelength}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+\frac{\text{Your speed}}{\text{Speed of light}}}{1-\frac{\text{Car speed}}{\text{Speed of light}}}} \] \[ \textrm{Car speed}=\frac{\textrm{c}\times\left ( \textrm{Red light wavelength}^2-\textrm{Green light wavelength}^2\right )}{\textrm{Green light wavelength}^2+\textrm{Red light wavelength}^2}\approx\frac{1}{6}c \] Bernoulli’s principle (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli's_principle#Incompressible_flow_equation) gives us this estimate of the air flow rate: \[ \text{Flow rate}=\sqrt{2\times\frac{\text{Sea level pressure}-\text{Mexico City pressure}}{\text{Density of air}}}=440\textrm{ mph} \] That’s fast enough to strip up the pavement from a parking lot. I suggest we put it in Kendall Square—the MIT folks are probably used to dealing with this kind of thing. This ... isn’t actually a question. [Image: image] But thank you for sharing!

items.model_answer:
Shooting a giant water hose at the Sun would not extinguish it; instead, it would make the Sun burn hotter, brighter, and faster. 

Unlike a campfire, the Sun is not a chemical fire that can be smothered or cooled by water. It is a giant nuclear fusion reactor powered by immense gravity and pressure. Because water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen, pouring water onto the Sun actually feeds it more hydrogen, which is its primary fuel for fusion. Furthermore, the oxygen in the water adds a tremendous amount of mass. 

This added mass would increase the Sun's overall gravitational pull, compressing its core even tighter. The resulting spike in core pressure and temperature would accelerate the nuclear fusion process, causing the Sun to release significantly more energy. If a truly massive amount of water were added—such as a volume equal to the Sun itself—the Sun would grow so heavy and hot that it could transform into a massive, blue-white star. Ultimately, "watering" the Sun would drastically shorten its lifespan and cause it to emit enough intense heat and radiation to completely incinerate the Earth and the rest of the inner solar system.

items.question: What If You Detonated a Nuclear Bomb at the Bottom of the Mariana Trench?
human_answers: Surprisingly little—especially compared to what would happen if you put it just under the surface. Evin isn’t the first person to think of setting off nuclear weapons underwater. In fact, we’ve actually tried it a bunch of times. This (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ggH-ObiUWEE) is what it looks like. Most of the tests, however, involved either small bombs or shallow water. Evin’s scenario concerns neither. At 53 megatons, the Tsar Bomba was the most powerful nuclear weapon ever detonated, and at 11 kilometers, the Mariana(s) Trench is the deepest part of the ocean. No underwater test has involved bombs anywhere near that size, nor depths anywhere near that deep. In 1962, physicist Freeman Dyson wrote a memo discussing eight possible novel weapon systems, all of which looked like they’d be possible in the near future, and outlined the potential military uses and dangers of each. This memo has been declassified, but was never published. Freeman’s son, science historian George Dyson, got a paper copy of the memo from his father, and was kind enough to show it to me. In the memo, one of the eight ideas Freeman discusses is the use of gigaton nuclear weapons as wave generators. It includes this rather terrifying passage describing the detonation of a submerged gigaton mine off the North American coast: “Quantitative study of the destructive effects has not been made. Rough estimates indicate that the inundation would reach to a height of 200-300 feet above sea level, or a distance of 200-300 miles inland, whichever limit is reached first.” [Image: image] Luckily for the coast, later research paints a less dire picture. The seminal work in the field of nuclear ocean waves is Water Waves Generated By Underwater Explosions (http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?Location=U2&doc=GetTRDoc.pdf&AD=ADA304244), a sprawling 400-page report produced for the Department of Defense by Bernard Le Mehaute and Shen Wang. The report, published in 1996, exhaustively examines and summarizes all available research about the ocean waves created by nuclear explosions. The report outlines how when a nuclear weapon goes off underwater, it produces a cavity of hot gasses, which then collapses. If the explosion happens near the surface, it can create some pretty big waves—under some circumstances, they can be hundreds of feet high near ground zero. [Image: image] Or is it ocean zero? Fortunately for the coast, these waves are fundamentally different from tsunamis. It turns out that if the waves are very large, they break early, and expend most of their energy creating a narrow surf zone on the continental shelf. This is potentially hazardous to some ships, but much less catastrophic than a direct nuclear attack. When they reached the coast, the waves would be no worse than those from a bad storm. But those are waves from an explosion close to the surface. A nuke set off deep underwater acts a bit differently. The explosion at the bottom of the Mariana Trench will create a quickly-expanding spherical cavity of hot steam. To figure out how big it gets, we can try a formula from the 1971 paper Evaluation of Various Theoretical Models For Underwater Explosion (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/737271.pdf): \[\text{Radius} = \left (\frac{3}{4\pi}\right )^\frac{1}{3}\left ( \frac{40 \% \times 53\text{ megatons of TNT}}{\text{Mariana Trench pressure}+\text{1 ATM}} \right)^\frac{1}{3}\approx580\text{ meters}\] The bubble grows to about a kilometer across in a couple of seconds. The water above bulges up, though only slightly, over a large area. Then the pressure from that six miles of water overhead causes it to collapse. Within a dozen or so seconds, the bubble shrinks to a minimum size, then ‘bounces’ back, expanding outward again. It goes through three or four cycles of this collapse and expansion before disintegrating into, in the words of the 1996 report, “a mass of turbulent warm water and explosion debris.” According to the report, as a result of such a deep-water closed bubble creation and dissipation, “no wave of any consequence will be generated.” That “turbulent warm water” is actually quite substantial. The rising column of heat creates a hot spot in the ocean—many degrees warmer than the surrounding water—that lingers for some time. [Image: image] Earlier this year, Severe Tropical Storm Sanvu passed over the Mariana Trench. The column of deep, hot water from our nuke could conceivably have been enough to strengthen it into a typhoon, much as the deep warm waters of the Gulf of Mexico’s Loop Current sometimes cause hurricanes to rapidly intensify. In addition to the heat energy from the water, Sanvu could whip up a spray containing fallout from the blast, and approach Iwo Jima as a radioactive whirlwind. Of course, that’s getting a little far-fetched. In the absence of an improbable typhoon interaction, the overall effect of the bomb isn’t quite as dramatic as Evin might have imagined. ... But. All that changes when this cat enters the equation: [Image: image] Literally. Let’s say that when I’m typing the above equation, the cat hops onto my desk and steps on the “0” key, which inserts six extra zeroes: \[\text{Radius} = \left (\frac{3}{4\pi}\right) ^\frac{1}{3}\left ( \frac{40 \% \times 53000000\text{ megatons of TNT}}{\text{Mariana Trench pressure}+\text{1 ATM}} \right)^\frac{1}{3}\approx35\text{ miles}\] If there was enough water, and if the model held up, this blast would expand into a bubble 70 miles across. In reality, the oceans aren’t that deep. Instead, it blows a hole in the Earth’s crust dozens of miles across, leaving a hole through which briefly glows the magma of the mantle. Around the early 1990s, scientists started discovering jumbled fields of petrified wood mixed with sand buried beneath the Louisiana and Texas coast. These turned out to be the remains of North American forests swept out to sea by a massive tsunami. The culprit was a comet or asteroid hitting the Yucatan—the impact that killed most of the dinosaurs. The debris played a key role in identifying the 65-million-year-old Chicxulub impact site—this book (http://www.amazon.com/Crater-Doom-Princeton-Science-Library/dp/0691131031) provides a wonderful account of the unraveling of that mystery. 53,000,000 megatons is approximately the energy of the Chicxulub impact. A blast this size in the Mariana Trench creates kilometer-high waves that engulf the forests of Indonesia, California, and the Pacific Northwest, along with most of coastal China and the rest of the Pacific rim. Huge volumes of rock and water are blasted into space. The debris takes less than an hour to encircle the Earth. As the chunks of rock fall back into the atmosphere, they heat to a glow—like meteors—igniting global firestorms. The hole fills in, with huge columns of steam and great convulsions. The Mariana Trench is gone, and with it Guam and the Mariana Islands. The area is now marked by a 100-kilometer-wide scar of magma sizzling beneath the waters of the Pacific. The majority of the world’s plants die and the food chain collapses completely. Between the famine and the fires, most life on Earth is wiped out. Stupid cat. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If You Detonated a Nuclear Bomb at the Bottom of the Mariana Trench?

criteria.name: Premise specification and scale fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer anchors the counterfactual to the Mariana Trench setting, the depth pressure, and the bomb yield rather than treating it like an atmospheric or shallow-water detonation.
criteria.1-2: Ignores depth, pressure, or yield; treats the event as a generic nuclear blast.
criteria.3-4: Mentions underwater depth but gives little sense of scale or uses implausible assumptions without noting them.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes extreme depth and high pressure; roughly distinguishes large nuclear yield from ocean/geologic scales.
criteria.7-8: Clearly ties effects to ~11 km depth, hydrostatic pressure, and yield-dependent scaling; avoids surface-blast intuition.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the scenario, states assumptions about yield, and uses scale comparisons to constrain all later consequences.

criteria.name: Deep underwater explosion mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the actual physical sequence: energy deposition, steam/gas cavity formation, shock propagation, bubble expansion, collapse, oscillation, and dissipation.
criteria.1-2: Describes fireballs, mushroom clouds, or crater effects as if the bomb detonated in air or on land.
criteria.3-4: Mentions steam or pressure but omits the main bubble-collapse dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Describes a hot cavity or bubble and its collapse under ocean pressure, with some correct qualitative physics.
criteria.7-8: Covers shock wave, temporary vapor cavity, expansion/collapse cycles, and conversion into turbulent hot water.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent mechanism chain with appropriate scaling, explaining why the deep-water bubble remains largely contained.

criteria.name: Surface waves and tsunami reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons about wave generation from a very deep detonation and distinguishes it from shallow underwater blasts or earthquake tsunamis.
criteria.1-2: Predicts world-destroying tsunamis or instant coastal devastation with no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Claims large waves but does not distinguish deep from shallow detonation effects.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that deep detonation reduces surface-wave generation, though details may be incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Explains that most energy remains in the deep bubble/shock system and that surface waves would likely be limited.
criteria.9-10: Accurately states that no consequential tsunami is expected for a plausible bomb at trench depth, while noting shallow detonations would differ.

criteria.name: Downstream environmental, radiological, and geological consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of longer-range effects such as local heating, radioactive contamination, marine impacts, sediment disturbance, and whether global geological consequences are plausible.
criteria.1-2: Invents global crust cracking, mantle exposure, mass extinction, or no effects at all without justification.
criteria.3-4: Lists dramatic consequences but poorly separates plausible local effects from implausible global ones.
criteria.5-6: Identifies local heating, contamination, and marine disturbance; avoids the worst geological exaggerations.
criteria.7-8: Explains lingering warm turbulent water, local fallout/activation concerns, ecological damage, and limited seabed effects.
criteria.9-10: Balances all major downstream effects, including possible contamination transport or storm interaction, while rejecting unsupported earthquakes, volcano triggering, or trench destruction.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence and uncertainty calibration
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a consistent causal chain over time and space, distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes, and avoids contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected claims, internal contradictions, or certainty about impossible outcomes.
criteria.3-4: Has a loose sequence but mixes likely, unlikely, and impossible effects without calibration.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly coherent timeline and uses some cautious language for uncertain effects.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates immediate shock/bubble effects, short-term water disturbance, and longer-term environmental dispersion.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous causal continuity, explicitly flags speculative branches, and only invokes catastrophic outcomes for vastly larger, Chicxulub-scale energies.

items.model_answer:
Detonating a nuclear bomb at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 kilometers (36,000 feet) below sea level, would be surprisingly anticlimactic for anyone watching from the surface. The outcome is dictated entirely by the immense hydrostatic pressure at that depth, which is roughly 1,000 times greater than the atmospheric pressure at sea level. 

Upon detonation, the bomb would release an enormous amount of energy, instantly vaporizing the surrounding water and creating a rapidly expanding bubble of superheated steam and radioactive plasma. However, the crushing weight of the 11-kilometer water column above it would act as a massive dampener. Even if you detonated the most powerful nuclear weapon ever created—the 50-megaton Tsar Bomba—the bubble would only expand to about a kilometer in diameter before the water pressure halted its growth. 

Instead of rising to the surface as a giant sphere, the immense pressure would force the bubble to violently collapse back in on itself. The bubble would oscillate, shrinking and expanding a few times, before breaking apart into a plume of smaller, highly radioactive bubbles of hot water that would gradually rise and cool. 

Because the explosion is contained so deep underwater, it would not create a massive, coastal-destroying tsunami. Tsunamis are typically caused by the displacement of massive tectonic plates, not localized point-source explosions. By the time the energy and displaced water reached the surface, it would likely manifest as a localized, relatively harmless swell, perhaps accompanied by a patch of frothy, turbulent water. Furthermore, the explosion would not trigger a catastrophic earthquake or crack the Earth's crust. While a nuclear blast is powerful, its energy is minuscule compared to the tectonic forces already at play in the subduction zone, and the rock would easily absorb the shockwave.

The primary consequence would be localized environmental devastation. The immense shockwave would instantly kill all deep-sea marine life within several kilometers of the blast. The radioactive isotopes generated by the explosion would largely be trapped in the deep ocean, mixing with the frigid bottom waters. Over hundreds or thousands of years, deep-sea currents would slowly circulate this radioactive material around the globe, though it would become highly diluted by the vast volume of the world's oceans.

nodes.text: Detonating a nuclear bomb at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, nearly 11 kilometers (36,000 feet) below sea level, would be surprisingly anticlimactic for anyone watching from the surface.
The outcome is dictated entirely by the immense hydrostatic pressure at that depth,
which is roughly 1,000 times greater than the atmospheric pressure at sea level.
Upon detonation, the bomb would release an enormous amount of energy,
instantly vaporizing the surrounding water and creating a rapidly expanding bubble of superheated steam and radioactive plasma.
However, the crushing weight of the 11-kilometer water column above it would act as a massive dampener.
Even if you detonated the most powerful nuclear weapon ever created—the 50-megaton Tsar Bomba—
the bubble would only expand to about a kilometer in diameter
before the water pressure halted its growth.
Instead of rising to the surface as a giant sphere, the immense pressure would force the bubble to violently collapse back in on itself.
The bubble would oscillate, shrinking and expanding a few times,
before breaking apart into a plume of smaller, highly radioactive bubbles of hot water
that would gradually rise and cool.
Because the explosion is contained so deep underwater,
it would not create a massive, coastal-destroying tsunami.
Tsunamis are typically caused by the displacement of massive tectonic plates,
not localized point-source explosions.
By the time the energy and displaced water reached the surface,
it would likely manifest as a localized, relatively harmless swell,
perhaps accompanied by a patch of frothy, turbulent water.
Furthermore, the explosion would not trigger a catastrophic earthquake or crack the Earth's crust.
While a nuclear blast is powerful,
its energy is minuscule compared to the tectonic forces already at play in the subduction zone,
and the rock would easily absorb the shockwave.
The primary consequence would be localized environmental devastation.
The immense shockwave would instantly kill all deep-sea marine life within several kilometers of the blast.
The radioactive isotopes generated by the explosion would largely be trapped in the deep ocean,
mixing with the frigid bottom waters.
Over hundreds or thousands of years, deep-sea currents would slowly circulate this radioactive material around the globe,
though it would become highly diluted by the vast volume of the world's oceans.

items.question: What If You Stayed in a Swimming Pool During a Thunderstorm?
human_answers: Before we go any further, I want to emphasize something: I am not an authority on lightning safety. I am a guy who draws pictures on the internet. I like when things catch fire and explode, which means I do not have your best interests in mind. The authorities on lightning safety are the folks at the US National Weather Service: http://www.lightningsafety.noaa.gov/ (http://www.lightningsafety.noaa.gov/) (http://www.lightningsafety.noaa.gov/) Ok. With that out of the way ... To answer these questions, we need to get an idea of where lightning is likely to go. There’s a cool trick for this, and I’ll give it away right here at the start: Roll an imaginary 60-meter sphere across the landscape and look at where it touches. They say lightning strikes the tallest thing around. That’s the kind of maddeningly inexact statement that immediately sparks all kinds of questions. How far is “around”? I mean, not all lightning hits Mt. Everest. But does it find the tallest person in a crowd? The tallest person I know is probably Ryan North (paleontologists estimate he stood nearly five meters tall at the shoulder). Should I try to hang around him for lightning safety reasons? What about other reasons? (This is probably why you people ask the questions on this blog, not me.) But how does lightning pick its targets? This video (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1mB5rM8WHU), captured by Tom A. Warner, might be the single coolest piece of footage I’ve ever seen. It shows a bolt of lightning recorded at 7,207 frames per second. The 33-second video represents barely a tenth of a second of real time. There are lots of slow-motion videos of lightning, but this is by far the best I’ve found. Tom’s video gives an idea of how lightning moves. It starts with a branching bundle of charge—the “leader”—descending from the cloud. This is what you see in the first part of the video. It spreads downward at speeds of tens to hundreds of kilometers per second, covering the few kilometers to the ground in a few dozen milliseconds. The leader carries comparatively little current—on the order of 200 amps. That’s still enough to kill you, but it’s nothing compared to what happens next. Once the leader makes contact with the ground, the cloud and the ground equalize with a massive discharge of more like 20,000 amps. This is the blinding flash you see. It races back up the channel at a significant fraction of the speed of light, covering the distance in under a millisecond—all within a single frame of that video. (Technical detail: while it’s called a “return stroke”, charge is still flowing downward. However, the discharge appears to propagate upward. This effect similar to how when a traffic light turns green, or whatever (http://xkcd.com/1116/) color, the cars in front start moving, then the cars in back, so the movement appears to spread backward.) So the place on the ground where we see a bolt “strike” is the spot where the leader first makes contact with the surface. The leader moves down through the air in little jumps. It’s ultimately feeling its way toward the (usually) positive charge in the ground. However, it only “feels” charges within a few tens of meters of the tip. If there’s something connected to the ground within that distance, the bolt will jump to it. Otherwise, it jumps out in a semi-random direction and repeats the process. [Image: image] This is where the 60-meter sphere comes in. It’s a way to imagine what spots might be the first thing the leader senses—the places it might jump to in its next (final) step. To figure out where lightning is likely to hit, you roll the imaginary 60-meter sphere across the landscape (for safety reasons, do not use a real sphere). This sphere climbs up over trees and buildings without passing through anything (or rolling it up). Places the surface makes contact—treetops, fenceposts, and golfers in fields—are potential lightning targets. This means you can calculate a lightning “shadow” around an object of height h on a flat surface. [Image: image] The shadow is the area where the leader is likely to hit the tall object instead of the ground around it: \[\text{Shadow Radius}=\sqrt{-h(h-2r)}\] Now, that doesn’t mean you’re safe on the ground around it—often, it means the opposite. After the current hits the tall object, it flows out into the ground. If you’re touching the ground nearby, it can travel through your body. Of the 28 people killed by lightning so far this year, 13 were standing under or near trees (http://www.lightningsafety.noaa.gov/fatalities.htm). With all this in mind, let’s look at possible lightning paths for the scenarios in the questions. How dangerous is it, really, to be in a pool during a thunderstorm? Pretty dangerous. Water is conductive, but that’s not the biggest problem—the biggest problem is that if you’re swimming, your head is poking up from a large flat surface. But lightning striking the water near you would still be bad. The 20,000 amps spread outward—mostly over the surface (http://www.pbs.org/wgbh/nova/earth/dwyer-lightning.html)—but how much of a jolt it will give you at what distance is hard to calculate My guess is that you’d be in significant danger anywhere within a minimum of a dozen meters—and further in fresh water, because the current will be happier to take a shortcut through you. What would happen if you were taking a shower when you were struck by lightning? Or standing under a waterfall? [Image: image] You’re not in danger from the spray—it’s just a bunch of droplets of water in the air. It’s the tub under your feet, and the puddle of water in contact with the plumbing, that’s the real threat. What would happen if you were in a boat or a plane that got hit by lightning? Or a submarine? [Image: image] A boat without a cabin is about as safe as a golf course. A boat with a closed cabin and a lightning protection system is about as safe as a car. A submarine is about as safe as a submarine safe (a submarine safe is not to be confused with a safe in a submarine—a safe in a submarine is substantially safer than a submarine safe). What if you were changing the light at the top of a radio tower and lightning struck? Or what if you were doing a backflip? Or standing in a graphite field? Or looking straight up at the bolt? [Image: image] What would happen if lightning struck a bullet in midair? The bullet won't affect the path the lightning takes. You'd have somehow to time the shot so the bullet was in the middle of the bolt when the return stroke happened. The core of a lightning bolt is a few centimeters in diameter (http://www.agu.org/pubs/crossref/1968/JB073i006p01889.shtml). A bullet fired from an AK-47 is about 26 mm long and moves at about 700 millimeters every millisecond. The bullet has a copper coating over a lead core. Copper is a fantastically good conductor of electricity, and much of the 20,000 amps could easily take a shortcut through the bullet. [Image: image] Surprisingly, the bullet handles it pretty well. If it were sitting still, the current would quickly heat and melt the metal. But it’s moving along so quickly that it exits the channel before it can be warmed by more than a few degrees. It continues on to its target relatively unaffected. There are some curious electromagnetic forces created by the magnetic field around the bolt and the current flow through the bullet, but none of the ones I examined changed the overall picture very much. What if you were flashing your BIOS during a thunderstorm and you got hit by lightning? [Image: image]

criteria.name: Lightning attachment and strike-path mechanism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly explains how lightning would choose targets around a swimming pool, including the role of upward/stepped leaders, nearby tall objects, and the swimmer's head protruding above a flat conductive surface.
criteria.1-2: Claims lightning simply seeks water or ignores target geometry; gives little or no mechanism.
criteria.3-4: Mentions tall objects or water attraction but with major simplifications or misleading causal claims.
criteria.5-6: Explains that nearby height and grounding affect strike likelihood, but omits leader attachment details or pool-specific geometry.
criteria.7-8: Accurately describes likely strike points, including the swimmer's exposed head, pool deck, ladders, and nearby structures.
criteria.9-10: Gives a precise, pool-specific account of leader attachment, local electric fields, tall-object shielding limits, and why the swimmer remains a plausible strike point.

criteria.name: Current propagation through pool water and surroundings
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly traces what happens after a strike: current spreading through water, over surfaces, into plumbing/metal fixtures, through the deck, and potentially through the swimmer.
criteria.1-2: Says the whole pool is uniformly electrified or that water fully protects the swimmer.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes electrocution risk but gives vague or physically confused current paths.
criteria.5-6: Describes current spreading through water and nearby conductors with some correct but incomplete detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains surface spreading, voltage gradients, metal fixtures, ladders, plumbing, and distance-dependent risk.
criteria.9-10: Coherently models multiple strike cases—direct hit, nearby water hit, deck/fixture hit—and how salinity, pool chemistry, geometry, and grounding change current distribution.

criteria.name: Human injury and survival consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer covers the likely physiological outcomes of remaining in the pool, from direct strike to nearby strike, including cardiac, neurological, burn, respiratory, and drowning risks.
criteria.1-2: Only says the person dies or is fine, with no injury mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Mentions electrocution but misses major outcomes such as cardiac arrest or drowning.
criteria.5-6: Identifies serious injury risks, including shock and possible death, but lacks causal depth.
criteria.7-8: Covers cardiac arrest, respiratory paralysis, burns, nervous-system effects, loss of consciousness, and secondary drowning risk.
criteria.9-10: Differentiates direct versus indirect strike outcomes and explains why even nonfatal shock in water can become fatal through incapacitation and drowning.

criteria.name: Long-range scenario coherence and downstream effects
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows the counterfactual over time: storm develops, swimmer remains exposed, strike probability changes, lightning event occurs or does not, rescue becomes hazardous, and post-event consequences unfold logically.
criteria.1-2: Gives a one-step answer with no temporal chain beyond 'lightning hits'.
criteria.3-4: Includes some sequence but jumps causally or ignores key downstream effects.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible short chain from exposure to injury but limited aftermath or alternative paths.
criteria.7-8: Traces exposure, strike likelihood, electrical effects, incapacitation, rescue constraints, emergency response, and possible survival.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a coherent branching timeline covering no-strike, nearby-strike, and direct-strike outcomes, including delayed medical and environmental consequences.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration, safety framing, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer communicates risk without overclaiming, avoids contradictions, and gives appropriate lightning-safety guidance specific to pools and thunderstorms.
criteria.1-2: Gives dangerous advice, dismisses the risk, or contradicts itself about whether water conducts electricity.
criteria.3-4: Warns against swimming but includes unsupported certainties or inconsistent claims.
criteria.5-6: Generally advises leaving the pool, with some uncertainty but limited precision.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states that staying in the pool is dangerous, recommends getting indoors or into a hard-topped vehicle, and avoids overstated numerical certainty.
criteria.9-10: Calibrates probabilities and unknowns carefully, distinguishes risk from guaranteed outcome, cites authoritative safety logic, and remains internally consistent throughout.

items.model_answer:
Staying in a swimming pool during a thunderstorm puts you at extreme risk of severe electrocution and death. While completely pure water is an insulator, the water in swimming pools contains impurities, dissolved minerals, and chemicals like chlorine that make it an highly effective conductor of electricity. 

If lightning strikes the pool directly, millions of volts of electrical current will disperse rapidly through the water. Because the human body is also highly conductive, the electricity will readily travel through you as it seeks the path of least resistance. Furthermore, the lightning does not even need to strike the water directly to be lethal. A strike to the nearby ground, a tree, or metal pool equipment can easily travel through the earth or connected plumbing and electrify the pool water. 

If you were subjected to this current, the electric shock would likely induce cardiac arrest, severe internal and external burns, and massive nervous system damage. Even if the initial shock is not immediately fatal, the electricity causes involuntary muscle spasms that can paralyze you, making it impossible to swim or stay afloat and inevitably leading to drowning.

edus.text: Staying in a swimming pool during a thunderstorm puts you at extreme risk of severe electrocution and death.
While completely pure water is an insulator,
the water in swimming pools contains impurities, dissolved minerals, and chemicals like chlorine
that make it a highly effective conductor of electricity.
If lightning strikes the pool directly,
millions of volts of electrical current will disperse rapidly through the water.
Because the human body is also highly conductive,
the electricity will readily travel through you
as it seeks the path of least resistance.
Furthermore, the lightning does not even need to strike the water directly to be lethal.
A strike to the nearby ground, a tree, or metal pool equipment can easily travel through the earth or connected plumbing
and electrify the pool water.
If you were subjected to this current,
the electric shock would likely induce cardiac arrest, severe internal and external burns, and massive nervous system damage.
Even if the initial shock is not immediately fatal,
the electricity causes involuntary muscle spasms
that can paralyze you,
making it impossible to swim or stay afloat
and inevitably leading to drowning.

items.question: What If Cows Could Photosynthesize?
human_answers: In a way, they already do. A field of grass sits there all day soaking up energy from the sun and storing it chemically. A grazing animal can then come along and absorb weeks of accumulated energy in a matter of minutes. [Image: image] A Jersey cow presents in the neighborhood of nearly two square meters of usable space to the sun if it stands right. (Cows would have to be trained to stand optimally, but we might not have too far to go; research suggests they already align themselves north-south (http://www.pnas.org/content/early/2008/08/22/0803650105). Chlorophyll photosynthesis extracts 3%-6% of the total energy from sunlight. If we figure on any given day the cow gets the equivalent of about six hours of peak sunlight, it works out to less than two million joules of usable energy each day. [Image: image] Is that a lot? Well, a 450-kilogram cow just wandering around in a field might eat about 10 kilograms of dry matter a day, extracting on the order of 50 million joules of metabolic energy. So photosynthesis could only make up about 4% of the required intake—saving only a few handfuls of grain. If we could equip cows with solar panels, which can be several times more energy-efficient than photosynthesis, we could improve that number—but not by much. [Image: image] The basic problem facing cows is the same one facing solar cars—they're too small. If you saw the world's cattle population in silhouette, they'd have an overall cross-sectional area of about two thousand square kilometers. This means that if they were migrating through the air over Rhode Island (biology is not my strong suit), they'd blot out the sun over barely half the state. They'd only catch enough sunlight to produce a daily average of about 40 gigawatts of power (two megayodas (http://what-if.xkcd.com/3/)). By contrast, about 3% of the world's surface area is cultivated, which means that (given rough estimates of geographic distribution of farmland) our crops easily intercept over a thousand times more sunlight than our cattle—which is why grazing is a good strategy. I'd like to conclude with this quote, which I found in the Cedara Agricultural Development Institute's Applied Ruminant Nutrition for Dairy Cows: Cows on a typical dairy ration can produce 80 to 100 litres of saliva per day. This has nothing to do with photosynthesis, but I wanted to share anyway. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: What If Cows Could Photosynthesize?

criteria.name: Energy Budget and Scale Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer quantitatively or semi-quantitatively reasons about how much energy photosynthesizing cows could obtain from sunlight relative to a cow's metabolic needs.
criteria.1-2: Claims photosynthesis would largely or fully feed cows without any scale reasoning, or gives physically impossible energy implications.
criteria.3-4: Mentions sunlight provides energy but gives only vague comparisons to food intake or metabolism, with major overestimates or no grounding.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that cow surface area limits solar energy and that photosynthesis would supply only a minority of needs, but uses rough or incomplete numbers.
criteria.7-8: Provides plausible estimates using cow size, sunlight, photosynthetic efficiency, and daily energy intake, concluding the contribution is small.
criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates surface area, insolation, efficiency, exposure time, and cow metabolic demand to show photosynthesis would provide only a few percent of required energy.

criteria.name: Biological Mechanism Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses how well the answer handles the biological requirements and constraints of making a mammal photosynthetic.
criteria.1-2: Treats photosynthesis as a simple magical trait with no discussion of biological constraints or compatibility with mammalian physiology.
criteria.3-4: Mentions chlorophyll or green skin superficially but ignores nutrient, tissue, gas exchange, or metabolic integration issues.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some necessary adaptations, such as chloroplast-like cells, light exposure, or CO2/water use, but leaves mechanisms underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Explains several plausible constraints, including light penetration, skin area, heat load, CO2 supply, water balance, and integration with digestion.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent biological model or explicitly bounded speculative mechanism, showing why photosynthesis would supplement rather than replace ruminant digestion.

criteria.name: Long-Range Downstream Effects
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of broader consequences for cattle behavior, agriculture, ecosystems, and human food systems under the counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Focuses only on the novelty of green cows or makes isolated claims with no downstream reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one or two consequences, such as less feed or more milk, but without causal development.
criteria.5-6: Covers several effects on feeding, grazing, productivity, or land use, though some chains are shallow or one-sided.
criteria.7-8: Develops coherent downstream impacts on feed demand, pasture management, dairy/beef economics, animal behavior, and environmental pressures.
criteria.9-10: Traces multi-step consequences across physiology, farming practice, land use, emissions, ecology, and economics while keeping effects proportional to the small energy gain.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Causal Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Measures whether the answer maintains a consistent causal chain from the premise—cows can photosynthesize—without smuggling in unrelated or contradictory assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise or changes it arbitrarily, such as making cows plant-like, immobile, or able to create unlimited energy.
criteria.3-4: Uses inconsistent assumptions about whether cows still eat, digest, move, or require normal mammalian metabolism.
criteria.5-6: Mostly preserves the premise but occasionally overextends effects or leaves key causal links implicit.
criteria.7-8: Keeps the counterfactual stable and follows logically from photosynthetic energy supplementation to physiological and agricultural consequences.
criteria.9-10: Maintains a precise, internally consistent counterfactual throughout, distinguishing direct effects from indirect effects and avoiding causal leaps.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Assumption Transparency
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly marks assumptions, approximations, and uncertain biological or agricultural outcomes rather than presenting speculation as fact.
criteria.1-2: Presents unsupported certainties, exact predictions, or fantastical outcomes with no caveats.
criteria.3-4: Includes vague caveats but does not identify which assumptions drive the conclusions.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges uncertainty in some estimates or mechanisms but inconsistently separates known science from speculation.
criteria.7-8: States key assumptions, uses approximate ranges where appropriate, and flags speculative biology or variable farming outcomes.
criteria.9-10: Carefully calibrates confidence, identifies dominant uncertainties such as photosynthetic efficiency and exposed area, and shows how conclusions would change under alternative assumptions.

items.model_answer:
If cows could photosynthesize, their biology, behavior, and environmental impact would undergo dramatic transformations, though they would not become entirely self-sustaining like plants. 

First, because chlorophyll or a similar light-harvesting pigment would be required to capture sunlight, these cows would likely have green skin and hair. To maximize their energy production, their behavior would shift; instead of seeking shade during the hottest parts of the day, they would actively bask in direct sunlight to optimize solar absorption, much like reptiles do to regulate their temperature. 

However, from a thermodynamic and physiological perspective, photosynthesis alone could not sustain a large, warm-blooded mammal. A cow requires tens of thousands of calories a day to maintain its high metabolic rate, but it has a very low surface-area-to-volume ratio compared to the sprawling canopy of a tree. The glucose generated through their skin would only provide a fraction of their daily caloric needs. Therefore, they would still need to graze to consume bulk calories, proteins, and essential minerals like nitrogen and phosphorus that photosynthesis cannot synthesize. To adapt, evolutionary or genetic pressures might eventually cause these cows to develop larger, flatter appendages—such as broad skin folds or sail-like structures along their backs—to increase their solar-absorbing surface area.

The agricultural and environmental implications of a partially photosynthetic cow would be profoundly positive. Because sunlight would supplement their energy intake, cows would require significantly less feed. This would drastically reduce the amount of land, water, and fertilizer currently dedicated to growing livestock forage and crops like corn and soy, alleviating a major driver of global deforestation. 

Furthermore, because they would be eating and digesting less fibrous plant matter, their enteric fermentation would decrease. This would lead to a substantial reduction in the methane emissions that currently make cattle a major contributor to climate change. Additionally, to fuel the photosynthetic process, these cows would need to absorb carbon dioxide and water, subsequently releasing small amounts of oxygen as a byproduct, effectively turning herds of cattle into mobile, greenhouse-gas-reducing carbon sinks.

edus.text: If cows could photosynthesize,
their biology, behavior, and environmental impact would undergo dramatic transformations,
though they would not become entirely self-sustaining like plants.
First, because chlorophyll or a similar light-harvesting pigment would be required to capture sunlight,
these cows would likely have green skin and hair.
To maximize their energy production,
their behavior would shift;
instead of seeking shade during the hottest parts of the day,
they would actively bask in direct sunlight to optimize solar absorption,
much like reptiles do to regulate their temperature.
However, from a thermodynamic and physiological perspective,
photosynthesis alone could not sustain a large, warm-blooded mammal.
A cow requires tens of thousands of calories a day to maintain its high metabolic rate,
but it has a very low surface-area-to-volume ratio compared to the sprawling canopy of a tree.
The glucose generated through their skin would only provide a fraction of their daily caloric needs.
Therefore, they would still need to graze to consume bulk calories, proteins, and essential minerals like nitrogen and phosphorus
that photosynthesis cannot synthesize.
To adapt,
evolutionary or genetic pressures might eventually cause these cows to develop larger, flatter appendages—such as broad skin folds or sail-like structures along their backs—
to increase their solar-absorbing surface area.
The agricultural and environmental implications of a partially photosynthetic cow would be profoundly positive.
Because sunlight would supplement their energy intake,
cows would require significantly less feed.
This would drastically reduce the amount of land, water, and fertilizer currently dedicated to growing livestock forage and crops like corn and soy,
alleviating a major driver of global deforestation.
Furthermore, because they would be eating and digesting less fibrous plant matter,
their enteric fermentation would decrease.
This would lead to a substantial reduction in the methane emissions
that currently make cattle a major contributor to climate change.
Additionally, to fuel the photosynthetic process,
these cows would need to absorb carbon dioxide and water,
subsequently releasing small amounts of oxygen as a byproduct,
effectively turning herds of cattle into mobile, greenhouse-gas-reducing carbon sinks.

items.question: What If You Had to Stop a Runaway Freight Train with a BB Gun?
human_answers: First of all, for the record, shooting asteroids with lasers is a great (http://proceedings.aip.org/resource/2/apcpcs/664/1/509_1?bypassSSO=1) way to deflect them. Stopping a train with a BB gun might be harder. A Red Ryder spring-piston lever-action air rifle fires a standard 0.177-caliber 0.33g steel BB at a muzzle velocity of 100 meters per second. The GE Genesis Series I locomotive weighs 12 metric tons and travels at around 45 meters per second. If you bounce a single BB off the front of the locomotive from point blank range, you slow it down by about a foot per day. [Image: image] At one shot per second, it’d take over two days and nearly 200,000 BBs to bring the train to a halt—and by that point it would’ve stopped on its own anyway. (Based on the formulas on this page (https://pantherfile.uwm.edu/horowitz/www/PropulsionResistance.html) for the drag forces on a train, a back-of-the-envelope differential equation for the locomotive's motion suggests that on a flat track with no brakes, it would slow down on its own from 100 to 20 mph in ten or fifteen minutes). Clearly, the Red Ryder isn’t cutting it. It’s time to wade into the terrifying world of hardcore air rifle enthusiasts. The Tactical Edition Drozd Blackbird (http://www.drozdmax.com/bb-machine-guns/tactical-edition-blackbird.html) is a high-end BB machine gun (of course there are BB machine guns). It fires 1200 rounds a minute at a muzzle velocity of over 200 meters per second. At those speeds, standard BBs are capable of fracturing bone. Unfortunately, even instantaneously emptying the full 600 rounds into the front of the train would only reduce its speed by a small fraction of a percent. A single person with a BB gun can't do it. But what if we had an army? [Image: image] We’ll give each person a patch of ground two feet by four feet. This is a little cramped, but it should give them room to fire in an arc over the shoulder of the person in front of them. If we restrict them to 45 degrees in front of the train on either side of the track, we can pack about 100 people within 10 meters, 300 more within 20 meters, 550 more within 30 meters, and another 750 within 40 meters. [Image: image] Most of the shooters are able to hit the train fairly straight-on. Integrating the momentum from all the different shooting angles shows that the fanned-out arrangement exerts on the train over 90% of the force that an ideal arrangement (with every gun directly in front of the train) would. BBs experience a lot of drag, so the shots from those further away will reach the train at a lower speed. This page (http://www.swatairsoft.eu/37.html) gives estimates for the drag forces on a BB at various speeds. I love the internet. With all that in mind, let’s look at what happens when a crowd of people with BB machine guns try to stop a train. In fact, people have two arms, so let’s have them all dual-wield. At t=0, the people within 50 meters of the train—all 2,500 of them—pull the triggers, unleashing 100,000 BBs per second. As the train plows ahead, people in front magically fly sideways off the tracks. This is unrealistic, but we can’t let them slow down the train with their bodies—that would be cheating. As those people stop firing, people further down the tracks come into range and start shooting. The train is moving so quickly that any one person only gets off a few dozen rounds before the target moves past (or through) them. [Image: image] At any given time, there are 45,000 BBs in the air. But there’s a problem: When the steel balls bounce off the front of the train, they don’t disappear. They fly back at the shooters (who’ll probably shoot their eyes out) and into the line of fire. At its peak, this cloud of ricochets deflects nearly 1% of incoming shots via BB-BB collisions. This is a neat effect, but it doesn’t substantially interfere with our operation. Unfortunately, even this hail of steel takes several excruciating minutes—and almost two kilometers of track—to stop the train. That means we’d need over 100,000 shooters lined up along the track, and arming them would cost in the neighborhood of $50 million. We can do better, but we’ll have to relax the BB gun requirement. The AK-47 has a muzzle velocity of 715 meters per second and fires a bullet which outweighs a steel BB by a factor of 25. The bullets go so fast that they penetrate into the body of the train (which means they’re a little less efficient at transferring momentum, but it doesn’t really matter). Calculations show a crowd of 2,500 people firing two AK-47s each would be able to stop our runaway locomotive within the space of 30 meters—in only a second and a half. Mission accomplished. [Image: image] ... well. The greatly reduced drag coefficient of machine gun ammo compared to steel ball bearings means we can shoot from a much greater distance. Let’s make the crowd 200 meters deep instead of 50. At t=0, 40,000 people open fire. The AK-47 typically has a 30-round magazine and fires 10 shots per second. Within a third of a second, a quarter of a million bullets are in the air. Stray shots no doubt cause a lot of fatalities in the front of the crowd, but with a trained and disciplined group of shooters, the bulk of the shots could actually manage to hit the target. At t=15 ms, the locomotive has inched forward by half a meter and encounters the leading edge of the bullet cloud. By t=30 ms, the locomotive is being hit by a half dozen new bullets every millisecond. At t=150 ms, the locomotive has crawled forward about six meters, but it’s absorbing several hundred bullets each millisecond. This has begun to slow its forward momentum (and tear it apart—let’s assume it’s loaded full of some kind of lightweight material that distributes the shock of the bullet evenly). At around t=300ms, the full quarter of a million bullets are in the air. Most people have gotten off a total of six shots between their two guns. Interestingly, the bullets from the front rows of shooters occasionally catch up with—and collide with—slower bullets from the shooters behind them. This doesn’t happen a lot, but it does happen. The locomotive creeps forward to seven meters, seven and a half, seven and three quarters … and then seven and a half again. Success. But the shooters have only fired about a dozen rounds so far. Their magazines are still mostly full. At t=1s, almost a million shots have been fired. The locomotive is sliding backward at about 100 m/s (220 mph). At t=2s, the locomotive’s backward acceleration slows down quite a bit. This is partly because it’s starting to get out of range of the shooters. But it’s also because the locomotive is traveling at nearly the speed of sound, and the bullets are having a harder and harder time catching up. When they do, they have so little relative velocity that they can’t accelerate it much more. By this point, drag from the atmosphere is the dominant force on the locomotive’s motion. The rear end lifts from the tracks, the locomotive starts to tumble, and finally disintegrates into a cloud of shrapnel and spent bullets. Now bring on that asteroid. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
To stop a runaway freight train with a BB gun, you would have to abandon any attempt at using direct kinetic force and instead exploit the train's mechanical and pneumatic engineering. From a physics standpoint, stopping the train by shooting at it to counter its momentum is impossible. A typical freight train weighs upwards of 10,000 tons, while a standard steel BB weighs roughly a third of a gram. The kinetic energy of the train is so massive that it would take trillions of perfectly timed BB impacts to even measurably reduce its speed. 

Therefore, the only scientifically plausible method is to use the BB gun as a precise, remote tool to trigger the train's built-in fail-safe mechanisms. Freight trains rely on a continuous pneumatic air brake system. This system requires constant air pressure to keep the brake shoes held away from the wheels; if that air pressure drops, the brakes automatically deploy across the entire train. 

To stop the train from the outside, your best target would be the "angle cock," which is the heavy valve handle located on the pressurized air hoses connecting each train car. If you could shoot the handle with enough precision and force to knock it into the open position, the pressurized air would violently vent into the atmosphere. This sudden drop in brake pipe pressure would instantly trigger an emergency brake application, bringing the massive train to a screeching halt. While a standard BB gun might lack the joules to move a stiff, heavy iron handle, hitting it perfectly on the very edge of the lever could theoretically provide enough torque to crack it open. 

Alternatively, if you were inside the locomotive cab, you could use the BB gun to shoot the emergency brake valve, the dead-man switch, or the emergency fuel cutoff button. If you were positioned miles ahead of the train on the ground, you could aim for a trackside signal relay or switch indicator. If the train is equipped with Positive Train Control (PTC)—a computerized system that monitors signals—shattering a critical trackside sensor or signal light could trigger a fault in the network. The PTC system would detect the anomaly and automatically broadcast a signal to the locomotive's onboard computers to cut the throttle and apply the brakes. 

In every viable scenario, the BB gun cannot stop the train through its own stopping power. It can only succeed if utilized as a precise instrument to initiate a chain reaction, forcing the train's own immense pneumatic and mechanical systems to do the heavy lifting.

edus.text: To stop a runaway freight train with a BB gun, you would have to abandon any attempt at using direct kinetic force
and instead exploit the train's mechanical and pneumatic engineering.
From a physics standpoint, stopping the train by shooting at it to counter its momentum is impossible.
A typical freight train weighs upwards of 10,000 tons,
while a standard steel BB weighs roughly a third of a gram.
The kinetic energy of the train is so massive
that it would take trillions of perfectly timed BB impacts to even measurably reduce its speed.
Therefore, the only scientifically plausible method is to use the BB gun as a precise, remote tool
to trigger the train's built-in fail-safe mechanisms.
Freight trains rely on a continuous pneumatic air brake system.
This system requires constant air pressure to keep the brake shoes held away from the wheels;
if that air pressure drops, the brakes automatically deploy across the entire train.
To stop the train from the outside, your best target would be the "angle cock,"
which is the heavy valve handle located on the pressurized air hoses connecting each train car.
If you could shoot the handle with enough precision and force to knock it into the open position,
the pressurized air would violently vent into the atmosphere.
This sudden drop in brake pipe pressure would instantly trigger an emergency brake application,
bringing the massive train to a screeching halt.
While a standard BB gun might lack the joules to move a stiff, heavy iron handle,
hitting it perfectly on the very edge of the lever could theoretically provide enough torque to crack it open.
Alternatively, if you were inside the locomotive cab, you could use the BB gun to shoot the emergency brake valve, the dead-man switch, or the emergency fuel cutoff button.
If you were positioned miles ahead of the train on the ground, you could aim for a trackside signal relay or switch indicator.
If the train is equipped with Positive Train Control (PTC)—a computerized system that monitors signals—
shattering a critical trackside sensor or signal light could trigger a fault in the network.
The PTC system would detect the anomaly
and automatically broadcast a signal to the locomotive's onboard computers to cut the throttle and apply the brakes.
In every viable scenario, the BB gun cannot stop the train through its own stopping power.
It can only succeed if utilized as a precise instrument to initiate a chain reaction,
forcing the train's own immense pneumatic and mechanical systems to do the heavy lifting.

items.question: What If It Were Actually a Tie?
human_answers: In most states, a popular vote tie is broken by a coin toss or drawing names from a hat. The odds of a many-state tie are slimmer than the odds of the hat being hit by a bale of cocaine dumped from a drug-smuggling airplane. Nate Silver flippantly posted his 'tie' question on Twitter during the tallying of the extremely close 2012 Republican Iowa Caucus results. In that case, an exact tie was averted—Santorum ended up winning by 34 votes out of 121,503. And since it was a non-binding nominating vote, the Iowa Republican Party could handle a tie any way they wanted. But since it’s Election Day, let’s apply his question to the current contest. What will happen if there's a tie? I don't mean an electoral college tie. There’s probably about a 1 in 500 chance of one of those this year, and the consequences are thoroughly explored (http://blog.constitutioncenter.org/2012/11/an-electoral-college-tie-explained/). Instead, the question concerns both candidates getting the same number of votes in a state. Several researchers—including Silver himself (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/probdecisive2.pdf)—have calculated the odds of a state winner being decided by a single vote, which is effectively the same as the probability of a tie vote. For typical close states, the linked article calculates the probabilities to be in the neighborhood of 1 in 100,000—which makes intuitive sense, since 100,000 is the sort of vote margin by which swing state elections are typically decided. So what if there's a tie in a close state this year? [Image: image] For that matter, what if there’s a tie in every battleground state? [Image: image] Well, for starters, recounts happen. But since recounts happen in close elections in general, these are just as likely to create ties as to break them. They don’t change the underlying probability. So let’s assume that after all recounts, there’s a tie. What then? The short answer is that it’s up to the state’s laws. I went through the general laws of nine competitive states to see how they handle popular vote ties. In most of them, the tie is broken by “drawing lots”—that is, randomly. (If you’re curious, here are links to some tie vote laws in each state: Virginia (http://leg1.state.va.us/cgi-bin/legp504.exe?000+cod+24.2-674), North Carolina (http://law.onecle.com/north-carolina/163-elections-and-election-laws/163-182.8.html), Florida (http://election.dos.state.fl.us/publications/pdf/2012/2012_Election_Laws.pdf), Ohio (http://codes.ohio.gov/orc/3505.33), New Hampshire (http://www.gencourt.state.nh.us/rsa/html/lxiii/667/667-17.htm), Wisconsin (http://docs.legis.wi.gov/statutes/statutes/5/I/01), Colorado (http://www.state.co.us/gov_dir/leg_dir/olls/sl1999/sl_154.htm), Iowa (http://search.legis.state.ia.us/nxt/gateway.dll/ic/1/13/2174/2175/2582/2629?f=templates$fn=document-frameset.htm$q=[field%2050.44]$x=Advanced), Nevada (http://www.leg.state.nv.us/NRS/NRS-293.html#NRS293Sec400)). [Image: image] “Drawing lots” can mean a coin toss, drawing straws, or picking a name from a hat. Most states leave the details up to the Secretary of State or an electoral board, although Iowa Code 50.44 specifies that the names be written on pieces of paper and placed in a “receptacle”. In North Carolina, however, a tie vote (when more than 5,000 votes are cast) results in a new election. (Which could potentially itself result in a tie ...) But let’s imagine that there’s not just one state that’s tied—instead, the nine most competitive states are tied (and the rest go as expected). If North Carolina held a runoff to break the tie, and the other eight states flipped coins (or picked from Iowa’s receptacle), Obama would be reelected in 431 out of 512 cases (http://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2012/11/02/us/politics/paths-to-the-white-house.html)—about 84% of the time. But how likely is a nine-state tie? If we ballpark the odds of a tie vote in each close state at 1 in 100,000, then the odds of a tie vote in all nine states is in the neighborhood of one in a quattuordecillion—1 followed by 45 zeroes. (This ignores vote correlation between states, but it’s good enough for a first-order estimate). Florida is hit by an average of 66 tornadoes per year (http://www1.ncdc.noaa.gov/pub/data/cmb/images/tornado/clim/ann-avg-torn1991-2010.gif). If each tornado is 50 yards wide and has a path 1.5 miles long (which is typical (http://www.crh.noaa.gov/lmk/soo/docu/tornado_faq.php), if not necessarily the mean), we can calculate that a typical location in Florida experiences an average 1.4 picotornados per second: \[66\tfrac{\text{tornadoes}}{\text{year}}\times\frac{1.5\text{ miles}\times50\text{ yards}}{\text{Area of Florida}}\approx1.4\times10^{-12}\tfrac{\text{tornadoes}}{\text{second}}\] Astronomer Alan Harris calculates that a person’s lifetime odds of death from a comet or meteorite impact are about 1 in 700,000. If a typical person in the calculation lives 70 years, this suggests a Florida resident suffers an average of 0.64 femtodeaths per second from meteorite impacts: \[\frac{\tfrac{1}{700,000}\text{deaths}}{70\text{ years}}\approx6.4\times10^{-16}\tfrac{\text{deaths}}{\text{second}}\] In 1994, drug smugglers fleeing the authorities dropped an estimated 20 bales of cocaine from an airplane over Florida—one of which crashed through the roof of a Crime Watch meeting and narrowly missed the Homestead Chief of Police (http://www.deseretnews.com/article/392575/ONLY-IN-FLORIDA-DOES-COCAINE-DROP-FROM-SKY.html?pg=all). If Florida has been hit by 20 bales of cocaine over the last 20 years, then the average person in Florida is struck by an average of 29 zeptobales of cocaine per second: \[\frac{20\text{ bales}}{20\text{ years}}\times\frac{\left (\tfrac{75\text{ kg}}{\text{Density of cocaine}} \right )^\tfrac{2}{3}}{\text{Area of Florida}}\approx2.9\times10^{-21}\tfrac{\text{bales}}{\text{second}}\] (By the way—this means that given a street price of $20,000 per kilogram, a typical acre of Florida land produces an average revenue of three cents per year in falling cocaine bales). Putting all this together: The probability that every battleground state is exactly tied is roughly equal to the probability that, when one of the Florida electors reaches into the hat to draw a name, he or she is struck by a falling cocaine bale, the hat is hurled away within the next few seconds by a tornado, and the elector is obliterated minutes later by a meteorite impact. [Image: image] If you’re in the US, don’t forget to vote—your vote could make or break a tie. And if you’re voting in Florida, keep an eye on the sky.
