items.question: What If My Printer Could Really Print Money?
human_answers: In today’s article, I give shorter answers to several reader questions. (Previous installment here (http://what-if.xkcd.com/14/).) You can fit four bills on an 8.5”x11” sheet of paper: [Image: image] If your printer can manage one page (front and back) of full-color high-quality printing per minute, that’s $200 million dollars a year. [Image: image] This is enough to make you very rich, but not enough to put any kind of dent in the world economy. Since there are 7.8 billion (http://www.federalreserve.gov/paymentsystems/coin_currcircvolume.htm) \$100 bills in circulation, and the lifetime of a \$100 bill is about 90 months, that means there are about a billion produced each year. Your extra two million bills a year would barely be enough to notice. This question gets submitted a lot. It turns out the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration—the agency which runs the National Hurricane Center—gets it a lot, too. In fact, they’re asked about it so often that they’ve published a response (http://www.aoml.noaa.gov/hrd/tcfaq/C5c.html). I recommend you read the whole thing, but I think the last sentence of the first paragraph says it all: “Needless to say, this is not a good idea.” It makes me happy that an arm of the US government has, in some official capacity, issued an opinion on the subject of firing nuclear missiles into hurricanes. [Image: image] A house in a very rainy place, like the Alaska panhandle, might receive close to four meters of rain per year. Water turbines can be pretty efficient. If the house has a footprint of 1,500 square feet and gutters five meters off the ground, it would generate an average of less than a watt of power from rainfall, and the maximum electricity savings would be: \[1500\text{ft}^2 \times 4\tfrac{\text{ meters}}{\text{year}}\times1\tfrac{\text{kg}}{\text{liter}} \times9.81\tfrac{\text{m}}{\text{s}^2}\times5\text{ meters}\times15\tfrac{\text{cents}}{\text{kWh}}=\frac{$1.14}{\text{year}}\] The rainiest hour on record occurred in 1947 in Holt, Missouri, where about 30 centimeters of rain fell in 42 minutes. For those 42 minutes, our hypothetical house could generate up to 800 watts of electricity, which might be enough to power everything inside it. For the rest of the year, it wouldn’t come close. If the generator rig cost $100, residents of the rainiest place in the US—Ketchikan, Alaska—could potentially offset the cost in under a century. There are about 300,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 stars in the universe. If you make a word pronounceable by alternating vowels and consonants (there are better ways to make pronounceable words, but this will do for an approximation), then every pair of letters you add lets you name 105 times as many stars (21 consonants times 5 vowels). 105 possibilities per two characters is about the same information density that numbers have, which suggests the name will end up being about as long as the total number of stars written out: [Image: image] I like doing math that involves measuring the lengths of numbers written out on the page—which is really just a way of loosely estimating log~10~x. It works, but it feels so wrong. Reentering spacecraft heat up because they’re compressing the air in front of them (not, as is commonly believed, because of air friction). According to this calculator (http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/BGH/stagtmp.html), to increase the temperature of the air layer in front of your body by twenty degrees Celsius (enough to go from freezing to room temperature), you would need to be biking at 200 m/s. The fastest human-powered vehicles at sea levels are recumbent bicycles enclosed in streamlined aerodynamic shells. These vehicles have an upper speed limit near 40 m/s. This is the speed at which the human can just barely produce enough thrust to balance the drag force from the air. Since drag increases with the square of the speed, this limit would be pretty hard to push any further. Biking at 200 m/s would require at least 25 times the power output needed to go 40 m/s. At those speeds, you don’t really have to worry about the heating from the air—a quick back-of-the-envelope calculation suggests that if your body were doing that much work, your core temperature would reach fatal levels in a matter of seconds. There are a lot of ways to estimate the amount of information stored on the internet, but we can put an interesting upper bound on the number just by looking at how much storage space we (as a species) have purchased. The storage industry produces in the neighborhood of 650 million hard drives per year. If most of them are 3.5” drives, then that’s eight liters (two gallons) of hard drive per second. This means the last few years of hard drive production—which, thanks to increasing size, represent a large chunk of global storage capacity—would just about fill an oil tanker. So, by that measure, the internet is smaller than an oil tanker. [Image: image] Aerodynamics aside, I’m curious what tactical advantage you’re expecting to gain by having the high explosive fly back at you if it misses the target.

rubrics.question_focus: What If My Printer Could Really Print Money?

criteria.name: Quantitative grounding of the money-printing premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer anchors the counterfactual in realistic order-of-magnitude calculations for a home printer producing usable currency.
criteria.1-2: Provides no meaningful calculation or gives wildly implausible amounts without basis.
criteria.3-4: Attempts arithmetic but misses key factors such as bills per page, duplex printing, print speed, or yearly output.
criteria.5-6: Estimates output in the right broad range but with incomplete assumptions or unclear unit handling.
criteria.7-8: Correctly uses plausible assumptions, such as four $100 bills per sheet and about one duplex page per minute, to estimate hundreds of millions per year.
criteria.9-10: Gives a clear, checked order-of-magnitude calculation and distinguishes bills, face value, print rate, operating time, and annual total.

criteria.name: Macroeconomic scale and inflation reasoning
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer compares the printer's output to existing money supply, currency circulation, and economic scale rather than assuming instant economic collapse.
criteria.1-2: Claims global hyperinflation or economic destruction from one printer with no scale comparison.
criteria.3-4: Mentions inflation or money supply but treats the effect qualitatively and exaggeratedly.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that one printer makes the owner rich but likely has limited macroeconomic impact, with weak quantitative support.
criteria.7-8: Compares the output to circulation or annual production of high-denomination bills and concludes the macro effect is small.
criteria.9-10: Accurately separates personal wealth effects from aggregate effects, noting that a few million extra $100 bills per year is tiny relative to existing currency and broader money supply.

criteria.name: Causal chain from physical printing to spendable wealth
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the mechanisms that determine whether printed money actually functions as money, including authenticity, detection, laundering, banking, and spending constraints.
criteria.1-2: Assumes printed pages automatically become usable wealth without considering authentication or circulation.
criteria.3-4: Briefly notes legality or counterfeiting but does not analyze how the bills enter the economy.
criteria.5-6: Discusses some practical constraints such as serial numbers, security features, suspicious deposits, or spending limits.
criteria.7-8: Builds a coherent chain from printing to attempted use, including counterfeit detection, banking scrutiny, law enforcement, and transaction bottlenecks.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly explains how physical realism, legal status, traceability, laundering difficulty, and behavioral responses govern the actual outcome under the premise.

criteria.name: Long-range downstream effects and institutional response
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer traces plausible longer-term consequences beyond the immediate windfall, including government, financial, and social responses.
criteria.1-2: Stops at 'you get rich' or 'the economy collapses' with no downstream reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a few consequences but as disconnected guesses.
criteria.5-6: Covers likely personal, legal, and economic consequences, though with limited causal depth.
criteria.7-8: Explains escalating effects such as spending patterns, audits, seizure, Secret Service involvement, changes to bill designs, or containment of the anomaly.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent long-range scenario showing how institutions detect, investigate, adapt to, and likely neutralize or exploit the money-printing capability.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles the ambiguous counterfactual consistently and flags uncertainties without undermining its own assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contradicts the premise or makes mutually incompatible claims without acknowledgment.
criteria.3-4: Uses inconsistent assumptions about whether the money is real, counterfeit, magical, or legally valid.
criteria.5-6: Mostly maintains a consistent interpretation but leaves important ambiguities unresolved.
criteria.7-8: Clearly states assumptions, such as whether the bills pass authentication or merely look real, and keeps conclusions aligned with them.
criteria.9-10: Separates multiple plausible interpretations, calibrates confidence in each, and avoids overclaiming while preserving causal consistency throughout.

items.model_answer:
If your home printer could produce perfect, indistinguishable legal tender, the immediate result would be immense personal wealth, but the ultimate consequences would be dictated by the strict laws of macroeconomics and law enforcement. 

On a small, personal scale, printing a few thousand dollars a week would allow you to live luxuriously. Because the bills are assumed to be indistinguishable from real currency, the physical cost of production would not be an issue. Even though standard printer ink is notoriously one of the most expensive liquids on Earth, printing $100 bills would still yield a massive profit margin. Your primary obstacle would instead be money laundering. Sudden, massive cash expenditures for real estate or luxury vehicles would immediately trigger IRS audits and attract the attention of the Secret Service. To stay out of federal prison, you would have to invent a legitimate cash-heavy business just to explain your sudden wealth and pay taxes on the money you printed.

However, if you scaled up your operation to print billions of dollars to buy out corporations, or if everyone’s printer suddenly gained this magical ability, it would trigger catastrophic hyperinflation. In economics, money is not actual wealth; it is simply a medium of exchange that represents the real goods and services available in an economy. Flooding the market with newly printed cash does not miraculously create more food, steel, cars, or homes. It simply means that a higher volume of dollars is now chasing the exact same limited supply of goods. 

As a direct result, sellers would rapidly raise their prices to adjust to the influx of cash. If you printed enough money, the purchasing power of the currency would plummet to near zero. You would quickly find yourself in a macroeconomic collapse mirroring historical crises in Weimar Germany or modern Zimbabwe, where it could cost a wheelbarrow full of your freshly printed $100 bills just to buy a loaf of bread. Ultimately, a machine that prints infinite money does not generate infinite wealth; on a large enough scale, it merely destroys the value of the currency itself.

edus.text: If your home printer could produce perfect, indistinguishable legal tender,
the immediate result would be immense personal wealth,
but the ultimate consequences would be dictated by the strict laws of macroeconomics and law enforcement.
On a small, personal scale, printing a few thousand dollars a week would allow you to live luxuriously.
Because the bills are assumed to be indistinguishable from real currency,
the physical cost of production would not be an issue.
Even though standard printer ink is notoriously one of the most expensive liquids on Earth,
printing $100 bills would still yield a massive profit margin.
Your primary obstacle would instead be money laundering.
Sudden, massive cash expenditures for real estate or luxury vehicles would immediately trigger IRS audits and attract the attention of the Secret Service.
To stay out of federal prison,
you would have to invent a legitimate cash-heavy business just to explain your sudden wealth and pay taxes on the money you printed.
However, if you scaled up your operation to print billions of dollars to buy out corporations, or if everyone’s printer suddenly gained this magical ability,
it would trigger catastrophic hyperinflation.
In economics, money is not actual wealth;
it is simply a medium of exchange that represents the real goods and services available in an economy.
Flooding the market with newly printed cash does not miraculously create more food, steel, cars, or homes.
It simply means that a higher volume of dollars is now chasing the exact same limited supply of goods.
As a direct result, sellers would rapidly raise their prices to adjust to the influx of cash.
If you printed enough money,
the purchasing power of the currency would plummet to near zero.
You would quickly find yourself in a macroeconomic collapse mirroring historical crises in Weimar Germany or modern Zimbabwe,
where it could cost a wheelbarrow full of your freshly printed $100 bills just to buy a loaf of bread.
Ultimately, a machine that prints infinite money does not generate infinite wealth;
on a large enough scale, it merely destroys the value of the currency itself.

items.question: What If You Tried to Launch a Real Rocket Using Only Model Rocket Engines?
human_answers: About 65,000, give or take a few. You’d have to arrange them like this: [Image: image] The rocket would weigh about as much as a tow truck. There wouldn’t be room for anything except the engines, aerodynamic shell, and minimal staging equipment. Each rocket motor would burn for about three seconds. The layer cake arrangement means that every three seconds, the bottom layer of spent rockets would detaches and the next stage would kick in. It would go through between 25 and 30 of these stages, burning for a total of a minute and a half, after which it would coast upward and just barely brush the edge of space. (For this design, I’m assuming something akin to Estes E9-4 engines, which are on the large end of the common model rocket engines. There are larger ones—the classes go all the way up to O and beyond—but at a certain point, they stop being model rocket engines, and just become rocket engines.) A 30-stage rocket is, to put it lightly, an engineering nightmare. This design assumes the non-engine portion of the vehicle is limited to the weight of a person (60 kg). In effect, the spaceship would be a solid block of rocket engines. They’d need to be insulated from each other so the upper stages didn’t ignite prematurely, and the staging and aerodynamics would both be a challenge. The stack of engines narrows as you go from bottom to top. By the time the top stages are firing, the rocket will have shed most of its mass, so it won’t need as much thrust to get the same acceleration. The reason the engine stack bulges in the middle is so that the acceleration profile will look like this: [Image: image] Rockets work best when their thrust is several times greater than the force of gravity. But you don’t want to accelerate too quickly while you’re low down. Air drag increases with the square of your speed, and if you accelerate too quickly, you’ll find yourself wasting all your fuel just to maintain your speed. You want to accelerate slowly at first, then ramp it up as the air starts getting thinner. [Image: image] Now, as you may have noticed, this rocket will get you into space (for a few seconds, at least), but not orbit. Can you use model rocket engines to dock with the ISS? No. Taking into account atmospheric drag, to get into space, you need a rocket capable of accelerating (in a vacuum) to about 2 kilometers per second. To get to orbit, you need a rocket capable of accelerating to about 10 kilometers per second. If you try to produce an orbital rocket using the same design math we used for the suborbital rocket, it spits out a description of a pancake-shaped mountain of model rocket engines over a mile wide. It would taper to a 10-meter-high spire in the center and would weigh about as much as the Great Pyramid. [Image: image] Not only would this vehicle never get out of the atmosphere, it would probably not stand up under its own weight. Frankly, the word “vehicle” is a bit misleading. Essentially, what you’ve created is an unstable pile of gunpowder the size of Central Park. If it went up in flames—which it would—it would break the record for the largest manmade non-nuclear explosion in history. (Interestingly, the current holder of that dubious record is also a rocket that exploded during launch (http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m79UO4HOQmc).) The bottom line is that it would be very difficult, but perhaps not impossible, to launch something up to the edge of space using model rocket engines. However, if you try to build a ship capable of getting to orbit, you will not go to space today.

criteria.3-4: Mentions clustering or staging but misses why spent engines must be discarded and how drag or acceleration matters.

criteria.9-10: Precisely explains that the model-engine stack might barely brush space briefly but cannot reach orbit; scaling to orbit produces an absurd, atmosphere-bound, structurally untenable mega-pile.

criteria.9-10: Shows how the counterfactual cascades into a near-solid block of motors, severe staging/aero/thermal control problems, structural collapse for orbital scaling, and possible record-scale non-nuclear explosion.

items.model_answer:
If you tried to launch a real, orbital-class rocket using only model rocket engines, the attempt would fail spectacularly, resulting in either a massive fire on the launchpad or a very brief, catastrophic crash. The fundamental barriers to this idea come down to thrust-to-weight ratio, structural mass fraction, burn time, and ignition synchronization.

First, consider the sheer number of engines required just to counteract gravity. A medium-lift rocket like the SpaceX Falcon 9 weighs roughly 550,000 kilograms fully fueled, meaning it needs over 5.4 million Newtons of thrust to lift off the pad. A standard hobbyist model rocket engine, such as an Estes C6, produces an average thrust of about 6 Newtons. You would need roughly one million C-class engines firing simultaneously just to make the Falcon 9 hover. Even if you used much larger, high-power amateur rocketry motors (like O-class motors), you would still need thousands of them.

However, strapping thousands or millions of model engines to a rocket introduces a fatal physics problem tied to the rocket equation. Model rocket engines have a terrible "mass fraction." Their thick cardboard, fiberglass, or plastic casings and clay nozzles are incredibly heavy compared to the actual solid propellant inside them. Adding a million small engines would add tens of thousands of kilograms of dead weight to the vehicle. To lift that new weight, you would need to add even more engines, which adds even more weight. This creates a cascading failure where the rocket becomes too heavy to ever lift itself, regardless of how many engines you attach. 

Even if you magically solved the weight problem and achieved a positive thrust-to-weight ratio, you would immediately run into the burn time problem. Model rocket engines are designed to burn for only one to three seconds. Real liquid-fuel rocket engines must burn continuously for several minutes to slowly push the vehicle through the thick lower atmosphere and build up the immense horizontal speed (roughly 28,000 km/h) required to reach orbit. With model engines, your massive rocket would violently leap a few meters into the air, run out of thrust almost instantly, and crash straight back down under its own weight.

Finally, there is the engineering nightmare of ignition. Igniting hundreds of thousands of solid rocket motors at the exact same millisecond is practically impossible. If the engines on one side of the rocket ignited even a fraction of a second before the other side, the asymmetric thrust would instantly tip the towering rocket over. The aerodynamic shear forces and gravity would snap the rocket in half, likely detonating its massive liquid fuel tanks in a colossal fireball. 

Ultimately, model rocket engines simply lack the energy density, sustained burn time, and structural efficiency required to move a multi-ton vehicle into space.

edus.text: If you tried to launch a real, orbital-class rocket using only model rocket engines,
the attempt would fail spectacularly,
resulting in either a massive fire on the launchpad or a very brief, catastrophic crash.
The fundamental barriers to this idea come down to thrust-to-weight ratio, structural mass fraction, burn time, and ignition synchronization.
First, consider the sheer number of engines required just to counteract gravity.
A medium-lift rocket like the SpaceX Falcon 9 weighs roughly 550,000 kilograms fully fueled,
meaning it needs over 5.4 million Newtons of thrust to lift off the pad.
A standard hobbyist model rocket engine, such as an Estes C6, produces an average thrust of about 6 Newtons.
You would need roughly one million C-class engines firing simultaneously just to make the Falcon 9 hover.
Even if you used much larger, high-power amateur rocketry motors (like O-class motors),
you would still need thousands of them.
However, strapping thousands or millions of model engines to a rocket introduces a fatal physics problem tied to the rocket equation.
Model rocket engines have a terrible "mass fraction."
Their thick cardboard, fiberglass, or plastic casings and clay nozzles are incredibly heavy compared to the actual solid propellant inside them.
Adding a million small engines would add tens of thousands of kilograms of dead weight to the vehicle.
To lift that new weight,
you would need to add even more engines,
which adds even more weight.
This creates a cascading failure where the rocket becomes too heavy to ever lift itself,
regardless of how many engines you attach.
Even if you magically solved the weight problem and achieved a positive thrust-to-weight ratio,
you would immediately run into the burn time problem.
Model rocket engines are designed to burn for only one to three seconds.
Real liquid-fuel rocket engines must burn continuously for several minutes
to slowly push the vehicle through the thick lower atmosphere and build up the immense horizontal speed (roughly 28,000 km/h) required to reach orbit.
With model engines, your massive rocket would violently leap a few meters into the air,
run out of thrust almost instantly,
and crash straight back down under its own weight.
Finally, there is the engineering nightmare of ignition.
Igniting hundreds of thousands of solid rocket motors at the exact same millisecond is practically impossible.
If the engines on one side of the rocket ignited even a fraction of a second before the other side,
the asymmetric thrust would instantly tip the towering rocket over.
The aerodynamic shear forces and gravity would snap the rocket in half,
likely detonating its massive liquid fuel tanks in a colossal fireball.
Ultimately, model rocket engines simply lack the energy density, sustained burn time, and structural efficiency required to move a multi-ton vehicle into space.

items.question: What If Humanity Sped Up Earth's Rotation to Eliminate Leap Seconds?
human_answers: The Earth’s spin is slowing down. This is annoying. One reason that it’s annoying is that it makes time standards more difficult. We already have way too many time standards (http://tycho.usno.navy.mil/systime.html), including: TAI, time based on an atomic clock, which ignores all motion of the Earth UT0 and UT1, time based on precise measurement of the Earth’s rotation GPS, the time standard used by GPS satellites UTC, the standard used in computing, which is like TAI but with leap seconds to keep it in sync with Earth TDT, TBT, TCB, and TCG, which are all even worse This leads to all kinds of little headaches, particularly for programmers. For example, the clock in your smartphone’s GPS is 16 seconds out of sync with the phone’s system clock. This is because the system clock uses Coordinated Universal Time (which has leap seconds), but GPS time doesn’t. They were in sync in January of 1980 and probably never will be again. Half a billion years ago (when the Earth was 4 billion years old, instead of 4.5), each day was 22 hours long instead of 24. The day has gotten longer because of tidal forces from the Moon. Loosely speaking, here’s how tidal drag works: The Moon’s tides raise bulges in the Earth, but the Earth’s rotation moves those bulges out of line with the Moon. The Moon’s gravity tries to tug the bulges back into line, which exerts a twisting force on the Earth, slowing it down: [Image: image] Strangely, the Earth is actually not slowing down as much as you’d expect from tidal drag. The biggest reason for the discrepancy is that during the last ice age, the continents were pushed down by the weight of the glaciers, and they’re still springing back into place. This has the effect of shifting mass toward the poles, closer to the axis of rotation: [Image: image] This makes us spin faster—or, at least, keeps us from slowing down as quickly. At the moment, each day is about 0.8 milliseconds longer than the 86,400 seconds it needs to be to avoid adding leap seconds. [Image: image] This difference fluctuates over time based on weather and other effects (it’s actually shortened a bit since the early 1990s), although in the long run, it will definitely get larger as the Earth slows. If we wanted to get rid of leap seconds, we’d need to keep the Earth spinning at a more constant rate. This means speeding up the Earth and shortening each day by about 0.8 milliseconds. This is a tough problem. Here are a few things that won’t work: Spinning counterclockwise (http://xkcd.com/162/) in a chair. It temporarily alters the Earth’s rate of rotation, but not enough to matter. Putting rocket engines on the Equator. This won’t work because the exhaust would go into the atmosphere, which transmits the force back to the ground as wind drag—it’d be like making a bike go forward by pushing on the handlebars. If the engines were somehow mounted above the atmosphere, they’d be able to slow the Earth, but not by enough to accomplish our goal. Triggering big earthquakes. This can alter the length of the day (http://www.nasa.gov/topics/earth/features/japanquake/earth20110314.html), but even those aren’t big enough to make a difference. In the end, there’s only one solution: Hitting the Earth with asteroids. Given enough time, we could send a spaceship (captained by an anti-Bruce Willis) to perform repeated flybys of a comet. Over time, the gravitational perturbation could steer the comet into a collision course with Earth. By hitting the Earth at the right angle, we would give it a push: [Image: image] Even if the comet burns up in the atmosphere, its momentum is transmitted to the surface by wind drag (taking a matter of days). It takes about a decade (http://www.researchgate.net/publication/227650235_Topographic_CoreMantle_Coupling_and_Polar_Motion_On_Decadal_TimeScales) for the core to sync up with the crust, so we’d have to plan the impact schedule carefully to avoid overshooting. Here’s the bad news: To get enough spin, we have to hit the Earth with on the order of a billion liters of rock per second (several times the volumetric discharge rate of the Amazon). This adds up to about one six-mile dinosaur-killing asteroid every couple days. Humanity—and life—wouldn’t survive the bombardment long. What about a steady stream of smaller asteroids? [Image: image] If asteroid B-612 in The Little Prince is four meters across and made of rock, we’d need an average of around fifty thousand of them to enter the atmosphere each second to keep up the pressure. [Image: image] Unfortunately, the steady high-altitude meteor shower would deliver just as much energy to the atmosphere that daily giant impacts would, and the eventual death toll would be the same: Seven billion humans, plus four billion Little Princes per day. But at least we could stop worrying about leap seconds.

criteria.name: Counterfactual Target and Timekeeping Framing
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly frames the counterfactual: eliminating leap seconds by changing Earth’s rotation rather than redefining time standards, and whether it identifies the relevant day-length mismatch and its causes.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise, treats leap seconds as purely administrative, or gives no connection between Earth rotation and timekeeping.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes leap seconds relate to Earth’s rotation but is vague or wrong about whether Earth must speed up or slow down.
criteria.5-6: Correctly says Earth must spin slightly faster to keep days near 86,400 SI seconds, but gives little quantitative context.
criteria.7-8: Accurately explains the current millisecond-scale day excess, tidal slowing, and UTC/leap-second motivation with minor omissions.
criteria.9-10: Precisely frames the target as shortening the day by about 0.8 ms, distinguishes atomic and rotational time, and notes short-term fluctuations versus long-term tidal slowdown.

criteria.name: Angular Momentum and Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses correct rotational dynamics to reason about how Earth’s spin could be changed under the counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Relies on magical, local, or internally impossible mechanisms with no angular-momentum reasoning.
criteria.3-4: Mentions force or energy but confuses torque, linear momentum, atmospheric coupling, or conservation laws.
criteria.5-6: Applies basic angular-momentum ideas and recognizes that external torque or mass redistribution is needed.
criteria.7-8: Correctly explains why many intuitive methods fail, such as ground-based engines or human motion, and why off-world momentum transfer could work.
criteria.9-10: Gives a physically faithful chain involving torque, impact angle, atmospheric momentum transfer, crust-core coupling, and conservation constraints.

criteria.name: Scale, Feasibility, and Quantitative Plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer captures the enormous scale required to measurably speed up Earth and avoids implausibly small fixes.
criteria.1-2: Claims the problem could be solved with ordinary engineering, rockets, earthquakes, or small impacts without scale analysis.
criteria.3-4: Acknowledges it would be difficult but gives no meaningful magnitude or severely underestimates the required intervention.
criteria.5-6: States that the required energy or momentum is enormous and likely impractical, with rough but incomplete support.
criteria.7-8: Uses plausible order-of-magnitude reasoning, e.g. asteroid-scale impacts or continuous mass influx, to show infeasibility.
criteria.9-10: Conveys the extreme scale comparable to repeated large asteroid impacts or vast continuous meteor streams and ties it quantitatively to the millisecond day adjustment.

criteria.name: Downstream Effects on Earth, Climate, and Life
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the long-range consequences of attempting to speed Earth’s rotation, especially collateral effects from realistic mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Ignores downstream consequences or says the change would be harmless because 0.8 ms is small.
criteria.3-4: Mentions generic disasters but does not connect them causally to the chosen spin-up method.
criteria.5-6: Identifies major hazards such as impacts, atmospheric heating, tsunamis, earthquakes, or biosphere damage.
criteria.7-8: Traces a coherent causal chain from momentum delivery to global energy deposition, environmental catastrophe, and civilizational failure.
criteria.9-10: Comprehensively explains that any sufficient asteroid or meteor bombardment would deliver lethal energy at planetary scale, making leap-second elimination survivability-negative.

criteria.name: Long-Range Coherence, Uncertainty, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer maintains a coherent causal narrative over time, calibrates uncertainty, and avoids contradictions with the counterfactual physics.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, unsupported certainty, or disconnected claims that break the scenario logic.
criteria.3-4: Has a partly coherent narrative but includes significant inconsistencies or unjustified leaps.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent, with some uncertainty acknowledged, but misses timing issues or mixes incompatible mechanisms.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a clear causal sequence, separates short-term and long-term effects, and flags uncertainties in Earth-rotation variability.
criteria.9-10: Provides a tightly consistent long-range analysis including feedbacks, scheduling/overshoot concerns, natural variability, and the distinction between solving leap seconds by physics versus by policy.

items.model_answer:
If humanity decided to speed up Earth's rotation to eliminate leap seconds, we would be undertaking a planetary mega-engineering project of catastrophic proportions merely to solve a minor software and timekeeping annoyance. Because Earth's rotation is gradually slowing down due to tidal friction from the Moon, a solar day is currently a fraction of a millisecond longer than exactly 86,400 atomic seconds. To permanently eliminate the need for leap seconds, humanity would have to artificially accelerate the planet's spin and continuously maintain that exact rotational velocity against the Moon's ongoing drag.

The energy required to alter Earth's rotational kinetic energy is incomprehensibly massive. To speed up the planet, humanity would need to employ highly advanced, futuristic technologies. This could involve constructing colossal equatorial mass drivers to fire streams of matter into space, building giant thrusters, or artificially shifting billions of tons of Earth's mass closer to its core to increase its angular velocity (similar to a figure skater pulling their arms in). The energy expenditure would dwarf the total power output of human history, and because the Moon would continuously pull on Earth's oceans and bulge, this planetary engine would have to run indefinitely to counteract natural tidal braking.

The physical consequences of applying such immense torque to the Earth would be devastating. The mechanical stress exerted on the planet's crust to force this acceleration would likely trigger catastrophic tectonic shifts, resulting in unprecedented global earthquakes and volcanic eruptions. Furthermore, increasing the Earth's rotational speed would alter the centrifugal force acting on the planet. This would cause the oceans to bulge slightly more at the equator, leading to a permanent sea-level rise in equatorial regions and a corresponding drop in sea levels near the poles. 

Technologically, while software engineers would no longer have to program complex leap second adjustments into global computing, financial, and GPS systems, the aerospace industry would face massive disruptions. Every geostationary satellite, which relies on matching Earth's exact current rotational period to stay fixed over a single location, would slowly drift out of position. Entire satellite constellations would require continuous orbital adjustments or total replacement to match the new, faster Earth.

Ultimately, the endeavor would be a cosmic absurdity. Rather than risking global geological collapse and expending planetary-scale energy to force Earth to match our atomic clocks, the actual solution is much simpler. In reality, the global scientific community has already voted to abandon the leap second by 2035, choosing instead to simply let atomic time and solar time slowly drift apart.

items.question: What If One Extra Person Died Randomly Every Second?
human_answers: Every second, 1.8 humans die and 4.2 humans are born. Under Mr. Petzall’s plan, the number of deaths would increase to 2.8. This randomized culling would obviously be a big deal—it would be responsible for over a third of all deaths—but, at least for a while, our population would continue to grow. At one death per second, any given person currently has a 0.464% chance of being chosen each year. Put another way, the scenario would result in 4.64 deaths per 1,000 people (or 464 per 100,000). [Image: image] There are about twenty countries with death rates below 4.64 per 1,000. It’s an odd bunch (https://www.cia.gov/library/publications/the-world-factbook/rankorder/2066rank.html), including the Dominican Republic, Brunei, Singapore, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the Maldives, and Paraguay. These are the countries where Guy’s program would be responsible for the majority of all deaths. The death rate in all of these countries is going to go up. It has to, because of math. It seems intuitively obvious that death rates below 10 per 1,000 are unsustainable. If fewer than one person out of every hundred dies each year (and enough are born to sustain the population) then the average person must have to wait over a hundred years to die—which is clearly not compatible with our current lifespans. In those countries with low single-digit death rates, the rates are guaranteed to rise in the future. This includes the United States, whose death rate is 8.40 per 1,000—a number which will go up substantially as the Baby Boomers age. A rate of one death per second isn’t enough to reverse population growth at present, but it would have been until recently. In 1950, the world’s population was only 2.52 billion. One death per second would mean 12.5 annual deaths per 1,000 people, almost triple the number in 2013. At the start of the early 20th century, this would have been enough to reverse population growth, and within a handful of decades—as population levels off—it will be again. Of course, if people die faster, this in turn has an effect on birth rates—as people change their behavior in response to the change in mortality—so the actual result would be more complicated. [Image: image] In the United States, Guy Petzall would be the leading cause of death for females between the ages of 1 and 55 and for males between the ages of 1 and 48. Currently, about 96% of infants survive to age 40, but in Guy’s scenario, only 80% would. When would these deaths happen? Given the numbers of aircraft in the air at any given time, it’s certain that some pilots would die while flying. This wouldn’t be a disaster, though, since large commercial airliners have multiple crew members who can take over. Cars would be a different story. Since about 10 million Americans are driving (http://what-if.xkcd.com/5/) at any given time, 127 will die behind the wheel each day (plus a smaller but still significant number of passengers, pedestrians, and other drivers). Interestingly, this is only a little larger than the number of Americans who die in car accidents every day already. (This number has been declining, as a percentage of population, since the 1960s, and as a percentage of miles traveled since at at least the 1920s (http://www.saferoads.org/federal/2004/TrafficFatalities1899-2003.pdf).) About 50 million (http://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nhsr/nhsr011.pdf) outpatient surgery procedures are performed each year. If they’re primarily performed by one surgeon and each last an average of half an hour, then about 13 surgeons per year will unexpectedly die mid-surgery (as will 13 extra patients). This is a scary thought. But to put it in perspective, that’s about the number of surgeons who will operate on the wrong body part or wrong patient every two days (http://www.cnn.com/2011/HEALTH/04/28/ep.wrong.side.surgery/index.html). It’s not that the scenario isn’t scary. It’s just that reality is far more terrifying. Lastly, what about our leaders? Members of Congress die in office at a rate of two or three per year, or about five per Congress. This used to be much higher, as explained in this strangely florid paper (http://home.gwu.edu/~forrest/fmdeathincongressps.pdf). 29 members of Congress died during 1939 and 1940, the two years the 76th Congress was in session. In Guy’s scenario, the current rate would double, leading to a loss of 10 per Congress. This would certainly be tragic, but it would be no higher than the levels seen as recently as the 1960s. All in all, the losses would be dramatic, but not devastating to our species as a whole. And really, in the end, the global death rate is 100%—everyone dies. [Image: image] … or do they? Strictly speaking, the observed death rate for the human condition is something like 93%—that is, around 93% of all humans have died. This means the death rate among humans who were not members of The Beatles is significantly higher than the 50% death rate among humans who were. [Image: image] I expect this significant[dubious–discuss] fact[citation needed] will pave the way[citation needed] for a great deal[dubious–discuss] of important[citation needed][dubious–discuss] research.

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly translates 'one extra random person dies every second' into annual deaths, individual risk, and effects on global population growth over time.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or gives wildly incorrect magnitudes, such as claiming immediate extinction or no meaningful added deaths.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes that deaths increase substantially but uses vague or mostly incorrect numbers and population-growth implications.
criteria.5-6: Gives approximately correct scale, such as about 31.5 million extra deaths per year, but only partially relates it to births, baseline deaths, or population growth.
criteria.7-8: Correctly compares extra deaths with current global births and deaths and explains that population would likely keep growing initially but more slowly.
criteria.9-10: Accurately quantifies annual deaths, per-person risk, share of total deaths, and explains how effects depend on population size, fertility, mortality trends, and future demographic transition.

criteria.name: Random-selection mechanics and demographic implications
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer respects the randomness of victim selection and derives realistic consequences across ages, countries, occupations, and risk groups.
criteria.1-2: Treats the deaths as targeted, disease-like, or concentrated without justification, contradicting the random premise.
criteria.3-4: Mentions randomness but fails to apply it consistently to age, location, or activity-based consequences.
criteria.5-6: Explains that everyone has roughly equal additional risk and notes some demographic effects, but with limited specificity.
criteria.7-8: Applies random risk to meaningful groups, such as children, working-age adults, low-mortality countries, leaders, pilots, drivers, or surgeons.
criteria.9-10: Shows nuanced demographic reasoning: equal per-person hazard changes relative mortality most for low-risk groups and young ages, while absolute deaths follow population distribution and time spent in activities.

criteria.name: Coverage of downstream physical and social hazards
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores major secondary consequences caused by people dying suddenly during critical activities.
criteria.1-2: Ignores downstream effects or asserts civilization collapses without mechanisms.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few sensational examples but does not estimate frequency or distinguish minor from severe effects.
criteria.5-6: Covers some plausible hazards, such as driving, aviation, surgery, childcare, or industrial operations, with limited causal detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains why some hazards would be manageable and others serious, using rough exposure reasoning or comparisons to existing accident rates.
criteria.9-10: Systematically analyzes cascading risks across transportation, medicine, infrastructure, governance, households, and workplaces while keeping consequences proportional to the added random mortality.

criteria.name: Long-range feedbacks and adaptation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reasons beyond the immediate death toll to behavioral, institutional, demographic, and technological adaptation over years to decades.
criteria.1-2: Only describes the first moments or gives a static conclusion with no longer-term causal chain.
criteria.3-4: Mentions long-term effects vaguely, such as fear or lower population, without tracing mechanisms.
criteria.5-6: Identifies some adaptations, such as safety automation, redundancy, insurance changes, or fertility responses, but does not connect them deeply.
criteria.7-8: Develops coherent medium- and long-term chains involving fertility, life expectancy, labor markets, public health, political stability, and risk management.
criteria.9-10: Balances demographic transition, psychological normalization, institutional redesign, economic effects, and possible fertility/mortality feedbacks, distinguishing transient disruption from equilibrium outcomes.

criteria.name: Plausibility, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer remains internally consistent, avoids overclaiming, and clearly separates robust implications from speculative ones under the counterfactual.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible claims, or confident conclusions unsupported by the premise.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible points but mixes incompatible assumptions or exaggerates outcomes without acknowledging uncertainty.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent and plausible, with occasional unsupported leaps or weak distinction between certain and speculative effects.
criteria.7-8: Clearly flags uncertainty, avoids deterministic collapse/extinction claims, and keeps conclusions consistent with the stated random one-per-second mechanism.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous causal consistency throughout, quantifies uncertainty where possible, presents alternative plausible trajectories, and avoids both alarmist and dismissive distortions.

items.model_answer:
If one extra person died randomly every second, the most surprising immediate outcome is that humanity would not go extinct; in fact, the global population would continue to grow. Currently, there are about 4.3 births and 1.8 deaths per second worldwide. Adding one extra death per second would raise the global mortality rate to roughly 2.8 deaths per second, equating to 31,536,000 additional deaths per year. While this would nearly halve our current annual population growth, global births would still outpace deaths by tens of millions annually. 

However, the true devastation of this scenario stems from the randomness of the deaths rather than the raw demographic numbers. Because this phenomenon could strike anyone at any moment regardless of age, health, or location, people would suddenly drop dead while engaged in critical tasks. Individuals would die instantly while driving in heavy traffic, piloting aircraft, operating heavy industrial machinery, or performing delicate surgeries. These sudden incapacitations would trigger countless secondary accidents, fires, and collateral fatalities, significantly inflating the actual death toll well beyond the baseline 31.5 million.

Statistically, the direct risk to any specific individual would remain relatively low. With a global population of roughly 8 billion, each person would face about a 1 in 250 (or 0.4%) chance of being the random victim in any given year. 

Despite this low individual probability, the unpredictable nature of the threat would fundamentally alter human infrastructure and society. Engineering would pivot entirely toward fail-safes. "Dead-man's switches," automatic braking, and autonomous takeover systems would become strictly mandatory in all vehicles. Strict human redundancies—such as requiring multiple operators for any dangerous equipment or public transport—would be enforced globally to prevent mass casualty events when a single operator randomly dies.

Scientifically and psychologically, the sudden onset of millions of causeless deaths would initially trigger immense global panic and the largest medical investigation in human history. Autopsies would reveal no underlying disease or trauma, baffling the scientific community. Once epidemiologists and statisticians realized the deaths were perfectly random and untreatable, society would be forced to adapt to a new, persistent baseline of existential anxiety, heavily inflated life insurance premiums, and a world entirely redesigned around the constant assumption of sudden human failure.

edus.text: If one extra person died randomly every second,
the most surprising immediate outcome is that humanity would not go extinct;
in fact, the global population would continue to grow.
Currently, there are about 4.3 births and 1.8 deaths per second worldwide.
Adding one extra death per second would raise the global mortality rate to roughly 2.8 deaths per second,
equating to 31,536,000 additional deaths per year.
While this would nearly halve our current annual population growth,
global births would still outpace deaths by tens of millions annually.
However, the true devastation of this scenario stems from the randomness of the deaths rather than the raw demographic numbers.
Because this phenomenon could strike anyone at any moment regardless of age, health, or location,
people would suddenly drop dead while engaged in critical tasks.
Individuals would die instantly while driving in heavy traffic, piloting aircraft, operating heavy industrial machinery, or performing delicate surgeries.
These sudden incapacitations would trigger countless secondary accidents, fires, and collateral fatalities,
significantly inflating the actual death toll well beyond the baseline 31.5 million.
Statistically, the direct risk to any specific individual would remain relatively low.
With a global population of roughly 8 billion,
each person would face about a 1 in 250 (or 0.4%) chance of being the random victim in any given year.
Despite this low individual probability,
the unpredictable nature of the threat would fundamentally alter human infrastructure and society.
Engineering would pivot entirely toward fail-safes.
"Dead-man's switches," automatic braking, and autonomous takeover systems would become strictly mandatory in all vehicles.
Strict human redundancies—such as requiring multiple operators for any dangerous equipment or public transport—
would be enforced globally
to prevent mass casualty events when a single operator randomly dies.
Scientifically and psychologically, the sudden onset of millions of causeless deaths would initially trigger immense global panic and the largest medical investigation in human history.
Autopsies would reveal no underlying disease or trauma,
baffling the scientific community.
Once epidemiologists and statisticians realized the deaths were perfectly random and untreatable,

society would be forced to adapt to a new, persistent baseline of existential anxiety, heavily inflated life insurance premiums, and a world entirely redesigned around the constant assumption of sudden human failure.

items.question: How Far Would You Have to Drop a Steak to Cook It?
human_answers: I hope you like your steaks Pittsburgh Rare. And you may need to defrost it after you pick it up. Things get really hot when they come back from space. This isn’t because of air friction, strictly speaking—it’s because of air compression. The air can’t move out of the way fast enough, and gets squished in front of the spaceship/meteor/steak. Compressing air heats it up. As a rule of thumb, you start to notice compressive heating above about Mach 2 (which is why the Concorde had heat-resistant material on the leading edge of its wings). A few months ago, skydiver Felix Baumgartner jumped from 39 kilometers, and hit Mach 1 around 30 kilometers. This was enough to heat the air by a few degrees, but the air was so far below freezing that it didn’t make a difference. (Early in his jump, it was about minus 40 degrees, which is that magical point where you don’t have to clarify whether you mean Fahrenheit or Celsius—it’s the same in both.) As far as I know, this steak question originally came up in a lengthy 4chan thread (http://m.chanarchive.org/4chan/sci/63224/5209640#p5209833), which quickly disintegrated into poorly-informed physics tirades intermixed with homophobic slurs. There was no clear conclusion. To try to get a better answer, I decided to run a series of simulations of a steak falling from various heights. This involved a lot of research. I used Mathematica models of atmospheric density to generate a set of descent profiles for the plummeting steak. For a nice tutorial on how to do this, see the Wolfram Blog’s analysis of Felix Baumgartner’s jump (http://blog.wolfram.com/2012/10/24/falling-faster-than-the-speed-of-sound/). An 8 oz. steak is about the size and shape of a hockey puck, so I based my steak’s drag coefficients on those given on page 74 of The Physics of Hockey (which author Alain Haché actually measured personally using some lab equipment). A steak isn’t a hockey puck, but the precise drag coefficient turned out not to make a big difference in the result. I used a handy NASA compressive heating calculator (http://www.grc.nasa.gov/WWW/BGH/stagtmp.html) to determine the temperature of the shock layer in front of the steak. Since this blog tends to wind up looking at unusual objects in extreme physical circumstances, often the only relevant research I can find is US military studies from the Cold War era. (Apparently, the US government was shoveling tons of money at anything even loosely related to weapons research.) To get an idea of how the air would heat the steak, I looked at research papers on the heating of ICBM nose cones as they reenter the atmosphere. Two of the most useful were Predictions of Aerodynamic Heating on Tactical Missile Domes (http://www.dtic.mil/cgi-bin/GetTRDoc?AD=ADA073217) and Calculation of Reentry-Vehicle Temperature History (http://www.dtic.mil/dtic/tr/fulltext/u2/a231552.pdf). Lastly, I had to figure out exactly how quickly heat spreads through a steak. I started by looking at some papers from industrial food production which simulated heat flow through various pieces of meat. It took me a while to realize there was a much easier way to learn what combinations of time and temperature will effectively heat the various layers of a steak: Check a cookbook. Jeff Potter’s excellent book Cooking for Geeks (http://www.amazon.com/Cooking-Geeks-Science-Great-Hacks/dp/0596805888) provides a great introduction to the science of cooking meat, and explains what ranges of heat produce what effects in steak and why. Cook’s The Science of Good Cooking (http://www.amazon.com/Science-Cooking-Cooks-Illustrated-Cookbooks/dp/1933615982) was also helpful. Putting it all together, I found that the steak will accelerate quickly until it reaches about an altitude of about 30-50 kilometers, at which point the air gets thick enough to start slowing it back down. The falling steak’s speed drops steadily as the air gets thicker. No matter how fast it’s going when it reaches the lower layers of the atmosphere, it quickly slows down to terminal velocity. It always takes six or seven minutes to drop from 25 kilometers to the ground. For much of those 25 kilometers, the air temperature is below freezing—which means the steak will spend six or seven minutes subjected to a relentless blast of subzero, hurricane-force winds. Even if it is cooked by the fall, you’ll probably have to defrost it when it lands. When the steak does finally hit the ground, no matter the initial height, it will be traveling at about 30 meters per second. To get an idea of what this means, imagine a steak flung at the ground by a major-league pitcher. If the steak is even partially frozen, it could easily shatter. However, if it lands in the water, mud, or leaves, it will probably be fine. (Not clean, but intact.) A steak dropped from 39 kilometers will, unlike Felix, probably not break the sound barrier. It also won’t be appreciably heated. This makes sense—after all, Felix’s suit wasn’t scorched when he landed. [Image: image] Steaks can probably survive breaking the sound barrier. In addition to Felix, pilots have ejected at supersonic speeds (http://www.ejectionsite.com/insaddle/insaddle.htm) and lived to tell about it. To break the sound barrier, you’ll need to drop the steak from about 50 kilometers. But this isn’t enough to cook it. We need to go higher. If dropped from 70 kilometers, the steak will go fast enough to be briefly blasted by 350°F air. Unfortunately, this blast of thin, wispy air barely lasts a minute—and anyone with some basic kitchen experience can tell you that a steak placed in the oven at 350 for 60 seconds isn’t going to be cooked. From 100 kilometers—the formally defined edge of space—the picture’s not much better. The steak spends a minute and a half over Mach 2, and the outer surface will likely be singed, but the heat is too quickly replaced by the icy stratospheric blast for it to actually be cooked. [Image: image] At supersonic and hypersonic speeds, a shockwave forms around the steak which helps protect it from the faster and faster winds. The exact characteristics of this shock front—and thus the mechanical stress on the steak—depend on how an uncooked 8 oz. filet tumbles at hypersonic speeds. I searched the literature, but was unable to find anything to help me estimate this. For the sake of this simulation, I assume that at lower speeds some type of vortex shedding creates a flipping tumble, while at hypersonic speeds it’s squished into a semi-stable spheroid shape. However, this is little more than a wild guess. If anyone puts a steak in a hypersonic wind tunnel to get better data on this, please, send me the video. If you drop the steak from 250 kilometers, things start to heat up. 250 kilometers puts us in the range of low earth orbit. However, the steak, since it’s dropped from a standstill, isn’t moving nearly as fast as an object re-entering from orbit. [Image: image] The steak reaches a top speed of Mach 6, and the outer surface may even get pleasantly seared. The inside, unfortunately, is still uncooked. Unless, that is, it goes into a hypersonic tumble and explodes into chunks. From higher altitudes, the heat starts to get really substantial. The shockwave in front of the steak reaches thousands of degrees (Fahrenheit or Celsius; it’s true in both). The problem with these levels of heat is that it burns the surface layer completely, converting it to little more than carbon. That is, it becomes charred. Charring is a normal consequence of dropping meat in the fire. The problem with charring meat at hypersonic speeds is that the charred layer doesn’t have much structural integrity, and is blasted off by the wind—exposing a new layer to be charred. (If the heat is high enough, it will simply blast the surface layer off as it flash-cooks it. This is referred to in the ICBM papers as the “ablation zone”) Even from those heights, the steak stilldoesn’t spend enough time in the heat to get cooked all the way through. (I know what some of you are probably thinking, and the answer is no—it doesn’t spend enough time in the Van Allen belts to be sterilized by radiation). We can try higher and higher speeds, and we might lengthen the exposure time via dropping it at an angle, from orbit. But if the temperature is high enough or the burn time long enough, the steak will slowly disintegrate as the outer layer is repeatedly charred and blasted off. If most of the steak makes it to the ground, the inside will still be raw. Which is why we should drop the steak over Pittsburgh. As the probably-apocryphal story goes, steel workers in Pittsburgh would cook steaks by slapping them on the glowing metal surfaces coming out of the foundry, searing the outside while leaving the inside raw. This is, supposedly, the origin of the term Pittsburgh Rare (http://www.livestrong.com/article/436635-how-to-cook-pittsburgh-style-steaks/). So drop your steak from a suborbital rocket, send out a collection team to recover it, brush it off, reheat it, cut away any badly charred sections, and dig in. Just watch out for salmonella. And the Andromeda Strain. [Image: image]

rubrics.question_focus: How Far Would You Have to Drop a Steak to Cook It?

criteria.name: Endpoint Plausibility for the Steak-Drop Question
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a physically plausible conclusion about how far a steak must be dropped to become cooked, including the distinction between searing, cooking through, freezing, and destruction.
criteria.1-2: Claims a simple modest height cooks the steak, or gives an arbitrary distance with no plausible physical endpoint.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes very high altitude is needed but incorrectly says the steak cooks through cleanly from a single drop.
criteria.5-6: States that tens to hundreds of kilometers may sear or heat the surface, but is vague about whether the interior cooks.
criteria.7-8: Correctly concludes that no practical drop cooks it through; around space/suborbital heights may singe or sear while the inside remains raw.
criteria.9-10: Accurately frames the best result as Pittsburgh-rare-like: high-altitude/suborbital drops can char or sear the outside, but full cooking fails because higher speeds cause ablation/destruction before heat penetrates.

criteria.name: Aerodynamic Heating Mechanism Fidelity
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer explains the correct cause and conditions of heating during the fall: compressive shock heating at high Mach numbers, not ordinary rubbing friction.
criteria.1-2: Attributes cooking mainly to simple air friction or impact heat with no discussion of compression or Mach effects.
criteria.3-4: Mentions fast fall heating but confuses friction, pressure, and atmospheric effects.
criteria.5-6: Identifies compression or shock heating but gives little detail about when it matters.
criteria.7-8: Explains that noticeable heating begins at supersonic/hypersonic speeds and depends on atmospheric density and shock-layer temperature.
criteria.9-10: Clearly links altitude, Mach number, shock/compressive heating, thin air, and rapid deceleration, avoiding the common misconception that friction alone cooks the steak.

criteria.name: Trajectory and Atmospheric Chain Coherence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer tracks the long-range causal chain from release altitude through acceleration, peak speed, deceleration, terminal velocity, and impact.
criteria.1-2: Treats the steak as falling at one constant speed or ignores atmospheric drag and altitude changes.
criteria.3-4: Mentions drag or terminal velocity but does not connect them to the changing atmosphere.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that higher drops produce faster speeds and later slowing, but the sequence is incomplete.
criteria.7-8: Describes acceleration in thin upper air, slowing in denser lower atmosphere, and arrival near terminal velocity rather than orbital reentry speed.
criteria.9-10: Gives a coherent end-to-end path: little heating at Baumgartner-like heights, supersonic near roughly 50 km, brief heating near 70–100 km, stronger heating from hundreds of km, followed by deceleration and low-altitude cold-air exposure.

criteria.name: Heat Transfer, Cooking, Freezing, and Ablation Coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer distinguishes surface temperature from internal doneness and accounts for heat penetration, cold stratospheric exposure, charring, and material loss.
criteria.1-2: Assumes hot outside air instantly cooks the whole steak or ignores the steak’s interior.
criteria.3-4: Mentions surface heating but misses heat-transfer time or cold-air effects.
criteria.5-6: Notes that short exposure may sear the surface while the center stays raw, with limited explanation.
criteria.7-8: Explains that brief hot blasts are followed by minutes of subfreezing high-speed airflow, preventing thorough cooking.
criteria.9-10: Fully captures the tradeoff: low altitudes do not heat enough, intermediate heights singe/sear briefly, and higher hypersonic drops char and ablate outer layers faster than heat can cook the interior.

criteria.name: Uncertainty Calibration and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer handles assumptions and uncertainties specific to a falling steak while avoiding internally inconsistent claims.
criteria.1-2: Presents overconfident numerical claims, contradicts itself, or ignores basic assumptions such as steak size, drag, and tumbling.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but still makes unsupported or conflicting claims about speed, cooking, or survival.
criteria.5-6: States reasonable assumptions but leaves key uncertainties underdeveloped.
criteria.7-8: Calibrates uncertainty about drag coefficient, orientation, tumbling, breakup, and landing while maintaining a consistent conclusion.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates robust conclusions from model-dependent details, noting uncertainties in steak shape/tumbling/ablation while preserving a contradiction-free causal story.

items.model_answer:
It is physically impossible to successfully cook a steak by dropping it from any height. 

If you drop a steak from a standard height, such as a tall building, it will quickly reach a relatively low terminal velocity. At this speed, air resistance does not generate any meaningful heat, and the steak will simply hit the ground completely raw. 

To generate enough heat to cook meat, the steak would need to be dropped from the edge of space—roughly 250 kilometers (155 miles) high—so that it has enough time in a near-vacuum to accelerate to hypersonic speeds (Mach 5 or higher) before hitting the thicker parts of the atmosphere. At these extreme speeds, the falling steak would heavily compress the air in front of it, creating a shockwave that reaches thousands of degrees. 

However, this still would not result in a cooked steak. Because meat is a very poor conductor of heat, the extreme temperature of the shockwave will not penetrate evenly to cook the meat. Instead, the intense heat and violent aerodynamic shear forces will instantly char and disintegrate the outer layers of the meat, while the inside remains completely raw or even frozen from the temperatures of the upper atmosphere. Ultimately, the steak would be torn apart into burnt fragments long before it hits the ground, meaning there is no drop height that will yield a cooked piece of meat.

items.question: What If You Went Swimming in a Spent Fuel Pool?
human_answers: Assuming you’re a reasonably good swimmer, you could probably survive treading water anywhere from 10 to 40 hours. At that point, you would black out from fatigue and drown. This is also true for a pool without nuclear fuel in the bottom. Spent fuel from nuclear reactors is highly radioactive. Water is good for both radiation shielding and cooling, so fuel is stored at the bottom of pools for a couple decades until it’s inert enough to be moved into dry casks. We haven’t really agreed on where to put those dry casks yet. One of these days we should probably figure that out. Here’s the geometry of a typical fuel storage pool: [Image: image] The heat wouldn't be a big problem. The water temperature in a fuel pool can in theory go as high as 50°C, but in practice they're generally between 25°C and 35°C—warmer than most pools but cooler than a hot tub. For the kinds of radiation coming off spent nuclear fuel, every 7 centimeters of water cuts the amount of radiation in half. The most highly radioactive fuel rods are those recently removed from a reactor. Based on the activity levels provided by Ontario Hydro in this report (http://www.osti.gov/energycitations/servlets/purl/7284014-xaMii9/7284014.pdf), this would be the region of danger for fresh fuel rods: [Image: image] Swimming to the bottom, touching your elbows to a fresh fuel canister, and immediately swimming back up would probably be enough to kill you. Yet outside the outer boundary, you could swim around as long as you wanted—the dose from the core would be less than the normal background dose you get walking around. In fact, as long as you were underwater, you would be shielded from most of that normal background dose. You may actually receive a lower dose of radiation treading water in a spent fuel pool than walking around on the street. [Image: image] That’s if everything goes as planned. If there’s corrosion in the spent fuel rod casings, there may be some fission products in the water. They do a pretty good job of keeping the water clean, and it wouldn’t hurt you to swim in it, but it’s radioactive enough that it wouldn’t be legal to sell it as bottled water. (Which is too bad—it’d make a hell of an energy drink). We know spent fuel pools can be safe to swim in because they’re routinely serviced by human divers. However, these divers have to be careful. On August 31st, 2010 (http://www.isoe-network.net/index.php/publications-mainmenu-88/isoe-news/doc_download/1756-ritter2011ppt.html), a diver was servicing the spent fuel pool at the Leibstadt nuclear reactor in Switzerland. He spotted an unidentified length of tubing on the bottom of the pool and radioed his supervisor to ask what to do. He was told to put it in his tool basket, which he did. Due to bubble noise in the pool, he didn’t hear his radiation alarm. When the tool basket was lifted from the water, the room’s radiation alarms went off. The basket was dropped back in the water and the diver left the pool. The diver’s dosimeter badges showed that he’d received a higher-than-normal whole-body dose, and the dose in his right hand was extremely high. The object turned out to be protective tubing from a radiation monitor in the reactor core, made highly radioactive by neutron flux. It had been accidentally sheared off while a capsule was being closed in 2006. It sank to a remote corner of the pool floor, where it sat unnoticed for four years. The tubing was so radioactive that if he’d tucked it into a tool belt or shoulder bag, where it sat close to his body, he could’ve been killed. As it was, the water protected him, and only his hand—a body part more resistant to radiation than the delicate internal organs—received a heavy dose. [Image: image] So, as far as swimming safety goes, the bottom line is that you’d probably be ok, as long as you didn’t dive to the bottom or pick up anything strange. But just to be sure, I got in touch with a friend of mine who works at a research reactor, and asked him what he thought would happen to you if you tried to swim in their radiation containment pool. “In our reactor?” He thought about it for a moment. “You’d die pretty quickly, before reaching the water, from gunshot wounds.”

items.model_answer:
If you went swimming in a spent nuclear fuel pool, your experience would depend entirely on how deep you dive. Assuming you stay near the surface, it would actually be a safe and surprisingly pleasant swim. The water in these pools is typically kept around 30°C (86°F) to absorb the decay heat from the spent radioactive fuel, so it would feel like a comfortably heated swimming pool. 

Furthermore, water is an incredibly effective radiation shield. Every 7 centimeters of water cuts the amount of radiation in half. Because the deep water completely shields you from the radioactive fuel at the bottom, while also blocking natural background radiation and cosmic rays from the sky, floating at the surface would actually expose you to a slightly lower dose of radiation than walking down the street outside.

The extreme danger lies at the bottom of the pool. The spent fuel assemblies stored there are highly radioactive. If you were to hold your breath, dive down, and get within a few feet of the fuel rods, the shielding effect of the water would diminish, and you would receive a lethal dose of radiation in a matter of seconds. 

Practically speaking, however, the greatest threat to your life wouldn't be the radiation. Because spent fuel pools are located inside highly secure nuclear facilities, the most immediate danger would be the heavily armed security guards who would swiftly detain or shoot you the moment you tried to enter the water.
