items.question: What If There Were Both a Space Elevator and a Stairway to Space?
human_answers: A week or two, if you're a champion stair-climber. Or 12 hours if you're on a motorcycle. A tower to space would be very different from a space elevator. A space elevator (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_elevator) would be about 100,000 kilometers tall, while a tower "to space" would only need to be 100 kilometers. As Ethan mentions, it would need to be pressurized, with an airlock every few miles. [Image: image] A stairway to space[1]If there's a bustle in your hedgerow, well, uh, boy, I don't know what to tell you. I guess ask it to leave? would have about half a million steps. World-champion stair-climbers[2]or "towerrunners" like Christian Riedl (http://stairsport.com/12h-stair-climbing-world-record-attempt-by-christian-riedl/) or Kristin Frey (http://www.kristinfrey.com/) can travel roughly a Mount Everest's height in a day; Riedl set the half-day record last October by climbing 13,145.65 meters (http://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/stair-climbing-vertical-height-%2812-hours%29) in 12 hours. At that pace—taking the other twelve hours to rest, eat, and sleep each day—it would take him a little over a week to reach the top. Climbing all those stairs would burn calories, which would mean you'd need to carry food. It turns out that the most efficient food you can carry, in terms of calories per pound, is butter—which is why Arctic explorers carry so much of it (http://abcnews.go.com/Technology/GlobalWarming/story?id=4853093). Suppose your backpack (http://www.amazon.co.uk/Disney-Frozen-Childrens-Multicoloured-FROZEN001018/dp/B00O2EO8XU) holds 9 liters. Climbing 10 stairs (http://journals.lww.com/acsm-msse/pages/articleviewer.aspx?year=2002&issue=04000&article=00021&type=abstract) burns about a calorie, which means climbing all the way up to space will burn about 72,000 calories. If you fill your backpack with butter, it would hold almost enough calories (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=9+liters+of+butter) to get you to the top. However, since it would take you weeks to climb all those stairs, you'd also need your normal dietary allowance of 2,000 calories (three sticks of butter) per day. Combining that with the 72,000 calories just from climbing the stairs, and you'd probably need to upgrade to a more serious 16-liter backpack (http://www.disneystore.com/anna-and-elsa-backpack-for-girls-personalizable/mp/1367267/1000290/). If you fill that backpack with butter, it will let you carry around 110,000 calories,[3]Coincidentally, about the amount you get (http://www.topatoco.com/merchant.mvc?Screen=PROD&Product_Code=QW-PERSON) from eating a human body. which should be enough to get you to the top if you're really dedicated. If you didn't want to eat 35 pounds of butter,[4]For whatever weird reason. you could try getting to the top by motorcycle. Based on how quickly this rider (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k8CZiqEjQDk) ascends 45 stairs, a motorcycle could conceivably make it to the top in a day. [Image: image] Ok, so you got to the top. Now what? Getting up to space isn't that hard, after all—the hard part is getting into orbit (http://what-if.xkcd.com/58/), and the tower doesn't help you very much with that. So what else could you do? Michael Longuet-Higgins (http://noc.ac.uk/about-us/history/national-oceanography-centre-southampton/influential-scientists/professor-michael-s) was a research professor at the University of Cambridge and an expert in fluid dynamics, bubbles, and unusual types of waves.[5]Given his apparent research interests, this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p70s1BNvBXI) would blow his mind.​[6]Or this one (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=711bZ_pLusQ), or this gadget (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/creatableslabs/project-nesm-never-ending-slinky-machine), or this (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JwohMl9Toww). In 1953, Dr. Longuet-Higgins was shown, by a colleague, an "interesting toy" which had recently appeared on the market. This toy, "Slinky," had some unusual properties. The professor immediately set to work analyzing it, and wrote up his results in a paper (http://www2.eng.cam.ac.uk/~hemh/TV/On_Slinky_the_dynamics_of_a_loose_heavy_spring.pdf). Dr. Longuet-Higgins first determined through mathematical modeling that the rate at which the Slinky descends steps should depend only on the properties of the spring itself, and not the size or shape of the stairs. He and his colleague conducted a series of experiments "on five different flights of stairs, of various dimensions, in Trinity College, Cambridge." Their conclusion: The Slinky descended a constant rate of about 0.8 seconds per step.[7]Except on some wide, flat stairs, where the Slinky "came to rest after three or four steps at most," which gives me a wonderful mental image of two disappointed British professors at the bottom of a staircase.​[8]Sadly, this was before the invention of the StairMaster. Fun fact: After a surprise StairMaster management shakeup in 2011, for some reason not a single newspaper ran the headline "StairMaster CEO steps down". Dr. Longuet-Higgins determined that the Slinky quickly reached a constant descent rate after first few steps. This tells us that if you placed a Slinky (similar to his) at top of the stairway to space, and gave it just the right nudge ... [Image: image] ... it would make it back to the bottom in just over five days. Or, to put that in more appetizing units: [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual setup fidelity: elevator vs stairway
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly preserves the key physical distinction in the prompt: a space elevator and a stairway/tower to 'space' are not equivalent structures and imply very different scales, endpoints, and engineering constraints.
criteria.1-2: Treats the stairway and space elevator as the same thing, or assumes both simply reach orbit with no distinction.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a difference between them but gives major wrong scales or endpoints, such as a 100 km elevator or a stairway reaching geostationary orbit.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes that the stairway only needs to reach near-space while the elevator must extend vastly farther, but gives limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains the approximate scale contrast, such as ~100 km for a stairway/tower to space versus tens of thousands to ~100,000 km for an elevator, and distinguishes reaching space from reaching orbit.
criteria.9-10: Precisely anchors the counterfactual around both structures coexisting, clearly separating the stairway's atmospheric/altitude role from the elevator's orbital transport role and using that distinction consistently throughout.

criteria.name: Mechanism coverage for human ascent on the stairway
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer plausibly reasons through what climbing or riding up a stairway to space would require, including atmosphere, pressure, food/energy, time, fatigue, and access infrastructure.
criteria.1-2: Ignores human survival and ascent mechanics, or says people can simply walk up into space unaided.
criteria.3-4: Mentions one issue such as oxygen or fatigue but leaves most survival and logistics mechanisms unexplained.
criteria.5-6: Covers several relevant constraints, such as pressurization, airlocks, time to climb, food, and rest, but with shallow or partially inconsistent reasoning.
criteria.7-8: Provides a coherent account of a pressurized stairway, repeated airlocks or stations, ascent times on the order of days to weeks for climbers, and energy/food requirements.
criteria.9-10: Integrates the stairway mechanics quantitatively and causally, including approximate step counts or altitude, climb-rate limits, calories, rest cycles, pressure management, and why vehicles might change the timescale.

criteria.name: Orbital mechanics and transport consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons about the major downstream consequence: getting to 100 km altitude is not the same as achieving orbital velocity, while a true space elevator can provide access to orbital energy and momentum regimes.
criteria.1-2: Claims that reaching the top of the stairway automatically puts a person or payload safely in orbit.
criteria.3-4: Vaguely mentions orbit but confuses altitude, escape velocity, and orbital velocity in ways that undermine the answer.
criteria.5-6: States that the hard part is getting into orbit, not merely reaching space, but does not develop the implication for the two structures.
criteria.7-8: Explains that the stairway mainly saves altitude while leaving most orbital velocity needs, whereas the elevator could lift payloads to orbital or beyond-orbital radii.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects altitude, tangential velocity, geostationary radius, tether rotation, and launch/reentry options, showing how the elevator and stairway would complement or fail to complement each other.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence under coexistence
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer follows a coherent chain of effects if both a stairway/tower to space and a space elevator existed, including infrastructure interaction, safety, economics, traffic, and plausible scientific or practical uses.
criteria.1-2: Lists disconnected jokes or effects with no causal chain and little relation to both structures existing.
criteria.3-4: Gives a few consequences but they are mostly isolated, speculative, or inconsistent with earlier assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Provides a plausible sequence of downstream effects, such as tourism, maintenance, launch support, or emergency access, but misses important interactions.
criteria.7-8: Develops multiple connected consequences: stairway as a novelty or access tower, elevator as cargo/orbit infrastructure, safety bottlenecks, maintenance, weather, and operational separation.
criteria.9-10: Builds a sustained long-range scenario in which physical constraints drive engineering design, costs, logistics, public use, failure modes, and societal or scientific impacts without losing the original premise.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer uses appropriate confidence, avoids overclaiming in speculative areas, and remains internally consistent with known physics and the counterfactual assumptions.
criteria.1-2: Contains severe contradictions, impossible claims presented as certain, or ignores the counterfactual premise entirely.
criteria.3-4: Has several internal inconsistencies or unsupported exact claims, such as incompatible ascent times or changing structure heights.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent but includes some uncalibrated speculation, vague numbers, or minor contradictions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly separates approximate estimates from firm physical constraints and avoids major contradictions about altitude, pressure, orbit, and travel time.
criteria.9-10: Maintains tight consistency across all estimates and assumptions, flags uncertainty where materials or engineering are counterfactual, and never lets humor or speculation override causal plausibility.

items.model_answer:
If both a space elevator and a stairway to space existed, the scenario would present a stark contrast between revolutionary aerospace efficiency and an absurd, extreme test of human biology. The space elevator would serve as the primary economic and logistical artery to the cosmos, using mechanical climbers on a high-tensile tether to haul cargo and passengers to geostationary orbit (GEO) at a fraction of the cost of chemical rockets. The stairway, whether integrated into the elevator’s tether or built as a parallel megastructure, would be functionally useless for actual space transit, serving instead as the ultimate extreme sport, a tourist attraction, or a highly impractical maintenance route.

From a biological and physical standpoint, climbing the stairway would be a lethal endeavor without heavy technological assistance. To reach the Kármán line—the widely recognized boundary of space at 100 kilometers (62 miles) above sea level—a person would have to climb roughly 500,000 steps. Long before reaching this milestone, climbers would face severe environmental hazards. At 8 kilometers high, they would enter the "Death Zone," requiring supplemental oxygen. By 19 kilometers, they would hit the Armstrong Limit, where atmospheric pressure is so low that the water in human lungs and saliva would boil at normal body temperature. From this point onward, climbers would be forced to wear heavy, fully pressurized spacesuits, making the physical exertion of climbing stairs vastly more difficult.

If the stairway extended all the way to the elevator's anchor in geostationary orbit (35,786 kilometers), the journey would become physically impossible for a single human lifetime. Even if a person could climb at a relentless pace of 10 kilometers a day, it would take nearly ten years of continuous climbing just to reach GEO. Because a human cannot carry a decade's worth of food, water, and oxygen on their back, the stairway would require pressurized waystations and life-support infrastructure at regular intervals. Furthermore, climbers would be exposed to lethal doses of solar radiation and the Van Allen radiation belts as they slowly ascended through the magnetosphere. 

From an engineering perspective, building both would be a nightmare of mass and tension. A space elevator relies on an incredibly light, strong material—like carbon nanotubes or macroscopic graphene—to support its own weight against Earth's gravity, balanced by the centrifugal force of the planet's rotation. Adding the physical mass of millions of stairs, plus the necessary life-support waystations, would drastically increase the weight and aerodynamic drag of the tether in the lower atmosphere, requiring an exponentially stronger material to keep the structure from snapping. 

Ultimately, the two structures would serve completely different purposes. The space elevator would handle the actual logistics of a spacefaring civilization, seamlessly moving thousands of tons of payload into orbit. The stairway to space would stand as a monumental engineering flex, but only the lowest few dozen kilometers would ever see human foot traffic before the hostile, freezing vacuum of the upper atmosphere forced everyone to simply step off the stairs and take the elevator.

edus.text: If both a space elevator and a stairway to space existed,
the scenario would present a stark contrast between revolutionary aerospace efficiency and an absurd, extreme test of human biology.
The space elevator would serve as the primary economic and logistical artery to the cosmos,
using mechanical climbers on a high-tensile tether to haul cargo and passengers to geostationary orbit (GEO) at a fraction of the cost of chemical rockets.
The stairway, whether integrated into the elevator’s tether or built as a parallel megastructure,
would be functionally useless for actual space transit,
serving instead as the ultimate extreme sport, a tourist attraction, or a highly impractical maintenance route.
From a biological and physical standpoint,
climbing the stairway would be a lethal endeavor without heavy technological assistance.
To reach the Kármán line—the widely recognized boundary of space at 100 kilometers (62 miles) above sea level—
a person would have to climb roughly 500,000 steps.
Long before reaching this milestone,
climbers would face severe environmental hazards.
At 8 kilometers high,
they would enter the "Death Zone,"
requiring supplemental oxygen.
By 19 kilometers,
they would hit the Armstrong Limit,
where atmospheric pressure is so low that the water in human lungs and saliva would boil at normal body temperature.
From this point onward,
climbers would be forced to wear heavy, fully pressurized spacesuits,
making the physical exertion of climbing stairs vastly more difficult.
If the stairway extended all the way to the elevator's anchor in geostationary orbit (35,786 kilometers),
the journey would become physically impossible for a single human lifetime.
Even if a person could climb at a relentless pace of 10 kilometers a day,
it would take nearly ten years of continuous climbing just to reach GEO.
Because a human cannot carry a decade's worth of food, water, and oxygen on their back,
the stairway would require pressurized waystations and life-support infrastructure at regular intervals.
Furthermore,
climbers would be exposed to lethal doses of solar radiation and the Van Allen radiation belts
as they slowly ascended through the magnetosphere.
From an engineering perspective,
building both would be a nightmare of mass and tension.
A space elevator relies on an incredibly light, strong material—like carbon nanotubes or macroscopic graphene—
to support its own weight against Earth's gravity,
balanced by the centrifugal force of the planet's rotation.
Adding the physical mass of millions of stairs, plus the necessary life-support waystations,
would drastically increase the weight and aerodynamic drag of the tether in the lower atmosphere,
requiring an exponentially stronger material to keep the structure from snapping.
Ultimately,
the two structures would serve completely different purposes.
The space elevator would handle the actual logistics of a spacefaring civilization,
seamlessly moving thousands of tons of payload into orbit.
The stairway to space would stand as a monumental engineering flex,
but only the lowest few dozen kilometers would ever see human foot traffic
before the hostile, freezing vacuum of the upper atmosphere forced everyone to simply step off the stairs and take the elevator.

items.question: What If Tug-of-War Teams Pulled on an Iron Rod Instead of a Rope?
human_answers: A couple dozen people could pull a half-inch iron rod apart. Tug-of-war, a simple game in which two teams try to pull a rope in opposite directions, has a surprisingly bloody history. I don't mean that there's some kind of gruesome historical forerunner of modern tug-of-war.[1]Although it's definitely an ancient sport (http://www.usatowa.com/history.html), so I'm sure people have come up with all kinds of horrific variations over the centuries that I don't really want to spend hours reading about. Humans seem to be creative when it comes to that kind of thing. I mean that modern tug-of-war involves a lot more death and mutilation than you might expect—precisely because people underestimate how few people it takes to break "strong" things like heavy rope. As detailed in a riveting article (http://priceonomics.com/a-history-of-tug-of-war-fatalities/) in Priceonomics, recent games of tug-of-war have resulted in hundreds of serious injuries and numerous deaths—all caused, one way or another, by ropes snapping. In particular, this seems to happen when large groups of students try to set a world record for largest tug-of-war game. When a rope under many tons of tension suddenly snaps, the recoiling ends can—and do—cause a terrifying variety of injuries. [Image: image] Before we answer Markus's question, it's worth noting that the physics of tug-of-war can be a little tricky (https://www.lhup.edu/~dsimanek/scenario/insight.htm#mechanics). It seems like common sense that the "stronger" team has an advantage, but that's not quite right. To win, you need to resist sliding forward better than the other team. If you can't resist sliding, then increasing your arm strength means you'll just pull yourself forward. Since sliding friction is often proportional to weight, tug-of-war on many surfaces is simply a contest over who's heavier.[2]Champion tug-of-war teams focus on body angle, footwork, digging into the ground, and timing pulls to throw off the other team. The strongest team in the world would lose a tug-of-war with a six-year-old and a sack of bricks, as long as the sack had a firm grip. [Image: image] So, how much force can tug-of-war players exert? A 2011 paper (http://web.nchu.edu.tw/~biosimulation/journal/pdf/vol-3-no01/vol-3-no-1-b-0003.pdf) analyzing the immune systems of several "elite tug-of-war players"[3]The paper notes that "Few studies have been done to examine the effects of [the] tug-of-war sport on physiological responses," which seems likely enough to me. measured their average pull force (on a school gym floor) to be about 102.5 kilograms-force, or about 1.5x their body weight. The ultimate tensile strength (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultimate_tensile_strength) of cast iron is about 200 megapascals (MPa), so we can use a simple formula to figure out how many players would be needed to break one. \[ \text{People required}=\frac{\pi\times\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\text{ inch} \right )^2\times200\text{ MPa}}{102.5\text{ kg}/\text{person}}\approx25\text{ people} \] Two teams of 25 people[4]I originally wrote 25 people total, forgetting that two people pulling with 100 units of force each will produce 100 units of tension on the rope, not 200! Thank you for Gordon McDonough for pointing this out. could probably pull a half-inch iron bar apart. An inch-thick iron bar could be torn in half by teams of 101 people,[5]People often play tug-of-war with their dogs. Going by weight alone, 30 humans would probably be about evenly matched against 101 dalmatians. and a 2-inch-diameter bar would need over 400. It's hard to have a tug-of-war with something thicker than about 2 inches. Since you're not allowed to install handles on the rope,[6]Or wrap it around your hand, for reasons which will become clear if you read some of the articles on tug-of-war injuries. it has to be narrow enough to grip easily. While "400 people" may be the limit for plain iron bars, there are much stronger substances out there. Common types of steel, for example, have a tensile strength about 10 times that of cast iron. Common half-inch rebar (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebar), for example, would in theory take teams of over 200 people to pull apart, compared to 25 for cast iron. Other substances are even stronger; a half-inch shaft made from high-grade steel or a polymer like Kevlar (or, theoretically, a solid silicon crystal) could handle the pulling force from teams of anywhere between 500 and 800 competitive tug-of-war players. If we limit ourselves to a two-inch diameter rope, which seems to be about the maximum size for tug-of-wars,[7](William Safire (http://www.theonion.com/articles/william-safire-orders-two-whoppers-junior,3351/) returns from the grave to point out that it should really be tugs-of-war.) then the maximum number of tug-of-war players given a super-strong rope like Kevlar is in the neighborhood of 10,000.[8]Or several times that many, if they're not very athletic. If we figured out how to manufacture large ropes out of graphene ribbons, which have tensile strengths over 10 times higher (http://arxiv.org/pdf/0709.0992.pdf) than existing materials, we could theoretically support a tug-of-war between teams of up to 100,000 players each. Such a rope would be over 200 miles long, and could stretch from New York to Washington. [Image: image] If our experience with nylon ropes failing is any indication, when the graphene finally snapped, the death toll could be enormous among both players and bystanders. Lengths of graphene would crack across the landscape like bullwhips, slicing down forests and demolishing buildings. In the end, trying to develop stronger ropes leads only to greater danger to everyone, both participants and bystanders. In the ultimate game of tug-of-war ... [Image: image] ... the only winning move is not to pull.

items.model_answer:
If tug-of-war teams pulled on an iron rod instead of a rope, the physics and dynamics of the game would change dramatically due to the rod's immense mass, lack of elasticity, and low surface friction. 

First, the sheer weight of the rod would alter the mechanics of the pull. An iron rod thick enough to grip comfortably (about 1.5 inches in diameter) and long enough for a standard match (around 100 feet) would weigh roughly 600 pounds. Teams would have to expend a massive amount of their physical energy just fighting gravity to keep the rod off the ground. This would transform the contest from a pure horizontal pulling match into a combined lifting and pulling endurance test. 

Second, the physics of force transmission would be entirely different. A standard tug-of-war rope has significant elasticity; as teams pull, the rope stretches and stores a massive amount of elastic potential energy. If the rope snaps or one team suddenly lets go, that stored energy is violently released, causing a dangerous whiplash effect that is responsible for severe injuries and amputations in competitive tug-of-war. An iron rod, however, has an incredibly high Young's modulus and is highly rigid. It would not stretch under human pulling force, meaning zero elastic potential energy would be stored. Force would be transmitted almost instantaneously with no slack, and if one team let go, the rod would simply shift backward with the winning team's momentum without any snapback effect.

Finally, the friction and safety hazards would shift. The smooth, unyielding surface of an iron rod provides far less friction than woven rope fibers, making it incredibly difficult to grip, especially as players' hands begin to sweat. While the rigid material means players would no longer suffer from rope burn or the deadly snapback of a broken rope, they would face a new, severe hazard: the blunt-force trauma of a massive, heavy iron beam instantly dropping onto their feet and legs the moment the match ends.

they would face a new, severe hazard:
the blunt-force trauma of a massive, heavy iron beam instantly dropping onto their feet and legs
the moment the match ends.

items.question: What If the Moon Were Replaced by a Black Hole of the Same Mass?
human_answers: "Not much" and "not much." [Image: image] A black hole the mass of the Moon would have an event horizon about the size of a sand grain. Specifically, according to one of my favorite charts (http://pubs.usgs.gov/of/2003/of03-001/htmldocs/images/chart.pdf), a black hole moon would be a grain of fine to medium-fine sand, and could pass through a sieve of size ASTM No. 70 or larger. I mean, I guess a black hole with the mass of the Moon would pass right through any sieve, destroying it in the process, but that's neither here nor there.[1]The expression "that's neither here nor there" can be kind of confusing and ambiguous, but I guess that's neither here nor there. Since the Moon's mass and position wouldn't change, the tides on Earth wouldn't change, either. When you're floating outside a spherical mass, its pull on you is the same regardless of whether the mass is concentrated at the center of the sphere or spread out throughout it. If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth's orbit wouldn't change, although life on Earth might (http://what-if.xkcd.com/49/). With the Moon gathered into a point, there'd be no moonlight, which would affect the life cycles of all kinds of nocturnal animals. But compared to a lot of the other (http://xkcd.com/1338/) things we've done, that would be fairly minor. The Earth's orbit is stabilized by the Moon (http://www.nature.com/nature/journal/v361/n6413/abs/361615a0.html), but the lunar-mass black hole would probably serve the same role. This black hole Moon (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mbBbFH9fAg) would be pretty low-profile. If it were much smaller, it would evaporate through Hawking radiation (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawking_radiation), but a black hole the size of the Moon actually absorbs more energy from the cosmic background radiation than it emits through the Hawking mechanism. Our black hole would really be black. [Image: image] At least, if it didn't eat anything. If the black hole devoured any objects, it would let off a tremendous blast of radiation. Black holes burn brightly as they devour things; the whirlpool of matter heats up as it falls inward (http://www.gothosenterprises.com/black_holes/outside_black_holes.html), causing it to glow brightly.[2]A black hole can't devour matter too fast, though, because at some point it would be producing so much radiation that it would blast its own "food" away. This is called the Eddington limit (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eddington_luminosity). If our black hole were devouring matter at the Eddington limit, it would be hot enough to sterilize the Earth. Fortunately, there's not a lot out there for it to eat, so it wouldn't glow very brightly for now. It would spend most of its time drastically altering the orbits of nearby dust particles—one sand grain pushing other sand grains around.[3]Even if it sucked in matter at the rate the Earth—with its much larger "collecting area"—sucks in interplanetary dust, it wouldn't necessarily be a problem for us. But there would be one interesting effect: In addition to getting darker, Earth would get colder, because moonlight warms the Earth. It's a very tiny contributor to our global energy balance; the Moon is five or six orders of magnitude dimmer than the Sun. But it's there. Measurements show that global temperature varies with a 28-day cycle (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2000GL011651/abstract); all else being equal, the Earth is hottest during the full moon. It's a tiny difference—small fractions of a degree—but it's there. But it turns out most of this effect is not due to moonlight. The largest contributor is the fact that the Earth is slightly closer to the Sun during a full Moon: [Image: image] Calculating the amount of energy radiated back to Earth by the Moon is deceptively tricky. The Moon reflects sunlight, but with some surprising twists. When the Moon is half-illuminated, you might think it would be half as bright as when full—but it's much less bright than that (http://home.earthlink.net/~kitathome/LunarLight/moonlight_gallery/technique/moonbright.htm). And once you account for that, there are even trickier effects to deal with, because science is the worst.[4]Like the fact that the waxing Moon is 20% brighter (http://www.jstor.org/discover/10.2307/2402251?sid=21105340972791&uid=2&uid=4&uid=3739808&uid=3739256) than the waning Moon, or that the Moon is a mild retroreflector (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_surge). Then, on top of all the weird visible-light effects, the Moon also heats up under the Sun, then radiates that heat as infrared light. There's a great discussion of the Moon's effect on the Earth's energy budget in this article (http://scitation.aip.org/content/aapt/journal/ajp/67/12/10.1119/1.19109?ver=pdfcov) by Robert Knox. The upshot is that the Moon's infrared heat radiation turns out to affect Earth's temperature about 10 times more than the visible moonlight, but still about 10 times less than the effect from gravity moving Earth closer and farther from the Sun. Knox even quantifies the effect this has on Earth's radiation balance—the presence of infrared moonlight warms the planet by 1.2 milli-degrees Fahrenheit (m°F). [Image: image] Without moonlight, the planet would cool down slightly. But given the accelerating rate at which we're adding (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keeling_Curve) CO2 to the atmosphere—which changes the Earth's energy balance—we'd make up the difference in a couple of weeks. So all in all, the conversion of the Moon to a black hole might not even be that big of a deal. Unless, of course, it happened on certain days between 1969 and 1972, in which case Nixon (http://www.archives.gov/presidential-libraries/events/centennials/nixon/images/exhibit/rn100-6-1-2.pdf) would've needed yet another one of those speeches (http://xkcd.com/1484/). [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual Premise and Gravitational Equivalence
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the answer correctly reasons from the premise that the Moon is replaced by a black hole of the same mass, preserving the Moon's external gravitational field while changing its size, luminosity, and surface properties.
criteria.1-2: Treats the black hole as vastly more massive or as immediately swallowing Earth; ignores the same-mass premise.
criteria.3-4: Mentions same mass but still predicts major orbital or tidal changes without justification.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that Earth's orbit and tides would be mostly unchanged, but gives limited explanation.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that external gravity depends on mass and distance, so tides, lunar orbit, and Earth-Moon dynamics remain broadly similar.
criteria.9-10: Accurately applies shell/external-field reasoning throughout, distinguishing unchanged gravitational effects from changed optical, accretion, and surface-related effects.

criteria.name: Black Hole Physical Scale, Stability, and Hawking Radiation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response correctly describes the physical properties of a lunar-mass black hole, including its tiny event horizon and negligible evaporation risk.
criteria.1-2: Claims the black hole would be planet-sized, explode, rapidly evaporate, or otherwise misstates basic black hole scale.
criteria.3-4: Identifies it as small but gives no reliable sense of scale or wrongly emphasizes Hawking radiation as dangerous.
criteria.5-6: States that the event horizon would be tiny and that evaporation is not an immediate threat, with minimal detail.
criteria.7-8: Gives an appropriate scale, such as sand-grain-sized, and explains that a lunar-mass black hole is stable over astronomical timescales.
criteria.9-10: Quantitatively or semi-quantitatively captures the Schwarzschild-radius scale and correctly notes that Hawking emission is negligible compared with environmental absorption.

criteria.name: Accretion, Radiation, and Hazard Assessment
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates treatment of whether the black-hole Moon would consume matter, emit radiation, or become dangerous through accretion rather than gravity alone.
criteria.1-2: Assumes it rapidly sucks in Earth, the atmosphere, or the Solar System without considering distance or accretion limits.
criteria.3-4: Mentions accretion but greatly exaggerates its rate or ignores that space near the Moon is mostly empty.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that little matter is available to eat, so immediate radiation hazards are probably small.
criteria.7-8: Explains that accretion could produce intense radiation if supplied with matter, but normal lunar-orbit conditions provide little fuel.
criteria.9-10: Balances low geometric capture rates, orbital perturbations of dust/debris, possible bright accretion episodes, and Eddington-limit-style self-regulation without sensationalism.

criteria.name: Downstream Earth Effects: Darkness, Climate, Biology, and Observation
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the main non-gravitational consequences on Earth, including loss of moonlight, lunar infrared emission, night ecology, human observation, and small temperature effects.
criteria.1-2: Claims no effects at all or invents dominant catastrophic climate consequences unrelated to the premise.
criteria.3-4: Mentions darkness but misses most downstream effects or overstates climate impacts.
criteria.5-6: Covers loss of visible moonlight and some ecological or cultural consequences, with rough plausibility.
criteria.7-8: Adds that thermal/climate effects would be tiny, while nocturnal ecosystems, sky brightness, tides' appearance, and lunar exploration would change.
criteria.9-10: Integrates visible light, reflected sunlight, lunar infrared, small 28-day energy-balance effects, ecological impacts, and observational consequences with correct relative magnitudes.

criteria.name: Long-Range Causal Coherence, Calibration, and Contradiction Control
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates whether the full answer maintains a coherent causal chain over short-, medium-, and long-term consequences without contradictions or unjustified certainty.
criteria.1-2: Presents disconnected or mutually contradictory claims, such as unchanged gravity plus immediate tidal destruction.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible points but mixes them with major contradictions or unsupported leaps.
criteria.5-6: Provides a mostly coherent sequence but lacks nuance about timescales, magnitudes, or conditional hazards.
criteria.7-8: Separates immediate effects from long-term effects and calibrates uncertainty about accretion, climate, and biological impacts.
criteria.9-10: Maintains consistent physics across all mechanisms, ranks effects by magnitude, flags speculative branches, and avoids both catastrophic exaggeration and false 'nothing changes' oversimplification.

items.model_answer:
If the Moon were suddenly replaced by a black hole of the exact same mass, the gravitational effects on Earth would remain completely unchanged, but the visual and ecological impacts would be profound. 

Because gravity depends only on mass and distance, a lunar-mass black hole would exert the exact same gravitational pull on Earth as our current Moon. The Earth-moon barycenter would remain the same, meaning our ocean tides, the length of our days, and the black hole's 27.3-day orbital period would continue exactly as they do now. The black hole would not "suck in" the Earth; it would simply orbit safely at the same 238,900-mile distance. 

However, the physical size of this black hole would be incredibly tiny. The Schwarzschild radius for a black hole with the Moon's mass is about 0.1 millimeters—roughly the size of a grain of sand. Because it is so unimaginably small and emits no light, the Moon would effectively vanish from the sky. Nights on Earth would become significantly darker, entirely devoid of moonlight, which would disrupt the navigation, hunting, and mating behaviors of countless nocturnal animal species. 

Additionally, solar and lunar eclipses as we know them would cease to exist. If the black hole passed in front of the Sun, it would be far too small to block any sunlight. Instead of an eclipse, it would merely act as a microscopic gravitational lens, bending the light of the Sun in a way that would be practically unnoticeable to the naked eye. 

Finally, a black hole of this mass would be perfectly stable. It is massive enough that its Hawking radiation temperature would be colder than the cosmic microwave background, meaning it would not evaporate away. At the same time, its physical cross-section is so tiny that it would rarely collide with stray atoms of solar wind, meaning it would not actively accrete matter or emit dangerous X-rays. It would simply remain a silent, invisible, grain-sized companion orbiting Earth for eons.

edus.text: If the Moon were suddenly replaced by a black hole of the exact same mass,
the gravitational effects on Earth would remain completely unchanged,
but the visual and ecological impacts would be profound.
Because gravity depends only on mass and distance,
a lunar-mass black hole would exert the exact same gravitational pull on Earth as our current Moon.
The Earth-moon barycenter would remain the same,
meaning our ocean tides, the length of our days, and the black hole's 27.3-day orbital period would continue exactly as they do now.
The black hole would not "suck in" the Earth;
it would simply orbit safely at the same 238,900-mile distance.
However, the physical size of this black hole would be incredibly tiny.
The Schwarzschild radius for a black hole with the Moon's mass is about 0.1 millimeters—roughly the size of a grain of sand.
Because it is so unimaginably small and emits no light,
the Moon would effectively vanish from the sky.
Nights on Earth would become significantly darker, entirely devoid of moonlight,
which would disrupt the navigation, hunting, and mating behaviors of countless nocturnal animal species.
Additionally, solar and lunar eclipses as we know them would cease to exist.
If the black hole passed in front of the Sun,
it would be far too small to block any sunlight.
Instead of an eclipse,
it would merely act as a microscopic gravitational lens,
bending the light of the Sun in a way that would be practically unnoticeable to the naked eye.
Finally, a black hole of this mass would be perfectly stable.
It is massive enough that its Hawking radiation temperature would be colder than the cosmic microwave background,
meaning it would not evaporate away.
At the same time, its physical cross-section is so tiny that it would rarely collide with stray atoms of solar wind,
meaning it would not actively accrete matter or emit dangerous X-rays.
It would simply remain a silent, invisible, grain-sized companion orbiting Earth for eons.

items.question: What If You Mounted a High-Power Microwave on a Car to Melt Ice?
human_answers: Believe it or not, your flamethrower idea is actually the more practical of the two. The flamethrower also has the advantage that, unlike the microwave, it won't interfere with wifi (unless you aim it directly at the router). [Image: image] I'm writing this article from Boston, which is currently buried under a truly ridiculous amount of snow (http://www.buzzfeed.com/mjs538/please-stop-snowing). We've had more snow in the past 30 days (http://weather.ou.edu/~splillo/misc.html) than Anchorage, Alaska usually gets in an entire winter.[1]Meanwhile, Anchorage is on Twitter wondering (https://twitter.com/NWSBoston/status/567172928593485824) where their snow went and threatening revenge (https://twitter.com/NWSAnchorage/status/567566488517619712). Here's (https://twitter.com/EricHolthaus/status/567350490912931840) a neat visualization of the atmospheric pattern during these polar vortexes. Vortices. Whatever. Our transit system has broken down (http://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2015/02/14/transportation/U7vNqP861gKQFRly2jmjdL/story.html) and our roofs[2]Tolkien prefers rooves. are collapsing (http://www.whdh.com/story/28133433/dozens-of-roof-collapses-reported-across-new-england). The mayor gave a press conference (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/2015/02/15/boston-mayor-seems-pretty-tired-all-this-dang-snow/OYtAnLLNQ2iMBMRaxTJYzJ/story.html?s_campaign=bcom%3Asocialflow%3Atwitter) in which he announced, "I don't know what to say to anybody anymore. Hopefully it will stop eventually." So snow removal is on all our minds. But snow is hard to melt. (And we've been trying (https://twitter.com/NotifyBoston/status/564524089017401347)[3]I love that tweet because it sort of sounds like it comes from an alternate fairy-tale universe where cities farm snow and snow-melters form the base of the economy.) Your microwave idea certainly sounds like it should be more practical than a flamethrower. Microwaves seem clean and efficient; after all, we don't use flamethrowers in our kitchens. [Image: image] But there's a big problem: Microwaves heat water very well, but they don't really work on ice (http://www.thenakedscientists.com/HTML/content/kitchenscience/exp/-324719c1f8/). Fortunately, there are other ways to get energy into the ice. In addition to your flamethrower suggestion, you could, for example, use infrared heat lamps or lasers.[4]Pick a frequency where snow has a low albedo; otherwise, the FBI may hunt you down for lasering aircraft (http://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/why-its-terrible-idea-point-lasers-airplanes-n28841). But whatever you use, you'll run into another problem: It takes an awful lot of energy to melt snow. Melting a gram of snow takes about 335 joules of energy. To put that another way, a 60-watt lightbulb is capable of melting about a pound of snow an hour. A foot of snow contains roughly the same amount of water as an inch of rain, give or take (http://www.theweatherprediction.com/habyhints/346/). Let's assume you've had a decent snowstorm of about a foot[5]For the record, by this standard, Boston has had a "decent snowstorm" every few days for the past month.—meaning an inch worth of water—and that you want to melt a 9-foot-wide swath while driving along at 55 mph. Luckily, this happens to be one of those happy physics situations where we can just multiply together every number we're looking at, and the answer (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=55+mph+*+water+density+*+1+inch+*+9+feet+*+335+J%2Fgram) turns out to be the measurement we want: \[55\text{ mph}\times1\text{ inch}\times9\text{ feet}\times\text{water density}\times335\tfrac{\text{J}}{\text{gram}}=574\text{ megawatts}\] Unfortunately, it's not the answer we'd like. The nuclear reactor on an aircraft carrier, for example, produces less than 200 megawatts. To melt snow in front of your car, you'd need three of those. [Image: image] What about your your original flamethrower idea? Gasoline may have a phenomenally high energy density (http://what-if.xkcd.com/128/), but it's not high enough. No matter how big the tank on your flamethrower was, you'd run out of fuel constantly. Gas mileage in the US is often measured in "miles per gallon" of gasoline. With your flamethrower guzzling fuel, your mileage would be about 17 feet per gallon. You might be better off dropping the flamethrower entirely. Instead, take a cue from the rail agencies, who use jet-engine-powered snowblowers (http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2011/01/23/mbtas_mattapan_line_relies_on_snowzilla_in_worst_weather/) to clear train tracks. In the end, it's easier to just move the snow out of your way. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
Mounting a high-power microwave on a car to melt ice would be completely impractical, highly inefficient, and incredibly dangerous. 

First, from a physics standpoint, microwaves are surprisingly bad at melting ice. Microwave emitters work via dielectric heating, which relies on rapidly flipping freely moving water molecules back and forth to generate friction and heat. In ice, the water molecules are locked in a rigid crystal lattice and cannot rotate easily, making ice largely transparent to microwave radiation. Instead of immediately melting the ice, the microwave energy would pass right through it and strike the road beneath. 

This leads to severe collateral damage. The asphalt or concrete would absorb the microwaves, rapidly heating any liquid water trapped inside the pavement's pores. This trapped water would flash into steam, causing the road surface to crack, shatter, or violently explode in a process called spalling. Furthermore, the microwaves would reflect off the ground and scatter in all directions. This stray radiation would fry your car’s electronics, heat the steel belts in your tires until the rubber melted, and inflict severe, deep-tissue radiation burns on any nearby pedestrians, animals, or other drivers. 

Even if you ignored the safety hazards and the physics of ice, the energy requirements make the concept impossible. The latent heat of fusion—the energy required to change water from a solid to a liquid—is massive. To melt just a one-centimeter-thick layer of ice in the path of a car driving at typical residential speeds, the microwave emitter would need to output tens of megawatts of continuous power. A standard car engine or electric vehicle battery produces only a tiny fraction of this, meaning you would need to tow a small commercial power plant just to generate enough electricity. 

Ultimately, a microwave-equipped car would fail to clear the road, destroy the pavement beneath the ice, and create a lethal hazard for everything in its vicinity.

edus.text: Mounting a high-power microwave on a car to melt ice would be completely impractical, highly inefficient, and incredibly dangerous.
First, from a physics standpoint, microwaves are surprisingly bad at melting ice.
Microwave emitters work via dielectric heating,
which relies on rapidly flipping freely moving water molecules back and forth to generate friction and heat.
In ice, the water molecules are locked in a rigid crystal lattice and cannot rotate easily,
making ice largely transparent to microwave radiation.
Instead of immediately melting the ice, the microwave energy would pass right through it and strike the road beneath.
This leads to severe collateral damage.
The asphalt or concrete would absorb the microwaves,
rapidly heating any liquid water trapped inside the pavement's pores.
This trapped water would flash into steam,
causing the road surface to crack, shatter, or violently explode in a process called spalling.
Furthermore, the microwaves would reflect off the ground and scatter in all directions.

This stray radiation would fry your car’s electronics, heat the steel belts in your tires until the rubber melted, and inflict severe, deep-tissue radiation burns on any nearby pedestrians, animals, or other drivers.
Even if you ignored the safety hazards and the physics of ice, the energy requirements make the concept impossible.
The latent heat of fusion—the energy required to change water from a solid to a liquid—is massive.
To melt just a one-centimeter-thick layer of ice in the path of a car driving at typical residential speeds, the microwave emitter would need to output tens of megawatts of continuous power.
A standard car engine or electric vehicle battery produces only a tiny fraction of this,
meaning you would need to tow a small commercial power plant just to generate enough electricity.
Ultimately, a microwave-equipped car would fail to clear the road, destroy the pavement beneath the ice, and create a lethal hazard for everything in its vicinity.

items.question: What If a Falling Person Grabbed a Flagpole and Swung Back to the Roof?
human_answers: If you're like me, your first thought on hearing this question was, "That's ridiculous; there's no way that could work." Your first thought is right. But just to be sure, let's take a closer look. Grip strength depends on a lot of factors, like hand slickness and surface material. But for the moment, let's assume Rex's hands are able to grab the pole tightly. What happens to the rest of his body? [Image: image] It's hard to find good numbers on how much force it takes to tear off a person's arm.[1]Which is probably a good thing, to be honest. There are threads on the question on MetaFilter (http://ask.metafilter.com/133821/How-much-force-to-tear-off-a-limb) and the Straight Dope message boards (http://boards.straightdope.com/sdmb/showthread.php?t=515612), and frequent discussion of the death of Robert-François Damiens (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert-Fran%C3%A7ois_Damiens),[2]Damiens was tortured to death for attempting to assassinate Louis XV, but a team of horses had trouble tearing him limb from limb. but not too much hard data. For the record, there are lots (https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article/215/20/3552/11014/Tendon-material-properties-vary-and-are) of studies (http://www.udel.edu/PT/PT%20Clinical%20Services/journalclub/sojc/95_96/apr96/itoi.pdf) and lectures (http://wings.buffalo.edu/eng/mae/courses/417-517/Orthopaedic%20Biomechanics/Lecture%203u.pdf) on the breaking strength of tendons, which tend to give values of around 50-150 MPa. That's stronger than skin (27 MPa (http://www.ircobi.org/downloads/irc12/pdf_files/59.pdf)) but weaker than bone (120 MPa (http://www.robmech.co.za/proceed/ROBMECH2011_Unene%20N.%20MAnganyi_Biological%20considerations%20in%20the%20structural%20design%20of%20smart%20prosthetics.pdf)). However, to figure out the overall strength of the arm, we need to tally up all the tendons, muscles, and tissues in the wrist, arm, and shoulder, their cross-sectional area, and figure out which parts would be put under strain in what order. Instead, it might be easier to consider people who try to pull off this maneuver in real life: Gymnasts. A gymnast on the uneven parallel bars pushes the human body to its limits while performing maneuvers very similar to Rex's flagpole stunt.[3]In some ways, at least. A 2009 study (http://www.jbiomech.com/article/S0021-9290(09)00609-5/fulltext) used 3D motion capture to measure the forces involved in an elite gymnast's routine. They found that the athlete's hands exerted a force of over 3 kN on the bar at the bottom of a swing. In other words, the gymnast was briefly supporting almost 700 lbs of weight. Let's be generous and assume that Rex is even better than the elite gymnast in the study. (After all, the gymnast has to worry about long-term injury, while Rex's concerns are a lot more short-term). Suppose Rex's arms can handle a swing force of over 10 kN, three times more than the gymnast (and twice as much as these (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V1JBx2Mm9e8) guys (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJYOs5VFjwk)!). How will he do? Let's see how much force Rex needs to withstand. The "tallest building in town" here in Boston is the 240-meter-tall Hancock Tower (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hancock_Tower); if he jumped off the top, he'd be going nearly 100 mph by the time he was halfway down. At that speed, the force on his arms (speed squared over the radius of his turn[4]Which is effectively somewhere between 1 and 2 meters here.) would be around ... 100 kN (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=100+lbs+*+(100+mph)%5E2+%2F+(1.5+meters)). [Image: image] Really, the numbers are just telling us what common sense told us from the start: You can't grab hold of something while going 100 mph, much less swing around it. If you want get a more vivid intuitive sense of the forces involved, consider this: In 2006, GQ put baseball star Albert Pujols in a lab and measured his swing. They clocked the speed of his bat at 87 mph, similar to the speed of the flagpole relative to our falling person. So if you want to pull off Rex's stunt, first go find Albert Pujols, have him swing his bat as hard as you can ... and try to grab it. [Image: image] And remember: You're just trying to stop the momentum of a 31-ounce piece of wood. When you're falling past the flagpole, you're going to be catching your whole body, so it's going to be up to 100 times worse. Good luck! [Image: image]

criteria.name: Core physical plausibility and conclusion
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a physically defensible conclusion about a falling person grabbing a flagpole at high speed and swinging back to the roof.
criteria.1-2: Claims the stunt would likely work or treats it as easy, with little or no physical justification.
criteria.3-4: Expresses doubt but leaves the outcome ambiguous or bases the conclusion on weak intuition only.
criteria.5-6: Concludes it is very unlikely or impossible, citing excessive force or speed in general terms.
criteria.7-8: Clearly explains that the person could not safely grab and swing back because the required deceleration/centripetal force far exceeds human limits.
criteria.9-10: Gives a decisive, physically grounded conclusion: grip, arms, shoulders, or tissues would fail or the person would be severely injured long before a successful swing back to the roof.

criteria.name: Force and motion mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of the relevant mechanics: fall speed, momentum change, circular motion around the pole, radius of swing, and forces transmitted through the hands and arms.
criteria.1-2: Ignores mechanics or relies on unrelated ideas such as bravery, agility, or cinematic timing.
criteria.3-4: Mentions falling speed or impact force but does not connect them to the pole grab or swing dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Identifies that grabbing the pole would require stopping or redirecting the body's momentum, but with limited detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains that the body must undergo rapid centripetal acceleration around a small radius, creating forces many times body weight.
criteria.9-10: Integrates fall velocity, swing radius, centripetal acceleration, grip load, and body-momentum redirection into a coherent mechanical account.

criteria.name: Biomechanical realism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer realistically treats human grip, tendons, shoulders, arms, and injury thresholds in the flagpole scenario.
criteria.1-2: Assumes hands and arms can withstand arbitrary loads or ignores injury entirely.
criteria.3-4: Mentions possible injury but does not specify what would fail or why.
criteria.5-6: Notes that grip strength or arm strength would be insufficient under the load.
criteria.7-8: Discusses likely failure modes such as losing grip, dislocated shoulders, torn tendons/ligaments, broken bones, or severe soft-tissue injury.

items.model_answer:
It is physically impossible for a falling person to grab a flagpole and swing back up to the roof they fell from due to the laws of energy conservation and human biomechanical limits. 

According to the conservation of energy, as a person falls, their gravitational potential energy converts into kinetic energy. To swing back up to the exact height of the roof, they would need to retain 100% of that initial energy. However, grabbing the flagpole initiates a highly inelastic collision. A massive amount of the person's kinetic energy would be instantly dissipated as heat, sound, and the physical deformation of both the flagpole and the person's body. Combined with further energy lost to air resistance and friction between their hands and the pole during the swing, the person would have a severe energy deficit and could never reach their starting altitude.

Furthermore, the human body cannot withstand the physical forces required for this maneuver. The sudden deceleration, combined with the extreme centripetal force needed to redirect a vertical drop into a circular swing, would generate forces many times the person's own body weight. This violent jerk would instantly exceed maximum human grip strength, causing the person's hands to slip off the pole. Even if their grip somehow held, the immense force would dislocate their shoulders, tear muscles and ligaments, and potentially break the flagpole. Ultimately, rather than swinging back to safety, the person would suffer catastrophic upper-body injuries and continue falling to the ground.

items.question: What Would Happen to a Human Body Left in Orbit?
human_answers: This isn't really relevant, but I have to ask: Is there a reason you specifically wanted your corpse to be naked? Just making things extra weird for the technicians loading up the capsule and/or throwing you out of the airlock? [Image: image] If you tried this, the first thing that would happen to your corpse would be that it would dry out. This would probably start before you made it to space; the dry, climate-controlled air in the pre-launch waiting area would help draw moisture from your body. In the Manual of Forensic Taphonomy, Franklin Damann and David Carter outline the process of human decomposition. According to them, it takes a lot of effort to keep corpses from drying out during the embalming process.[1]The citation they give for that fact is "(C. A. Wacker, pers. comm.)," which I like to think means it was shared in a conversation that totally broke up the dinner party they were both at. In extremely dry environments like the Atacama Desert in Chile, "spontaneous mummification" can occur—and space is even drier than Chile.[2]The space tourism industry has not adopted this as a slogan. Also, "Chile: Not as Dry as Space!" was probably nixed by the Chilean tourism board. Once your body made it to space, this process would ramp up quickly. Most of the "ecology" responsible for decomposing your corpse would be killed off quickly by the drying process (along with the lack of oxygen, temperature swings, and solar radiation levels), so your body wouldn't decay very much. Instead, you'd become a freeze-dried mummy, after losing about 80% of your body weight in water.[3]This is how much liquid you can remove from fresh animal tissue, according to lab experiments reported in Arthur C. Aufderheide's book The Scientific Study of Mummies. That makes sense; after all, according to that commonly-repeated piece of trivia, human bodies are around 70% water. Or is it 65%? Or 80%? The exact number is a little vague, and seems to depend on who you ask. In a footnote in her wonderful book, Stiff: The Curious Lives of Human Cadavers, writer Mary Roach mentioned that she had methodically Googled the phrase "human body is <X> percent water", for X from 0 to 100. She reported a wide range of claims, including several pages asserting that we're 98% water. It's really gratifying to know I'm not the only person who spends a lot of time carefully cataloging weird stuff like that. What happens next depends on exactly where in space you are. If you're in an orbit that passes near the Earth, your orbit will quickly decay, and before long you'll re-enter the atmosphere and burn up. If you're in a slightly higher orbit, you'll last longer, but you'd also be in the zone where space debris (http://commons.erau.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1000&context=stm) was thickest. Impacts with small bits of debris would start to leave pits and scars on your surface; they would often find these on Space Shuttle windows after a flight. Eventually, probably after a few decades, you'd probably have a violent collision with something. Higher orbits are safer. If you were some distance away from the Earth, near where geosynchronous satellites orbit, there would be less debris to run into. Furthermore, for large, dense objects, orbits out there are stable (http://www.readcube.com/articles/10.1029%2F92JE00032?show_checkout=1) for a very long time. You could spend centuries drifting among TV broadcast satellites. [Image: image] If you wanted to last even longer, you could launch yourself away from Earth completely, finding a quiet and stable orbit somewhere in interplanetary space. There, over the course of millennia, you'd be slowly baked by the Sun's radiation and pitted and powdered by micrometeorites. But if your goal is to weird out future space travelers, that might not be the best plan. Space is big; if someone randomly stumbles on your corpse, it suggests that there must be a lot of people zipping around the solar system. And if space travel has become that common, there will be lots of corpses floating around;[4]Weird that "lots of corpses floating around" is somehow an optimistic prediction about the future of space travel. discovering yours will be more archaeologically exciting than anything. You'll be stuck in a lab or museum somewhere and contribute to someone's research paper—a bland end to your exciting prank. Unless, of course, you happen to be found by the only people in space even weirder than you. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If a human body were left in Earth orbit, it would not explode as often depicted in science fiction, but would instead undergo a rapid process of freeze-drying and mummification. In the vacuum of space, the sudden lack of atmospheric pressure would cause the liquid on the surface of the eyes, skin, and lungs to vaporize almost instantly. While human skin is strong and elastic enough to keep the body's internal organs intact, the corpse would quickly lose its moisture. Because space lacks an atmosphere to conduct heat, the body's internal temperature would drop gradually, but the exterior would face extreme temperature fluctuations—baking at over 250°F (120°C) in direct sunlight and freezing at minus 250°F (-150°C) in Earth's shadow. 

Initially, anaerobic bacteria in the gut would begin decomposing the body from the inside out, but this putrefaction would halt entirely as soon as the body froze or fully desiccated. Over the long term, the body would become a rigid, floating mummy. Unfiltered ultraviolet and cosmic radiation would severely bleach the skin and slowly break down the molecular bonds of the organic tissue. Additionally, constant bombardment by microscopic space debris and micrometeoroids would gradually pit and erode the corpse over time. 

The ultimate fate of the body depends entirely on its orbital altitude. If left in Low Earth Orbit (LEO), the faint traces of atmospheric drag would gradually degrade its orbit over a few years or decades. Eventually, the body would be pulled back into Earth's atmosphere, where the extreme friction of re-entry would cause it to completely incinerate like a shooting star. items.question: What If You Dug Straight Down at One Foot per Second?
human_answers: This question is the reverse of question #64 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/64/), which asked how you'd die if you rose steadily at a foot per second. Digging at the same rate would kill you more quickly. [Image: image] After you get through the surface layers,[1]See question #132 (http://what-if.xkcd.com/132/) for more on that. temperatures rise pretty steadily as you go deeper, a trend that continues all the way to the core. In some areas, where the hot magma[2](Lava (http://xkcd.com/1405/).) is closer to the surface, the ground gets hotter more quickly. The Southern Methodist University Geothermal Lab has produced some superb maps (http://www.smu.edu/Dedman/Academics/Programs/GeothermalLab/DataMaps/TemperatureMaps) showing the temperature of deep rocks in different parts of the United States. If you look at the map of the 3.5 km layer (http://www.smu.edu/~/media/Site/Dedman/Academics/Programs/Geothermal%20Lab/Graphics/TemperatureMaps/SMU_2011_35kmTemperature.ashx?la=en), you see that at that depth, most of the US is colored greenish-yellow, representing temperatures somewhere around 100°C—with one glaring exception. In northwest Wyoming, there's a circle of ground colored bright red, where the rock is much hotter than normal. That circle is the Yellowstone supervolcano (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_Caldera). [Image: image] The SMU maps show that even if you avoided digging in Yellowstone, you'd quickly encounter temperatures too hot for an unprotected human. The ground typically gets hotter at an average of about 35°C per kilometer, so at a rate of a foot per second, you'd encounter lethal heat within an hour or two. But wait a moment. Let's say your hole is about a meter wide. At the rate you're digging, you have to remove roughly half a ton of material every second. No human would be capable of lifting that first foot of material out of the hole so quickly, and it only gets worse after that. After a minute of digging, you'd be 60 feet down, and would have to lift all that rock and dirt a huge distance vertically to get it out of the hole. The power required to do that lifting—just after the first minute—would be roughly 150 horsepower. [Image: image] Even if you're not doing the lifting yourself, the way your question is worded makes it pretty clear that you are in this hole. Whatever process you're using is going to require huge amounts of energy to lift all that rock, and that energy is inevitably going to result in the hole being heated somehow. Even if the layer you're digging through wasn't hot when you started, it will be. What if we assume you're protected against the heat from the ground (and the digging mechanism)? Well, in that case, the pressure would become a problem. As you go deeper, air pressure increases. Below about 5 km, the pressure is high enough that oxygen (http://www.scuba-doc.com/oxygentox.html) becomes toxic (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LOZuxwVk7TU). So what if you're protected against the heat, pressure, and the digging process? Well, at that point, we've redefined the rules so much that I'm not sure it makes sense to try to calculate an answer. The question—"what would kill you if you kept digging downward"—has left the realm of physics and become fantasy. Which, come to think of it, makes the answer perfectly clear. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you possessed an indestructible suit and magical digging equipment that allowed you to dig straight down at a constant rate of one foot per second, it would take you approximately 242 days to reach the center of the Earth, and about 484 days (roughly a year and four months) to pop out on the exact opposite side of the globe. 

The Earth's radius is about 3,959 miles, which translates to nearly 21 million feet. At one foot per second, you are traveling at a sluggish 0.68 miles per hour. Within the first day, you would pass through soil, bedrock, and the water table. After about 15 days, you would surpass the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia, the deepest hole ever dug by humanity. Beyond this point, the journey becomes physically impossible without fictional technology. 

As you breach the Earth's crust and enter the mantle, the temperature would quickly rise to thousands of degrees, and the pressure would become crushing. For the next 200 days, you would be digging through incredibly dense, semi-solid rock that flows like plastic under immense pressure. Around day 215, you would hit the outer core, a churning ocean of liquid iron and nickel that generates Earth's magnetic field. Because it is liquid, your tunnel would instantly fill with molten metal reaching temperatures up to 9,000 degrees Fahrenheit. By day 230, you would hit the inner core, a sphere of solid iron and nickel that is as hot as the surface of the sun but kept solid by the unfathomable weight of the entire planet pressing down on it.

Throughout your journey, you would experience two bizarre physical phenomena. First, due to the Coriolis effect, the Earth's rotation would cause you to constantly drift and scrape against the eastern wall of your tunnel unless you started digging exactly at the North or South Pole. Second, your experience of gravity would change. As you get closer to the center, there is more of the Earth's mass above you pulling you upward, canceling out the gravitational pull from below. By the time you reached the exact center of the Earth on day 242, you would experience zero gravity and float weightlessly. 

If you continued digging past the center, "down" would suddenly become "up." You would have to dig upward against gravity for another 242 days, pushing through the inner core, outer core, mantle, and crust, until you finally broke the surface on the other side of the world.

items.question: What If You Dropped a Submarine into Jupiter?
human_answers: Nope! Jupiter's pressure, density, and temperature curves are different from ours. At the point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the density is high enough for a submarine to float, the pressure is high enough to crush the submarine,[1]Which makes it more dense. and the temperature is high enough to melt it.[2]Which makes it harder to drive. [Image: image] But there's another problem: Jupiter is a gas giant, but submarines—as you can figure out from etymology—go under water. [Image: image] Air and water are different. This seems straightforward enough, but they're also the same in a lot of ways. They're both "fluids," and some of the same rules apply to each. In some sense, when you look up at the sky (http://xkcd.com/1556/), you're looking up from the bottom of a deep sea of air. Things float when they're less dense than the fluid around them. This works the same for balloons in air and boats in water. The late Terry Pratchett wrote a truly beautiful passage about this, in the prologue to his book Going Postal. He says that since water is in many respects a wetter form of air,[3]Sounds reasonable enough to me. as ships sink, eventually they reach a point where the water was too dense to sink any further. This layer forms an underwater surface on which shipwrecks collect, drifting around beneath the waves but far above the sea floor:It’s calm there. Dead calm.Some stricken ships have rigging; some even have sails. Many still have crew, tangled in the rigging or lashed to the wheel.But the voyages still continue, aimlessly, with no harbour in sight, because there are currents under the ocean and so the dead ships with their skeleton crews sail on around the world, over sunken cities and between drowned mountains, until rot and shipworms eat them away and they disintegrate.Sometimes an anchor drops, all the way to the dark, cold calmness of the abyssal plain, and disturbs the stillness of centuries by throwing up a cloud of silt. I love that passage. It's also completely wrong. Ships sink all the way to the bottom. (Sir Terry knew this, as the rest of the passage makes clear, but he's describing how ships work on Discworld, not Earth.) Air follows the ideal gas law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law). The more pressure you put on it, the smaller (and denser) it gets. Water, on the other hand, is pretty much incompressible. When you dive into the ocean, the pressure increases as you go deeper (rising by one atmosphere every 10 meters or so) but the water's density barely changes all the way down to the sea floor. Buoyancy depends on density, not pressure. There's a point in Jupiter's atmosphere where the pressure is equal to a little more than an Earth atmosphere—which is the pressure a submarine is used to—but the air there is barely a tenth as dense as ours. A submarine in that layer would fall even faster than it would in the air on Earth. [Image: image] To reach a depth where it could "float" in Jupiter, the submarine would have to go halfway to the center of the planet, where the intense pressure turns the air into a metallic soup (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metallic_hydrogen) that's hotter than the surface of the Sun. The pressure there would be so high that not only would the submarine be crushed, the substances that make it up would probably be converted into new and exciting forms. It's hard to create those kinds of conditions in a lab, so we don't know a lot about how materials behave with that much pressure pushing down on them. [Image: image] In the sea, on the other hand, the density of the fluid stays relatively constant. That means the submarine can find its appropriate pressure range and float there. In other words, submarines only work because water doesn't follow the ideal gas law. But there's one more twist: Water sort of does obey the ideal gas law. The equations governing water under normal pressure are similar to (http://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.0534.pdf) the equation for a gas under about twenty thousand atmospheres of pressure. In a sense, this is why water seems incompressible to us—it behaves as if it's already compressed so much that an extra atmosphere or two hardly makes a difference. So, in some ways, water and air are more similar than they seem, but in the ways that matter for a submarine, they really are different. Which, of course, brings us back to why it's called a submarine—it operates under a "mare". A vehicle designed to operate beneath a sea of air would be called a subaerine.[5]The "gas" in "gas giant" is from the Greek word for void (χάος, kháos), so maybe a vessel (σκάφη, skáphē) that travels through a gas giant's atmosphere would be a khaoskaphe. Which, come to think of it, is a perfectly good description of a car. [Image: image]
