items.question: What If You Tried to Drink Niagara Falls through a Straw?
human_answers: One would get in trouble with the International Niagara Committee, the International Niagara Board of Control, the International Joint Commission, the International Niagara Board Working Committee, and probably the Great Lakes–St. Lawrence River Adaptive Management Committee.[2]Which is, if I'm understanding these organizational charts right, itself a supergroup made up of three committees for individual bodies of water. Also, the Earth would be destroyed. [Image: image] Well, that's not quite right. At the risk of stating the obvious, the real answer is, "Niagara Falls wouldn't fit through a straw." There are limits to how fast you can push fluids through things. If you pump a fluid through a narrow opening, it speeds up. If the fluid is a gas,[3]Gasses are fluids. I know that's weird, but many things are weird. it becomes "choked" when the speed of the gas flowing through the opening reaches the speed of sound. At that point, the gas flowing through the hole can't move any faster—although you can still get more mass to flow through per second by increasing the pressure, which compresses the gas further. For water, a different effect causes it to choke. When a fluid flows through an opening fast enough, the pressure within the fluid drops due to the Bernoulli principle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli%27s_principle). Water always "wants" to boil, but is held together by air pressure. Without enough pressure, bubbles of steam form in the water. This is called cavitation. When the water is forced through an opening at high speed, cavitation bubbles cause it to become less dense overall. Increasing the pressure—to try to push the water through harder—only makes it boil faster. (See page 17 here (http://www.controlglobal.com/assets/Media/MediaManager/RefBook_Cashco_Fluid.pdf) for a description of this process.)[4]Valve designers try to avoid creating these steam bubbles, because after the bubbles form, they quickly collapse as the pressure rises back up past the valve, and the force from that collapse can gradually eat away at plumbing. This keeps the total amount of water making it through the opening from rising, even if the water-steam mix moves at a higher speed. Another limit on the water flow rate comes from the speed of sound. You can't use pressure to accelerate water through an opening faster than the speed of sound (in water).[5]It's sort of like a traffic jam—forcing more cars into the back of a traffic jam won't make the ones in the front come out faster. The analogy between traffic jams and choked flows isn't perfect, but I still like it, because it's fun to imagine someone trying to solve traffic jams by using a bulldozer to push more cars into them. However, water very rarely reaches this point, because "the speed of sound in water" is very fast. If you try to make water—which is pretty heavy—go that fast, it tends to start ignoring the turns in your pipes. [Image: image] So how fast does Niagara Falls need to go to fit through a straw, and is it faster than the speed of sound? This is easy to figure out; all we need to know is the flow rate over the falls and how much area it needs to fit through. The flow rate over Niagara Falls is at least 100,000 cubic feet per second (http://niagara.nypa.gov/ALP%20working%20documents/finalreports/html/IS23WL.htm), which is actually mandated by law. The Niagara river supplies a total of about 292,000 cubic feet per second to the falls, but much of it is diverted into tunnels to generate electric power. However, since people get mad if you turn off the world's most famous waterfall, they're required to leave at least 100,000 of those cubic feet per second flowing over the falls for everyone to look at. (50,000 at night or during the off-season). Sometime in the next few years, the falls may be turned off (http://www.buffalonews.com/city-region/niagara-falls/niagara-falls-is-going-to-go-dry-x2013-again-20160123) for maintanence. And probably to see what cool stuff they can find. [Image: image] (Important note: If you divert the water into a straw, you'll be in violation of the 1950 treaty establishing the "100,000 cubic feet per second" limit. This is monitored by the International Niagara Committee (http://www.appointments-nominations.gc.ca/prflOrg.asp?OrgID=INNC&lang=eng), which consists of one American and one Canadian.[6]Currently (http://ijc.org/files/tinymce/uploaded/INBC/20150910_NiagaraPublicMeetingPresentation_Final.pdf), they are Aaron Thompson of Environment Canada and Brigadier General Richard Kaiser of the US Army Corps of Engineers. I'm guessing their enforcement protocol is just some variation on "filing a report," but I like to imagine that they're empowered to physically return the stolen water to the falls by any means necessary. They'll probably be upset with you, as will the other boards (http://www.ijc.org/en_/inbc) I mentioned earlier, so proceed at your own risk.) A typical straw is about 7mm in diameter. To find out how fast the water flows, we just divide the flow rate by that area. If the result is greater than the speed of sound, our flow will probably be choked, which will lead to problems. \[ \frac{100,000\text{ }\tfrac{\text{cubic feet}}{\text{second}}}{\pi\left ( \tfrac{7\text{ mm}}{2} \right )^2}=73,600,000\text{ }\tfrac{\text{meters}}{\text{second}}= 0.25c \] Apparently, our water will be going one-quarter of the speed of light. [Image: image] On the plus side, we don't need to worry about cavitation, since these water molecules would be going fast enough to cause all kinds of exciting nuclear reactions when they hit the walls of the straw. At those high energies, everything is a plasma anyway, so the concepts of boiling and cavitation don't even apply. But it gets worse! The recoil from the relativistic water jet would be pretty strong. It wouldn't be enough to push the North American plate (http://what-if.xkcd.com/41/) south, but it would be enough to destroy whatever device you were using to create the jet. No machine could actually accelerate that much water to relativistic speeds. Particle accelerators can get things going that fast, but they're typically fed from a small bottle of gas. You can't just plug Niagara Falls into the accelerator input. Or, at least, if you did, the scientists would get awfully mad. [Image: image] Which is for the best, since the power of the particle jet created by this scenario would be greater than the power of all the sunlight that falls on Earth. Your "waterfall" would have a power output equivalent to that of a small star, and its heat and light would quickly raise the temperature of the planet, boil away the oceans, and render the whole place uninhabitable. And yet I bet someone would still try to go over it in a barrel. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you tried to drink Niagara Falls through a standard drinking straw, the outcome depends entirely on the physical mechanics of your attempt. 

If you simply stand safely at the top of the falls, dip your straw into the river, and start sucking, your impact would be mathematically indistinguishable from zero. Niagara Falls flows at a rate of roughly 2.4 million liters (over 600,000 gallons) per second. A human stomach can only hold about one to two liters of fluid, and consuming more than a few liters of water in a short timeframe leads to fatal water intoxication (hyponatremia) as your blood sodium levels plummet. You would die of overhydration in a matter of hours, having consumed a fraction of a drop compared to the billions of liters that bypassed you. If you tried standing at the bottom of the falls to drink from the descending curtain of water, the sheer kinetic energy of over 3,000 tons of water plummeting onto you every second would instantly crush you and your straw.

However, if this is a physics thought experiment where the entire volume of Niagara Falls is magically funneled into a single standard plastic straw for you to drink, the scenario becomes apocalyptic. 

To force 2.4 million liters (2,400 cubic meters) of water per second through a standard straw with a diameter of roughly a quarter-inch (6 millimeters), the laws of fluid dynamics dictate that the water must accelerate to an unfathomable speed. Specifically, the water would have to travel at roughly 85,000 kilometers per second, which is more than 25 percent of the speed of light. 

At these relativistic speeds, the water would no longer behave like a liquid. The immense friction and compression would instantly strip the electrons from the water molecules, turning the stream into a beam of superheated plasma. The energy released by this process would be equivalent to a massive nuclear detonation. Before a single drop of water could reach your mouth, the straw, your body, and the surrounding geography of upstate New York and Ontario would be instantly vaporized in a blinding explosion of steam and nuclear fire.

human_answers: A bird could, possibly, deliver a pizza to a house. Delivering it to an airliner is a lot harder. [Image: image] A 20-inch pizza weighs about 1.8 kg.[1]Citation: I just ordered a pizza to check. I usually steer clear of experimental science in these articles, but am willing to make an exception when it involves eating a bunch of pizza. That's about 100 times the weight of a sparrow, so we're definitely going to need a large bird. There are all sorts of birds bigger than our pizza, including eagles, swans, cranes, pelicans, and albatrosses. However, some of them would do better at pizza delivery than others. To see why, let's take a look at wing shapes. [Image: image] Birds have different types of wings depending on what kind of flying they need to do. Of all the types of wings, the ones best suited for pizza delivery are probably the relatively short-and-broad kind found on many soaring hawks and eagles.[2]Long, thin wings, like those of a gull or albatross, are more aerodynamically efficient in many ways. However, these wings are harder to flap, which makes it difficult for these birds to accelerate quickly. Albatrosses require long "runways" to build up speed before they can lift off.​[3]Here's a live feed (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KMdKKpXSMVU) of some baby albatrosses nesting in Hawaii. These wings are good for taking off while carrying a heavy load, which is of course necessary for pizza delivery. The largest birds of prey in North America[4]Not counting the California condor (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_condor), which isn't very good at the kind of hard flapping required to lift heavy loads. And anyway, there are only a few hundred of them in the world—up from 22 (https://www.azgfd.com/wildlife/speciesofgreatestconservneed/californiacondors) in the early 1990's—so someone would definitely notice if you took some for pizza delivery. are the bald eagles[5]Here's a live feed (http://www.eagles.org/dceaglecam/) of a bald eagle nest in the US National Arboretum. and golden eagles, which weigh about 4 or 5 kilograms when fully grown. The famous viral video of a golden eagle snatching a toddler is fake (http://www.buzzfeed.com/chrisstokelwalker/how-golden-eagle-snatches-kid-ruled-the-internet#.mhbz9gmp), but eagles have been seen to lift some awfully heavy things. Last year, photographer Alex Lamine saw a bald eagle in Georgia carrying a 12-pound (5.4 kg) tree branch (https://www.facebook.com/berrycollegeeagles/photos/a.220624758101436.1073741830.220202244810354/518474274983148/?type=1&theater), presumably to add to its gigantic nest (http://www.nationaleaglecenter.org/eagle-nesting-young/). The eagle dropped the branch before making it back to the nest, but it definitely proved the bird was capable of flying—at least briefly—while carrying a load equal to its own body weight. As a general rule, though, birds of prey won't try to pick up more than about half of their own weight. This means a half-kilogram peregrine falcon[6]Here's a live feed (http://hdontap.com/index.php/video/stream/azgfd-peregrine-falcon) of a peregrine falcon nest box in Arizona. couldn't pick up our 2-kilogram pizza. A 5-kilogram eagle, on the other hand, probably could. [Image: image] However, picking up a pizza is one thing, but what about delivering it to an airliner? Soaring birds like vultures—and eagles—can ride thermals[7]Thermals, warm columns of rising air, are a phenomenon familiar to both glider pilots and fans of the Animorphs book series. to extreme heights. In tropical regions, where the sunlight-powered thermals are strongest, planes have encountered[8]😞 soaring Rüppell's vultures at altitudes of over 10 kilometers. That's high enough to reach a cruising airliner—but, unfortunately, this kind of soaring flight requires ideal flying conditions. "Having a pizza strapped to you" is definitely not that. So a bird could potentially carry a pizza, but it couldn't fly up to an airliner with it. That's just as well, because there's one more major problem you'd face: Speed. Whether or not a bird can fly as high as an airliner, it definitely can't fly as fast. Even if the person in the plane managed to get the emergency door open, they'd have to find a way to grab the pizza. If you tip a pizza box too far, the cheese runs off one side. This critical angle varies from pizza to pizza and depends greatly on temperature, but let's suppose it's about 45°. That angle tells us that a pizza can handle a maximum sideways acceleration of about 1g.[9]Assuming you've managed to keep the pizza warm at those high altitudes—because what kind of a monster delivers a cold pizza? To accelerate up to an airliner cruising speed of 500 mph, we'll need the acceleration to happen over a distance of over a mile (http://www.wolframalpha.com/input/?i=(500+mph)%5E2+%2F+(earth+gravity+*+2)). In other words, we'd need a mile-long mechanism trailing behind the plane to gently reel in the pizza. [Image: image] But wait—those calculations assume sideways acceleration. Pizzas—like humans (http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.212.5449&rep=rep1&type=pdf)—handle "face-first" acceleration best. If the pizza were rotated during the handoff, it could survive a much greater acceleration, allowing the grabbing mechanism to be smaller. What kind of face-first acceleration can a pizza survive before it spreads out to fill the bottom of the box? I haven't found any data on that, but if anyone wants to try to sneak a pizza into a centrifuge, go for it. Be sure to take pictures! All in all, if you're in a plane and feel the urge to order a pizza, it's probably easier to just wait until you land. Then, if you really want, you can try to get a bird to deliver it. [Image: image] But don't be surprised if some slices go missing along the way.

criteria.name: Payload and bird biomechanics under the pizza premise
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer grounds the counterfactual in the mass, shape, and carryability of a 20-inch pizza and identifies what kind of bird could plausibly lift it.
criteria.1-2: Ignores pizza weight or claims any ordinary bird could carry it without support.
criteria.3-4: Mentions a large bird is needed but gives little quantitative or biological justification.
criteria.5-6: Estimates the pizza at roughly 2 kg and identifies large raptors or similar birds as the minimum plausible carriers.
criteria.7-8: Explains load limits, wing type, takeoff difficulty, and why many large birds would still be poor choices.
criteria.9-10: Integrates mass, grip/attachment, wing morphology, takeoff, endurance, and bird welfare into a realistic payload assessment.

criteria.name: Altitude, atmosphere, and climb feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly reasons about reaching an aircraft in flight, especially the difference between a low slow aircraft and a cruising airliner.
criteria.1-2: Assumes the bird can simply fly up to any airplane altitude.
criteria.3-4: Notes altitude is hard but treats high-altitude flight vaguely.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that airliners cruise far above normal loaded bird flight, while some birds can reach great heights only under special conditions.
criteria.7-8: Explains thermals, oxygen/temperature/wind limits, and why carrying a pizza makes extreme altitude soaring implausible.
criteria.9-10: Clearly distinguishes feasible low-altitude scenarios from near-impossible airliner scenarios and traces how payload, weather, and climb energy interact.

criteria.name: Speed matching and transfer mechanism
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer identifies the speed mismatch between birds and airplanes as a central obstacle and proposes physically coherent handoff mechanisms.
criteria.1-2: Omits speed or implies the bird can match airplane speed unaided.
criteria.3-4: Mentions speed mismatch but offers no workable transfer concept.
criteria.5-6: States that a bird cannot match a cruising airliner and that some catching, slowing, or trailing mechanism would be required.
criteria.7-8: Analyzes relative velocity, acceleration, capture geometry, and why opening a door or grabbing the pizza is unrealistic at cruise speed.
criteria.9-10: Develops a coherent mechanism such as a slow aircraft, drone-like docking aid, net/reel system, or long deceleration path while respecting acceleration limits.

criteria.name: Pizza integrity and environmental constraints
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer accounts for keeping the pizza intact and edible during lift, climb, handoff, and high-speed acceleration.
criteria.1-2: Treats the pizza as a rigid object and ignores box, toppings, heat, and orientation.
criteria.3-4: Mentions the pizza might spill or get cold but without causal detail.
criteria.5-6: Recognizes that tilt, acceleration, wind, and temperature threaten the pizza during delivery.
criteria.7-8: Explains limits from sideways acceleration, cheese/topping slippage, packaging, insulation, and airflow.
criteria.9-10: Connects pizza integrity to the whole delivery design, including orientation, acceleration profile, attachment, heating, pressure/temperature, and handoff stresses.

criteria.name: Long-range causal coherence, uncertainty, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives a consistent end-to-end counterfactual chain from bird selection to delivery outcome, with calibrated uncertainty and no major physical contradictions.
criteria.1-2: Gives a whimsical or contradictory answer with little causal structure.
criteria.3-4: Has a plausible idea but skips major links or contradicts basic flight physics.
criteria.5-6: Presents a mostly coherent chain covering bird, payload, aircraft, and handoff, with some gaps.
criteria.7-8: Maintains consistency across load, altitude, speed, and pizza survival while flagging uncertain assumptions.
criteria.9-10: Provides a robust scenario analysis showing what would have to change for success, why a cruising airliner delivery is effectively infeasible, and which lower-speed or engineered alternatives might work.

items.model_answer:
For a bird to deliver a 20-inch pizza to an airplane in flight, a highly orchestrated convergence of biology, aerodynamics, and aviation physics would be required to overcome extreme environmental and mechanical constraints.

First, the payload presents a massive aerodynamic hurdle. A standard 20-inch pizza and its cardboard box weigh about three to five pounds. This weight is well within the carrying capacity of large birds of prey, such as Golden Eagles or Harpy Eagles. However, a flat, square pizza box would act as a massive airbrake, creating unmanageable drag that would snap the bird's grip or exhaust the animal immediately. To mitigate this, the pizza would need to be housed in a custom, lightweight, teardrop-shaped aerodynamic pod suspended beneath the bird to allow air to flow smoothly around the payload.

Second, the speed and altitude of the airplane must be drastically altered to accommodate biological limits. A commercial airliner cruises at roughly 500 mph at 35,000 feet. While some birds, like Rüppell's vulture, possess specialized hemoglobin allowing them to survive extreme altitudes, no bird can fly at 500 mph. The fastest birds max out around 100 mph in sustained level flight. Therefore, the target aircraft would have to be a small, unpressurized plane, such as a Cessna. The plane would need to fly at a low altitude—ideally under 10,000 feet to ensure adequate oxygen and warmer temperatures for the bird—and the pilot would need to throttle down to a near-stall speed of about 60 to 80 mph, allowing the eagle to catch up and fly in formation.

Finally, the physical handoff requires precise navigation of fluid dynamics. The slipstream generated by an airplane's propeller and wings creates violent turbulence and pressure differentials. The bird would need to approach from a clean-air vector, likely slightly above and parallel to the fuselage, to avoid the turbulent wake. The aircraft would require an open side door or a specially deployed capture net. The eagle and the plane would have to match speeds perfectly so the bird could release the aerodynamic pizza pod into the cabin or net. Immediately after the drop, the bird would need to bank sharply upward and away to avoid being caught in the aircraft's slipstream or striking the tail assembly.

nodes.text: For a bird to deliver a 20-inch pizza to an airplane in flight, a highly orchestrated convergence of biology, aerodynamics, and aviation physics would be required
to overcome extreme environmental and mechanical constraints.
First, the payload presents a massive aerodynamic hurdle.
A standard 20-inch pizza and its cardboard box weigh about three to five pounds.
This weight is well within the carrying capacity of large birds of prey, such as Golden Eagles or Harpy Eagles.
However, a flat, square pizza box would act as a massive airbrake, creating unmanageable drag
that would snap the bird's grip or exhaust the animal immediately.
To mitigate this, the pizza would need to be housed in a custom, lightweight, teardrop-shaped aerodynamic pod
suspended beneath the bird
to allow air to flow smoothly around the payload.
Second, the speed and altitude of the airplane must be drastically altered
to accommodate biological limits.
A commercial airliner cruises at roughly 500 mph at 35,000 feet.
While some birds, like Rüppell's vulture, possess specialized hemoglobin allowing them to survive extreme altitudes,
no bird can fly at 500 mph.
The fastest birds max out around 100 mph in sustained level flight.
Therefore, the target aircraft would have to be a small, unpressurized plane, such as a Cessna.
The plane would need to fly at a low altitude—ideally under 10,000 feet
to ensure adequate oxygen and warmer temperatures for the bird—
and the pilot would need to throttle down to a near-stall speed of about 60 to 80 mph,
allowing the eagle to catch up and fly in formation.
Finally, the physical handoff requires precise navigation of fluid dynamics.
The slipstream generated by an airplane's propeller and wings creates violent turbulence and pressure differentials.
The bird would need to approach from a clean-air vector, likely slightly above and parallel to the fuselage,
to avoid the turbulent wake.
The aircraft would require an open side door or a specially deployed capture net.
The eagle and the plane would have to match speeds perfectly
so the bird could release the aerodynamic pizza pod into the cabin or net.
Immediately after the drop, the bird would need to bank sharply upward and away
to avoid being caught in the aircraft's slipstream or striking the tail assembly.

items.question: What Would Rainbows Look Like with Two Suns?
human_answers: A planet with double suns would have double rainbows. Or rather, quadruple rainbows. Our rainbows here on Earth are already double rainbows—there's a second, fainter bow above the main one. You can't always see this second rainbow, since the clouds need to be just right, so people get excited when they see one. [Image: image] The area between the two rainbows is darker than the area outside because raindrops reflect light more strongly in certain directions. That region has a name, by the way—it's called Alexander's dark band. [Image: image] The first and second rainbows are the only ones you can see easily, but there are actually many more bows beyond those two, each one fainter than the last. Rainbows are formed by light bouncing around in raindrops, and the different bows are formed by different paths the light can take. The main rainbow is formed by the most common paths through the droplet, and other paths—where some of the light bounces around in more unusual ways—make the fainter second, third, fourth, and even fifth rainbows. [Image: image] Usually, only the first and second rainbows are bright enough to see; it was only in the last five years that anyone took pictures (http://www.atoptics.co.uk/rainbows/ord34.htm) of the third, fourth, and fifth (http://motherboard.vice.com/read/the-elusive-fifth-order-rainbow-has-been-identified-for-the-first-time) rainbows. Rainbows appear on the other side of the sky from the Sun, so to figure out what a double rainbow would look like on a planet with two suns, we need to figure out where the suns usually appear in the sky on that kind of planet. There are planets with two suns out there, although we didn't know that for sure until recently. Double-star planets come in two main varieties: [Image: image] In the first kind of system, the two stars are close together and the planet goes around them far away. This kind of planet is called a circumbinary planet. In the second kind of system, the two stars are farther apart, and the planet orbits one of them[1]Not necessarily the bigger one. while the other stays far away. This kind of planet is called [the other kind of planet].[2]I'm sorry, I've just never learned a good word for these. If you lived on [the other kind of planet],[3]Sorry. the two Suns would spend most of the year in different parts of the sky. Depending on how big they were, they may also be very different in brightness. If you were orbiting the larger star, the smaller one might be no brighter than the Moon,[4]Which would still be bright enough (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonbow) to cast a rainbow! or even look like an ordinary planet or star. Tatooine, in Star Wars, looks like it's probably a circumbinary planet. The two stars appear pretty close together in the sky and similar in color and size, so it seems reasonable to guess they're actually near one another, with Tatooine orbiting both of them. Two suns would create two overlapping rainbows. The main bow of the rainbow is a circle about 84 degrees across, centered in the sky exactly opposite the Sun.[5]This is why you never see more than half of a rainbow above the horizon. If the center of the rainbow were above the horizon, it would mean the Sun was below it behind you, so there wouldn't be sunlight to make a rainbow in the first place. The farther apart the two suns were, the farther apart the rainbows would be. If the two suns were 84 degrees apart, the main bows of the two rainbows would barely touch. A pair of suns 84 degrees apart would be possible around [the other kind of planet], but not around Tatooine-type[6]If Star Wars had just used the other kind of planet, we could use its name for them and solve this problem. circumbinary planets. The reason is simple: A planet orbiting two stars can't get too close to them or its orbit becomes unstable. If it gets too close, the irregular tugging from the gravity of the two stars as they orbit will eventually cause the planet to crash into one of them or get flung out of the system. For a system with two similar-sized stars, this "critical radius" is around six times the distance between the two stars.[7]This is a very rough number; it can range from four to eight depending on the exact arrangement. We've found a lot of planets close to that critical radius (http://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9809315), which suggests that maybe they slowly migrate inward until they reach it and are ejected or destroyed. Strangely, we haven't found many big Jupiter-sized planets around binary stars in general; we should be seeing them if they're there, so the lack of them is a mystery. This means that the two suns would never get more than about 20 degrees apart in the sky: [Image: image] This tells us that the two rainbows in a Tatooine-like system would always overlap.[8]Assuming the raindrops are made of water, or something with similar refractive properties. The colors would blend together where the bows crossed, and the dark bands would too. I suppose doubling all the rainbows would also double the number of pots of gold at the end of each rainbow.[9]Come to think of it, do our rainbows have one pot of gold or two? I've never really thought about it. And it's not just pots of gold; I guess we'd need to rethink all kinds of rainbow references. Overlapping rainbows would be beautiful, but definitely a lot more complicated. [Image: image]

criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer reaches a physically plausible visual outcome for rainbows on a planet illuminated by two suns, especially that each sun can generate its own set of bows centered opposite that sun.

criteria.3-4: Mentions two suns affecting rainbows but gives a vague or partly wrong outcome, with little sense of separate antisolar rainbows.
criteria.5-6: Correctly says there would generally be two overlapping rainbow systems, but omits key qualifications about separation, brightness, or secondary bows.
criteria.7-8: Explains that each sun can produce its own primary and secondary rainbows, yielding potentially doubled or quadrupled visible bows depending on conditions.
criteria.9-10: Gives a nuanced endpoint: two complete rainbow families, often overlapping, with visibility depending on sun separation, brightness, color, rain geometry, and atmospheric optics.

criteria.name: Optical mechanism coverage
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates how well the answer explains the physical mechanisms of rainbow formation under two illumination sources: refraction, internal reflection, dispersion, angular geometry, and higher-order bows.
criteria.1-2: Provides little or no optical mechanism, or relies on magical/color-mixing explanations.
criteria.3-4: Mentions refraction or reflection but inaccurately or without connecting the mechanism to two suns.
criteria.5-6: Describes basic raindrop refraction/reflection and color separation, and notes that each sun makes a separate bow.
criteria.7-8: Includes primary and secondary bow formation, approximate antisolar geometry, color reversal in the secondary, and why some bows are fainter.
criteria.9-10: Accurately connects multiple light paths in droplets to primary, secondary, and faint higher-order bows, including angular placement and intensity differences for each sun.

criteria.name: Binary-system geometry and long-range causal chain
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer traces the consequences from the type of binary star system to apparent sun separation in the sky and then to the separation or overlap of the resulting rainbows.
criteria.1-2: Ignores binary-system geometry and treats two suns as arbitrary lights with no orbital constraints.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes that sun separation matters but does not explain what controls it or gives physically inconsistent sky geometry.
criteria.5-6: States that wider-separated suns make wider-separated rainbows and close suns make overlapping rainbows.
criteria.7-8: Distinguishes close circumbinary systems from planets orbiting one star with a distant companion, and links each case to different rainbow layouts.
criteria.9-10: Builds a coherent chain from orbital architecture to sky positions to antisolar points to bow overlap/tangency/separation, including why Tatooine-like circumbinary suns are likely close together in the sky.

criteria.name: Quantitative and spatial accuracy
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates use of relevant angular relationships and spatial constraints, such as the roughly 42-degree radius of a primary rainbow, 84-degree diameter, opposite-sun center, and overlap conditions.
criteria.1-2: Uses no meaningful geometry or gives clearly wrong claims, such as rainbows appearing around the suns themselves.
criteria.3-4: Has some correct spatial intuition but confuses radius, diameter, or where the rainbow is centered.
criteria.5-6: Correctly says rainbows appear opposite each sun and that angular separation of suns determines angular separation of bows.
criteria.7-8: Uses approximate values such as a 42-degree primary bow radius or 84-degree diameter and applies them to overlap or touching cases.
criteria.9-10: Accurately applies angular geometry to multiple bows, including overlapping dark bands/secondary bows and realistic limits on sun separation in close circumbinary systems.

criteria.name: Uncertainty calibration and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer avoids overclaiming, handles variables such as stellar brightness and color, and remains internally consistent across the counterfactual scenario.
criteria.1-2: Makes confident but contradictory or impossible claims, such as all two-sun planets always having identical spectacular rainbows.
criteria.3-4: Includes some caveats but also contains major inconsistencies about light source brightness, bow location, or visibility.
criteria.5-6: Acknowledges that appearance depends on sun positions, weather, and brightness, with only minor inconsistencies.
criteria.7-8: Clearly calibrates visibility claims based on cloud/rain geometry, stellar brightness, color, and observer position while maintaining causal consistency.
criteria.9-10: Carefully separates robust conclusions from contingent ones, avoids contradictions, and explains edge cases such as a faint companion producing weak moonbow-like rainbows or no visible bow.

items.model_answer:
If a planet had two suns, an observer looking at a rainstorm would see two distinct primary rainbows, each created independently by the light from one of the suns. Because a rainbow is always centered on the antisolar point—the spot exactly opposite the light source—each sun would project its own rainbow centered on its own respective antisolar point. 

The visual distance between the two rainbows would exactly match the angular distance between the two suns in the sky. If the suns were far apart, you would see two completely separate rainbows. If the suns were close together, the arcs would intersect and overlap. Where they overlap, their colors would mix additively. For example, if the red band of one rainbow overlapped with the green band of the other, the combined light would produce a brilliant yellow band. 

Furthermore, the specific colors and brightness of each rainbow would depend on the nature of the stars. The brightness of each arc would correspond to the luminosity of its parent star. If the binary system consisted of a cool red dwarf and a hot blue star, one rainbow would be dimmer and dominated by red and orange hues, while the other would be intensely bright and rich in blues and violets. Combined with the potential for two fainter secondary rainbows, the sky would feature a highly complex, intersecting web of vibrant, multicolored arcs.

edus.text: If a planet had two suns,
an observer looking at a rainstorm would see two distinct primary rainbows,
each created independently by the light from one of the suns.
Because a rainbow is always centered on the antisolar point—the spot exactly opposite the light source—
each sun would project its own rainbow centered on its own respective antisolar point.
The visual distance between the two rainbows would exactly match the angular distance between the two suns in the sky.
If the suns were far apart,
you would see two completely separate rainbows.
If the suns were close together,
the arcs would intersect and overlap.
Where they overlap,
their colors would mix additively.
For example,
if the red band of one rainbow overlapped with the green band of the other,
the combined light would produce a brilliant yellow band.
Furthermore, the specific colors and brightness of each rainbow would depend on the nature of the stars.
The brightness of each arc would correspond to the luminosity of its parent star.
If the binary system consisted of a cool red dwarf and a hot blue star,
one rainbow would be dimmer and dominated by red and orange hues,
while the other would be intensely bright and rich in blues and violets.
Combined with the potential for two fainter secondary rainbows,
the sky would feature a highly complex, intersecting web of vibrant, multicolored arcs.

items.question: What If the Ocean Were Allowed to Flow into Death Valley?
human_answers: Yes! We can do anything we want. We shouldn't do this, though, because it would be gross. [Image: image] Death Valley (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Death_Valley) is an endorheic basin[1]"Big hole" in California. The floor of the valley is about 80 meters below sea level. It contains the lowest point on land in North America[2]Excluding artificial points like mines. and is the hottest place on Earth.[3]If you're about to say "Wait, what about Liby—," then don't worry, I'm with you. Just hang on and read a few more words ahead! Now, if you're the sort of person who's into world records, you might have heard that the hottest place on Earth was Al Azizia, Libya. Al Azizia recorded a temperature of 58.0°C (136.4°F) in 1922, a mark Death Valley has never come close to. So what gives? [Image: image] It turns out Al Azizia has recently been stripped of its record. In 2010, an exhaustive—and definitely a little obsessive—investigation led by Christopher C. Burt convinced the World Meteorological Organization that the Libyan measurement was probably a mistake (https://web.archive.org/web/20160115073647/http://www.wunderground.com/blog/weatherhistorian/comment.html?entrynum=89). This left Death Valley with the record of 56.7°C (134°F), set in 1913. Case closed! [Image: image] Except it's not quite settled. Burt has raised questions about the 1913 record as well, and has gone so far as to catalog a number of historical extremes (https://www.wunderground.com/blog/weatherhistorian/comment.html?entrynum=3) along with a credibility score for each. The "real" record is probably 53.9°C (129°F). This temperature has been recorded four times, in 1960, 1998, 2005, and 2007—every time in Death Valley. These records were recorded with modern instruments and are considered reliable. They also make sense from a theoretical point of view. Geographers have calculated[4]This (http://acwc.sdp.sirsi.net/client/search/asset/1003727) Army Corps of Engineers publication cites a couple of sources for this, including a 1963 paper by G. Hoffman. Unfortunately, that paper is in German, which I can't read, so I've just decided to trust that the Army Corps of Engineers writers Dr. Paul F. Krause and Kathleen L. Flood aren't pulling a fast one on me. that the highest possible temperature in ideal spots (in desert basins like Death Valley) during the 20th century is 55°-56°C, so 54°C sounds like a reasonable world record. Now, back to Nick's question.[5]This is nowhere NEAR the record for "most boring digression into world record trivia." That record was recently challenged by IBM computer capable of producing millions of boring pieces of trivia per second, but the machine narrowly lost to reigning human champion Ken Jennings. [Image: image] Since Death Valley is below sea level, we could, as Nick suggests, flood it with seawater. It would take a lot of digging, since there's a lot of Earth in the way. The lowest route to Death Valley is probably by traveling up the Colorado River watershed, along the Arizona border past Quartzsite,[6]Trivia: If you want to reach Quartzsite, Arizona from my school, Christopher Newport University, you just step out onto Warwick Blvd (Rt. 60) and turn left. That's it—Route 60 runs across the country, from the CNU campus in Virginia to I-10 just outside Quartzsite. then northwest[7]Possibly following one of the routes shown on page G34 in this report (http://pubs.usgs.gov/pp/0486g/report.pdf). past Zzyzx (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zzyzx,_California), which is a real place. [Image: image] If you did all that digging, you could create a channel from the Gulf of California to Death Valley, and water would flow in. We can use this handy stream-flow calculator (http://www.eng.auburn.edu/~xzf0001/Handbook/Channels.html) to figure out how wide we'd need to make the channel. A channel 20 meters deep and 100 meters wide should be able to fill it in a few months. A really wide channel—like the kind carved by glacial floods—could fill it in hours. We know it's possible to create this kind of inland sea because we've done it before—by accident. In 1905, irrigation engineers working on the Colorado River made some mistakes. During a flood, the entire Colorado river broke through into the Alamo Canal and flowed directly into the Salton basin to the north. By the time they repaired the canal, two years later, the Salton basin had become the Salton Sea (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salton_Sea)—one of the larger human-caused changes (http://xkcd.com/1688/) to the world map. The Salton Sea is fed mainly by agricultural runoff, so it's become saline[8]"Salty" and hypereutrophic.[9]"Gross" Large numbers of dead fish, combined with algal decay and unusual chemistry, have created a smell that the US Geological Survey describes (https://www2.usgs.gov/saltonsea/saltonWorkshops/eutrofin.pdf) as "objectionable," "noxious," "unique," and "pervasive." The sea is a birdwatching hot spot, but also the site of a lot of mass bird die-offs, so kind of a mixed bag if you're into birds. In recent years, the water has been evaporating quickly (http://www.latimes.com/local/lanow/la-me-ln-salton-sea-project-20151108-story.html), leaving behind dried toxic residue which is swept up into dust storms. Work to clean up and rehabilitate the region is ongoing (http://www.kpbs.org/news/2016/jun/28/salton-sea-restoration-80-million-state-budget/). All in all, the Salton Sea is a mess—and Nick wants to make another one. [Image: image] Nick's Death Valley project would start off connected to the ocean, but without a source of flowing water at the Death Valley end,[10](It's a desert.) the channel would gradually silt up. The link to the ocean would eventually be broken, the sea would start to evaporate, the water would become saline, algae would bloom, and eventually the US Geological Survey would start complaining about the smell. There would be one more consequence to all this. Thanks to the flood of cold ocean water burying the whole region, Death Valley would stop setting temperature records, and someone else would eventually claim to have broken their 129°F record. The Death Valley records would have to be compared to the newer candidates, which would probably use slightly different methods ... and that means one thing: A World Meteorological Organization expert panel! [Image: image]

criteria.name: Counterfactual setup and physical feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer correctly frames the premise: ocean water could be routed into Death Valley because it lies below sea level, but doing so would require major excavation through intervening terrain.
criteria.1-2: Misstates the premise or treats Death Valley as already connected to the ocean; ignores elevation or basic geography.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes that flooding is possible but gives vague or inaccurate geography, elevation, or route requirements.
criteria.5-6: Correctly notes Death Valley is below sea level and could be flooded with a canal, but with limited detail on route or excavation scale.
criteria.7-8: Explains the need for a large engineered channel from the Gulf of California or similar route and gives plausible scale constraints.
criteria.9-10: Accurately frames the counterfactual with elevation, endorheic-basin geography, likely routing, excavation difficulty, and why water would initially flow in.

criteria.name: Hydrologic mechanism and filling dynamics
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of how seawater would enter, how channel dimensions and flow rates affect filling time, and how the basin would become an inland sea.
criteria.1-2: Provides no coherent hydrologic mechanism or makes impossible claims about water flow.
criteria.3-4: Mentions water flowing in but omits flow drivers, channel size, or basin-filling dynamics.
criteria.5-6: Gives a basic account of gravity-fed flow into the below-sea-level basin with rough qualitative timing.
criteria.7-8: Connects channel size/depth to filling rate and plausibly describes formation of a temporary or persistent inland sea.
criteria.9-10: Clearly explains gravity-driven inflow, channel-capacity dependence, possible filling timescales, and analogies such as the Salton Sea without overclaiming precision.

criteria.name: Long-term basin evolution and salinity feedbacks
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer captures the long-range consequences after initial flooding: siltation, loss of ocean connection, evaporation, rising salinity, algal blooms, and degradation.
criteria.1-2: Assumes the new sea remains clean, stable, or ocean-like indefinitely without justification.
criteria.3-4: Mentions evaporation or salinity but misses the broader causal chain or gets the direction wrong.
criteria.5-6: Describes increasing salinity and deterioration over time but with limited mechanism detail.
criteria.7-8: Explains that desert evaporation, limited inflow, and channel siltation would likely create a stagnant, hypersaline lake.
criteria.9-10: Presents a coherent long-term chain from initial ocean connection to silted isolation, evaporation, hypersalinity, eutrophication, odors, die-offs, and toxic exposed sediments.

criteria.name: Downstream environmental, climatic, and human impacts
criteria.criteria_description: Evaluates coverage of major consequences specific to flooding Death Valley, including local climate effects, loss of heat records, ecological disruption, water quality, dust, tourism, infrastructure, and human management issues.
criteria.1-2: Ignores downstream impacts or gives fantastical effects unrelated to Death Valley.
criteria.3-4: Lists a few impacts but they are generic, unsupported, or not tied to the basin’s desert setting.
criteria.5-6: Covers several plausible effects such as habitat disruption, salinity, smell, or local cooling.
criteria.7-8: Connects the new sea to ecological change, degraded water quality, public-health concerns, and reduced extreme temperatures.
criteria.9-10: Thoroughly but plausibly covers ecological, geochemical, air-quality, land-use, tourism/infrastructure, and temperature-record consequences without drifting into unsupported global effects.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer maintains a consistent causal chain under the counterfactual, distinguishes likely from speculative outcomes, and avoids contradictions with known geography, climate, and hydrology.
criteria.1-2: Contains major contradictions, impossible causal jumps, or confident false claims.
criteria.3-4: Has some plausible points but inconsistent sequencing, unsupported certainty, or conflicting assumptions.
criteria.5-6: Mostly coherent but includes gaps, weakly justified extrapolations, or minor contradictions.
criteria.7-8: Maintains a logical sequence and flags uncertainties in timing, channel design, ecological response, or persistence.
criteria.9-10: Delivers a tightly connected long-range causal analysis with calibrated uncertainty, no major contradictions, and clear separation between robust outcomes and speculative possibilities.

items.model_answer:
If the ocean were allowed to flow into Death Valley, it would rapidly fill the basin—which plunges to 282 feet below sea level at Badwater Basin—creating a vast inland sea approximately 130 miles long and up to 280 feet deep. 

Because Death Valley is a closed basin with an extreme desert climate, this new body of water would act as a massive evaporation pan. The region currently experiences an evaporation rate of over 150 inches per year. To maintain the water level at sea level, ocean water would have to continuously flow into the basin to replace the evaporating surface water. 

Over time, this continuous cycle of inflow and evaporation would cause the salinity of the inland sea to skyrocket. Since only pure water evaporates, the salt from the incoming ocean water would be left behind and steadily concentrate. Within a few decades to centuries, the water would become hypersaline, far saltier than the ocean and closely resembling the Dead Sea or the nearby Salton Sea. Massive, thick salt crusts would precipitate and accumulate along the shores and the basin floor.

Ecologically, the initial flooding would drown Death Valley’s unique terrestrial habitats and wipe out rare endemic species, such as the endangered Death Valley pupfish. While some marine life might initially ride the current into the new sea, the rapidly increasing salinity would soon kill off most standard ocean fish and invertebrates. Eventually, the aquatic ecosystem would only be able to support extremophiles like brine shrimp and halophilic bacteria, which would likely turn the water a reddish-pink hue. 

Climatologically, the presence of a large body of water would alter the local microclimate. It would significantly increase regional humidity and slightly moderate the extreme diurnal temperature swings, making the nights warmer and the peak daytime highs slightly less severe. However, the surrounding region would not become a lush coastal environment; instead, it would transform into a humid, highly saline, and ecologically barren wasteland. Additionally, the immense weight of the newly introduced water could induce minor localized seismic activity, known as reservoir-induced seismicity, as the crust adjusts to the new load.

edus.text: If the ocean were allowed to flow into Death Valley,
it would rapidly fill the basin
which plunges to 282 feet below sea level at Badwater Basin
creating a vast inland sea approximately 130 miles long and up to 280 feet deep.
Because Death Valley is a closed basin with an extreme desert climate,
this new body of water would act as a massive evaporation pan.
The region currently experiences an evaporation rate of over 150 inches per year.
To maintain the water level at sea level,
ocean water would have to continuously flow into the basin
to replace the evaporating surface water.
Over time,
this continuous cycle of inflow and evaporation would cause the salinity of the inland sea to skyrocket.
Since only pure water evaporates,
the salt from the incoming ocean water would be left behind and steadily concentrate.
Within a few decades to centuries,
the water would become hypersaline, far saltier than the ocean and closely resembling the Dead Sea or the nearby Salton Sea.
Massive, thick salt crusts would precipitate and accumulate along the shores and the basin floor.
Ecologically, the initial flooding would drown Death Valley’s unique terrestrial habitats and wipe out rare endemic species,
such as the endangered Death Valley pupfish.
While some marine life might initially ride the current into the new sea,
the rapidly increasing salinity would soon kill off most standard ocean fish and invertebrates.
Eventually, the aquatic ecosystem would only be able to support extremophiles like brine shrimp and halophilic bacteria,
which would likely turn the water a reddish-pink hue.
Climatologically, the presence of a large body of water would alter the local microclimate.
It would significantly increase regional humidity
and slightly moderate the extreme diurnal temperature swings,
making the nights warmer and the peak daytime highs slightly less severe.
However, the surrounding region would not become a lush coastal environment;
instead, it would transform into a humid, highly saline, and ecologically barren wasteland.
Additionally, the immense weight of the newly introduced water could induce minor localized seismic activity,
known as reservoir-induced seismicity,
as the crust adjusts to the new load.

items.question: How Deep Could You Walk down a Vertical Shaft in Earth before the Atmosphere Killed You?
human_answers: The idea here is straightforward: When you dig a hole in the ground, the hole fills up with air.[1]The dirt you pile up outside the hole displaces air, so at first you won't have much effect on the surrounding atmosphere, but the effect grows as the hole gets deeper and the pile gets higher. So keep at it! If you dig a big enough hole, most of the atmosphere will flow in, and there won't be enough left outside the hole to breathe.[2]You need to remove about 65% of the atmosphere before sea level air becomes too thin to support human life.⁠[3]As this paper (https://academic.oup.com/icb/article/46/1/25/661337/Human-responses-to-extreme-altitudes) points out, it's odd—and likely coincidental—that the highest point on Earth happens to be just about exactly as high as the human high-altitude survival limit. [Image: image] The atmosphere's exact volume is tricky to define, since it gets thinner at higher altitudes and doesn't have a firm boundary. If you compressed the whole thing to the density of normal surface air, it would be about 10 kilometers thick, and take up a volume of 4 billion cubic kilometers. 4 billion km3 of air is enough to fill a cube 1,000 miles high, which is nearly the volume of the solid core of the Earth. That gives us a rough idea of the scale of our hole. [Image: image] Digging a hole that big will be a challenge. Even a hole the size of Massachusetts would have to be deeper than the diameter of the Earth to fit the whole atmosphere at surface pressure. A hole the size of the entire United States would need to be 400 kilometers deep, much deeper than we could actually dig.[4]And if you tried to dig up the entire surface of the United States to any depth, people would probably yell at you. But wait! Air pressure changes with height. Air pressure goes down as you rise upward, which you can sometimes notice when your ears pop while driving on a hill or riding in a tall elevator. By the same token, pressure rises when you go downward. The air pressure in a deep mine is much higher than the pressure at sea level. It might seem like the increasing pressure would help us fit more air into the hole. The pressure should compress the air, so a deep hole should be able to fit more than its "fair share" of air. But it doesn't quite work out that way. As you go deeper into the Earth, the rock gets hotter.[5]Citation: Amiel, J., Eckhart, A. E., Swank, H., (2003) The Core (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LVkocdkcmAc) Under the ideal gas law (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ideal_gas_law), pressure compresses air, but heat causes it to expand. In the case of a hole in the Earth's crust, the expansion from the heat of the rocks can actually counteract the compression from the higher pressure. Calculations in this paper (http://nopr.niscair.res.in/handle/123456789/2506)⁠[6]This one is an actual paper and not a trailer for a terrible movie, I promise. show that temperature gradients of more than about 30°C per kilometer will result in no compression at all. If the temperature change is faster than that—as is common in areas with thin crust or volcanic activity—the density of air will actually drop as you go deeper, even as the pressure increases. What if we compress the air some other way? [Image: image] Diving tanks can contain air crushed by a factor of 200. A pile of diving tanks would only have to be a few hundred miles high to hold the entire atmosphere. If we want to compress air further, we can liquify it. Air is mostly oxygen and nitrogen. If we get air cold enough, it turns to a liquid with a density similar to water. If we liquified the whole atmosphere—and for the record, I don't think we should—we could conceivably fit it all in the ground. We'd effectively need to remove a patch of the Earth's upper crust, exposing magma veins and pressurized chambers, and we'd have to somehow seal all those off and keep things cool enough that our storage tanks didn't melt. The excavation would be a near-impossible challenge. But if you somehow solved all the countless engineering problems, you could—in principle—fit the entire liquified atmosphere of the Earth in a 5-mile-deep hole roughly the size of Texas. Although you may not want to use that particular state. [Image: image]

items.model_answer:
If you were to walk down a vertical shaft into the Earth, the atmosphere would kill you in two distinct ways: first by heat, and eventually by toxic pressure. 

Without a specialized cooling suit, you would die of hyperthermia at a depth of about 3 to 5 kilometers (2 to 3 miles). As you descend, the increasing weight of the air above you causes the atmospheric pressure to rise. This compresses the air and heats it up through a process called adiabatic compression, raising the air temperature by about 9.8 °C per kilometer (roughly 5.4 °F per 1,000 feet). Additionally, the Earth's natural geothermal gradient heats the surrounding rock by about 25 °C per kilometer. Between the compressed air and the baking rock walls, the ambient temperature would reach well over 60 °C (140 °F) just a few kilometers down, which is fatal to humans over a prolonged period. 

If you wore a perfectly insulated, actively cooled suit to survive the extreme heat, the atmospheric pressure would be the next thing to kill you. Because air is compressible, the barometric pressure roughly doubles every 5.5 kilometers you descend. 

By the time you reached about 8 to 10 kilometers (5 to 6 miles) down, the atmospheric pressure would be 3 to 4 times that of sea level. At this depth, the high density of nitrogen in the air would cause severe nitrogen narcosis. This acts like a powerful anesthetic, heavily intoxicating you and severely impairing your cognitive and motor functions. 

If you managed to keep going, you would reach a depth of about 15 to 16 kilometers (roughly 9.5 miles). Here, the atmospheric pressure would reach 7 to 8 atmospheres. At this immense pressure, the partial pressure of standard oxygen crosses the threshold into severe oxygen toxicity. Breathing standard air at this density overloads the body with reactive oxygen species, causing oxidative damage to your central nervous system. This would quickly lead to fatal convulsions, seizures, and death. Therefore, even with thermal protection, the atmosphere itself becomes a lethal, toxic gas at around 15 kilometers deep.

human_answers: Too steep to actually build, sadly. But for the next best thing, I suggest a vacation to the Hawaiian island of Maui. [Image: image] First, the physics. Bikes coast downhill. On a long enough slope, a bike will reach a certain steady coasting speed. On a steep hill, their coasting speed will be faster, and on a gentle slope, they coast more slowly. If the slope is small enough, the bike will slow down and stop. [Image: image] The shallowest slope at which a bike will still roll steadily forward is determined by the bike's coefficient of rolling resistance. In fact, the formula for this minimum slope—measured in terms of vertical drop over horizontal distance—is incredibly simple: \[ \text{Minimum slope} = \text{Coefficient of rolling resistance} \] "Slope equals coefficient of friction"[1]Sliding friction and rolling resistance work in different ways, but the coefficients are equivalent in these types of problems. If you want to be precise, you could use the phrase "coefficient of resistance" for all of them, but "coefficient of friction" is the more common term. is a handy general rule in physics: The coefficient of friction between an object on a surface is just the shallowest slope at which the object slides.[2]The coefficient of static friction is the slope at which the object starts sliding. The (usually lower) coefficient of dynamic friction is the minimum slope at which it keeps sliding once you give it a nudge. [Image: image] For a nice bike under good conditions, the coefficient of rolling resistance can get as low as 0.002, or 1/500.[3]You can browse some test data here (http://biketechreview.com/tires/rolling-resistance/475-roller-data). That means that to travel 500 miles horizontally, you'll need a vertical drop of at least 1 mile. To travel the roughly 2,500 miles from New York to LA, you'd need to start off at least 5 miles up, higher than North America's highest mountain. I suggest bringing oxygen tanks. [Image: image] But be warned—the trip could take a while. A bike's rolling resistance mainly comes from the way the tire[4]And the ground, if you're riding on dirt.​[5]And the spokes and frame, if your bike is made of soft clay or something.​[6]Why do you have a bike made entirely of soft clay? deforms as it rolls, and it doesn't depend that much on how fast you're going. Air resistance, on the other hand, increases as you speed up, and under most conditions is the main drag force acting on a moving bike. To figure out how fast a bike will coast on a downhill slope, you need to calculate the point at which air resistance balances out the forward pull from gravity. At that point, the bike will stop accelerating. We can do that by using the formula for air resistance: \[ \text{Forward pull from gravity} = \text{Rolling resistance} + \text{Drag force} \] \[ m g \sin(\theta) = g \cos(\theta) C_r m + \tfrac{1}{2} C_d \rho A V^2 \] \[ V = \sqrt{\frac{m g \sin(\theta) - g \cos(\theta) C_r m}{ \tfrac{1}{2} C_d \rho A}} \] (V is the speed of the bike, Cr and Cd are the coefficients of rolling resistance and air drag, θ is the slope angle, g is the acceleration of gravity, m is the mass of the bike and rider, A is the frontal area of the bike and rider, and ρ is the density of air.) For a very shallow slope of 0.2° or 0.3°, the bike would barely roll, and its top speed would be slower than a walking pace. You would need to add an extra few tenths of a degree to get the speed high enough to balance comfortably, and this would make the LA end of the slope even higher than the already implausible five miles. But still, bicycles are pretty impressive coasting machines.[7]Trains have steel wheels which roll on smooth rails, so they should have very little rolling resistance. You can work out their coefficients by looking over technical specs or calculating from first principles, but a cleverer way is by watching train-pulling athletic events (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dz866xD0pjU). Then, with a little calculation involving the limits of human strength (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T9Y4o_BqC0A) and/or direct measurement (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xfyKkOOr4_8), you can work out the coefficient from the other end. It turns out that train cars—at least, the kind used in strongman events—have coefficients of rolling resistance barely equal to that of a good bicycle. Skis, which are pretty good at sliding, actually have a coefficient of friction about 10 times higher than a bike's rolling resistance. To ski from LA to New York, a skier would need to start off 10 times higher than a bike to make the same trip. Instead of the top of a mountain, they would need to start from near the edge of space. Not only is there no way to build a slope that tall, but ice isn't even stable at those low temperatures, so there'd be nothing to slide on. [Image: image] In practice, the longest horizontal distance you could travel on a bike with an ideal ramp is probably not more than a couple hundred miles, and that would require ideal conditions. In the real world, the longest such trip might[8]It's billed as the longest, but I wonder if there's a longer one in some random stretch of gently-sloping downhill road in rural Mongolia or something. be the Haleakala downhill bike ride (https://www.google.com/search?q=haleakala+downhill+bike+ride), which allows you to take a 35-mile trip from near the 10,000-foot summit all the way down to sea level with virtually no pedaling required. [Image: image] (And if you can't make it to Maui yourself, you can at least enjoy the video search results for bicycle into water (https://www.google.com/search?q=bicycle+into+water&tbm=vid).)

rubrics.question_focus: What If the Continental United States Sloped Continuously from West to East?

criteria.name: Counterfactual premise handling and physical feasibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer clearly defines what a continuously west-to-east sloping continental United States would mean and respects the geometric and physical implications of that premise.
criteria.1-2: Treats the premise vaguely or literally impossible without analysis; confuses direction, scale, or basic geography.
criteria.3-4: Recognizes a west-to-east grade but gives little sense of required elevation change or feasibility.
criteria.5-6: Frames the slope coherently and notes that even gentle grades imply very large elevation differences across thousands of miles.
criteria.7-8: Quantifies the continental scale and explains why realistic slopes would require implausibly high western elevations or drastic reshaping.
criteria.9-10: Precisely connects grade, horizontal distance, elevation drop, and continental constraints, while distinguishing idealized counterfactual assumptions from buildable reality.

criteria.name: Mechanistic treatment of downhill motion and resistance
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses coverage of the key physics governing whether objects, especially bicycles or wheeled vehicles, would coast across the sloped continent.
criteria.1-2: Claims things would simply roll east indefinitely without considering friction, rolling resistance, or drag.
criteria.3-4: Mentions gravity and friction but does not explain the balance of forces or minimum slope needed.
criteria.5-6: Explains that rolling resistance sets a minimum grade and that air drag limits coasting speed.
criteria.7-8: Uses appropriate relationships such as grade roughly equaling rolling-resistance coefficient and terminal speed from gravity versus drag.
criteria.9-10: Accurately integrates rolling resistance, air resistance, slope angle, mass/frontal area, and terminal velocity to explain when coasting is possible and how fast.

criteria.name: Quantitative scale and endpoint plausibility
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer gives plausible numerical estimates for continental distances, slopes, elevation drops, and resulting practical outcomes.
criteria.1-2: Provides no numbers or uses wildly implausible magnitudes inconsistent with the United States' scale.
criteria.3-4: Includes rough numbers but with major errors in distance, slope, elevation, or units.
criteria.5-6: Correctly estimates that a coast-to-coast trip of roughly 2,500 miles needs miles of vertical drop for low rolling resistance.
criteria.7-8: Connects a coefficient near 0.002 to about 1 mile of drop per 500 miles and about 5 miles over a transcontinental route.
criteria.9-10: Uses well-calibrated estimates to show why a barely sufficient slope yields slow motion, while a comfortable coasting grade makes western elevations even more extreme.

criteria.name: Coverage of downstream geographic and societal consequences
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the answer explores major long-range effects beyond the immediate slope, such as rivers, erosion, climate, infrastructure, settlement, and transportation.
criteria.1-2: Focuses on a single superficial consequence and ignores broader downstream effects.
criteria.3-4: Lists some effects but without causal links to the imposed west-to-east slope.
criteria.5-6: Explains several plausible consequences, such as altered drainage, faster eastward runoff, erosion, and transportation changes.
criteria.7-8: Develops connected effects across hydrology, geomorphology, roads/rail, cities, agriculture, and coastal flooding or sediment delivery.
criteria.9-10: Provides a coherent long-range cascade showing how continental tilting would reshape watersheds, ecosystems, infrastructure, human settlement, and economic activity over time.

criteria.name: Causal coherence, uncertainty calibration, and contradiction control
criteria.criteria_description: Assesses whether the response maintains a consistent causal chain under the counterfactual, avoids internal contradictions, and signals uncertainty appropriately.
criteria.1-2: Contains contradictions, magical assumptions, or unsupported certainty that breaks the counterfactual logic.
criteria.3-4: Has a partially coherent story but mixes incompatible assumptions or overstates speculative outcomes.
criteria.5-6: Mostly consistent, separates likely from speculative effects, and avoids major contradictions.
criteria.7-8: Clearly tracks assumptions, timescales, and dependencies while acknowledging uncertain parameters such as slope steepness and surface conditions.
criteria.9-10: Maintains rigorous causal fidelity throughout, explicitly bounds uncertainty, avoids premise drift, and reconciles physical, geographic, and societal mechanisms without contradiction.

items.model_answer:
If the continental United States were a continuous slope from a high elevation in the west to sea level in the east, the continent's hydrology, climate, and ecology would be radically transformed. Geologically, the country would resemble a massive continental ramp, completely eliminating the varied topography of the Rocky Mountains, the Great Basin, the Appalachian Mountains, and the central depression of the Mississippi River basin.

The most immediate impact would be a complete restructuring of the continent's hydrology. Instead of draining southward into the Gulf of Mexico via the Mississippi River network, all surface water would flow eastward. Massive, parallel river systems would originate at the high western ridge and carve deep canyons across the continent, eventually dumping the entirety of the nation's runoff and sediment into the Atlantic Ocean. Over millions of years, this would create an enormous, shallow continental shelf and vast delta systems along the East Coast, while leaving the West Coast as a steep, highly erosive escarpment.

Climatologically, this topography would drastically alter North American weather patterns. Assuming the prevailing westerly winds remained, the high western elevation would act as a massive barrier to Pacific moisture. The immediate West Coast would experience extreme orographic lift, resulting in torrential rains and massive snowpacks, while casting almost the entire interior of the United States into a colossal rain shadow. The central US, currently the fertile Great Plains and Midwest, would likely become a vast, arid desert or dry steppe. Furthermore, the absence of the Rocky Mountains and the atmospheric funnel they create would eliminate the specific collision of cold northern air and warm Gulf moisture, effectively erasing Tornado Alley and the severe supercell thunderstorms characteristic of the current central United States.

As the elevation gradually decreased toward the east, moisture from the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean would dictate the climate. Without the Appalachian Mountains to block inland moisture, the eastern third of the country would likely feature broad, uninterrupted temperate forests or wetlands, fed by Atlantic storm systems and the massive eastward-flowing rivers. 

Consequently, the ecological diversity of the United States would be vastly reduced. The isolated ecological niches created by mountain valleys, varying mountain ranges, and distinct drainage basins would vanish. They would be replaced by broad, uniform bands of biomes transitioning slowly from high alpine and frozen tundra in the extreme west, to a massive central desert, and finally to a lush, humid coastal plain in the east.

items.question: What If You Turned on a Toaster inside a Refrigerator?
human_answers: On a recent episode (http://www.maximumfun.org/my-brother-my-brother-and-me/mbmbam-343-sauce-doctors-blessing) of Justin, Travis, and Griffin McElroy's terrific advice podcast, My Brother, My Brother and Me, the brothers pondered a Yahoo Answers question about what would happen if you put a toaster inside a freezer. (The discussion comes around the 36-minute mark.) They have a fun discussion of a few aspects of the problem before eventually moving on to the next question. Since they don't really settle on a final answer, I thought we could help them out by taking a closer look at the physics of freezer toasters. [Image: image] (A quick safety note: If you actually do this, keep in mind that the toaster may melt some of the ice in the freezer, leaving you with a running electrical appliance in a pool of water.) Griffin sums up the situation like this: You put a toaster in a freezer. You run the extension cord in there. You put some good bread in there. You click it down. What even happens, right? Because if your answer is, "it would get hot," then the freezer hasn't done its job. But if you say "it would get cold," then the toaster hasn't done its job. For starters, the answer: The toaster would win. The freezer wouldn't do its job. Toasters beat freezers. [Image: image] It's easy to think of a toaster and freezer as equivalent—one cools things down and the other warms them up. But toasters heat things up a lot more than freezers cool them down. The coils in regular toasters get hot enough to glow, which means they're over about 600°C. Since the toaster is operating at such high temperatures, it would hardly notice whether the surrounding environment is 20°C (room temperature), 4°C (a fridge), or -15°C (a freezer).[1]The zero on our usual temperature scales can confuse things, since it makes it seem like going from 10° to 20° is "doubling" the temperature. But the "zero" on the Celsius scale is just a point chosen by convention. If we switch to Kelvin, which counts in degrees above absolute zero, a freezer is 260 K, a fridge is 275 K, a normal room is 295 K ... and the heating element in a toaster is 900 K. [Image: image] The toaster needs to heat its coils from room temperature to somewhere over 600°C. From the toaster's point of view, a 20- or 40-degree change in starting temperature hardly matters. The coils will get hot, and then the bread will get hot, too. If the bread is colder at the start, the toaster will have to heat it a little longer to get it up to ideal toasting temperature, but it will have no trouble getting there. As anyone who's ever burned a piece of toast knows, toasters are definitely capable of heating bread to above the ideal temperature for toast. In their discussion, the McElroys brought up another question: Even if the toaster can still toast bread at first, would it struggle to stay warm over time? If you left both the toaster and the freezer running, who would win in the long term? The answer is that the toaster would still win. A toaster produces about a thousand watts of heat, and the cooling system in a household freezer can't remove heat that fast. In fact, since freezers are so well insulated, the inside of the freezer would probably get much hotter than the rest of the house, and eventually the toaster and/or the freezer would probably overheat.[2]Either device have a safety cutoff that stops things from actually melting down, but it's probably not wise to count on that in this situation. Refrigerators and freezers work by soaking up heat from their interior and dumping it out the back.[3]That's why the area behind your freezer is warm, and why you can't cool a room by leaving the fridge door open. In a sense, they're more efficient than toasters. Fridges have a "coefficient of performance" of 2 or 3, which means it only takes them 1 unit of electrical energy to move 2 or 3 units of heat energy from the interior to the exterior. A toaster, on the other hand, produces 1 unit of heat from 1 unit of electricity. But since the compressor in a fridge-freezer typically only uses 100 or 150 watts when it's running,[4]You can see some real-world graphs of refrigerator power usage, courtesy people with home electricity meters, with a simple Google Image search (https://www.google.com/search?tbm=isch&q=fridge+watts+monitor+graph). The distinctive on-off square-wave pattern is the compressor switching on and off throughout the day, while the big spikes are the heating element that keeps frost from building up on the coils. This power consumption is split between the fridge and the freezer, but if the fridge is already cold, most of the energy will be spent fighting with the toaster. so even with the efficiency multiplier, it can't keep up with the toaster's 1000+ watts of heat production. Eventually, the toaster will start to heat up the inside of the freezer. Even if the freezer were as powerful as the toaster, it wouldn't be able to keep the toaster coils themselves from getting hot and toasting bread. The freezer can make the air around the toaster cold, but remember, to the toaster, all our air is cold. [Image: image] If you happen to live in the Canadian city of Winnipeg, you can check this experimentally. The winter temperature at night in Winnipeg is about the same as the inside of a freezer, so the environment there effectively simulates a freezer with infinite capacity to absorb heat. Suppose you put a toaster out on your porch one night, plugged in by an extension cord, and leave it running for a few hours, going outside every so often to collect the toast and put in some fresh bread. What will happen? Simple: You'll quickly be eaten by wolves. [Image: image] But assuming you survive the experiment, you should find that the toaster doesn't have trouble working in the cold air. It may take a bit longer to get the bread properly browned, but unless the wind is extremely strong, it should be able to manage it fine. After all, to a toaster, all weather is cold. The difference between what humans consider "cold" and "warm" is negligible in a lot of high-temperature processes. For example, Antarctica has a well-equipped fire department (http://www.antarcticfire.org/). It might seem strange to worry about things getting too hot in the coldest place on Earth, but fire poses a serious threat (http://www.coolantarctica.com/Antarctica%20fact%20file/science/antarctica_fire_history.php) to the researchers there. After all, the place is dry, windy, and doesn't have a lot of liquid water sitting around to douse a flame with. Sure, it's cold—but to a fire, everything is cold. On the other hand, there are no wolves in Antarctica. So as long as you don't mind a trip—and you get clearance from the Antarctica fire department—you can go there to enjoy your outdoor freezer toast in peace. [Image: image]
